0.title: In the Beginning Was the Word
0.overview:
The Gospel of John is the most theological document ever written. Where Matthew presents Jesus as the King of Israel, Mark as the Servant-Son, and Luke as the Saviour of the world, John presents Jesus as the eternal Word of God who became flesh and dwelt among us — the visible form of the invisible God. John wrote last, having lived longest with the mystery of the incarnation, and every sentence carries the weight of that lifelong meditation.

John's purpose is stated with unusual precision at the end of the book: "these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name" (20:31). Two things — belief and life. Not mere assent to facts, but faith in a person; and not mere existence, but the eternal life that is knowing God and knowing Jesus Christ whom he has sent (17:3). The entire Gospel is an extended argument for this faith, structured around seven signs and seven "I AM" declarations.

The seven signs escalate in power and publicity: water to wine (private), healing the official's son (at a distance), healing the invalid (Sabbath controversy), feeding five thousand (crowd), walking on water (disciples alone), healing the blind man (Jerusalem), raising Lazarus (public, four days dead). Each sign is a window into who Jesus is; together they build the case that "no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him" (3:2) — and more than that: unless he is God. The eighth and final sign is the resurrection itself, which the prologue has been anticipating from its first verse.

The seven "I AM" statements are the theological spine of the Gospel. Each one appropriates the divine name revealed at the burning bush (Exod 3:14 — "I AM WHO I AM") and fills it with the content of Jesus' saving work: I am the bread of life; the light of the world; the door; the good shepherd; the resurrection and the life; the way, the truth, and the life; the true vine. These are not metaphors about a human teacher but divine self-disclosures of the Son of God. When Jesus says "Before Abraham was, I am" (8:58), his hearers pick up stones to throw at him — they know exactly what he is claiming.

Who wrote it? The Gospel names its author only as the disciple whom Jesus loved, who is bearing witness about these things, and who has written these things (21:24; cf. 19:35). He was one of the inner circle at the Last Supper, and he never names himself or his brother James, though he names almost every other disciple. The early church, from Irenaeus on, identified him as John the son of Zebedee, writing in old age at Ephesus, probably between AD 80 and 95. Some scholars think the beloved disciple was a Jerusalem follower other than one of the Twelve, or that the Gospel was finished by his community. But the internal evidence fits John, the son of Zebedee, best, and the church’s testimony is early and consistent.

Why is it so different from Matthew, Mark and Luke? John has no parables, few miracles and long discourses; much of his story is set in Judea and Jerusalem, across at least three Passovers; and the great “I am” sayings are his alone. He was not correcting the others but completing them. He chose his material deliberately, so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God (20:30–31), and says plainly that he left out much more than he included (21:25). Where the others mostly give the Galilean ministry, John adds what happened in Jerusalem and what it meant.

Unique to John is the Farewell Discourse (chapters 13–17) — five chapters of intimate instruction given to the disciples on the night of his betrayal. Here Jesus gives his most extended teaching on the Holy Spirit ("another Helper"), on union with him ("abide in me"), on the world's hatred, on the coming joy, and on the prayer that will sustain the church to the end of the age. The High Priestly Prayer of chapter 17 — Jesus praying for his disciples and for all who will believe through their word — is the most sacred text in Scripture. John's Gospel ends not with a great commission on a mountain but with a question on a beach: "Do you love me?" Everything hangs on the answer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — The Prologue: The Word Became Flesh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before anything existed, the Word already was. He was with God, and he was God. Everything came into being through him, and in him was the life that is light for humanity, a light that darkness has never put out. God sent John to testify about the light so that all might believe, though John himself was not the light. The true light was coming into the world he had made, yet the world did not recognise him, and his own people did not welcome him. But to all who received him and trusted in his name, he gave the right to become God’s children, born not by human descent or decision but of God. The Word became human and lived among us, and we saw his glory, the glory of the Father’s one and only Son, full of grace and truth. John testified that the one coming after him outranked him, because he existed before him. From his abundance we have all received grace on top of grace. The law came through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. No one has ever seen God, but the only Son, himself God and closest to the Father, has made him known.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Word (Logos) is not an abstract philosophical principle but the personal Son of God through whom all things were made and in whom life and light reside. John's Christology is the highest in the New Testament: Jesus is fully God, co-eternal with the Father, the agent of creation, the source of life. The incarnation does not diminish his deity — 'the Word became flesh' while remaining the Word. Grace and truth come through Jesus Christ; the law came through Moses. The contrast is not abolition but fulfillment: the law pointed to the one in whom grace and truth are personally embodied.

Verse 2 is a safeguard rather than a repetition. Having said the Word was God, John at once restores the distinction — He was in the beginning with God — so that the identification cannot swallow the persons. The Prologue's architecture is carried by its verbs: the Word simply was, while all things were made, and in verse 14 the Word himself became flesh. He never became God; he became flesh.

The new birth of verse 13 is stated in three negatives before its single positive: not by descent, not by natural desire, not by the decision of any human head of a house — and therefore not by anything a person can inherit, produce or decide. Sonship is conferred, not achieved. The right of verse 12 is exousia, a granted legal standing, and the word used of believers in this Gospel is children (1:12; 11:52), while the Son is reserved for Jesus alone — a distinction that protects the uniqueness of Christ and enlarges rather than reduces the gift.

Grace and truth in verses 14 and 17 echo the name God proclaimed over Moses at Sinai — abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness (Exod. 34:6) — which is why verse 17 must not be read as setting Moses against Christ — a reading Jesus himself forbids at 5:46. Moses was shown the glory from behind and told to write it down; the Prologue claims that the same grace and truth have now arrived in person. And verse 18 closes the door natural religion keeps trying: God has never been seen as he is, and the only one who has never left his side has come out and told us — the telling being a life rather than a lecture.
verseByVerse.examples:
The Prologue is the key that opens the entire Gospel: whoever grasps who Jesus is before reading a single miracle will interpret everything correctly. 'The Word was God' (not 'a god') is one of the clearest affirmations of Christ's full deity in all of Scripture. And the Logos would have resonated with both Jewish (the creative Word of God) and Greek (the rational principle of the universe) audiences — John is announcing that the one both traditions were groping toward has arrived in person.

The darkness has not overcome it is the sentence a reader in a dark season needs: the light has never yet been extinguished, however far it has been reduced — and the church's own history is the evidence, since it has been down to a very few candles more than once and has never gone out. The verse does not promise that the darkness will feel defeated; it says the dark did not put the light out, and the shining verb is in the present tense while the failure to overcome is in the past.

The pastoral force of the three denials in verse 13 is usually missed. Because nothing whatever in the new birth was contributed by the one being born, there is nothing in it he can later fail to keep up — which is the answer to the Christian who cannot locate a moment of conversion and has concluded it never happened. No one remembers being born; the evidence of a birth is not a memory but a pulse. John gives the tests himself in his first letter, where believing the Son is the present-tense proof of a birth already completed in the past (1 Jn. 5:1).

verseByVerse.quote: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God.

The Gospel of John. Written by the apostle John, the son of Zebedee, “the disciple whom Jesus loved” (21:20–24), probably in Ephesus late in the first century. John tells us why he wrote: so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name (20:31). His Gospel is different from the other three: it focuses on Jesus’ long discourses, his signs, his ministry in Judea, and above all his identity. The prologue (vv. 1–18) is the overture to the whole book, introducing its themes: Word, life, light, darkness, witness, belief, glory, grace, truth.

In the beginning. “In the beginning” deliberately echoes the first words of Genesis 1:1. John begins a new Genesis, a new creation. But he goes further back than Genesis. Genesis says what happened in the beginning; John says what already existed in the beginning.

Was the Word. Key word. “Word” (logos). Before creation, the Word already “was”: not “came into being”, but existed. The tense (imperfect) means continuous existence. The Word had no beginning. Why “Word”? In the Old Testament, God created by his word (Genesis 1:3; Psalm 33:6), revealed himself by his word, and acted by his word (Isaiah 55:11). To Greek readers, logos meant reason, the rational principle behind the universe. John uses a word both Jews and Greeks would understand, and fills it with new content: the Word is a person, God’s self-expression, his full revelation of himself. A word expresses what is in the mind; Jesus expresses who God is.

And the Word was with God. “With” (pros): face to face with, in relationship with. The Word is distinct from God the Father, in eternal fellowship with him. Two persons.

And the Word was God. Key words. The Word is fully God, not a lesser being. In Greek, “God” comes first for emphasis (theos ēn ho logos): “God was the Word”. The Word is distinct from the Father, yet himself God. Here is the foundation of the doctrine of the Trinity: one God, in more than one person.

Where Christians differ, and beyond. Jehovah’s Witnesses translate “the Word was a god”, arguing from the absence of the article before theos. Verdict: this is grammatically mistaken. In Greek, a noun before the verb without the article describes the nature or quality of the subject; it does not mean “a god”. John means the Word was fully divine, all that God is, without being the same person as the Father. A “god” alongside God would be polytheism, which John, a Jew, utterly rejected. The church confessed it at Nicaea (325): true God from true God, of one substance with the Father.

He was in the beginning with God. John repeats it for emphasis: eternally existing, eternally with God.

In a sentence. Before anything existed, the Word already was, in eternal fellowship with God, and the Word himself was God.

For worship. The Jesus you trust is the eternal God. Bow before him.
verseByVerse.note: “In the beginning” deliberately echoes the first words of Genesis. “The Word” (Greek logos) was a term both Jews and Greeks understood: God’s self-expression, through which he created and revealed himself.

parallels.desc: in the beginning God created
by the word of the LORD the heavens were made
his name is the Word of God

verseByVerse.quote: "All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made. In him was life, and the life was the light of men."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made. In him was life, and the life was the light of men.

All things were made through him. The Word is the agent of creation. The Father created through the Son (Colossians 1:16; Hebrews 1:2; 1 Corinthians 8:6). If all things were made through him, he himself was not made. He is the Creator, not a creature.

And without him was not any thing made that was made. Said twice, positively and negatively, to exclude any exception. Nothing exists that the Word did not make. This refutes the ancient heresy (Arianism) that the Son was the first and highest created being.

In him was life. Key word. “Life” (zōē): occurs 36 times in John. Not just biological life but life in its fullest sense, eternal life, the life of God himself. The Word has life in himself (5:26), and gives it.

And the life was the light of men. Key word. “Light”: the revelation of God, truth, goodness, salvation, as opposed to darkness (sin, ignorance, death). In Genesis, light was the first thing created (Genesis 1:3). The life in the Word shines as light to humanity. Jesus will say: I am the light of the world (8:12).

In a sentence. Everything was created through the Word, and nothing exists that he did not make; in him was life, and that life was humanity’s light.

For worship. The one who made everything, including you, is the source of life and light. Come to him for both.

parallels.desc: “Let there be light”
all things were created through him

verseByVerse.quote: "The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it. There was a man sent from God, whose name was John."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it. There was a man sent from God, whose name was John.

The light shines in the darkness. Present tense: it keeps shining. Darkness is the world in rebellion against God, sin, ignorance and death. The light is not afraid of the darkness; it shines into it.

And the darkness has not overcome it. The ESV notes that “overcome” can also be rendered “understood”. The Greek (katelaben) can mean grasp, seize, either in understanding or in defeating. Both are true. The darkness did not understand the light, and it could not extinguish it. Even at the cross, when darkness seemed to win, the light was not overcome. It rose again.

There was a man sent from God, whose name was John. John the Baptist. This Gospel never calls him “the Baptist”, because the only John it needs to name is him; the author never names himself. “Sent from God”: a true prophet with a divine commission. A man, in contrast to the Word who was God.

In a sentence. The light keeps shining in the darkness, and the darkness has neither understood it nor put it out; and God sent a man named John.

On a Tuesday. However dark your circumstances, the light of Christ is not overcome. Trust it.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “overcome” can also be rendered “understood.” The John of verse 6 is John the Baptist.

parallels.desc: John’s ministry begins

verseByVerse.quote: "He came as a witness, to bear witness about the light, that all might believe through him. He was not the light, but came to bear witness about the light."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He came as a witness, to bear witness about the light, that all might believe through him. He was not the light, but came to bear witness about the light.

He came as a witness. Key word. “Witness” (martyria, martyreō): about 47 times in John. John the Baptist, the Father, the Scriptures, Jesus’ works, the Spirit, the disciples: all bear witness to Jesus. A witness testifies to what he has seen. The Gospel is presented like a court case: the evidence for who Jesus is.

That all might believe through him. Key word. “Believe” (pisteuō): about 98 times in John, but the noun “faith” never. For John, faith is an action: believing, trusting, coming, receiving. The goal of all witness is belief (20:31).

He was not the light. Some of John’s followers apparently continued as a separate group, and may have thought John was the Messiah (Acts 19:1–7). The Gospel firmly puts John in his place: a witness, not the light. John himself said so (v. 20; 3:28–30).

In a sentence. John came as a witness to testify about the light, so that all might believe through his testimony; he was not the light himself.

On a Tuesday. Like John, you are not the light, but a witness to it. Point people to Jesus.

parallels.desc: he was a burning and shining lamp

verseByVerse.quote: "The true light, which gives light to everyone, was coming into the world. He was in the world, and the world was made through him, yet the world did not know him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The true light, which gives light to everyone, was coming into the world. He was in the world, and the world was made through him, yet the world did not know him.

The true light. “True” (alēthinon): genuine, real, as opposed to imitations and shadows. A favourite word in John: the true bread (6:32), the true vine (15:1). Jesus is the reality to which all other lights point.

Which gives light to everyone. Every human being receives some light from the Word: the light of reason, conscience, and the knowledge of God through creation (Romans 1:19–20; 2:14–15). Not that everyone is saved, but that everyone is accountable.

Was coming into the world. The incarnation.

He was in the world, and the world was made through him. He came into the world he had made.

Yet the world did not know him. “The world” (kosmos): about 78 times in John. Here humanity in rebellion against God. The creatures did not recognise their Creator. The tragedy of human sin.

In a sentence. The true light that gives light to every person was coming into the world he had made, yet the world did not recognise him.

On a Tuesday. The world still does not know its Creator. Do you?

parallels.desc: a light for the nations

verseByVerse.quote: "He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him. But to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him. But to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God.

He came to his own. Literally “to his own things”, his own home, his own property. “His own” is Israel, God’s own people, to whom he had given the law, the prophets and the promises.

And his own people did not receive him. The deepest rejection. Not strangers, but his own family. The whole Gospel records this rejection, climaxing at the cross.

But to all who did receive him. Some did. “All”: whoever they are, Jew or Gentile.

Who believed in his name. To receive him is to believe in him. “His name”: who he is, as he has revealed himself.

He gave the right to become children of God. “Right” (exousian): authority, privilege, legal standing. Not by nature, but by gift. We are not children of God by birth; we become his children by adoption, through faith in Christ (Galatians 3:26; 4:4–7; Romans 8:14–17; 1 John 3:1). The greatest privilege in the universe.

In a sentence. He came to his own people and they rejected him, but to all who received him by believing in his name, he gave the right to become God’s children.

For worship. If you believe in Jesus, you are a child of God. Live in the joy of your adoption.
verseByVerse.note: “His own” is Israel, God’s own people.

parallels.desc: sons of God through faith

verseByVerse.quote: "who were born, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God. And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who were born, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God. And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth.

Who were born, not of blood. Not by physical descent. Being born a Jew, or into a Christian family, does not make you a child of God.

Nor of the will of the flesh. Not by human desire or effort.

Nor of the will of man. Not by any human decision, whether a husband’s, a parent’s, or one’s own.

But of God. Becoming God’s child is a new birth, and its source is God alone (3:3–8; James 1:18; 1 Peter 1:3). Three negatives exclude every human cause.

Where Christians differ: faith and new birth. Arminians teach that a person, enabled by grace, chooses to believe, and is then born again. Verdict: Reformed theology reads verses 12–13 together: those who believe are those born of God, not of the will of man. The new birth is God’s sovereign work, which produces faith (1 John 5:1, where “everyone who believes … has been born of God”, perfect tense). We believe because we have been born of God, not the reverse. Yet we truly believe, and are commanded to.

And the Word became flesh. Key words. The heart of the prologue, and of the Christian faith. The eternal Word, who was God, became flesh: a real human being, with a real human body and soul. Not merely appeared to be human, as the Docetists taught (1 John 4:2–3). Not changed into a man, ceasing to be God. He took human nature to himself, while remaining God. This is the incarnation. “Flesh” (sarx): human nature in its weakness and mortality. God became what we are, so that we could become what he made us to be.

And dwelt among us. “Dwelt” means literally “pitched his tent” (eskēnōsen), “tabernacled”. God’s presence in the tabernacle in the wilderness (Exodus 25:8; 40:34–35), and later in the temple, is now in the flesh of Jesus. He is the true tabernacle, the place where God meets his people.

And we have seen his glory. “We”: John and the apostles, eyewitnesses (1 John 1:1–3). “Glory” (doxa): the visible radiance of God’s presence, which filled the tabernacle. Seen in his signs (2:11), at the transfiguration, and supremely at the cross, which John calls his glorification (12:23; 17:1).

Glory as of the only Son from the Father. “Only Son” (monogenēs): unique, one of a kind, the only one of his kind. Not “only begotten” in the sense of having a beginning, but unique in his relationship to the Father.

Full of grace and truth. “Grace and truth” echo the Hebrew words of Exodus 34:6, where God revealed his glory to Moses: abounding in steadfast love (hesed) and faithfulness (emet). The God who passed by Moses is now seen in Jesus.

In a sentence. God’s children are born not by human descent or decision, but of God; and the Word became flesh and lived among us, and we saw his glory, the glory of the Father’s unique Son, full of grace and truth.

For worship. God became flesh and pitched his tent among us. Worship the incarnate Word, full of grace and truth.
verseByVerse.note: “Dwelt” means literally “pitched his tent” — God’s presence among his people, as in the tabernacle.

parallels.desc: that I may dwell in their midst
abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness
born of the Spirit

verseByVerse.quote: "(John bore witness about him, and cried out, 'This was he of whom I said, "He who comes after me ranks before me, because he was before me."') For from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace."
verseByVerse.commentary:
(John bore witness about him, and cried out: this was he of whom I said, he who comes after me ranks before me, because he was before me.) For from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace.

John bore witness about him, and cried out. “Cried out”: loudly, publicly, like a herald.

He who comes after me ranks before me, because he was before me. John was born about six months before Jesus (Luke 1:26, 36); “he was before me” points to Christ’s eternal existence. Jesus came after John in time, but ranks above him in dignity, because he existed before him, eternally (8:58).

For from his fullness we have all received. “Fullness” (plērōmatos): the complete abundance of grace and truth in him (v. 14; Colossians 1:19; 2:9). An inexhaustible supply.

Grace upon grace. Literally “grace in place of grace”: one grace after another, wave upon wave, continually. Or: the grace of the new covenant in place of the grace of the old (v. 17). Either way, endless grace.

In a sentence. John testified that the one coming after him ranks above him because he existed before him, and from his fullness we have all received grace upon grace.

For worship. Christ’s fullness never runs out. Receive grace upon grace from him today.
verseByVerse.note: John was born about six months before Jesus; “he was before me” points to Jesus’ existence before his birth.

parallels.desc: in him all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell

verseByVerse.quote: "For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. No one has ever seen God; God the only Son, who is at the Father's side, he has made him known."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. No one has ever seen God; God the only Son, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known.

For the law was given through Moses. The law was a gift of God, good and holy (Romans 7:12). It revealed God’s will and exposed sin.

Grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. Not that there was no grace in the law, but that the fullness of grace and truth came in Jesus. The law could command but not give the power to obey; Christ brings the grace that saves. The first time the name “Jesus Christ” appears in the Gospel.

No one has ever seen God. God in his essence is invisible (Exodus 33:20; 1 Timothy 6:16). Even Moses saw only his back (Exodus 33:23).

God the only Son. The ESV notes the readings “the only One, who is God” and, in some manuscripts, “the only Son”. The best manuscripts read monogenēs theos, “the only God”, or “God the only Son”. The prologue ends as it began: the Word is God (v. 1).

Who is at the Father’s side. Literally “in the bosom of the Father”: the place of closest intimacy, as John reclined next to Jesus at the supper (13:23). Eternal fellowship.

He has made him known. “Made known” (exēgēsato), from which comes “exegesis”: explained, interpreted, revealed. Jesus is the exegesis of God. To know what God is like, look at Jesus (14:9: whoever has seen me has seen the Father).

In a sentence. The law came through Moses, but grace and truth through Jesus Christ; no one has ever seen God, but the unique Son, himself God and at the Father’s side, has made him known.

For worship. Do you want to know what God is like? Look at Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes the readings “the only One, who is God” and, in some manuscripts, “the only Son.” “At the Father’s side” is literally “in the bosom of the Father” — the place of closest intimacy.

parallels.desc: no one may see me and live
whoever has seen me has seen the Father

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–51 — The Testimony of John and the First Disciples
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When priests and Levites from Jerusalem ask John who he is, he states plainly that he is not the Messiah, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet, but the voice in the wilderness Isaiah spoke of, calling people to make the Lord’s road straight. Asked why he baptises, he says he baptises with water, but among them stands one they do not know, whose sandal he is unfit to untie. Next day, seeing Jesus, John calls him the Lamb of God who takes away the world’s sin, the one who ranks above him because he was before him. John testifies that he saw the Spirit come down like a dove and remain on Jesus, the sign God had given him of the one who baptises with the Spirit; so he declares that this is the Son of God. The following day two of John’s disciples hear him call Jesus the Lamb of God and follow Jesus. He asks what they are looking for; they ask where he is staying, and he invites them to come and see. One of them, Andrew, brings his brother Simon, telling him they have found the Messiah, and Jesus names Simon Cephas, Peter. Next day Jesus calls Philip, who tells Nathanael they have found the one Moses and the prophets wrote about, Jesus of Nazareth. Nathanael scoffs at Nazareth, but comes, and Jesus greets him as a true Israelite without deceit and says he saw him under the fig tree before Philip called him. Nathanael confesses him Son of God and King of Israel. Jesus promises he will see greater things: heaven opened and God’s angels going up and down on the Son of Man.
verseByVerse.theology:
The gathering of the first disciples in John 1 is a theology of testimony: John testifies to Jesus; Andrew testifies to Simon; Philip testifies to Nathanael. The gospel spreads through personal witness. Each person who encounters Jesus becomes a testimony to others. The titles accumulate — Lamb of God, Son of God, Rabbi, Messiah, King of Israel, Son of Man — each one true, each one partial, each one pointing toward the one who exceeds all titles. Faith begins with testimony, but it must end with personal encounter: 'Come and see.'

Two guards belong to this section. The first concerns the phrase the Jews, which appears here for the first time and some seventy times in the Gospel: in John it functions as shorthand for the Jerusalem religious authorities, not for a people. The author is a Jew, every disciple is a Jew, and Jesus says in this same book that salvation is from the Jews (4:22). What is recorded is an argument inside a family about the family's own hope, and reading it as one people's verdict on another inverts it — a misreading Christians have made at terrible cost.

The second concerns the Lamb. Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world (v. 29) should not be assigned lazily to one background. John's own frame is Passover: he alone dates the condemnation to the hour the lambs were killed (19:14) and applies the Passover regulation about unbroken bones to the body on the cross (19:36). But the words spoken here — takes away the sin — echo Isaiah, since of all the candidate lambs only the servant of Isaiah 53 bears sin. Genesis 22 supplies the unanswered question (where is the lamb?), and the daily sacrifice explains why there had to be a last one. The verb is a present participle and the noun is singular: not a list of offences but the whole condition, taken up in order to be carried away.

The gathering of the disciples also settles the relation between this Gospel and the others. The call by the Sea of Galilee in Matthew and Mark is not an alternative version of this meeting but a later and decisive summons; here men are introduced to Jesus and begin to believe, and later they leave the nets for good. Faith by stages is the normal pattern, not a defective one — which is also the burden of vv. 50-51, where a man who has believed for minutes is told he will see greater things, and the greater things turn out to include a cross.
verseByVerse.examples:
'Behold, the Lamb of God' is the most comprehensive atonement statement in the New Testament: the lamb of Passover (Exod. 12), the lamb of the daily sacrifice (Exod. 29:38-42), the suffering servant who is led like a lamb to slaughter (Isa. 53:7), and the apocalyptic Lamb who alone is worthy (Rev. 5) — all in one person. And Andrew's first act after meeting Jesus is to find his brother: the natural overflow of genuine encounter with Christ is the desire for others to share it.

The pastoral centre of this section is that nobody in it recruits by argument. Andrew fetches his own brother — the hardest possible person, and the one least impressed by him — with a five-word sentence containing no case at all. Philip's testimony is theologically magnificent and incomplete twice over (Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph — nothing of Bethlehem, nothing of the virgin birth), and John lets both gaps stand on the page because Nathanael came anyway. Nobody is waiting for a witness to be finished before he is useful.

Two cautions worth carrying out of it. Andrew won his brother the same day, and that is the exception rather than the pattern; Jesus' own brothers did not believe during his lifetime (7:5). Anyone who has prayed for a relative for decades is not being rebuked by this chapter. And I saw you under the fig tree should be handled on both sides: it is the comfort of the believer whose faithfulness nobody is counting, and it is exposure for the reader who would rather his private life stayed private — with the point being that the one who has complete access to it is the one who came to take away the sin of the world, and he mentions the tree and says nothing else.

verseByVerse.quote: And this is the testimony of John, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him, "Who are you?" He confessed, and did not deny, but confessed, "I am not the Christ."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the testimony of John, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him: who are you? He confessed, and did not deny, but confessed: I am not the Christ.

The narrative begins. After the prologue, John’s Gospel opens with a week of testimony (1:19–2:11), ending at the wedding in Cana.

The Jews. In John’s Gospel “the Jews” often means the Jewish religious authorities in Jerusalem who opposed Jesus, not the Jewish people as a whole. Jesus, his disciples and John were all Jews (4:22). The term must not be used to justify hatred of Jewish people.

Sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem. An official delegation, perhaps from the Sanhedrin, to investigate this new prophet. Levites assisted the priests, and also served as temple police.

Who are you? The question of the whole Gospel is: who is Jesus? First they ask John.

He confessed, and did not deny, but confessed. Emphatic.

I am not the Christ. “I” is emphatic: I am not; someone else is. John’s first word is to deny that he is the Messiah.

In a sentence. When the Jerusalem authorities sent priests and Levites to ask John who he was, he openly declared that he was not the Messiah.

On a Tuesday. True witnesses point away from themselves. Be clear about who you are not.
verseByVerse.note: In John’s Gospel “the Jews” often means the Jewish religious authorities in Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: whether he might be the Christ

verseByVerse.quote: And they asked him, "What then? Are you Elijah?" He said, "I am not." "Are you the Prophet?" And he answered, "No."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They asked him: what then? Are you Elijah? He said: I am not. Are you the Prophet? And he answered: no.

Are you Elijah? Many expected Elijah to return before the Messiah (Malachi 4:5). John dressed like Elijah (2 Kings 1:8; Mark 1:6). Jesus said John was Elijah, in the sense of fulfilling Elijah’s role (Matthew 11:14; 17:12–13). But John denies being Elijah literally returned.

I am not. Shorter and shorter answers.

Are you the Prophet? “The Prophet” refers to Deuteronomy 18:15–18, the prophet like Moses whom God would raise up. Peter later identified him with Jesus (Acts 3:22).

No. One word. John refuses every title.

In a sentence. Asked whether he was Elijah or the Prophet, John said no to each.

On a Tuesday. John refused all titles of honour. Humility is a mark of a true servant of Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Many expected Elijah to return before the Messiah; “the Prophet” is the prophet like Moses whom Moses promised.

parallels.desc: I will send you Elijah
a prophet like me
he is Elijah who is to come

verseByVerse.quote: So they said to him, "Who are you? We need to give an answer to those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?" He said, "I am the voice of one crying out in the wilderness, 'Make straight the way of the Lord,' as the prophet Isaiah said."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they said to him: who are you? We need to give an answer to those who sent us. What do you say about yourself? He said: I am the voice of one crying out in the wilderness, make straight the way of the Lord, as the prophet Isaiah said.

Who are you? Again.

We need to give an answer to those who sent us. They must report back.

I am the voice of one crying out in the wilderness. Isaiah 40:3. John describes himself not as a person with a title, but as a voice. A voice is heard and then gone; what matters is the message. Jesus is the Word; John is only the voice.

Make straight the way of the Lord. Prepare the road for the Lord himself, by repentance.

As the prophet Isaiah said. John knows his role from Scripture.

In a sentence. Pressed for an answer, John said he was the voice Isaiah spoke of, crying in the wilderness to make straight the way of the Lord.

On a Tuesday. Be a voice for Christ. It is the message, not the messenger, that matters.

parallels.desc: the voice in the wilderness

verseByVerse.quote: (Now they had been sent from the Pharisees.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
(Now they had been sent from the Pharisees.)

Sent from the Pharisees. John’s aside. The Pharisees, strict interpreters of the law, would be concerned with John’s authority to baptise. Some manuscripts read “some of them were Pharisees”.

In a sentence. The delegation had been sent by the Pharisees.

On a Tuesday. Religious authorities are often the first to question genuine work of God. Don’t be discouraged by it.

verseByVerse.quote: They asked him, "Then why are you baptizing, if you are neither the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet?" John answered them, "I baptize with water, but among you stands one you do not know."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They asked him: then why are you baptising, if you are neither the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet? John answered them: I baptise with water, but among you stands one you do not know.

Then why are you baptizing. Baptism was associated with the coming of the messianic age, the cleansing God promised (Ezekiel 36:25; Zechariah 13:1). Who gave him the right?

I baptize with water. Only water: an outward sign.

But among you stands one you do not know. Already present, unrecognised. The Messiah is among them, perhaps in the very crowd. They are investigating the wrong man.

In a sentence. Asked why he baptised if he was none of these, John said he baptised with water, but among them stood one they did not know.

On a Tuesday. Christ may be nearer than you think. Look for him.

verseByVerse.quote: "even he who comes after me, the strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to untie." These things took place in Bethany across the Jordan, where John was baptizing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even he who comes after me, the strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to untie. These things took place in Bethany across the Jordan, where John was baptising.

The strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to untie. Untying a master’s sandals was a slave’s job, the lowest task. Rabbis said a disciple should do anything for his teacher that a slave would do, except this. John says: I am not worthy even to be his slave.

In Bethany across the Jordan. This Bethany lay east of the Jordan, in Perea, not the Bethany near Jerusalem where Lazarus lived. Its exact location is uncertain. John’s concern for precise places reflects an eyewitness.

In a sentence. John said that the one coming after him was so great that he was not worthy to untie his sandal; this happened at Bethany beyond the Jordan.

For worship. The greatest prophet felt unworthy to untie Jesus’ sandal. How great is our Lord!
verseByVerse.note: Untying a master’s sandals was a slave’s job. This Bethany lay east of the Jordan — not the Bethany near Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: where John had been baptizing at first

verseByVerse.quote: The next day he saw Jesus coming toward him, and said, "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world! This is he of whom I said, 'After me comes a man who ranks before me, because he was before me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next day he saw Jesus coming toward him, and said: behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world! This is he of whom I said, after me comes a man who ranks before me, because he was before me.

The next day. John marks the days of this first week (vv. 29, 35, 43; 2:1).

Behold, the Lamb of God. Key words. What lamb? Several streams flow together. The Passover lamb, whose blood saved Israel from death in Egypt (Exodus 12); John’s Gospel will show Jesus dying at the time the Passover lambs were slaughtered (19:14, 36). The lambs offered daily in the temple, morning and evening (Exodus 29:38–42). The lamb God provided in place of Isaac (Genesis 22:8: God will provide for himself the lamb). And the suffering servant of Isaiah 53:7: like a lamb that is led to the slaughter, who bears the sin of many. Jesus is the sacrifice God provides.

Who takes away the sin of the world! “Takes away” (airōn): lifts up, carries away, removes, by bearing it himself (Isaiah 53:4, 11–12; 1 Peter 2:24). “The sin”: singular, the whole mass of human sin and guilt. “Of the world”: not of Israel only, but of people from every nation (11:51–52; 1 John 2:2).

Where Christians differ: “the sin of the world”. Arminians take “the world” to mean that Christ died for every person equally, making salvation possible for all. Verdict: in John, “the world” usually means humanity in rebellion against God, not every individual, and the point is the scope of Christ’s work: not Jews only, but Gentiles from every nation (10:16; 11:52). Christ’s death actually takes away sin; it does not merely make removal possible. It takes away the sin of all who are his, from all over the world. The gospel is offered freely to everyone (3:16), and none who come will be turned away (6:37).

After me comes a man who ranks before me, because he was before me. As in v. 15: the eternal Word.

In a sentence. The next day John saw Jesus and declared him the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, the one he had said ranked above him because he existed before him.

For worship. Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away your sin. Look to him and live.
verseByVerse.note: Lambs were offered daily in the temple and at Passover; Isaiah’s servant goes “like a lamb that is led to the slaughter.”

parallels.desc: the Passover lamb
God will provide the lamb

verseByVerse.quote: "I myself did not know him, but for this purpose I came baptizing with water, that he might be revealed to Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I myself did not know him, but for this purpose I came baptising with water, that he might be revealed to Israel.

I myself did not know him. John and Jesus were relatives (Luke 1:36), and may have known each other. But John did not know him as the Messiah until God revealed it (v. 33).

But for this purpose I came baptizing with water, that he might be revealed to Israel. The whole purpose of John’s ministry: to reveal Jesus. Not to build his own following.

In a sentence. John said he had not known who Jesus was, but had come baptising so that he would be revealed to Israel.

On a Tuesday. The purpose of your life and ministry is to reveal Christ to others.

verseByVerse.quote: And John bore witness: "I saw the Spirit descend from heaven like a dove, and it remained on him. I myself did not know him, but he who sent me to baptize with water said to me, 'He on whom you see the Spirit descend and remain, this is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And John bore witness: I saw the Spirit descend from heaven like a dove, and it remained on him. I myself did not know him, but he who sent me to baptise with water said to me: he on whom you see the Spirit descend and remain, this is he who baptises with the Holy Spirit.

I saw the Spirit descend from heaven like a dove. At Jesus’ baptism (Mark 1:10). John’s Gospel does not describe the baptism itself, but John the Baptist’s testimony to it.

And it remained on him. Key word. “Remained” (emeinen): abode, stayed. In the Old Testament, the Spirit came on prophets and kings for particular tasks, and could depart (1 Samuel 16:14). On Jesus, the Spirit rests permanently (Isaiah 11:2; 42:1; 61:1). He has the Spirit without measure (3:34).

He who sent me. God.

This is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit. John baptises with water; Jesus with the Spirit. The one on whom the Spirit rests will give the Spirit to others (7:38–39; 20:22). Fulfilled at Pentecost, and in every believer’s new birth (3:5).

In a sentence. John testified that he saw the Spirit come down like a dove and remain on Jesus, the sign God had given him that Jesus is the one who baptises with the Holy Spirit.

For worship. The Spirit who rested on Jesus has been given to you. Thank God for his presence.

parallels.desc: the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him

verseByVerse.quote: "And I have seen and have borne witness that this is the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I have seen and have borne witness that this is the Son of God.

I have seen and have borne witness. Perfect tenses: a settled testimony. The language of a witness in court.

That this is the Son of God. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read the Chosen One of God (Isaiah 42:1). Either way, the climax of John’s testimony. Jesus is the unique Son of God (v. 18), the purpose of the Gospel (20:31).

In a sentence. John declared that he had seen and testified that Jesus is the Son of God.

For worship. Join John’s testimony: this is the Son of God.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “the Chosen One of God.”

parallels.desc: my Chosen One

verseByVerse.quote: The next day again John was standing with two of his disciples, and he looked at Jesus as he walked by and said, "Behold, the Lamb of God!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next day again John was standing with two of his disciples, and he looked at Jesus as he walked by and said: behold, the Lamb of God!

Two of his disciples. Andrew (v. 40), and probably John, the author, who never names himself.

He looked at Jesus as he walked by. “Looked” (emblepsas): gazed intently.

Behold, the Lamb of God! Shorter, repeated. John points his own disciples to Jesus, knowing they will leave him. He must decrease (3:30).

In a sentence. The next day John again pointed to Jesus as he passed, telling two of his disciples: look, the Lamb of God.

On a Tuesday. Point people to Jesus, even if it means they leave you to follow him.

verseByVerse.quote: The two disciples heard him say this, and they followed Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The two disciples heard him say this, and they followed Jesus.

And they followed Jesus. “Followed” (ēkolouthēsan): literally walked after him, and the word for discipleship. They heard the testimony, and followed. Witness leads to following. The first disciples come to Jesus through the testimony of John.

In a sentence. Hearing John, the two disciples followed Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Has the witness you have heard about Jesus led you to follow him?

verseByVerse.quote: "Jesus turned and saw them following and said to them, 'What are you seeking?' And they said to him, 'Rabbi' (which means Teacher), 'where are you staying?' He said to them, 'Come and you will see.' So they came and saw where he was staying, and they stayed with him that day, for it was about the tenth hour."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus turned and saw them following and said to them: what are you seeking? And they said to him: Rabbi (which means Teacher), where are you staying? He said to them: come and you will see. So they came and saw where he was staying, and they stayed with him that day, for it was about the tenth hour.

What are you seeking? Jesus’ first words in John’s Gospel. A question every person must answer. What do you want from Jesus?

Rabbi (which means Teacher). John translates Hebrew and Aramaic words for Greek readers.

Where are you staying? “Staying” (meneis): the same word as “remained” (v. 32), abiding. They want to be with him, to know him, not just ask a question.

Come and you will see. An invitation to discover him for themselves. Not an argument, but an experience of being with him. Philip will repeat it (v. 46).

And they stayed with him that day. “Stayed” (emeinan): abode. The beginning of abiding with Christ (15:4).

For it was about the tenth hour. The ESV notes that the tenth hour was about 4 p.m., late enough that they stayed the night. A precise detail, remembered by an eyewitness who never forgot the hour he met Jesus.

In a sentence. Jesus asked what they wanted, they asked where he was staying, and he invited them to come and see, and they spent the day with him from about four in the afternoon.

For worship. Jesus invites you: come and see. Spend time with him today.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the tenth hour was about 4 p.m. — late enough that they stayed the rest of the day.

verseByVerse.quote: One of the two who heard John speak and followed Jesus was Andrew, Simon Peter's brother. He first found his own brother Simon and said to him, "We have found the Messiah" (which means Christ).
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the two who heard John speak and followed Jesus was Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother. He first found his own brother Simon and said to him: we have found the Messiah (which means Christ).

Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother. Always known in relation to his more famous brother. Andrew appears three times in John, each time bringing someone to Jesus: his brother here, the boy with the loaves (6:8–9), and the Greeks (12:22).

He first found his own brother Simon. His first act as a disciple: tell his family. Personal evangelism begins at home.

We have found the Messiah. “Messiah” (Hebrew) and “Christ” (Greek) both mean “anointed one”, the promised King. Only John uses the Hebrew word in the New Testament (also 4:25). After one evening with Jesus, Andrew was convinced.

In a sentence. Andrew, one of the two, first found his brother Simon and told him they had found the Messiah.

On a Tuesday. Who in your family or circle can you tell about Jesus? Be an Andrew.
verseByVerse.note: “Messiah” (Hebrew) and “Christ” (Greek) both mean “anointed one” — the promised king.

parallels.desc: Andrew and Simon called by the lake

verseByVerse.quote: He brought him to Jesus. Jesus looked at him and said, "You are Simon the son of John. You shall be called Cephas" (which means Peter).
verseByVerse.commentary:
He brought him to Jesus. Jesus looked at him and said: you are Simon the son of John. You shall be called Cephas (which means Peter).

He brought him to Jesus. The greatest thing Andrew ever did. The man who would preach at Pentecost was brought by his brother.

Jesus looked at him. “Looked” (emblepsas): a penetrating gaze, seeing who he was and who he would become.

You are Simon the son of John. Jesus knows him already.

You shall be called Cephas. The ESV notes that Cephas (Aramaic) and Peter (Greek) both mean “rock”. A new name, as God renamed Abram and Jacob, signifying a new identity and calling. Simon was impulsive and unstable; Jesus would make him a rock. Not what he was, but what grace would make him.

In a sentence. Andrew brought Simon to Jesus, who looked at him and said that he would be called Cephas, meaning Peter, rock.

For worship. Jesus sees not only who you are, but who his grace will make you.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that Cephas (Aramaic) and Peter (Greek) both mean “rock.”

verseByVerse.quote: The next day Jesus decided to go to Galilee. He found Philip and said to him, "Follow me." Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The next day Jesus decided to go to Galilee. He found Philip and said to him: follow me. Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter.

Jesus decided to go to Galilee. North, from the Jordan to Galilee.

He found Philip. Here Jesus takes the initiative. Andrew found Peter; Jesus found Philip. Ultimately it is always Jesus who finds us (Luke 19:10).

Follow me. The call to discipleship.

Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter. Bethsaida was a fishing town at the north end of the Sea of Galilee. Mark says Peter and Andrew lived at Capernaum (Mark 1:29), perhaps having moved there.

In a sentence. The next day, about to leave for Galilee, Jesus found Philip, from Bethsaida like Andrew and Peter, and told him to follow him.

On a Tuesday. Jesus is the one who seeks and finds. Respond to his call: follow me.
verseByVerse.note: Bethsaida was a fishing town at the north end of the Sea of Galilee.

verseByVerse.quote: Philip found Nathanael and said to him, "We have found him of whom Moses in the Law and also the prophets wrote, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Philip found Nathanael and said to him: we have found him of whom Moses in the Law and also the prophets wrote, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.

Philip found Nathanael. Nathanael is not named in the other Gospels; he is often identified with Bartholomew, who is paired with Philip in the lists of apostles (Matthew 10:3). He was from Cana in Galilee (21:2).

We have found him of whom Moses in the Law and also the prophets wrote. The whole Old Testament points to Jesus (5:39, 46; Luke 24:27). Moses wrote of the prophet to come (Deuteronomy 18:15), the seed of the woman (Genesis 3:15), the offspring of Abraham (Genesis 22:18). The prophets wrote of the Messiah.

Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph. How people knew him. Philip did not yet know of the virgin birth. John’s readers know more (1:14).

In a sentence. Philip found Nathanael and told him they had found the one Moses and the prophets wrote about, Jesus of Nazareth, Joseph’s son.

On a Tuesday. Read the Old Testament as Philip did: it is about Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: Nathanael is not named in the other Gospels; he is often identified with Bartholomew, who is paired with Philip in their lists.

parallels.desc: Nathanael of Cana

verseByVerse.quote: Nathanael said to him, "Can anything good come out of Nazareth?" Philip said to him, "Come and see." Jesus saw Nathanael coming toward him and said of him, "Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nathanael said to him: can anything good come out of Nazareth? Philip said to him: come and see. Jesus saw Nathanael coming toward him and said of him: behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit!

Can anything good come out of Nazareth? Nazareth was an obscure village; it is never named in the Old Testament. Perhaps local rivalry: Nathanael was from nearby Cana. The Messiah was expected to come from Bethlehem (7:41–42). Prejudice.

Come and see. Philip does not argue. He invites Nathanael to meet Jesus himself, using Jesus’ own words (v. 39). The best answer to objections is often an encounter with Christ.

Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit! A true Israelite, honest, sincere, without guile. A contrast with Jacob, the father of Israel, whose name meant “deceiver” and who deceived his father and brother (Genesis 27:35–36). Nathanael is an Israel without Jacob’s deceit. Psalm 32:2: blessed is the man … in whose spirit there is no deceit. Even his objection was honest.

In a sentence. Nathanael doubted that anything good could come from Nazareth, but Philip told him to come and see, and Jesus greeted him as a true Israelite with no deceit.

On a Tuesday. Honest doubts can be brought to Jesus. Come and see.
verseByVerse.note: Nazareth was an obscure village; it is never named in the Old Testament. “No deceit” may contrast Nathanael with Jacob, the deceiver who became Israel.

parallels.desc: your brother came deceitfully
in whose spirit there is no deceit

verseByVerse.quote: Nathanael said to him, "How do you know me?" Jesus answered him, "Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nathanael said to him: how do you know me? Jesus answered him: before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.

How do you know me? Surprise. They had never met.

When you were under the fig tree, I saw you. Sitting under one’s own fig tree was a picture of peace and security in the messianic age (Micah 4:4; Zechariah 3:10). The rabbis also used the shade of a fig tree as a place to study and pray. Perhaps Nathanael had been praying or meditating on the Scriptures there, perhaps about Jacob (v. 51). Jesus saw him, supernaturally, and knew what was in his heart (2:25).

In a sentence. When Nathanael asked how Jesus knew him, Jesus said he had seen him under the fig tree before Philip called him.

For worship. Jesus sees you when no one else does, and knows your heart. You are fully known and loved.
verseByVerse.note: Sitting under one’s own fig tree was a picture of peace and security.

parallels.desc: every man under his vine and under his fig tree

verseByVerse.quote: Nathanael answered him, "Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!" Jesus answered him, "Because I said to you, 'I saw you under the fig tree,' do you believe? You will see greater things than these."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nathanael answered him: Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel! Jesus answered him: because I said to you, I saw you under the fig tree, do you believe? You will see greater things than these.

Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel! A great confession. “Son of God” and “King of Israel” were both messianic titles (Psalm 2:6–7). Nathanael believes Jesus is the Messiah. He may not yet understand all that “Son of God” means, but it is true in the fullest sense.

Because I said to you, I saw you under the fig tree, do you believe? Not a rebuke, but a promise. His faith was based on one small sign.

You will see greater things than these. The signs of the Gospel, and the glory of the cross and resurrection.

In a sentence. Nathanael declared Jesus to be the Son of God and King of Israel, and Jesus said that he believed on account of a small thing, but would see greater things.

For worship. Whatever you have seen of Christ so far, there are greater things to come.

parallels.desc: my King, my Son
the King of Israel, the LORD, is in your midst

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, "Truly, truly, I say to you, you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to him: truly, truly, I say to you, you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.

Truly, truly. “Amen, amen”: a double “truly” found only in John (25 times). A solemn introduction to an important statement.

I say to you, you will see. The ESV notes that “you” is plural: the promise is for all the disciples.

Heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending. Genesis 28:12, Jacob’s dream at Bethel: a ladder set up on the earth, reaching to heaven, and the angels of God ascending and descending on it. Jacob said: this is the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven (Genesis 28:17).

On the Son of Man. Jesus is the ladder. He is the meeting place of heaven and earth, the true Bethel, the house of God, the gate of heaven. The way between God and humanity is open through him alone (14:6). Nathanael, the true Israelite (Israel was Jacob), will see what Jacob saw, fulfilled in Jesus. “Son of Man”: Jesus’ favourite title for himself, from Daniel 7:13.

In a sentence. Jesus solemnly promised that they would see heaven opened and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.

For worship. Jesus is the ladder between heaven and earth. Through him, you have access to God.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “you” is plural: the promise is for all the disciples. “Truly, truly” is a solemn formula found only in John.

parallels.desc: Jacob’s ladder, angels ascending and descending

1.title: The Word Made Flesh
1.text: <sup>1</sup>In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.<sup>2</sup>He was in the beginning with God.<sup>3</sup>All things were made through him, and without him was not any thing made that was made.<sup>4</sup>In him was life, and the life was the light of men.<sup>5</sup>The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it.<sup>6</sup>There was a man sent from God, whose name was John.<sup>7</sup>He came as a witness, to bear witness about the light, that all might believe through him.<sup>8</sup>He was not the light, but came to bear witness about the light.<sup>9</sup>The true light, which gives light to everyone, was coming into the world.<sup>10</sup>He was in the world, and the world was made through him, yet the world did not know him.<sup>11</sup>He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him.<sup>12</sup>But to all who did receive him, who believed in his name, he gave the right to become children of God,<sup>13</sup>who were born, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God.<sup>14</sup>And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father, full of grace and truth.<sup>15</sup>(John bore witness about him, and cried out, “This was he of whom I said, ’He who comes after me ranks before me, because he was before me.’”)<sup>16</sup>For from his fullness we have all received, grace upon grace.<sup>17</sup>For the law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.<sup>18</sup>No one has ever seen God; God the only Son, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known.<sup>19</sup>And this is the testimony of John, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to ask him, “Who are you?”<sup>20</sup>He confessed, and did not deny, but confessed, “I am not the Christ.”<sup>21</sup>And they asked him, “What then? Are you Elijah?” He said, “I am not.” “Are you the Prophet?” And he answered, “No.”<sup>22</sup>So they said to him, “Who are you? We need to give an answer to those who sent us. What do you say about yourself?”<sup>23</sup>He said, “I am the voice of one crying out in the wilderness, ’Make straight the way of the Lord,’ as the prophet Isaiah said.”<sup>24</sup>(Now they had been sent from the Pharisees.)<sup>25</sup>They asked him, “Then why are you baptizing, if you are neither the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the Prophet?”<sup>26</sup>John answered them, “I baptize with water, but among you stands one you do not know,<sup>27</sup>even he who comes after me, the strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to untie.”<sup>28</sup>These things took place in Bethany across the Jordan, where John was baptizing.<sup>29</sup>The next day he saw Jesus coming toward him, and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!<sup>30</sup>This is he of whom I said, ’After me comes a man who ranks before me, because he was before me.’<sup>31</sup>I myself did not know him, but for this purpose I came baptizing with water, that he might be revealed to Israel.”<sup>32</sup>And John bore witness: “I saw the Spirit descend from heaven like a dove, and it remained on him.<sup>33</sup>I myself did not know him, but he who sent me to baptize with water said to me, ’He on whom you see the Spirit descend and remain, this is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit.’<sup>34</sup>And I have seen and have borne witness that this is the Son of God.”<sup>35</sup>The next day again John was standing with two of his disciples,<sup>36</sup>and he looked at Jesus as he walked by and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God!”<sup>37</sup>The two disciples heard him say this, and they followed Jesus.<sup>38</sup>Jesus turned and saw them following and said to them, “What are you seeking?” And they said to him, “Rabbi” (which means Teacher), “where are you staying?”<sup>39</sup>He said to them, “Come and you will see.” So they came and saw where he was staying, and they stayed with him that day, for it was about the tenth hour.<sup>40</sup>One of the two who heard John speak and followed Jesus was Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother.<sup>41</sup>He first found his own brother Simon and said to him, “We have found the Messiah” (which means Christ).<sup>42</sup>He brought him to Jesus. Jesus looked at him and said, “You are Simon the son of John. You shall be called Cephas” (which means Peter).<sup>43</sup>The next day Jesus decided to go to Galilee. He found Philip and said to him, “Follow me.”<sup>44</sup>Now Philip was from Bethsaida, the city of Andrew and Peter.<sup>45</sup>Philip found Nathanael and said to him, “We have found him of whom Moses in the Law and also the prophets wrote, Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.”<sup>46</sup>Nathanael said to him, “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?” Philip said to him, “Come and see.”<sup>47</sup>Jesus saw Nathanael coming toward him and said of him, “Behold, an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no deceit!”<sup>48</sup>Nathanael said to him, “How do you know me?” Jesus answered him, “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.”<sup>49</sup>Nathanael answered him, “Rabbi, you are the Son of God! You are the King of Israel!”<sup>50</sup>Jesus answered him, “Because I said to you, ’I saw you under the fig tree,’ do you believe? You will see greater things than these.”<sup>51</sup>And he said to him, “Truly, truly, I say to you, you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man.”
1.overview:
John opens not at Bethlehem but before creation. The prologue (vv. 1–18) is the overture to the whole Gospel: the Word who was with God and was God, through whom all things were made, has become flesh and lived among us, and in him we have seen the glory of the Father’s only Son, full of grace and truth. The great themes of the book appear here first: life and light, darkness that cannot overcome the light, witness, the world that does not know him, his own people who do not receive him, and the gift of becoming God’s children through faith, by a birth from God.

The narrative then begins with a week of witness. John the Baptist tells the Jerusalem delegation that he is not the Messiah, not Elijah, not the Prophet, only a voice preparing the way. He points to Jesus as the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, the one on whom the Spirit came and remained, the Son of God. Two of John’s disciples follow Jesus; Andrew brings his brother Simon, whom Jesus renames Cephas; Philip finds Nathanael, who doubts that anything good comes from Nazareth until Jesus shows he knows him, and then confesses him Son of God and King of Israel. Jesus promises greater things: heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man, Jacob’s ladder fulfilled in himself. One title after another is given to Jesus in this chapter: Word, God, Light, Lamb, Son of God, Rabbi, Messiah, King of Israel, Son of Man. The rest of the Gospel shows what they mean.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — The Wedding at Cana: Water into Wine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three days later there is a wedding in Cana of Galilee, and Jesus’ mother is there; Jesus and his disciples have also been invited. When the wine runs out, his mother tells him they have no wine. Jesus answers, addressing her as “woman”, that this is not their concern, for his hour has not yet come. She tells the servants to do whatever he says. Nearby stand six stone water jars used for Jewish purification rites, each holding twenty to thirty gallons. Jesus tells the servants to fill them with water, and they fill them to the brim. Then he tells them to draw some out and take it to the man in charge of the feast. He tastes the water that has become wine, not knowing where it came from, though the servants know. He calls the bridegroom over and remarks that people normally serve the best wine first and the cheaper wine once the guests have drunk freely, but he has saved the best until now. This, the first of his signs, Jesus does at Cana, revealing his glory, and his disciples believe in him. Afterwards he goes down to Capernaum with his mother, brothers and disciples, and stays there a few days.
verseByVerse.theology:
John calls the miracles of Jesus 'signs' (semeia) — they are not mere wonders but pointers to a deeper reality. The water-into-wine sign points to who Jesus is (the one who brings the new wine of the kingdom) and what his mission accomplishes (the transformation of the old into the new, abundance replacing scarcity, joy replacing labor). 'His hour had not yet come' — the hour of the cross, the hour of glorification, which will be the ultimate sign to which all others point. The disciples see the sign, believe, and their faith is the intended fruit of every sign in this Gospel.

The material of the sign is the point of the sign. The six jars were there for the Jewish rites of purification — the physical apparatus of a whole system for dealing with uncleanness — and Jesus does not replace the vessels but fills them. The water of ceremonial cleansing becomes the wine of a wedding feast: not the destruction of the old order but its transformation into joy. The quantity settles the tone. A hundred and twenty to a hundred and eighty gallons, at a village wedding, is not a measured response to a stated need; the disproportion is itself the message.

Semeion is established here as this Gospel's word for a miracle, and the choice is deliberate: John never uses the Synoptics' dynamis (mighty work). A sign is a signpost, valueless if you stop at it, and the crowds of chapter 6 will do exactly that. Seven signs are selected, and 20:30-31 states the purpose. He manifested his glory pays the claim of 1:14 — and the first instalment of that glory is a wedding present given anonymously in an unknown village. And his disciples believed in him, though they had already believed (1:41, 45, 49): faith in this Gospel grows and is tested rather than being settled once.
verseByVerse.examples:
The abundance of the provision — six jars of twenty to thirty gallons each — is a sign of the inexhaustible generosity of the kingdom. Jesus honors the institution of marriage by performing his first miracle at a wedding. And 'the best wine last' is the pattern of the gospel: the world offers its best first and then disappoints, but Christ gives his best at the end — the resurrection, the new creation, the eternal feast.

The pastoral register of the first sign is lower than readers expect and deliberately so. Nobody is ill and nobody is dying; a family has run out of drink and will be humiliated for years in a culture where hospitality was an obligation with teeth. The first miracle of the incarnate Son was performed because somebody was going to be embarrassed — which sets the threshold for what may be brought to him far below where most praying puts it. Mary's four words state the trouble and propose nothing: They have no wine.

You have kept the good wine until now is the gospel's shape against the world's. Everything else front-loads — the advertisement better than the product, youth spent early, the decline negotiated afterwards. But the promise must be guarded: it is not an assurance that circumstances improve, and it should not be handed to a suffering Christian as though it were. Plenty of lives get harder. What is promised is a better end, not an easier road — which is precisely why it speaks to the reader who has concluded his best years are behind him.

verseByVerse.quote: On the third day there was a wedding at Cana in Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there. Jesus also was invited to the wedding with his disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the third day there was a wedding at Cana in Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there. Jesus also was invited to the wedding with his disciples.

On the third day. After the call of Philip and Nathanael (1:43). Counting the days from 1:19, this is the seventh day of a new creation week. And “the third day” hints at the resurrection, when his glory would be fully revealed.

A wedding at Cana in Galilee. Cana was a village in Galilee, a few miles north of Nazareth, Nathanael’s home town (21:2). Weddings were the great celebrations of village life, lasting up to a week, with the whole community invited.

And the mother of Jesus was there. John never names her; she is always “the mother of Jesus”. Perhaps she was helping, as a relative or friend of the family.

Jesus also was invited to the wedding with his disciples. Jesus’ first sign is at a wedding. He honoured marriage by his presence (Hebrews 13:4). He was not an ascetic; he came eating and drinking (Luke 7:34), sharing in human joy.

In a sentence. On the third day, Jesus, his mother and his disciples were invited to a wedding at Cana in Galilee.

On a Tuesday. Jesus is at home at a celebration. Invite him into your joys as well as your sorrows.
verseByVerse.note: Cana was a village in Galilee, a few miles north of Nazareth. A wedding feast could last a week.

verseByVerse.quote: When the wine ran out, the mother of Jesus said to him, "They have no wine."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the wine ran out, the mother of Jesus said to him: they have no wine.

When the wine ran out. Running out of wine would have shamed the family publicly. Hospitality was a sacred duty, and a wedding host was expected to provide generously. There may even have been legal liability for gifts expected in return. A social disaster for the bridegroom.

They have no wine. Mary states the problem. She does not tell Jesus what to do. She brings the need to him, trusting him to act. A model of prayer.

The deeper meaning. In the prophets, abundant wine is a sign of the messianic age (Isaiah 25:6; Joel 3:18; Amos 9:13–14). Running out of wine may picture the emptiness of the old order: Israel’s religion had run dry. Jesus brings the new wine of the kingdom.

In a sentence. When the wine ran out, Jesus’ mother told him that they had no wine.

On a Tuesday. Bring your needs to Jesus, simply, and trust him with the answer.
verseByVerse.note: Running out of wine would have shamed the family publicly.

verseByVerse.quote: "And Jesus said to her, 'Woman, what does this have to do with me? My hour has not yet come.' His mother said to the servants, 'Do whatever he tells you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Jesus said to her: woman, what does this have to do with me? My hour has not yet come. His mother said to the servants: do whatever he tells you.

Woman. “Woman” was a respectful form of address, not a rude one. Jesus uses it from the cross, tenderly, as he entrusts her to John (19:26). But it is not the word a son would usually use for his mother. It signals a change: his relationship with her is now that of Lord, not son under parental authority.

What does this have to do with me? Literally “what to me and to you?”, a Hebrew idiom meaning: what do we have in common in this? This is not your business to direct. Jesus acts on his Father’s timing, not his mother’s, however well meant (Luke 2:49).

My hour has not yet come. Key words. “The hour” in John is the time of Jesus’ death, resurrection and glorification (7:30; 8:20; 12:23, 27; 13:1; 17:1). Everything in his life moves toward that hour, set by the Father. The full revelation of his glory, and the abundance of the messianic age, will come through the cross.

Do whatever he tells you. Mary’s last recorded words in the Gospels, and the best advice she ever gave. She does not take offence. She trusts him, and directs others to obey him. The words echo Pharaoh’s about Joseph: Go to Joseph. What he says to you, do (Genesis 41:55).

Where Christians differ: Mary’s intercession. Roman Catholic devotion has seen Cana as a picture of Mary’s power as intercessor, obtaining favours from her Son. Verdict: the passage shows the opposite emphasis: Jesus gently declines her direction, acts in his own time, and Mary points away from herself to him: do whatever he tells you. She is a model of faith and of pointing to Christ, not a mediator between us and him. There is one mediator (1 Timothy 2:5).

In a sentence. Jesus told his mother that this was not her concern to direct, for his hour had not yet come, but she told the servants to do whatever he said.

For worship. Mary’s word is for you: do whatever he tells you.
verseByVerse.note: “Woman” was a respectful form of address, not a rude one. Jesus’ “hour” in John is the time of his death and glorification.

parallels.desc: “Go to Joseph. What he says to you, do”

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were six stone water jars there for the Jewish rites of purification, each holding twenty or thirty gallons. Jesus said to the servants, "Fill the jars with water." And they filled them up to the brim.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there were six stone water jars there for the Jewish rites of purification, each holding twenty or thirty gallons. Jesus said to the servants: fill the jars with water. And they filled them up to the brim.

Six stone water jars there for the Jewish rites of purification. Stone jars did not become ritually unclean, so they were used to hold water for ceremonial washing (Mark 7:3–4). Washing hands and vessels before and during a meal. Six: perhaps a hint of incompleteness (one short of seven). The old order of ritual purification.

Each holding twenty or thirty gallons. Literally “two or three measures”. About 75–115 litres each. Together, 120–180 gallons (450–680 litres). An enormous quantity.

Fill the jars with water. An ordinary command. No explanation.

And they filled them up to the brim. Obedience, as Mary had said. Full: no room for anything else to be added. What follows is not a trick.

In a sentence. Six large stone jars for ritual washing stood there, holding about twenty or thirty gallons each, and Jesus told the servants to fill them with water, and they filled them to the brim.

On a Tuesday. Obey Jesus in the ordinary instructions. Miracles often begin with simple obedience.
verseByVerse.note: Stone jars did not become ritually unclean, so they were used for purification water. The ESV notes that each held two or three measures — twenty to thirty gallons: well over a hundred gallons in all.

parallels.desc: the washings of the Jews

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Now draw some out and take it to the master of the feast." So they took it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said to them: now draw some out and take it to the master of the feast. So they took it.

Now draw some out. No prayer, no touch, no word over the water. Just a command to draw it out. The change happened silently, by his will.

And take it to the master of the feast. The master of the feast was the guest put in charge of the celebration, the head steward, responsible for the food and drink.

So they took it. More obedience. They took a risk: what if it was still water?

In a sentence. Jesus told the servants to draw some out and take it to the master of the feast, and they did.
