On a Tuesday. Faith obeys before it sees the result.
verseByVerse.note: The master of the feast was the guest put in charge of the celebration.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the master of the feast tasted the water now become wine, and did not know where it came from (though the servants who had drawn the water knew), the master of the feast called the bridegroom and said to him, 'Everyone serves the good wine first, and when people have drunk freely, then the poor wine. But you have kept the good wine until now.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the master of the feast tasted the water now become wine, and did not know where it came from (though the servants who had drawn the water knew), the master of the feast called the bridegroom and said to him: everyone serves the good wine first, and when people have drunk freely, then the poor wine. But you have kept the good wine until now.

The water now become wine. A real miracle of transformation. Not grape juice, but wine.

And did not know where it came from (though the servants who had drawn the water knew). The humble servants knew; the important master did not. Those who obey Christ see his works.

Everyone serves the good wine first, and when people have drunk freely, then the poor wine. Normal practice: serve the best first, when people can taste it, and the cheap wine later.

But you have kept the good wine until now. The best comes last. A picture of God’s ways: the old covenant was good, but the new is better (Hebrews 8:6). And the best is still to come: the wedding supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:9).

Where Christians differ: wine and alcohol. Some Christians argue that biblical wine was unfermented grape juice, and that Christians should abstain completely. Verdict: the wine Jesus made was real wine, as the master’s comment shows. Scripture praises wine as God’s gift (Psalm 104:15) while forbidding drunkenness (Ephesians 5:18; Proverbs 23:29–35). Christians are free to drink in moderation, and free to abstain; they must never get drunk, and must be willing to abstain out of love for weaker brothers (Romans 14:21). Abstinence is a wise choice for many, but not a command.

In a sentence. The master of the feast tasted the water that had become wine and, not knowing where it came from, praised the bridegroom for keeping the best wine until last.

For worship. With Jesus, the best is always kept until last. Look forward to the wedding feast to come.

parallels.desc: a feast of well-aged wine
the mountains shall drip sweet wine

verseByVerse.quote: "This, the first of his signs, Jesus did at Cana in Galilee, and manifested his glory. And his disciples believed in him. After this he went down to Capernaum, with his mother and his brothers and his disciples, and they stayed there for a few days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This, the first of his signs, Jesus did at Cana in Galilee, and manifested his glory. And his disciples believed in him. After this he went down to Capernaum, with his mother and his brothers and his disciples, and they stayed there for a few days.

The first of his signs. Key word. John calls Jesus’ miracles “signs” (sēmeia), pointers to who he is. Not just displays of power, but signs that reveal his identity. John records seven signs before the resurrection: water into wine (2:1–11), the official’s son (4:46–54), the paralysed man (5:1–15), the five thousand (6:1–15), walking on water (6:16–21), the man born blind (9), and Lazarus (11). Each reveals something of who Jesus is.

And manifested his glory. His divine glory (1:14), hidden in his humanity, shone through. What does this sign show? That Jesus is the Creator, who turns water into wine every year through the vine, now doing it instantly. That he brings the abundance and joy of the messianic age. That the old order of purification is replaced by the new wine of the kingdom. And it is done quietly, for a poor family, to save them from shame.

And his disciples believed in him. The purpose of the signs (20:30–31). They already believed (1:41–49); now their faith deepened.

His mother and his brothers. His brothers did not believe in him yet (7:5). The most natural reading is that they were Mary’s younger children.

In a sentence. This first sign at Cana revealed Jesus’ glory and his disciples believed in him, and then he went to Capernaum with his mother, brothers and disciples.

For worship. Jesus’ glory is seen in his care for ordinary people. Believe in him, and let your faith grow.
verseByVerse.note: John calls Jesus’ miracles “signs” — pointers to who he is. Capernaum was a fishing town on the lake shore.

parallels.desc: these are written so that you may believe

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–25 — The Temple Cleansing and the New Temple
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Near Passover Jesus goes up to Jerusalem and finds the temple courts full of dealers in cattle, sheep and doves, and money-changers at their tables. He plaits a whip from cords and drives out the traders and their animals, flings the coins to the ground, upsets the tables and orders the dove-sellers to take their goods away: his Father’s house is not a place of business. The disciples recall the psalm about zeal for God’s house devouring the righteous one. The authorities demand a sign to back his action. Jesus tells them that if they tear this temple down, he will rebuild it in three days. They scoff that Herod’s temple has been forty-six years in the building. But Jesus is speaking of his own body, and after he rises the disciples remember and believe both Scripture and his word. At the festival many trust in him because of his signs, yet Jesus does not trust himself to them, for he knows human hearts without being told.
verseByVerse.theology:
The temple cleansing is an act of prophetic authority: Jesus acts as the Lord coming suddenly to his temple (Mal. 3:1), purifying the house of prayer from the commercial transactions that have turned worship into a market. The zeal that consumes him is zeal for the Father's house — the passion of the Son for the honor of the Father. 'My Father's house' — his first recorded words in Luke (2:49) and his claim here: the temple belongs to his Father, and he has authority over it because he is the Son.

The temple thread runs the length of Scripture and this passage is its hinge. In 1:14 the Word dwelt among us and we have seen his glory; here the tabernacle has become the temple, and John states that the temple is a body (v. 21); and the Bible ends with a city in which John saw no temple at all, for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb (Rev. 21:22). My Father's house (v. 16) is the claim that licenses the whip — the same phrase Luke records from him at twelve years old in the same building (Lk. 2:49).

Verse 22 supplies this Gospel's account of how understanding arrives. The disciples heard the saying at the time and grasped nothing of it for three years; the resurrection made the old sentence legible and the memory surfaced with its meaning attached — which is the promise of 14:26 in operation. They believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken, two objects of one verb, with no distinction drawn between them.

Verses 23-25 must not be used to unsettle the wrong reader. What is described is faith produced by spectacle and not yet tested — the crowd of chapter 6 who turn back at the first hard saying (6:66). John uses of them the identical phrase he used of the saved in 1:12, believed in his name: the difference is not in the vocabulary but in what the faith does when the wine runs out. Anxiety about whether one's faith is real is not a symptom of this condition; the people described here were entirely untroubled. And Jesus withholding himself is not Jesus withdrawing — the next thing he does is give Nicodemus the fullest account of the new birth in the Bible.
verseByVerse.examples:
The buying and selling were not wicked in themselves but had invaded the sacred space set apart for prayer, turning the house of God into a place of commerce. The sign of the temple's destruction and raising in three days is the central sign of the entire Gospel: the cross and resurrection are the ultimate manifestation of Jesus's glory, the event to which all other signs point.

The anger of this scene needs handling in both directions. It is not incompatible with meekness: anger is what love does when what it loves is being damaged, and he stops to make the whip of cords himself (v. 15) — this is deliberate, not a loss of temper. But the passage is not a warrant for aggression on God's behalf. Two things separate it from that: all of it is aimed at the dishonouring of God and the exclusion of the powerless, and none of it at a slight to himself, since under personal injury he did not open his mouth (Isa. 53:7; 1 Pet. 2:23); and it is the Son acting in his own house with the owner's authority.

The searching application is not the easy one about churches selling things. It is the Court of the Gentiles question: whether anything in the ordinary operation of a congregation — its assumptions, its vocabulary, the things everyone knows and nobody explains — makes it hard for an outsider to get near God. Nobody in Jerusalem had decided to exclude the nations. They had simply needed the space.

And the chapter's last word runs straight into the next scene: the printers' chapter break hides a joint. Verse 25 ends he himself knew what was in man (anthropos), and John's next sentence begins Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus — the general statement and its illustration set against each other like a caption and a photograph.

verseByVerse.quote: The Passover of the Jews was at hand, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. In the temple he found those who were selling oxen and sheep and pigeons, and the money-changers sitting there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Passover of the Jews was at hand, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. In the temple he found those who were selling oxen and sheep and pigeons, and the money-changers sitting there.

The Passover of the Jews was at hand. John mentions three Passovers (2:13; 6:4; 11:55), which is why we think Jesus’ ministry lasted about three years.

In the temple he found those who were selling oxen and sheep and pigeons. The trading happened in the outer court, the Court of the Gentiles. Animals for sacrifice, conveniently sold on the spot to pilgrims, at a price.

And the money-changers sitting there. Money-changers exchanged coins with images of pagan rulers for the Tyrian shekel used to pay the temple tax, taking a commission. This trade was under the control of the high priestly family.

In a sentence. At Passover Jesus went to Jerusalem and found people selling animals and changing money in the temple courts.

On a Tuesday. What has crept into the worship of God that should not be there?
verseByVerse.note: The trading happened in the outer court. Money-changers exchanged coins into the currency accepted for the temple tax. John places this cleansing early; the other Gospels record one in the last week.

verseByVerse.quote: And making a whip of cords, he drove them all out of the temple, with the sheep and oxen. And he poured out the coins of the money-changers and overturned their tables. And he told those who sold the pigeons, "Take these things away; do not make my Father's house a house of trade."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Making a whip of cords, he drove them all out of the temple, with the sheep and oxen. And he poured out the coins of the money-changers and overturned their tables. And he told those who sold the pigeons: take these things away; do not make my Father’s house a house of trade.

Making a whip of cords. Perhaps from the rushes used for animal bedding. To drive out the animals, not to beat people. A deliberate, considered act, not a loss of temper.

He drove them all out. With righteous anger.

And he poured out the coins … and overturned their tables. Coins scattering across the stone floor.

Take these things away. To the pigeon sellers, he speaks: the birds were in cages and could not be driven.

Do not make my Father’s house a house of trade. “My Father’s house”: Jesus claims a unique relationship with God (Luke 2:49). A house of trade: perhaps an echo of Zechariah 14:21: there shall no longer be a trader in the house of the Lord on that day. The day of the Lord has come.

One cleansing or two? John places a cleansing at the start of Jesus’ ministry; the other Gospels place one at the end (Mark 11:15–17). Some think John moved it to the beginning for theological reasons. But the details and wording differ, and it is quite possible that Jesus did it twice, at the beginning and end of his ministry.

In a sentence. Jesus made a whip of cords, drove out the traders and animals, scattered the coins, overturned the tables, and told them not to make his Father’s house a marketplace.

For worship. Jesus is zealous for the purity of God’s worship. Ask him to cleanse your worship today.

parallels.desc: no longer a trader in the house of the LORD
my Father’s house

verseByVerse.quote: "His disciples remembered that it was written, 'Zeal for your house will consume me.' So the Jews said to him, 'What sign do you show us for doing these things?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
His disciples remembered that it was written: zeal for your house will consume me. So the Jews said to him: what sign do you show us for doing these things?

His disciples remembered. Perhaps later, after the resurrection (v. 22).

Zeal for your house will consume me. Psalm 69:9, a psalm of the righteous sufferer, often applied to Jesus in the New Testament (15:25; 19:28–29; Romans 15:3). “Consume”: devour, eat me up. His zeal for God’s house would literally consume him: it would lead to his death. The cleansing of the temple was one cause of his execution.

What sign do you show us for doing these things? By what authority? Prove it with a miracle. The prophets sometimes did symbolic acts; let him prove he is a prophet.

In a sentence. His disciples remembered the Scripture that zeal for God’s house would consume him, and the Jewish leaders demanded a sign to prove his authority.

On a Tuesday. Are you zealous for God’s honour? Jesus’ zeal cost him his life.

parallels.desc: zeal for your house has consumed me

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." The Jews then said, "It has taken forty-six years to build this temple, and will you raise it up in three days?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered them: destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. The Jews then said: it has taken forty-six years to build this temple, and will you raise it up in three days?

Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up. The sign he offers: his resurrection. “Destroy”: a command meaning “if you destroy”. You will destroy it; I will raise it. “Raise up” (egerō): the word for resurrection. The words were twisted at his trial into a threat to destroy the temple (Mark 14:58).

It has taken forty-six years to build this temple. Herod the Great began rebuilding the temple around 20 BC; forty-six years later puts this at about AD 27. The work went on until AD 63, just seven years before it was destroyed.

And will you raise it up in three days? They take him literally, and mock.

In a sentence. Jesus answered that if they destroyed this temple, he would raise it up in three days, and they scoffed that it had taken forty-six years to build.

For worship. The sign of Jesus’ authority is his resurrection. Believe it.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the Great began rebuilding the temple around 20 BC; forty-six years brings us to about AD 27. The work went on for decades more.

parallels.desc: the charge at his trial

verseByVerse.quote: But he was speaking about the temple of his body. When therefore he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he was speaking about the temple of his body. When therefore he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.

But he was speaking about the temple of his body. John’s explanation. Jesus’ body is the true temple, the place where God dwells with his people (1:14: he tabernacled among us). The temple building will be replaced by Jesus himself. Through his death and resurrection, he becomes the meeting place of God and humanity (4:21–24). And his people, united to him, become God’s temple (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21–22).

When therefore he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered. Understanding came after the resurrection, with the help of the Spirit (14:26).

And they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken. Scripture (perhaps Psalm 16:10) and Jesus’ own words are placed side by side. Jesus’ word has the authority of Scripture.

In a sentence. He was speaking of his body as the temple, and after his resurrection his disciples remembered and believed Scripture and his words.

For worship. Jesus is the true temple. In him you meet God. And you are part of his temple.

parallels.desc: they remembered his words

verseByVerse.quote: Now when he was in Jerusalem at the Passover Feast, many believed in his name when they saw the signs that he was doing. But Jesus on his part did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When he was in Jerusalem at the Passover Feast, many believed in his name when they saw the signs that he was doing. But Jesus on his part did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people.

Many believed in his name when they saw the signs. Faith based on miracles. Real, but shallow. John recognises different kinds of belief. Some who believed would later turn away (6:66; 8:31, 59).

But Jesus on his part did not entrust himself to them. A play on words: they believed (episteusan) in him, but he did not believe (episteuen), entrust himself, to them. He did not commit himself to their enthusiasm.

Because he knew all people. He knew the shallowness of their faith.

In a sentence. At Passover many believed in Jesus because of his signs, but he did not entrust himself to them, because he knew everyone.

On a Tuesday. Faith based only on miracles may not last. Is your faith rooted in who Jesus is?

parallels.desc: I the LORD search the heart

verseByVerse.quote: and needed no one to bear witness about man, for he himself knew what was in man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And needed no one to bear witness about man, for he himself knew what was in man.

He himself knew what was in man. He knows the human heart perfectly, as only God does (1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:9–10; Psalm 139:1–4). He knew Nathanael (1:47–48), and will know the Samaritan woman’s past (4:18), and Judas’ betrayal (6:64). The next chapter shows him with a man, Nicodemus, whose heart he reads.

A comfort and a warning. Jesus knows the worst about us, and still loves us. And we cannot deceive him with shallow profession.

In a sentence. He needed no one to tell him about people, for he knew what was in every heart.

For worship. Jesus knows everything in your heart, and still loves you. Be honest with him.

parallels.desc: you alone know the hearts of all

2.title: The First Sign: Water into Wine
2.text: <sup>1</sup>On the third day there was a wedding at Cana in Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there.<sup>2</sup>Jesus also was invited to the wedding with his disciples.<sup>3</sup>When the wine ran out, the mother of Jesus said to him, “They have no wine.”<sup>4</sup>And Jesus said to her, “Woman, what does this have to do with me? My hour has not yet come.”<sup>5</sup>His mother said to the servants, “Do whatever he tells you.”<sup>6</sup>Now there were six stone water jars there for the Jewish rites of purification, each holding twenty or thirty gallons.<sup>7</sup>Jesus said to the servants, “Fill the jars with water.” And they filled them up to the brim.<sup>8</sup>And he said to them, “Now draw some out and take it to the master of the feast.” So they took it.<sup>9</sup>When the master of the feast tasted the water now become wine, and did not know where it came from (though the servants who had drawn the water knew), the master of the feast called the bridegroom<sup>10</sup>and said to him, “Everyone serves the good wine first, and when people have drunk freely, then the poor wine. But you have kept the good wine until now.”<sup>11</sup>This, the first of his signs, Jesus did at Cana in Galilee, and manifested his glory. And his disciples believed in him.<sup>12</sup>After this he went down to Capernaum, with his mother and his brothers and his disciples, and they stayed there for a few days.<sup>13</sup>The Passover of the Jews was at hand, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.<sup>14</sup>In the temple he found those who were selling oxen and sheep and pigeons, and the money-changers sitting there.<sup>15</sup>And making a whip of cords, he drove them all out of the temple, with the sheep and oxen. And he poured out the coins of the money-changers and overturned their tables.<sup>16</sup>And he told those who sold the pigeons, “Take these things away; do not make my Father’s house a house of trade.”<sup>17</sup>His disciples remembered that it was written, “Zeal for your house will consume me.”<sup>18</sup>So the Jews said to him, “What sign do you show us for doing these things?”<sup>19</sup>Jesus answered them, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”<sup>20</sup>The Jews then said, “It has taken forty-six years to build this temple, and will you raise it up in three days?”<sup>21</sup>But he was speaking about the temple of his body.<sup>22</sup>When therefore he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.<sup>23</sup>Now when he was in Jerusalem at the Passover Feast, many believed in his name when they saw the signs that he was doing.<sup>24</sup>But Jesus on his part did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people<sup>25</sup>and needed no one to bear witness about man, for he himself knew what was in man.
2.overview:
Two scenes open Jesus’ public ministry, one in a village home and one in the temple, and both announce that something new has come. At a wedding in Cana, when the wine runs out, Jesus turns some 150 gallons of water standing in stone jars for Jewish purification into wine better than any served before. It is the first of the seven “signs” John records, and through it Jesus reveals his glory and his disciples believe. The prophets pictured the messianic age as a feast overflowing with wine (Isaiah 25:6; Amos 9:13); the water of the old purification rites gives way to the wine of the kingdom.

At Passover in Jerusalem Jesus drives the traders and money-changers from the temple court with a whip of cords, forbidding them to make his Father’s house a market. Asked for a sign to justify his authority, he says, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” His hearers think of Herod’s building, forty-six years in the making; John explains that he meant his body, and the disciples understood after the resurrection. The meeting place of God and people is now Jesus himself. Many in Jerusalem believe because of his signs, but Jesus does not entrust himself to them, for he knows what is in every human heart.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — Nicodemus and the New Birth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Nicodemus, a Pharisee on the ruling council, visits Jesus by night and acknowledges him as a teacher sent by God, because of his signs. Jesus tells him that without a birth from above no one can see God’s kingdom. Nicodemus takes it literally: can an old man be born a second time? Jesus explains that entry to the kingdom requires birth by water and the Spirit. Human nature can only reproduce itself; the Spirit gives new life, unseen and unpredictable as the wind. Israel’s teacher should have understood. Jesus speaks of what he has seen, yet his testimony is refused. The Son of Man, who alone has come down from heaven, must be raised up as Moses raised the bronze serpent, so that all who trust him may have eternal life. The reason is God’s love for the world: he gave his unique Son, so that no one who believes in him will be lost, but will live for ever. The Son came to rescue, not to condemn. Believers face no condemnation; unbelievers are condemned already. The light has come, but people chose darkness because their deeds were evil and they feared exposure, while those who practise the truth come to the light gladly.
verseByVerse.theology:
The new birth is the work of the Spirit, who blows where he wills. No human being can produce it, control it, or predict it; the Spirit sovereignly regenerates those whom God has given to the Son. The lifting up of the Son of Man — as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness — is the means by which eternal life comes to those who look in faith. God's motive is love for the world; his means is the gift of his Son; his purpose is salvation, not condemnation. The light has come, and the verdict of each person is revealed by whether they come to the light or flee from it.

The kingdom of God — the dominant phrase of the other three Gospels — occurs in John only here, at verses 3 and 5, and never again. And the verb shifts between them: without this birth a man cannot see the kingdom (v. 3) and cannot enter it (v. 5). The problem is not that he is outside a door he can see; he cannot perceive the country. This is why argument alone never works, and why Nicodemus is the proof of it.

Verse 6 states the impossibility as a principle of kind, not of quantity: like produces like, and nothing in creation generates something of a higher order than itself. Flesh here is not the body — this Gospel has just said the Word became flesh and meant it as the highest news in the world — but human nature working with its own resources, including the best of them. So the failure of religious effort is not a failure of sincerity or degree. Effort was never the mechanism.

Verse 16 requires two corrections that make it larger rather than smaller. So loved renders houtos, an adverb of manner rather than degree: in this way God loved — he gave. The size of the love is not asserted but demonstrated. And the world in this Gospel is not a neutral term for the planet's population but humanity organised against God (1:10; 7:7; 15:18-19). The object of the love was the thing set against him. Verse 17's not to condemn is a statement of purpose, not a denial that judgement exists — verse 18 says the opposite in the same breath. A lifeboat does not go out to drown anyone; that the drowning is real is why it was launched.
verseByVerse.examples:
'Born again' (or 'born from above') is among the most comprehensive descriptions of salvation in the New Testament: it captures the totality of the transformation (rebirth, not reform), its source (from above, from God), and its necessity (without it, the kingdom cannot be seen). Nicodemus's night visit is the first of several encounters in John where the darkness represents the condition of the human soul before the light breaks in. John 3:16 is not a formula to be memorized but a universe to be explored: every word contains inexhaustible depth.

Nicodemus is not finished at the end of this conversation, and the arc is the answer to anyone who thinks the night visit was a failure. He appears twice more, each time further into the open: in chapter 7 he speaks up in the council for due process and is shouted down (7:50-51); and after the crucifixion, when the twelve have scattered and there is nothing left to gain, he comes to a Roman execution in daylight with about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes (19:39) — a quantity fit for the burial of a king, carried through the streets by a member of the Sanhedrin. The man who came at night buried him in the afternoon.

The bronze serpent repays being staged rather than cited. Israel complains; snakes come; people are dying through the camp. God's remedy is not to remove the snakes but to have Moses cast an image of the very thing killing them and raise it on a pole — an image, commanded by the God who forbade images, of the instrument of death — and the only requirement laid on a dying man is that he look. It is deliberately the one thing someone face down in the sand can still do. (Israel kept the bronze snake, and seven centuries later Hezekiah found them burning incense to it and smashed it, calling it Nehushtan — 2 Kgs. 18:4. Even the instrument of mercy becomes an idol if the look lands on it rather than through it.)

Verse 10 is the verse for the reader who knows his Bible and feels nothing. Nicodemus knows the texts and can almost certainly recite them; what he has never done is apply the promise of a new heart to himself, because he has spent his life being told, accurately, that his conduct is exemplary. Note the tone of the rebuke, though: Jesus asks a question, does not end the conversation, and goes on to give this one bewildered official more sustained teaching on the new birth than anyone else receives in the Gospels.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. This man came to Jesus by night and said to him, "Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. This man came to Jesus by night and said to him: Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him.

The link. John has just said that Jesus knew what was in man (2:25). Now he shows us a man: Nicodemus, and Jesus reading his heart.

A man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus. A Pharisee: devout, learned, moral, strict in keeping the law. The best of Jewish religion. If anyone could enter the kingdom by his own goodness, he could.

A ruler of the Jews. Nicodemus was a member of the Sanhedrin, the ruling council. He appears again defending Jesus (7:50–51) and helping to bury him (19:39). He seems to have become a believer.

This man came to Jesus by night. Perhaps for fear of being seen (12:42; 19:38). Perhaps for a quiet, uninterrupted talk, as rabbis often studied at night. And in John, night is symbolic: he came out of the darkness to the light (v. 2; 13:30).

Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God. Respectful, and true as far as it goes. “We”: perhaps other Pharisees thought the same. But “a teacher” is not enough.

For no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him. The signs had convinced him that God was with Jesus. A faith like that of 2:23, based on signs.

In a sentence. Nicodemus, a Pharisee and member of the ruling council, came to Jesus at night and acknowledged him as a teacher from God because of his signs.

On a Tuesday. Respect for Jesus as a great teacher is not enough. You need what he told Nicodemus.
verseByVerse.note: Nicodemus was a member of the Sanhedrin, the ruling council. Coming by night may have been for secrecy or simply for quiet conversation.

parallels.desc: Nicodemus speaks up in the council
he brings spices for Jesus’ burial

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered him: truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God.

Jesus answered him. Answered what? Nicodemus had not asked a question. Jesus answers the question of his heart, cutting through polite compliments to his deepest need.

Truly, truly, I say to you. A solemn statement.

Unless one is born again. Key words. The ESV notes that “again” (Greek anōthen) can also be rendered “from above”. Both meanings are intended: a second birth, and a birth from God above. Not improvement, but a completely new beginning, a new life given by God. Nicodemus needed not more religion, but new life.

He cannot see the kingdom of God. Cannot experience it, enter it, perceive it. Without the new birth, a person is blind to the kingdom. Not a few people, but every person. Even the most religious.

In a sentence. Jesus told Nicodemus that unless a person is born again, from above, he cannot see the kingdom of God.

For worship. If you see the kingdom of God, it is because God has given you new birth. Praise him.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “again” (Greek anōthen) can also be rendered “from above.” Nicodemus hears one sense; Jesus means both.

parallels.desc: born of God
born again to a living hope

verseByVerse.quote: Nicodemus said to him, "How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother's womb and be born?" Jesus answered, "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nicodemus said to him: how can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born? Jesus answered: truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.

How can a man be born when he is old? Nicodemus takes it literally, or perhaps means: how can someone my age change completely? A whole life of religious habit cannot be undone. You cannot start over.

Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born? Impossible. Exactly right. A person cannot cause his own birth. That is the point.

Unless one is born of water and the Spirit. Water and Spirit together recall Ezekiel’s promise of cleansing and a new heart: I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean from all your uncleannesses … And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you … And I will put my Spirit within you (Ezekiel 36:25–27). Water: cleansing from sin. Spirit: new life. One birth, with two aspects. Nicodemus, the teacher of Israel, should have known this (v. 10).

Where Christians differ: “born of water”. Roman Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and some Anglican teaching take the water to be baptism, and teach that baptism is the means of regeneration (baptismal regeneration). Others take water to mean physical birth. Verdict: the best reading, in context, is Ezekiel 36: water and Spirit describe one spiritual birth, the cleansing and renewing work of the Spirit. Nicodemus could not have understood a reference to Christian baptism, not yet instituted, and Jesus expected him to understand (v. 10). Baptism is the sign of this new birth, not its cause. The thief on the cross entered paradise without baptism (Luke 23:43).

He cannot enter the kingdom of God. Not just see it, but enter it.

In a sentence. Nicodemus asked how an old man could be born again, and Jesus answered that unless a person is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter God’s kingdom.

On a Tuesday. You cannot make yourself born again. Ask God for the cleansing and new life only his Spirit can give.
verseByVerse.note: Water and Spirit together recall Ezekiel’s promise of cleansing and a new heart.

parallels.desc: I will sprinkle clean water on you and put my Spirit within you
the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit

verseByVerse.quote: "That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit.

That which is born of the flesh is flesh. “Flesh”: human nature, mortal and fallen. Like produces like. Natural birth produces natural life. Human beings, by nature, can only produce more human nature. Religion, morality and effort, however good, are still flesh.

And that which is born of the Spirit is spirit. Only the Spirit can produce spiritual life. New birth is not the improvement of the old nature, but the creation of a new one (2 Corinthians 5:17). Flesh cannot become spirit by trying.

In a sentence. Natural birth produces only natural life, but birth by the Spirit produces spiritual life.

On a Tuesday. No amount of self-improvement can make you spiritual. You need to be born of the Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not marvel that I said to you, 'You must be born again.' The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not marvel that I said to you: you must be born again. The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.

Do not marvel that I said to you, You must be born again. “You” is plural: all of you, all Israel, everyone. “Must”: no exceptions.

The wind blows where it wishes. The ESV notes that the same Greek word (pneuma) means both “wind” and “spirit”. Perhaps a breeze was blowing as they spoke on a rooftop at night. The wind is sovereign: it blows where it wills. You cannot control it, command it, or predict it.

And you hear its sound. You see its effects: rustling leaves, moving clouds.

But you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. Its source and destination are hidden.

So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit. The new birth is the sovereign work of God’s Spirit. It cannot be controlled, manufactured or explained by human methods. It comes where he wills (1:13). But its effects can be seen: a changed life. This is a foundation of the Reformed doctrine of effectual calling and irresistible grace: the Spirit gives new birth sovereignly, as he wills.

In a sentence. Jesus told Nicodemus not to be surprised that all must be born again, for the Spirit, like the wind, blows where he wills, unseen but known by his effects.

For worship. If you are born again, the sovereign Spirit blew on you. Thank him. And pray for him to blow on those you love.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the same Greek word (pneuma) means both “wind” and “spirit.”

parallels.desc: you do not know the way the spirit comes
come from the four winds, O breath

verseByVerse.quote: "Nicodemus said to him, 'How can these things be?' Jesus answered him, 'Are you the teacher of Israel and yet you do not understand these things?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nicodemus said to him: how can these things be? Jesus answered him: are you the teacher of Israel and yet you do not understand these things?

How can these things be? Nicodemus’ last words in this conversation. He fades from view. Bewildered.

Are you the teacher of Israel. Jesus calls him “the teacher of Israel”, a recognised authority, perhaps one of the most respected rabbis.

And yet you do not understand these things? The Old Testament had promised the new birth: a new heart and a new spirit (Ezekiel 36:25–27; 11:19), the circumcision of the heart (Deuteronomy 30:6), the new covenant (Jeremiah 31:33), and the valley of dry bones brought to life by the Spirit (Ezekiel 37). He should have known. Learning without the Spirit leaves even the greatest teachers blind.

In a sentence. When Nicodemus asked how this could be, Jesus asked how the teacher of Israel could fail to understand.

On a Tuesday. Theological knowledge is not the same as spiritual understanding. Ask the Spirit to open your eyes.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus calls him “the teacher of Israel” — a recognised authority who should have known the prophets’ promises.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, we speak of what we know, and bear witness to what we have seen, but you do not receive our testimony. If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how can you believe if I tell you heavenly things?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, truly, I say to you, we speak of what we know, and bear witness to what we have seen, but you do not receive our testimony. If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how can you believe if I tell you heavenly things?

We speak of what we know. “We”: Jesus, and perhaps his disciples, or the Father and the Son, or Jesus speaking with authority. Eyewitness testimony.

But you do not receive our testimony. The ESV notes that “you” in these verses is plural: Jesus is now addressing Nicodemus’ group, or Israel’s teachers.

If I have told you earthly things. The new birth, which happens on earth, in people’s lives, illustrated by earthly things like birth and wind.

How can you believe if I tell you heavenly things? Truths about heaven itself, God’s plan, the Son’s relationship to the Father, which only one from heaven could reveal (v. 13).

In a sentence. Jesus said they spoke of what they knew and had seen, but their testimony was rejected, and if earthly things were not believed, how could heavenly things be?

On a Tuesday. Believe what Jesus tells you, even what you cannot fully understand.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “you” in these verses is plural: Jesus is addressing Nicodemus’s whole circle.

verseByVerse.quote: "No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man. And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man. And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up.

No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven. No human being has gone up to heaven to bring back knowledge of God (Deuteronomy 30:12; Proverbs 30:4). Only the Son of Man, who came down from heaven, can reveal heavenly things. He is from above (v. 31).

The Son of Man. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “who is in heaven”.

As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness. Numbers 21:4–9. When Israel grumbled against God, he sent poisonous snakes, and many died. When the people repented, God told Moses to make a bronze serpent and put it on a pole. Anyone bitten who looked at it lived. Not by medicine, not by effort, but by looking in faith at what God provided.

So must the Son of Man be lifted up. “Must” (dei): divine necessity. “Lifted up” (hypsōthēnai): a double meaning, used three times in John (8:28; 12:32–34). Lifted up on the cross, and lifted up in exaltation and glory. The cross is his glory. As the serpent, a symbol of the curse, was lifted up, so Jesus, made a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), would be lifted up on the cross. And those who look to him in faith will live.

In a sentence. Only the Son of Man, who came from heaven, can reveal heaven, and as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up.

For worship. Look to the crucified Christ and live. That is all the dying Israelites had to do.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “who is in heaven.” In John, “lifted up” means both the cross and his exaltation.

parallels.desc: the bronze serpent on a pole
he said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die

verseByVerse.quote: "that whoever believes in him may have eternal life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
That whoever believes in him may have eternal life.

Whoever believes in him. As the Israelites looked at the serpent, we look to Christ in faith. “Whoever”: anyone.

May have eternal life. Key words. “Eternal life” (zōē aiōnios): the life of the age to come, the life of God himself, given now and lasting for ever. Not just endless existence, but knowing God (17:3). It begins now, at the new birth, and continues for ever.

Where do Jesus’ words end? The ESV notes that some interpreters end Jesus’ words at verse 15, with verses 16–21 as John’s comment. Ancient Greek had no quotation marks. Either way, the words are true.

In a sentence. So that whoever believes in him may have eternal life.

For worship. If you believe in Jesus, you have eternal life now. Rejoice.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some interpreters end Jesus’ words at verse 15 and read verses 16–21 as John’s comment.

verseByVerse.quote: "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him.

The best-known verse in the Bible. Martin Luther called John 3:16 “the gospel in miniature”.

For God so loved the world. The ESV notes that verse 16 can also be rendered: For this is how God loved the world. “So” (houtōs) means “in this way”, more than “so much”. The verse describes how God showed his love: by giving his Son. “The world”: in John, humanity in rebellion against God (1:10). The wonder is not that the world is big, but that it is bad. God loved those who hated him.

That he gave his only Son. “Gave”: in the incarnation, and supremely on the cross (Romans 8:32). “His only Son” (monogenē): unique, beloved, like Isaac (Genesis 22:2). The cost of love.

That whoever believes in him. The way to receive it: faith. “Whoever”: no one who believes is excluded.

Should not perish. “Perish” (apolētai): be destroyed, be lost for ever. The alternative to eternal life is not nothing, but eternal ruin.

But have eternal life. Present tense: have it now.

For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world. The purpose of his first coming was salvation, not judgement (12:47).

But in order that the world might be saved through him. Through him alone (14:6; Acts 4:12).

Where Christians differ: God’s love and the extent of the atonement. Some take this verse to prove that Christ died equally for every individual, making salvation possible for all. Verdict: the verse teaches God’s love for a rebellious world, the gift of his Son, and the promise of life to everyone who believes. It is the foundation of the free offer of the gospel to all people: anyone who believes will be saved. It does not say Christ died in the same way for every individual. Elsewhere John shows that Christ lays down his life for his sheep (10:11, 15), and that those who believe are those the Father gives him (6:37, 44). Both truths stand: the gospel is offered to all, and those who believe are saved by a Saviour whose death secured their salvation.

In a sentence. This is how God loved the rebellious world: he gave his unique Son, so that everyone who believes in him will not perish but have eternal life; for God sent his Son not to condemn the world but to save it through him.

For worship. God loved you, a rebel, by giving his only Son. Believe in him, and you will never perish.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that verse 16 can also be rendered “For this is how God loved the world” — the stress is on the manner of his love.

parallels.desc: your son, your only son

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever believes in him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe is condemned already, because he has not believed in the name of the only Son of God. And this is the judgment: the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever believes in him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe is condemned already, because he has not believed in the name of the only Son of God. And this is the judgement: the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil.

Whoever believes in him is not condemned. No condemnation, now or ever (5:24; Romans 8:1). The verdict is settled.

But whoever does not believe is condemned already. Not that God condemns them for not believing alone, but that they are already under condemnation for their sin, and by refusing Christ, they refuse the only rescue. They remain where they are (v. 36).

Because he has not believed in the name of the only Son of God. Unbelief is the final sin, because it rejects the cure.

And this is the judgment. “Judgement” (krisis): the verdict, the dividing line.

The light has come into the world. Jesus (1:9).

And people loved the darkness rather than the light. The real reason for unbelief: not lack of evidence, but love of sin. People do not reject Jesus because they cannot believe, but because they will not give up the darkness.

Because their works were evil. They prefer to keep their evil deeds hidden.

In a sentence. Whoever believes is not condemned, but whoever does not believe is already condemned, for the light has come, and people loved darkness because their deeds were evil.

On a Tuesday. Is there any darkness you love more than the light? Bring it to Jesus.

parallels.desc: no condemnation

verseByVerse.quote: "For everyone who does wicked things hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works should be exposed. But whoever does what is true comes to the light, so that it may be clearly seen that his works have been carried out in God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For everyone who does wicked things hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works should be exposed. But whoever does what is true comes to the light, so that it may be clearly seen that his works have been carried out in God.

Everyone who does wicked things hates the light. Light exposes. The wicked avoid it, as thieves avoid daylight.

Lest his works should be exposed. “Exposed” (elenchthē): convicted, brought to light, shown for what they are.

But whoever does what is true comes to the light. “Does what is true”: lives honestly, sincerely, by God’s truth. Such a person is not afraid of the light.

So that it may be clearly seen that his works have been carried out in God. His works were done by God’s grace and in union with him, and the light shows it. Perhaps an encouragement to Nicodemus, who had come by night: come into the light.

In a sentence. Those who do evil hate the light and avoid it so that their deeds will not be exposed, but those who live by the truth come to the light, so that it is seen that their deeds were done in God.

On a Tuesday. Come out of hiding. Bring your life into Christ’s light, and let him show what is true.

parallels.desc: expose the works of darkness

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–36 — John's Final Testimony: The Bridegroom's Friend
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus and his disciples spend time in the Judean countryside, baptising, while John is still free and baptising at Aenon near Salim, where water is plentiful. After a dispute about purification, John’s disciples complain that everyone is now going to Jesus. John answers that people receive only what heaven gives. He is not the Messiah but the one sent ahead, like the friend of the bridegroom, whose joy is complete when he hears the groom’s voice. Jesus’ influence must grow while John’s shrinks. The one from heaven is over all and speaks what he has seen, though few accept it; those who do confirm that God tells the truth. God gives him the Spirit without limit, and the Father, who loves the Son, has entrusted everything to him. To trust the Son is to have eternal life; to refuse him is to remain under God’s wrath.
verseByVerse.theology:
John the Baptist's final words in this Gospel are also its most concentrated theological summary: Jesus comes from above, speaks the words of God, gives the Spirit without measure, and holds in his hands both eternal life and God's wrath. There is no middle ground: whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him. The Baptist who began by pointing to the Lamb of God ends by declaring the eternal stakes of the decision about him.

Verse 30 contains a word that is usually missed: both verbs carry must. Not I ought to step back graciously but a divine necessity — the same word Jesus used at verse 14 of the Son of Man being lifted up. The rise of one and the waning of the other are a single arrangement, and it was not the Baptist's to negotiate. These are among his last recorded words in this Gospel (some think he speaks on to verse 36); he does not appear again except in the past tense.

The closing verses hold eternal life and wrath in the same frame, and the pairing at verse 36 is deliberately asymmetrical: not believes against does not believe, but believes against does not obey (apeitheo, refuses to be persuaded). The unbelief in view is not doubt politely held but the refusal of a person who has a right to be obeyed.

And the final verb is this Gospel's own great word. The wrath of God remains on him is menei, from meno — the abiding word, whose first appearance was the Spirit coming down and remaining on Jesus (1:32-33), which reappeared when the first disciples asked where he was staying and then stayed (1:38-39), and which carries the whole of chapter 15. Something abides on everyone. On Christ the Spirit rests and does not lift; in his people he himself abides; and on the one who refuses him the wrath he was already under simply stays, because nothing has happened to move it. Nothing arrives — which is the same truth as condemned already at verse 18, said with a different verb, and which is also where the mercy lies: what remains can be lifted, and this chapter has already said how.
verseByVerse.examples:
'He must increase, but I must decrease' is the defining characteristic of all genuine ministry — the minister who builds his own kingdom rather than Christ's has misunderstood the calling. The image of the friend of the bridegroom captures perfectly the joy of the one who serves another's marriage rather than his own: he is not jealous, not diminished, but fulfilled in the fulfillment of the one he loves.

The friend of the bridegroom is sharper than a general lesson in humility once the role is understood. He stood beside the groom and served the wedding. The wedding was in a real sense his project — and the moment the bridegroom's voice was heard inside, his work was finished and his job was to go home. The Greek doubles the joy for emphasis: he rejoices with joy, and the perfect tense of verse 29 says that joy is now standing complete, at the exact moment the crowds transfer. He is not managing a loss. He is at the height of his life. And if Jesus is the bridegroom there is a bride, and she is not the audience at the wedding — she is the one being married.

Verse 30 must not be left sentimental, because of what it cost, as the other Gospels tell it. Within months John was arrested for telling the truth about a marriage, and from that cell he sent to ask whether Jesus was after all the one who was to come (Matt. 11:2-3) — not the question of a serenely fulfilled man, but of one whose decrease had gone further than he bargained for. He was beheaded without trial to settle a promise made in front of dinner guests. And Jesus' verdict, delivered while he was in that cell doubting, was that among those born of women no one greater had arisen (Matt. 11:11).

This is the passage for anyone being replaced — the younger colleague who is plainly better at it, the role handed on, the retirement that arrived before the sense of usefulness did, the body doing less than last year. The world has no account of those except loss. Note where the weight of the sentence actually falls: he must increase is doing all the work, and the second clause is only its shadow. Nobody in Scripture is asked to shrink for the sake of shrinking; the decrease is bearable, and is even a completed joy, solely because of who fills the space.

verseByVerse.quote: After this Jesus and his disciples went into the Judean countryside, and he remained there with them and was baptizing. John also was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because water was plentiful there, and people were coming and being baptized.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this Jesus and his disciples went into the Judean countryside, and he remained there with them and was baptising. John also was baptising at Aenon near Salim, because water was plentiful there, and people were coming and being baptised.

Into the Judean countryside. An early ministry in Judea, before the main Galilean ministry, recorded only in John.

He remained there with them and was baptizing. John clarifies later that Jesus himself did not baptise, but his disciples did (4:2).

At Aenon near Salim. The location of Aenon (“springs”) near Salim is uncertain, perhaps in the Jordan valley, or in Samaria.

Because water was plentiful there. Plenty of water: which suggests immersion. Baptists note this; it is not conclusive.

In a sentence. Jesus and his disciples went into the Judean countryside, where they baptised, while John was baptising at Aenon near Salim.

On a Tuesday. God’s servants can work side by side without rivalry.
verseByVerse.note: The location of Aenon (“springs”) near Salim is uncertain.

verseByVerse.quote: (for John had not yet been put in prison)
verseByVerse.commentary:
(For John had not yet been put in prison.)

For John had not yet been put in prison. The other Gospels begin Jesus’ Galilean ministry after John’s arrest (Mark 1:14). John explains that this Judean ministry came earlier, overlapping with John’s. He assumes his readers know the other Gospels.

In a sentence. This was before John had been imprisoned.

On a Tuesday. The Gospels complement each other. Read them together.
verseByVerse.note: The other Gospels begin Jesus’ Galilean ministry after John’s arrest; John fills in an earlier period.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a discussion arose between some of John's disciples and a Jew over purification. And they came to John and said to him, "Rabbi, he who was with you across the Jordan, to whom you bore witness — look, he is baptizing, and all are going to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A discussion arose between some of John’s disciples and a Jew over purification. And they came to John and said to him: Rabbi, he who was with you across the Jordan, to whom you bore witness, look, he is baptising, and all are going to him.

A discussion arose … over purification. Perhaps about the value of John’s baptism compared with Jesus’, or with Jewish ritual washings.

He who was with you across the Jordan, to whom you bore witness. They do not name Jesus. A hint of resentment: the one you helped is now taking your followers.

Look, he is baptizing, and all are going to him. Jealousy. John’s disciples are upset that Jesus is more popular.

In a sentence. After a dispute about purification, John’s disciples complained to him that the one he had testified about was baptising and everyone was going to him.

On a Tuesday. Jealousy of other ministries is a constant temptation. Rejoice when others are blessed.

verseByVerse.quote: John answered, "A person cannot receive even one thing unless it is given him from heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
John answered: a person cannot receive even one thing unless it is given him from heaven.

A person cannot receive even one thing unless it is given him from heaven. Everything comes from God: John’s ministry, Jesus’ ministry, every gift, every success. Jesus’ popularity is God’s gift, so there is no reason for jealousy. And John’s role is God’s gift too, and he is content with it (1 Corinthians 4:7).

In a sentence. John answered that no one can receive anything unless it is given from heaven.

On a Tuesday. Whatever role God has given you, receive it gladly. And don’t envy what he has given others.

parallels.desc: what do you have that you did not receive?

verseByVerse.quote: "You yourselves bear me witness, that I said, 'I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him.' The one who has the bride is the bridegroom. The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice. Therefore this joy of mine is now complete."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You yourselves bear me witness, that I said: I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him. The one who has the bride is the bridegroom. The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom’s voice. Therefore this joy of mine is now complete.

I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him. John had always said so (1:20, 23).

The one who has the bride is the bridegroom. In the Old Testament, God is the bridegroom of his people (Isaiah 54:5; 62:5; Hosea 2:19–20). Jesus is the bridegroom; his people are the bride (Mark 2:19–20; Ephesians 5:25–32; Revelation 19:7; 21:2).

The friend of the bridegroom. The friend of the bridegroom arranged the wedding and brought the bride to the groom, like a best man. His joy is to see the marriage happen, not to take the bride for himself.

Who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom’s voice. Perhaps the bridegroom’s shout of joy on receiving his bride.

Therefore this joy of mine is now complete. John is not jealous; he is overjoyed. People going to Jesus is the fulfilment of his whole life.

In a sentence. John reminded them that he had said he was not the Christ, but sent ahead, and like the bridegroom’s friend who rejoices at the bridegroom’s voice, his joy was now complete.

For worship. Your joy, like John’s, is to see people brought to Christ, the bridegroom.
verseByVerse.note: The friend of the bridegroom arranged the wedding and brought bride and groom together — his joy was the groom’s joy.

parallels.desc: as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride

verseByVerse.quote: "He must increase, but I must decrease."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He must increase, but I must decrease.

He must increase. “Must” (dei): divine necessity. Jesus must grow in prominence, in followers, in glory.

But I must decrease. John must fade from view. Not reluctantly, but gladly. One of the greatest statements of humility in the Bible. The motto of every true servant of Christ.

In a sentence. He must become greater, and I must become less.

For worship. Make John’s words your prayer today: Lord, may you increase, and may I decrease.

verseByVerse.quote: "He who comes from above is above all. He who is of the earth belongs to the earth and speaks in an earthly way. He who comes from heaven is above all. He bears witness to what he has seen and heard, yet no one receives his testimony."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who comes from above is above all. He who is of the earth belongs to the earth and speaks in an earthly way. He who comes from heaven is above all. He bears witness to what he has seen and heard, yet no one receives his testimony.

Who is speaking? Verses 31–36 may be John the Baptist’s words continuing, or the Gospel writer’s reflection. Either way, they explain why Jesus must increase.

He who comes from above is above all. Jesus, from heaven, is supreme over all.

He who is of the earth belongs to the earth and speaks in an earthly way. John the Baptist, and every human teacher. Even the greatest prophets speak as earthly men, with limited knowledge.

He bears witness to what he has seen and heard. Jesus speaks from direct knowledge of heaven (v. 11).

Yet no one receives his testimony. Generally speaking, rejection (1:11). Not literally no one, as the next verse shows.

In a sentence. The one from heaven is above all, speaking from what he has seen and heard, unlike those from earth, yet few receive his testimony.

On a Tuesday. Listen to the one who comes from heaven above all other voices.

parallels.desc: you are from below, I am from above

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever receives his testimony sets his seal to this, that God is true."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever receives his testimony sets his seal to this, that God is true.

Sets his seal to this. To set one’s seal to something is to certify it as true, as a seal on a document certifies its authenticity.

That God is true. To believe Jesus’ testimony is to affirm that God is truthful, since Jesus speaks God’s words (v. 34). And to refuse it is to call God a liar (1 John 5:10).

In a sentence. Whoever accepts his testimony certifies that God is true.

For worship. When you believe Jesus, you put your seal on God’s truthfulness. Trust him completely.
verseByVerse.note: To set one’s seal to something is to certify it as true.

parallels.desc: let God be true

verseByVerse.quote: "For he whom God has sent utters the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure. The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he whom God has sent utters the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure. The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand.

He whom God has sent utters the words of God. Jesus’ words are God’s words (7:16; 12:49–50; 14:10).

For he gives the Spirit without measure. God gives the Spirit to Jesus without limit (1:32–33; Isaiah 11:2). Prophets received the Spirit in measure, for particular tasks. Jesus has the fullness of the Spirit. Or: Jesus gives the Spirit without measure to his people. Both are true.

The Father loves the Son. The eternal love within the Trinity (5:20; 17:24).

And has given all things into his hand. All authority (13:3; Matthew 28:18). Everything is in his hands, including salvation and judgement.

In a sentence. The one God has sent speaks God’s words, for God gives him the Spirit without limit, and the Father loves the Son and has put everything in his hands.

For worship. Everything is in the hands of the Son whom the Father loves. Rest in that.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him.

Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life. Present tense: has it now.

Whoever does not obey the Son. Unbelief is disobedience. Faith in Christ is obedience to God’s command (1 John 3:23). Refusing to believe is rebellion.

Shall not see life. Will not experience eternal life.

But the wrath of God remains on him. Key words. “Wrath” (orgē): God’s settled, holy opposition to sin. The only time it appears in John’s Gospel. “Remains” (menei): abides, stays. Not that God becomes angry when someone rejects Christ, but that all people are already under his wrath because of sin (Ephesians 2:3), and it remains on those who refuse the only one who can remove it. Christ bore God’s wrath for those who believe (Romans 5:9; 1 Thessalonians 1:10).

In a sentence. Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life, but whoever disobeys the Son will not see life, and God’s wrath remains on him.

For worship. If you believe in the Son, God’s wrath has been removed from you, borne by Christ. Thank him for your eternal life.

parallels.desc: the wrath of God is revealed

3.title: You Must Be Born Again
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Now there was a man of the Pharisees named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews.<sup>2</sup>This man came to Jesus by night and said to him, “Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God, for no one can do these signs that you do unless God is with him.”<sup>3</sup>Jesus answered him, “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God.”<sup>4</sup>Nicodemus said to him, “How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born?”<sup>5</sup>Jesus answered, “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.<sup>6</sup>That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit.<sup>7</sup>Do not marvel that I said to you, ’You must be born again.’<sup>8</sup>The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.”<sup>9</sup>Nicodemus said to him, “How can these things be?”<sup>10</sup>Jesus answered him, “Are you the teacher of Israel and yet you do not understand these things?<sup>11</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, we speak of what we know, and bear witness to what we have seen, but you do not receive our testimony.<sup>12</sup>If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how can you believe if I tell you heavenly things?<sup>13</sup>No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man.<sup>14</sup>And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up,<sup>15</sup>that whoever believes in him may have eternal life.<sup>16</sup>“For God so loved the world, that he gave his only Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life.<sup>17</sup>For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but in order that the world might be saved through him.<sup>18</sup>Whoever believes in him is not condemned, but whoever does not believe is condemned already, because he has not believed in the name of the only Son of God.<sup>19</sup>And this is the judgment: the light has come into the world, and people loved the darkness rather than the light because their works were evil.<sup>20</sup>For everyone who does wicked things hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works should be exposed.<sup>21</sup>But whoever does what is true comes to the light, so that it may be clearly seen that his works have been carried out in God.”<sup>22</sup>After this Jesus and his disciples went into the Judean countryside, and he remained there with them and was baptizing.<sup>23</sup>John also was baptizing at Aenon near Salim, because water was plentiful there, and people were coming and being baptized<sup>24</sup>(for John had not yet been put in prison).<sup>25</sup>Now a discussion arose between some of John’s disciples and a Jew over purification.<sup>26</sup>And they came to John and said to him, “Rabbi, he who was with you across the Jordan, to whom you bore witness—look, he is baptizing, and all are going to him.”<sup>27</sup>John answered, “A person cannot receive even one thing unless it is given him from heaven.<sup>28</sup>You yourselves bear me witness, that I said, ’I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him.’<sup>29</sup>The one who has the bride is the bridegroom. The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom’s voice. Therefore this joy of mine is now complete.<sup>30</sup>He must increase, but I must decrease.”<sup>31</sup>He who comes from above is above all. He who is of the earth belongs to the earth and speaks in an earthly way. He who comes from heaven is above all.<sup>32</sup>He bears witness to what he has seen and heard, yet no one receives his testimony.<sup>33</sup>Whoever receives his testimony sets his seal to this, that God is true.<sup>34</sup>For he whom God has sent utters the words of God, for he gives the Spirit without measure.<sup>35</sup>The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand.<sup>36</sup>Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him.
3.overview:
Nicodemus, a Pharisee and member of the ruling council, comes to Jesus at night with a respectful compliment: Jesus must be a teacher from God. Jesus answers with a statement that sweeps away all religious achievement: no one can see the kingdom of God unless he is born again, or born from above. The Greek word means both, and Nicodemus hears only the first. Jesus explains that this birth is “of water and the Spirit”, the cleansing and new heart God promised through Ezekiel; it is as free and mysterious as the wind. The teacher of Israel ought to have known. The Son of Man, who came down from heaven, must be lifted up as Moses lifted the bronze serpent, so that whoever believes may have eternal life.

Then come the most famous words in the Bible: God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, so that whoever believes in him should not perish but have eternal life. God sent his Son to save, not to condemn; but those who refuse him stand condemned already, because they love darkness rather than light. In the second half of the chapter John the Baptist, told that everyone is going to Jesus, rejoices like the bridegroom’s friend: “He must increase, but I must decrease.” The chapter ends with the choice that runs through the whole Gospel: whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son will not see life, but God’s wrath remains on him.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–42 — The Woman at the Well
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Leaving Judea for Galilee, Jesus takes the road through Samaria and rests at noon by Jacob’s well near Sychar. When a Samaritan woman comes to draw water, he asks her for a drink, to her amazement, since Jews and Samaritans keep apart. He tells her that if she knew who was asking, she would ask him for living water. She objects that he has no bucket; is he greater than Jacob? He answers that well water leaves people thirsty again, but the water he gives becomes a spring of eternal life within. She asks for it. He tells her to call her husband, and when she says she has none, he reveals that she has had five, and her present partner is not her husband. She calls him a prophet and raises the dispute over whether to worship on Gerizim or in Jerusalem. Jesus says the time has come when the place will not matter: the Father, who is spirit, seeks worshippers in spirit and truth, though salvation comes from the Jews. She mentions the coming Messiah, and Jesus tells her that he is the one. The returning disciples are surprised but silent. Leaving her jar, she brings the townspeople to see the man who knew her whole life. Jesus tells the disciples his food is doing his Father’s will, and the fields are ripe for harvest now. Many Samaritans believe through her word, and more through his, confessing him the Saviour of the world.
verseByVerse.theology:
The living water Jesus offers is not a religious program or a moral reformation; it is himself — the inexhaustible source of eternal life. 'The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life.' Jesus does not merely point to the source of life; he is the source. The worship in Spirit and truth for which the Father seeks is not worship in a particular location but worship in the reality of who God is (truth) and by the power of God's own Spirit — the worship that the new covenant makes possible through the regeneration that Nicodemus could not understand.

The living water is explained by John himself later in the book. Standing in the temple Jesus cries out about rivers of living water, and the narrator adds the interpretation — this he said about the Spirit (7:38-39). So the gift offered at the well is the indwelling Spirit, the same new birth from above that Nicodemus could not grasp one chapter earlier, now pictured as a spring rather than a well. The distinction matters: a well is a store that must be gone to, lowered into and hauled from; a spring is water arriving from underneath under its own pressure, and the verb for welling up means to leap. What Jesus gives does not merely satisfy the drinker — it turns the drinker into a source.

Worship in spirit and truth is not sincerity set against ritual. Spirit is the Holy Spirit who enables it, and truth in this Gospel is a person before it is a quality (14:6) — so both halves are gifts rather than techniques. What is ruled out is worship that is correct and dead, and worship that is warm and invented: truth without Spirit is a corpse, Spirit without truth is a mood. And God is spirit (v. 24) does not mean God is vague or impersonal — the God described here speaks, seeks, loves and sends — but that he has no body and no location, and therefore cannot be arrived at or run out of.

The decisive clause is the Father is seeking such people to worship him (v. 23). Worship is ordinarily conceived as the search conducted from this end; here God is the one out looking, which is precisely what the chapter has been narrating since verse 4. A woman went to a well to fetch water and found somebody already sitting there who had come by a road many of his countrymen avoided. Note too that salvation is from the Jews is from, not for: the privilege was a channel and never a possession.
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus's method with the Samaritan woman is a model of contextual evangelism: he begins with her felt need (water), moves to her deeper need (the living water), exposes the root issue (her relationships), and leads her to the question of worship and the identity of the Messiah. He does not condemn; he illumines. The woman's testimony — 'Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did' — is the most basic form of Christian witness: here is someone who knows me completely and has not rejected me.

The five husbands deserve more care than they usually get. John never calls this woman immoral; Jesus never mentions sin to her, never calls her to repent, and never says sin no more — which he does say to the woman of chapter 8 and the man of chapter 5. A woman could not divorce in that world, so five marriages behind her means five times widowed or five times dismissed, or some mixture — things done to her at least as readily as by her. The town does not behave as a town behaves toward someone it has cast out: she speaks, they listen, they come (vv. 29-30, 39). The honest answer is that we are not told, and it matters that it be said, because women have sat through sermons on this chapter and been handed a shame the passage never assigns. (The old reading of the five husbands as an allegory of the five nations resettled in Samaria in 2 Kgs. 17 should also be resisted: it dissolves a real woman into a diagram, which is the one thing this passage refuses to do to her.)

Her testimony is instructive precisely because it is so poor by our standards. One fact, about herself; overstated (all that I ever did, when he had named one arrangement); no doctrine; and a closing line phrased in Greek to expect the answer no — nearer to this couldn't be the Christ, could it? And the town emptied. What travels is not the completeness of the account but the evidence that something has happened to the person giving it. Notice what her sentence leaves out: she never says and he did not despise me, because that is the tone of the whole remark. Being completely known had turned out not to be the disaster she would have predicted — which is the thing most people are most afraid of.

The harvest section is for the discouraged sower, and there are many. One sows and another reaps contains no promise that the sower sees it; the parent who prayed for thirty years, the teacher whose class drifted, the missionary who left with nothing to report are all inside that saying. The promise is in the verse before: sower and reaper rejoice together. In ordinary farming the reaper takes the visible result; here the arrangement is deliberately made so that neither can celebrate without the other.
