verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus learned that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John (although Jesus himself did not baptize, but only his disciples),
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus learned that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptising more disciples than John (although Jesus himself did not baptise, but only his disciples),

The contrast. Chapter 3 showed Jesus with Nicodemus: a man, a Jew, a respected teacher, who came at night. Chapter 4 shows him with a Samaritan woman: a woman, an outsider, a moral outcast, met at noon. Both need the same gift.

The Pharisees had heard. Jesus’ growing popularity attracted the attention of the Pharisees, who had already investigated John (1:24). Conflict was coming, but his hour had not yet come.

Making and baptizing more disciples than John. As John had said: he must increase (3:30).

Although Jesus himself did not baptize, but only his disciples. John clarifies 3:22. Perhaps to prevent people boasting that they had been baptised by Jesus himself (1 Corinthians 1:13–17).

In a sentence. Jesus learned that the Pharisees had heard he was making and baptising more disciples than John, though it was his disciples who baptised.

On a Tuesday. Jesus avoided unnecessary conflict. Wisdom sometimes means moving on.

verseByVerse.quote: he left Judea and departed again for Galilee. And he had to pass through Samaria.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He left Judea and departed again for Galilee. And he had to pass through Samaria.

He left Judea and departed again for Galilee. To avoid a premature confrontation.

And he had to pass through Samaria. Samaria lay between Judea and Galilee. Many Jews travelled round it, crossing the Jordan and going through Perea, to avoid contact with Samaritans. The direct route through Samaria took about three days. “Had to” (edei): the word of divine necessity. Not just geography, but God’s plan. There was a woman, and a town, that the Father had prepared to hear him.

In a sentence. Jesus left Judea for Galilee, and it was necessary for him to go through Samaria.

On a Tuesday. Your route today may be part of God’s plan for someone you will meet.
verseByVerse.note: Samaria lay between Judea and Galilee. Many Jews travelled round it by the Jordan valley; the direct route went through it.

parallels.desc: Philip preaches in Samaria

verseByVerse.quote: So he came to a town of Samaria called Sychar, near the field that Jacob had given to his son Joseph. Jacob's well was there; so Jesus, wearied as he was from his journey, was sitting beside the well. It was about the sixth hour.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So he came to a town of Samaria called Sychar, near the field that Jacob had given to his son Joseph. Jacob’s well was there; so Jesus, wearied as he was from his journey, was sitting beside the well. It was about the sixth hour.

A town of Samaria called Sychar. Probably near ancient Shechem, at the foot of Mount Gerizim.

Near the field that Jacob had given to his son Joseph. Genesis 33:18–19; 48:22; Joshua 24:32, where Joseph’s bones were buried. Sacred history.

Jacob’s well was there. Jacob’s well is still shown near Shechem (modern Nablus) at the foot of Mount Gerizim. One of the most certainly identified sites in the Gospels.

Jesus, wearied as he was from his journey. Truly human: tired, thirsty (v. 7), hungry (v. 8). The Word made flesh (1:14) gets tired. The one who made the stars sat down because his legs ached.

Was sitting beside the well. Literally “on the well”, on the low wall around it.

It was about the sixth hour. Noon, by Jewish reckoning: the hottest time of day. Women usually drew water in the cool of the morning or evening, together. A woman coming alone at noon was probably avoiding the others.

In a sentence. Jesus came to Sychar in Samaria, near Jacob’s well, and tired from the journey, sat down by the well at about noon.

For worship. Jesus knows your weariness. He was tired too.
verseByVerse.note: Jacob’s well is still shown near Shechem (modern Nablus) at the foot of Mount Gerizim. The ESV notes that the sixth hour was about noon — the heat of the day.

parallels.desc: Jacob buys land at Shechem
Joseph buried there

verseByVerse.quote: A woman from Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her, "Give me a drink."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A woman from Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her: give me a drink.

A woman from Samaria came to draw water. Alone, at noon. Unnamed.

Give me a drink. A Jewish teacher would not normally speak with a woman in public, let alone a Samaritan woman, let alone ask for a drink from her vessel, which would make him ceremonially unclean in strict Jewish eyes. Jesus breaks three barriers: gender, race and religion. He begins by asking for help. He makes himself dependent on her. A gracious way to open a conversation.

In a sentence. A Samaritan woman came to draw water, and Jesus asked her for a drink.

On a Tuesday. Jesus crossed every barrier to reach this woman. Who can you reach across a barrier today?
verseByVerse.note: A Jewish teacher would not normally speak with a woman in public, still less a Samaritan.

parallels.desc: meetings at a well

verseByVerse.quote: (For his disciples had gone away into the city to buy food.) The Samaritan woman said to him, "How is it that you, a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a woman of Samaria?" (For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
(For his disciples had gone away into the city to buy food.) The Samaritan woman said to him: how is it that you, a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a woman of Samaria? (For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.)

For his disciples had gone away into the city to buy food. So Jesus was alone, and the conversation private. And the disciples were willing to buy food from Samaritans.

How is it that you, a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a woman of Samaria? She is astonished.

For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans. Or “do not use vessels in common with Samaritans”. Samaritans were a mixed people descended from Israelites and foreigners settled in the land after the fall of Samaria in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:24–41). They accepted only the five books of Moses and worshipped on Mount Gerizim. Jews regarded them as half-breeds and heretics. The Jews had destroyed the Samaritan temple on Gerizim in 128 BC. Hatred ran deep on both sides (Luke 9:52–54).

In a sentence. With the disciples gone to buy food, the woman asked how Jesus, a Jew, could ask her, a Samaritan woman, for a drink, since Jews have nothing to do with Samaritans.

On a Tuesday. The gospel breaks down ancient hatreds. Is there a group you treat as she was treated?
verseByVerse.note: Samaritans were a mixed people descended from Israelites and settlers brought in by Assyria; Jews and Samaritans had centuries of hostility. The ESV notes that the last sentence may mean Jews did not share vessels with Samaritans.

parallels.desc: the settling of Samaria

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered her, "If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that is saying to you, 'Give me a drink,' you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered her: if you knew the gift of God, and who it is that is saying to you, give me a drink, you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.

If you knew the gift of God. God’s gift: eternal life, the Spirit, Christ himself (3:16; Romans 6:23). A gift is free.

And who it is that is saying to you. If you knew who I am. The theme of the conversation: who Jesus is.

You would have asked him, and he would have given you living water. The roles reverse: the one asking for water is the one who gives it. “Living water” normally meant fresh, flowing water from a spring or river, as opposed to still water in a cistern. But in the Old Testament, God is the fountain of living waters (Jeremiah 2:13; 17:13), and living water pictures the life and Spirit God gives (Isaiah 44:3; 55:1; Zechariah 14:8; Ezekiel 47). Jesus explains later that living water is the Spirit (7:37–39).

In a sentence. Jesus answered that if she knew God’s gift and who was asking her for a drink, she would have asked him and he would have given her living water.

For worship. Ask Jesus for living water. He gives it freely to all who ask.
verseByVerse.note: “Living water” normally meant fresh, flowing water from a spring, as opposed to still water in a cistern.

parallels.desc: the fountain of living waters

verseByVerse.quote: The woman said to him, "Sir, you have nothing to draw water with, and the well is deep. Where do you get that living water? Are you greater than our father Jacob? He gave us the well and drank from it himself, as did his sons and his livestock."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The woman said to him: sir, you have nothing to draw water with, and the well is deep. Where do you get that living water? Are you greater than our father Jacob? He gave us the well and drank from it himself, as did his sons and his livestock.

Sir, you have nothing to draw water with. Travellers carried a leather bucket and rope. Jesus had none.

And the well is deep. Said to be over 100 feet (30 m).

Where do you get that living water? She takes him literally, as Nicodemus did (3:4).

Are you greater than our father Jacob? An ironic question, expecting the answer no. The answer is yes. Jacob gave a well; Jesus gives living water. Jacob saw a ladder; Jesus is the ladder (1:51). The Samaritans claimed Jacob as their father.

In a sentence. The woman pointed out that he had no bucket and the well was deep, and asked if he was greater than Jacob, who gave them the well.

For worship. Jesus is greater than Jacob, greater than every hero of faith. Worship him.
verseByVerse.note: The well is deep — said to be over 100 feet.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to her: everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again.

Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again. Ordinary water satisfies only for a while. So does everything the world offers: pleasure, money, relationships, success. The woman knew this; she had tried five husbands (v. 18). Human beings have a thirst that no earthly thing can satisfy (Ecclesiastes 1:8; Jeremiah 2:13).

In a sentence. Jesus said that everyone who drinks this water will be thirsty again.

On a Tuesday. What are you drinking from that leaves you thirsty? Only Christ satisfies.

verseByVerse.quote: "'but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again. The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life.' The woman said to him, 'Sir, give me this water, so that I will not be thirsty or have to come here to draw water.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again. The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life. The woman said to him: sir, give me this water, so that I will not be thirsty or have to come here to draw water.

Whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again. “Never”: a strong negative. The deepest thirst of the soul is satisfied for ever.

A spring of water welling up to eternal life. Not just a drink, but a spring within, an inner source of life that never runs dry. “Welling up” (hallomenou): leaping, springing up, the word used of the lame man leaping (Acts 3:8). The life of the Spirit within the believer (7:38–39).

Sir, give me this water. She asks, but still misunderstands. She wants to be spared the daily trip to the well, perhaps the shame of coming alone at noon.

In a sentence. Jesus said that the water he gives becomes a spring within, welling up to eternal life, and the woman asked for it so she would no longer need to come to the well.

For worship. If you believe in Christ, you have a spring of living water within. Drink deeply today.

parallels.desc: like a spring of water whose waters do not fail

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Go, call your husband, and come here." The woman answered him, "I have no husband." Jesus said to her, "You are right in saying, 'I have no husband';"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to her: go, call your husband, and come here. The woman answered him: I have no husband. Jesus said to her: you are right in saying, I have no husband.

Go, call your husband, and come here. An abrupt change. Why? Because she cannot receive living water without facing her thirst, and her sin. Jesus goes straight to the wound.

I have no husband. True, as far as it went. A half-truth to close the subject.

You are right in saying, I have no husband. Jesus takes her words and opens them up.

In a sentence. Jesus told her to go and call her husband, and when she said she had none, he said she was right.

On a Tuesday. Jesus deals gently but directly with sin. Let him touch the wound.

verseByVerse.quote: "for you have had five husbands, and the one you now have is not your husband. What you have said is true."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you have had five husbands, and the one you now have is not your husband. What you have said is true.

You have had five husbands. Jesus knows everything about her (2:25). Whether through death or divorce, five marriages. In that culture a woman could not divorce her husband, so she may have been divorced by several, perhaps rejected over and over. Jewish teachers thought three marriages the most a woman should have.

And the one you now have is not your husband. She was living with a man without marriage. Hence her coming to the well alone at noon: shunned by the other women.

What you have said is true. Jesus exposes her, but without contempt. He does not condemn or lecture. He simply tells the truth, and in telling it, shows her that he knows her completely, and still speaks to her.

In a sentence. Jesus told her that she had had five husbands, and the man she was living with was not her husband.

For worship. Jesus knows everything you have done, and still offers you living water. That is grace.

parallels.desc: he knew what was in man

verseByVerse.quote: The woman said to him, "Sir, I perceive that you are a prophet. Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, but you say that in Jerusalem is the place where people ought to worship."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The woman said to him: sir, I perceive that you are a prophet. Our fathers worshipped on this mountain, but you say that in Jerusalem is the place where people ought to worship.

Sir, I perceive that you are a prophet. Only a prophet could know such things. Her understanding grows: from “a Jew” (v. 9) to “sir” to “a prophet”.

Our fathers worshiped on this mountain. “This mountain” is Mount Gerizim, where the Samaritans worshipped. It towered above them as they spoke. The Samaritans believed it was the chosen place of worship, based on Deuteronomy 11:29; 27:12. Their temple there had been destroyed by the Jews, but they still worshipped on the mountain.

But you say that in Jerusalem is the place where people ought to worship. The great dispute between Jews and Samaritans. Is she changing the subject, to avoid her sin? Perhaps. Or is she asking, as one convicted of sin, where she can find God and forgiveness: where should I go to offer sacrifice?

In a sentence. The woman said she could see he was a prophet, and raised the question of whether God should be worshipped on Mount Gerizim or in Jerusalem.

On a Tuesday. When people change the subject to religious debates, gently bring the conversation back to Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: “This mountain” is Mount Gerizim, where the Samaritans worshipped; a Samaritan temple had stood there until the Jews destroyed it more than a century before.

parallels.desc: the blessing on Mount Gerizim
the place the LORD will choose

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to her, "Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you worship the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to her: woman, believe me, the hour is coming when neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you worship the Father.

Woman, believe me. A solemn, respectful address (2:4).

The hour is coming. The new age that Jesus is bringing, through his death and resurrection.

When neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you worship the Father. The question of the place of worship will no longer matter. Jesus is the new temple (2:19–21). After his resurrection, God can be worshipped anywhere, through him. The Jerusalem temple would be destroyed in AD 70. And “the Father”: worship will be the worship of children.

In a sentence. Jesus told her that the time was coming when the Father would be worshipped neither on that mountain nor in Jerusalem.

For worship. You can worship God anywhere, through Christ. Your kitchen can be a temple.

parallels.desc: in every place incense will be offered to my name

verseByVerse.quote: "You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews. But the hour is coming, and is now here, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father is seeking such people to worship him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews. But the hour is coming, and is now here, when the true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father is seeking such people to worship him.

You worship what you do not know. The Samaritans accepted only the five books of Moses, rejecting the prophets and writings. Their knowledge of God was incomplete and distorted.

We worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews. Jesus does not pretend all religions are equal. God revealed himself to Israel, and the Messiah came from the Jews (Romans 9:4–5). Salvation is from the Jews: Jesus himself is a Jew. He does not flatter her; he tells her the truth.

But the hour is coming, and is now here. Already present, in Jesus.

When the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth. “In spirit”: not tied to a place, but from the heart, by the Holy Spirit, who gives new birth (3:5). “In truth”: according to God’s true revelation of himself, now fully given in Jesus, who is the truth (14:6). Not Samaritan worship, which lacked truth, nor merely Jewish worship, tied to a temple, but worship through Christ, by the Spirit.

For the Father is seeking such people to worship him. A wonderful statement. God seeks worshippers. He was seeking this woman, through Jesus at the well. Not that he needs our worship, but he seeks us for our good and his glory.

In a sentence. Jesus said the Samaritans worshipped what they did not know, while salvation is from the Jews, but the time has come when true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for he seeks such worshippers.

For worship. The Father is seeking you to worship him. Worship him today, in spirit and in truth.
verseByVerse.note: The Samaritans accepted only the five books of Moses.

parallels.desc: out of Zion shall go the law

verseByVerse.quote: "God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.

God is spirit. One of the great definitions of God in John’s writings, with God is light (1 John 1:5) and God is love (1 John 4:8). God is not a physical being, limited to a place. He is invisible, everywhere present, not confined to a mountain or a temple (1 Kings 8:27; Acts 17:24–25).

And those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth. “Must”: necessary. Because of who God is, worship must match his nature. Spiritual, not merely external. True, according to his revelation, not human invention.

Where Christians differ: how should we worship? Some traditions emphasise elaborate liturgy, ritual and visual symbols; others, free and spontaneous worship. Verdict: Reformed churches have drawn from this verse, among others, what is called the regulative principle: worship should be shaped by what God has revealed in his word, not by human invention, and offered from the heart by the Spirit. External forms matter less than the heart, but worship must be true to Scripture: the reading and preaching of the word, prayer, singing, the sacraments. Held charitably toward brothers who differ in practice.

In a sentence. God is spirit, and his worshippers must worship him in spirit and truth.

For worship. Check your worship this Sunday: is it from the heart, by the Spirit, according to God’s word?

verseByVerse.quote: "The woman said to him, 'I know that Messiah is coming (he who is called Christ). When he comes, he will tell us all things.' Jesus said to her, 'I who speak to you am he.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The woman said to him: I know that Messiah is coming (he who is called Christ). When he comes, he will tell us all things. Jesus said to her: I who speak to you am he.

I know that Messiah is coming. The Samaritans expected a coming prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15–18), called the Taheb (“the one who returns” or “restorer”).

When he comes, he will tell us all things. He will settle these questions. Perhaps she is postponing the matter. Or perhaps she is wondering.

I who speak to you am he. Literally “I am, the one speaking to you” (egō eimi). Jesus’ first open declaration that he is the Messiah, in John, is to a Samaritan woman with a broken past. Not to the Sanhedrin, not to Nicodemus. And “I am” echoes God’s name (Exodus 3:14), which Jesus will use of himself throughout this Gospel (6:20; 8:58). Jesus’ open claim is safer in Samaria, where it carried less political danger.

In a sentence. The woman said that the Messiah would come and explain everything, and Jesus told her: I who am speaking to you am he.

For worship. The Messiah revealed himself to an outcast. He reveals himself to you.
verseByVerse.note: The Samaritans expected a coming prophet like Moses. Jesus’ “I who speak to you am he” is literally “I am, the one speaking to you.”

verseByVerse.quote: Just then his disciples came back. They marveled that he was talking with a woman, but no one said, "What do you seek?" or, "Why are you talking with her?" So the woman left her water jar and went away into town.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Just then his disciples came back. They marvelled that he was talking with a woman, but no one said: what do you seek? or: why are you talking with her? So the woman left her water jar and went away into town.

They marveled that he was talking with a woman. A rabbi did not talk with women in public. Rabbinic sayings warned against it. Not even that she was a Samaritan; just a woman.

But no one said … Why are you talking with her? They had learned not to question him.

So the woman left her water jar. A small, vivid detail. She came for water and forgot it. She had found living water. She left in a hurry.

In a sentence. The disciples returned, astonished that Jesus was talking to a woman, though no one questioned him, and the woman left her water jar and went into town.

On a Tuesday. What will you leave behind when you meet Christ?

verseByVerse.quote: and said to the people, "Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did. Can this be the Christ?" They went out of the town and were coming to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And said to the people: come, see a man who told me all that I ever did. Can this be the Christ? They went out of the town and were coming to him.

And said to the people. The woman who had avoided people now runs to them.

Come, see. The words of Jesus and Philip (1:39, 46). She becomes an evangelist.

A man who told me all that I ever did. She does not hide her past. The very thing that made her ashamed becomes her testimony. Jesus knew everything, and still offered her life.

Can this be the Christ? A tentative question, expecting perhaps “no”, or genuinely wondering. She does not preach; she invites them to decide for themselves.

They went out of the town and were coming to him. Her testimony worked.

In a sentence. She told the townspeople to come and see a man who had told her everything she had done, asking if he could be the Christ, and they came out to him.

On a Tuesday. You don’t need a theology degree to witness. Tell people what Jesus has done for you, and invite them to come and see.

verseByVerse.quote: Meanwhile the disciples were urging him, saying, "Rabbi, eat." But he said to them, "I have food to eat that you do not know about."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Meanwhile the disciples were urging him, saying: Rabbi, eat. But he said to them: I have food to eat that you do not know about.

Rabbi, eat. They had brought food.

I have food to eat that you do not know about. As with the water (v. 10), Jesus speaks of a spiritual reality, and is misunderstood.

In a sentence. The disciples urged Jesus to eat, but he said he had food they did not know about.

On a Tuesday. There is a nourishment deeper than food. What feeds your soul?

parallels.desc: man shall not live by bread alone

verseByVerse.quote: So the disciples said to one another, "Has anyone brought him something to eat?" Jesus said to them, "My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the disciples said to one another: has anyone brought him something to eat? Jesus said to them: my food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.

Has anyone brought him something to eat? Literal again.

My food is to do the will of him who sent me. His deepest satisfaction and sustenance is doing the Father’s will (Deuteronomy 8:3; Matthew 4:4). Talking to this woman had refreshed him more than food. Obedience to God nourishes the soul.

And to accomplish his work. “Accomplish” (teleiōsō): complete, finish. The work the Father gave him to do (5:36; 17:4), finished on the cross: It is finished (tetelestai, 19:30).

In a sentence. When the disciples wondered if someone had brought him food, Jesus said his food was to do the will of the one who sent him and to finish his work.

For worship. Doing God’s will feeds the soul. Find your nourishment in obedience.

parallels.desc: having accomplished the work

verseByVerse.quote: "Do you not say, 'There are yet four months, then comes the harvest'? Look, I tell you, lift up your eyes, and see that the fields are white for harvest. Already the one who reaps is receiving wages and gathering fruit for eternal life, so that sower and reaper may rejoice together."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do you not say: there are yet four months, then comes the harvest? Look, I tell you, lift up your eyes, and see that the fields are white for harvest. Already the one who reaps is receiving wages and gathering fruit for eternal life, so that sower and reaper may rejoice together.

There are yet four months, then comes the harvest. Crops were sown in winter and harvested in spring; “four months” was the usual wait, perhaps a proverb.

Lift up your eyes, and see that the fields are white for harvest. Perhaps at that moment the Samaritans were streaming out of the town toward them across the fields, in their white robes (v. 30). The harvest of people is ready now, not in four months. Ripe grain turns pale, white-gold.

Already the one who reaps is receiving wages. The reward of gospel work.

And gathering fruit for eternal life. People saved for ever.

So that sower and reaper may rejoice together. In God’s harvest, sowing and reaping happen together. Joy shared.

In a sentence. Jesus told his disciples not to wait four months for harvest, but to look and see that the fields were already ripe, and the reaper was already gathering fruit for eternal life.

On a Tuesday. Lift up your eyes. Who around you is ready to hear about Christ?
verseByVerse.note: Crops were sown in winter and harvested in spring; “four months” was roughly the gap between sowing and harvest, and the saying may have been proverbial.

parallels.desc: the ploughman shall overtake the reaper

verseByVerse.quote: "For here the saying holds true, 'One sows and another reaps.' I sent you to reap that for which you did not labor. Others have labored, and you have entered into their labor."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For here the saying holds true: one sows and another reaps. I sent you to reap that for which you did not labour. Others have laboured, and you have entered into their labour.

One sows and another reaps. A proverb.

I sent you to reap that for which you did not labor. The disciples will reap a harvest prepared by others.

Others have labored. Who? The prophets, John the Baptist, and here, Jesus himself and the Samaritan woman. And in Acts, the disciples would reap in Samaria what Jesus sowed here (Acts 8:4–25).

And you have entered into their labor. Every gospel worker builds on others’ work. No room for pride (1 Corinthians 3:6–9).

In a sentence. Jesus said that the saying is true, one sows and another reaps, and he had sent them to reap where others had done the work.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for those who sowed the gospel in your life. And sow faithfully, even if others reap.

parallels.desc: cities you did not build
I planted, Apollos watered

verseByVerse.quote: Many Samaritans from that town believed in him because of the woman's testimony, "He told me all that I ever did." So when the Samaritans came to him, they asked him to stay with them, and he stayed there two days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many Samaritans from that town believed in him because of the woman’s testimony: he told me all that I ever did. So when the Samaritans came to him, they asked him to stay with them, and he stayed there two days.

Many Samaritans from that town believed in him because of the woman’s testimony. The power of a simple personal testimony. A woman with a broken past became the means of a town’s salvation.

They asked him to stay with them. “Stay” (meinai): abide. Samaritans asking a Jew to stay. Barriers broken.

And he stayed there two days. A Jewish rabbi staying two days among Samaritans.

In a sentence. Many Samaritans believed because of the woman’s testimony, and asked Jesus to stay, and he stayed two days.

On a Tuesday. Your testimony, however humble, can lead others to Christ.

parallels.desc: Samaria receives the word

verseByVerse.quote: And many more believed because of his word. They said to the woman, "It is no longer because of what you said that we believe, for we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this is indeed the Savior of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And many more believed because of his word. They said to the woman: it is no longer because of what you said that we believe, for we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this is indeed the Saviour of the world.

And many more believed because of his word. Testimony brings people to Jesus; his word brings them to faith.

It is no longer because of what you said that we believe. Not an insult, but a natural development. Second-hand faith becomes first-hand faith.

For we have heard for ourselves. A personal encounter with Christ through his word.

And we know that this is indeed the Savior of the world. A remarkable confession from Samaritans. “Savior of the world”: not just the Jewish Messiah, but the Saviour of all peoples, including Samaritans. The title was used of Roman emperors. The only other place in the New Testament it appears is 1 John 4:14. Outsiders understood what insiders missed.

In a sentence. Many more believed through Jesus’ own word and told the woman that they now believed not because of her testimony but because they had heard him and knew he was the Saviour of the world.

For worship. Jesus is the Saviour of the world, of every nation. Make sure your faith is your own, from hearing him yourself.

parallels.desc: the Father has sent his Son to be the Savior of the world

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 43–54 — The Official's Son: The Second Sign
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After two days Jesus goes on to Galilee, though he has said a prophet is not honoured in his own country. The Galileans receive him, having seen what he did at the festival in Jerusalem. He returns to Cana, where he turned water into wine. A royal official from Capernaum, whose son is dying, hears that Jesus is back and comes to beg him to come and heal the boy. Jesus says that unless people see miraculous signs they will not believe. The official pleads with him to come before his child dies. Jesus tells him to go home: his son will live. The man takes Jesus at his word and sets off. On the way his servants meet him with news that the boy is alive and well. Asking when he improved, he learns the fever left at one in the afternoon the day before, the very hour Jesus spoke. He and his whole household believe. This is the second sign Jesus performs after coming from Judea to Galilee.
verseByVerse.theology:
The second sign illustrates the highest form of faith: believing the word of Jesus without the supporting evidence of a visible miracle. Jesus speaks ('your son will live'), the official believes, and he goes. The confirmation comes later — the servants meet him with the news, and when he checks the timing, it matches exactly. This is the progression of faith in John's Gospel: sign-faith (the disciples at Cana), word-faith (the official), and ultimately cross-and-resurrection-faith (Thomas). Each stage is genuine faith; each stage is a step deeper into trust in the person of Jesus.

The two Cana signs are numbered (2:11; 4:54) and the counting then stops for the rest of the book, which means the numbering exists only to tie these two together. They frame everything between: a member of the ruling council who could not follow the plainest thing, and a Samaritan woman who understood enough to fetch a town.

Watch what changes between them. At the wedding Jesus was present, the water was in front of him, and he instructed servants who were standing there. Here he is twenty miles away and does nothing but speak. The first sign needed his hands on the situation; the second needed only his voice, and the voice worked across a day's journey as though the journey were not there. The escalation is the direction of the whole book — and it prepares the position every reader after the ascension occupies: no touch, no presence, no visible confirmation, only a word and a distance and the walking. John says at the close that he wrote it down so that people who were never in the room might believe (20:30-31).

Note also that the man believes twice. In verse 50 he believed the word — trust in a promise about his son. In verse 53 he himself believed, with no object named, which in this Gospel is the word for what a person does about Christ rather than about a request. The household followed him; that is not a formula and must never be used to reproach faithful people whose households have not, but it is worth noting what they had to go on — a man who came home, a boy who was well, and a father who could tell them the hour.
verseByVerse.examples:
The official's faith is remarkable because he believes before he sees — he accepts the word of Jesus as sufficient ground for confidence when everything he can see argues for despair. This is the pattern of all mature faith: not the absence of evidence but trust in the word of the one who cannot lie, prior to the confirming experience.

The finest detail in the episode is one word in the servants' report: the fever left him yesterday at the seventh hour. Jesus spoke at about one in the afternoon, and Capernaum is some twenty miles away and downhill — a distance a determined man could nearly cover by nightfall. The father did not cover it. He stopped for the night and came down the next day. Nobody whose only son is dying stops for the night if any part of him is still calculating. The most convincing evidence that this man took Christ at his word is that he did not hurry home.

Verse 50 is where the miracle actually sits, and it happens before the other one is known about. He had walked all day for one thing — to bring Jesus back down to the house — and he is sent home without him. Everything he came for is refused. What he has instead is five words about a child who was at the point of death when he left. And he went. Every hour of that walk the alternative explanation was available: that he had been fobbed off, that he should have insisted, that a real healer would have come.

The pastoral note belongs to the father's prayer, which was a bad one by any measure — no theology, no composure, one sentence repeated under pressure — and was answered immediately and generously. Nothing in the account suggests Jesus was waiting for a better-formed request. And his original assumption, that God must be brought to the place, should be treated gently rather than corrected: it is what people ask when they love somebody and are frightened. The answer he received was not smaller than the one he asked for. It was the same answer, delivered without the twenty miles.

verseByVerse.quote: After the two days he departed for Galilee. (For Jesus himself had testified that a prophet has no honor in his own hometown.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the two days he departed for Galilee. (For Jesus himself had testified that a prophet has no honour in his own home town.)

For Jesus himself had testified that a prophet has no honor in his own hometown. A puzzle: why go to Galilee if a prophet has no honour there? Perhaps “his own home town” here means Judea, the land of his birth, or Jerusalem, where he was rejected; so he left it for Galilee. Or it explains why the Galilean welcome (v. 45) was shallow: they welcomed him for his signs, not truly honouring him.

In a sentence. After two days Jesus left for Galilee, though he had said a prophet has no honour in his own home town.

On a Tuesday. Those closest to Jesus are not always those who honour him most.

verseByVerse.quote: So when he came to Galilee, the Galileans welcomed him, having seen all that he had done in Jerusalem at the feast. For they too had gone to the feast.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So when he came to Galilee, the Galileans welcomed him, having seen all that he had done in Jerusalem at the feast. For they too had gone to the feast.

The Galileans welcomed him. Because of his signs in Jerusalem (2:23), not because of who he was. A contrast with the Samaritans, who believed because of his word (v. 41).

In a sentence. The Galileans welcomed him, because they had seen what he did in Jerusalem at the feast.

On a Tuesday. Is your welcome for Jesus based on what he can do for you, or on who he is?

verseByVerse.quote: So he came again to Cana in Galilee, where he had made the water wine. And at Capernaum there was an official whose son was ill. When this man heard that Jesus had come from Judea to Galilee, he went to him and asked him to come down and heal his son, for he was at the point of death.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So he came again to Cana in Galilee, where he had made the water wine. And at Capernaum there was an official whose son was ill. When this man heard that Jesus had come from Judea to Galilee, he went to him and asked him to come down and heal his son, for he was at the point of death.

Cana in Galilee, where he had made the water wine. The site of the first sign. This will be the second (v. 54).

An official. A royal official (basilikos), probably in the service of Herod Antipas. Capernaum was about 20 miles (30 km) from Cana, downhill.

Whose son was ill … at the point of death. A desperate father. Wealth and position could not save his son.

He went to him and asked him to come down and heal his son. A day’s journey. He believes Jesus can heal, but thinks Jesus must be present.

In a sentence. When Jesus returned to Cana, a royal official from Capernaum, whose son was dying, came and begged him to come down and heal him.

On a Tuesday. Bring your desperate needs to Jesus, as this father did.
verseByVerse.note: The official was probably in the service of Herod Antipas. Capernaum lay down by the lake, about 20 miles from Cana.

parallels.desc: a similar healing of a centurion’s servant

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus said to him, "Unless you see signs and wonders you will not believe."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Jesus said to him: unless you see signs and wonders you will not believe.

Unless you see signs and wonders you will not believe. The “you” here is plural: Jesus speaks to the Galileans in general (v. 45). Faith that depends on miracles is weak faith. They want signs; the Samaritans believed his word. Jesus tests the official’s faith: will he believe without seeing?

In a sentence. Jesus said that unless they saw signs and wonders they would not believe.

On a Tuesday. Do you need to see miracles to believe? Trust Jesus’ word.
verseByVerse.note: The “you” here is plural — Jesus speaks to the Galileans in general.

verseByVerse.quote: The official said to him, "Sir, come down before my child dies." Jesus said to him, "Go; your son will live." The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him and went on his way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The official said to him: sir, come down before my child dies. Jesus said to him: go; your son will live. The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him and went on his way.

Sir, come down before my child dies. He persists. He does not argue; he begs. “Child” (paidion): little child, a tender word.

Go; your son will live. No journey, no touch. Just a word, from twenty miles away.

The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him. Key words. Faith in Jesus’ word, without a sign. He asked Jesus to come; Jesus gave him only a word; he took the word and went. This is the faith that Jesus looks for: believing his word.

And went on his way. He did not wait for proof.

In a sentence. The official begged Jesus to come before his child died, and Jesus told him to go, for his son would live, and the man believed Jesus’ word and left.

For worship. Take Jesus at his word, and go on your way trusting him.

parallels.desc: he sent out his word and healed them

verseByVerse.quote: As he was going down, his servants met him and told him that his son was recovering.
verseByVerse.commentary:
As he was going down, his servants met him and told him that his son was recovering.

As he was going down. To Capernaum, the next day (v. 52).

His servants met him and told him that his son was recovering. Literally “was living”: the very word Jesus had used. His word had come true.

In a sentence. On his way home, his servants met him with news that his son was living.

On a Tuesday. Jesus’ word does what it says, even at a distance.

verseByVerse.quote: So he asked them the hour when he began to get better, and they said to him, "Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him." The father knew that was the hour when Jesus had said to him, "Your son will live." And he himself believed, and all his household.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So he asked them the hour when he began to get better, and they said to him: yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him. The father knew that was the hour when Jesus had said to him: your son will live. And he himself believed, and all his household.

He asked them the hour. He wanted to confirm.

Yesterday at the seventh hour. The ESV notes that the seventh hour was about 1 p.m.

The father knew that was the hour. The exact moment Jesus spoke. Not coincidence.

And he himself believed. His faith deepened: from faith in a healer, to faith in his word, to full faith in Jesus.

And all his household. His whole family and servants believed (Acts 16:15, 34). The first household conversion in John.

In a sentence. Asking when his son improved, the official learned it was the very hour Jesus had spoken, and he and his whole household believed.

For worship. Pray for your whole household to believe.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the seventh hour was about 1 p.m.

parallels.desc: he believed, with his entire household

verseByVerse.quote: This was now the second sign that Jesus did when he had come from Judea to Galilee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This was now the second sign that Jesus did when he had come from Judea to Galilee.

The second sign. Both signs at Cana. The first revealed his glory at a wedding; the second, his power over sickness and death at a distance. Both show that his word has creative power. Both lead to faith (2:11; 4:53).

In a sentence. This was the second sign Jesus did after coming from Judea to Galilee.

For worship. Each of Jesus’ signs reveals who he is. Let this one deepen your faith in his word.

parallels.desc: the first sign

4.title: The Woman at the Well
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when Jesus learned that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John<sup>2</sup>(although Jesus himself did not baptize, but only his disciples),<sup>3</sup>he left Judea and departed again for Galilee.<sup>4</sup>And he had to pass through Samaria.<sup>5</sup>So he came to a town of Samaria called Sychar, near the field that Jacob had given to his son Joseph.<sup>6</sup>Jacob’s well was there; so Jesus, wearied as he was from his journey, was sitting beside the well. It was about the sixth hour.<sup>7</sup>A woman from Samaria came to draw water. Jesus said to her, “Give me a drink.”<sup>8</sup>(For his disciples had gone away into the city to buy food.)<sup>9</sup>The Samaritan woman said to him, “How is it that you, a Jew, ask for a drink from me, a woman of Samaria?” (For Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.)<sup>10</sup>Jesus answered her, “If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that is saying to you, ’Give me a drink,’ you would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.”<sup>11</sup>The woman said to him, “Sir, you have nothing to draw water with, and the well is deep. Where do you get that living water?<sup>12</sup>Are you greater than our father Jacob? He gave us the well and drank from it himself, as did his sons and his livestock.”<sup>13</sup>Jesus said to her, “Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again,<sup>14</sup>but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again. The water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life.”<sup>15</sup>The woman said to him, “Sir, give me this water, so that I will not be thirsty or have to come here to draw water.”<sup>16</sup>Jesus said to her, “Go, call your husband, and come here.”<sup>17</sup>The woman answered him, “I have no husband.” Jesus said to her, “You are right in saying, ’I have no husband’;<sup>18</sup>for you have had five husbands, and the one you now have is not your husband. What you have said is true.”<sup>19</sup>The woman said to him, “Sir, I perceive that you are a prophet.<sup>20</sup>Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, but you say that in Jerusalem is the place where people ought to worship.”<sup>21</sup>Jesus said to her, “Woman, believe me, the hour is coming when neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem will you worship the Father.<sup>22</sup>You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, for salvation is from the Jews.<sup>23</sup>But the hour is coming, and is now here, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father is seeking such people to worship him.<sup>24</sup>God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.”<sup>25</sup>The woman said to him, “I know that Messiah is coming (he who is called Christ). When he comes, he will tell us all things.”<sup>26</sup>Jesus said to her, “I who speak to you am he.”<sup>27</sup>Just then his disciples came back. They marveled that he was talking with a woman, but no one said, “What do you seek?” or, “Why are you talking with her?”<sup>28</sup>So the woman left her water jar and went away into town and said to the people,<sup>29</sup>“Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did. Can this be the Christ?”<sup>30</sup>They went out of the town and were coming to him.<sup>31</sup>Meanwhile the disciples were urging him, saying, “Rabbi, eat.”<sup>32</sup>But he said to them, “I have food to eat that you do not know about.”<sup>33</sup>So the disciples said to one another, “Has anyone brought him something to eat?”<sup>34</sup>Jesus said to them, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work.<sup>35</sup>Do you not say, ’There are yet four months, then comes the harvest’? Look, I tell you, lift up your eyes, and see that the fields are white for harvest.<sup>36</sup>Already the one who reaps is receiving wages and gathering fruit for eternal life, so that sower and reaper may rejoice together.<sup>37</sup>For here the saying holds true, ’One sows and another reaps.’<sup>38</sup>I sent you to reap that for which you did not labor. Others have labored, and you have entered into their labor.”<sup>39</sup>Many Samaritans from that town believed in him because of the woman’s testimony, “He told me all that I ever did.”<sup>40</sup>So when the Samaritans came to him, they asked him to stay with them, and he stayed there two days.<sup>41</sup>And many more believed because of his word.<sup>42</sup>They said to the woman, “It is no longer because of what you said that we believe, for we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this is indeed the Savior of the world.”<sup>43</sup>After the two days he departed for Galilee.<sup>44</sup>(For Jesus himself had testified that a prophet has no honor in his own hometown.)<sup>45</sup>So when he came to Galilee, the Galileans welcomed him, having seen all that he had done in Jerusalem at the feast. For they too had gone to the feast.<sup>46</sup>So he came again to Cana in Galilee, where he had made the water wine. And at Capernaum there was an official whose son was ill.<sup>47</sup>When this man heard that Jesus had come from Judea to Galilee, he went to him and asked him to come down and heal his son, for he was at the point of death.<sup>48</sup>So Jesus said to him, “Unless you see signs and wonders you will not believe.”<sup>49</sup>The official said to him, “Sir, come down before my child dies.”<sup>50</sup>Jesus said to him, “Go; your son will live.” The man believed the word that Jesus spoke to him and went on his way.<sup>51</sup>As he was going down, his servants met him and told him that his son was recovering.<sup>52</sup>So he asked them the hour when he began to get better, and they said to him, “Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him.”<sup>53</sup>The father knew that was the hour when Jesus had said to him, “Your son will live.” And he himself believed, and all his household.<sup>54</sup>This was now the second sign that Jesus did when he had come from Judea to Galilee.
4.overview:
Chapter 3 showed Jesus with a respected Jewish teacher at night; chapter 4 shows him with an unnamed Samaritan woman at noon. Travelling north through Samaria, tired and thirsty, he sits by Jacob’s well and asks her for a drink, crossing three barriers at once: race, sex and religion. He offers her “living water”, a spring of eternal life welling up inside, and she misunderstands, as Nicodemus did. Then he gently exposes her life: five husbands, and the present man not her husband. She turns to the old dispute between Samaritans and Jews about where to worship; Jesus answers that the hour has come when the place no longer matters, for the Father seeks worshippers in spirit and truth. When she speaks of the coming Messiah, he tells her plainly, “I who speak to you am he.”

She leaves her water jar and brings the town to “come, see a man who told me all that I ever did.” Meanwhile Jesus tells his puzzled disciples that his food is to do his Father’s will, and that the fields are already white for harvest. Many Samaritans believe, first through her testimony and then through his own word, and confess him as “the Savior of the world.” Back in Cana, a royal official begs Jesus to come and heal his dying son; Jesus simply says, “Go; your son will live,” and the man believes and goes. His servants meet him with the news that the fever left at the very hour Jesus spoke. This is the second sign: the word of Jesus gives life at a distance. Together the stories show the gospel crossing every boundary, and faith growing from hearing to trusting his word.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — The Healing at the Pool of Bethesda
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At a festival in Jerusalem, Jesus visits the pool of Bethesda by the Sheep Gate, where crowds of the blind, lame and paralysed lie under its colonnades. One man has been disabled for thirty-eight years. Jesus asks whether he wants to be healed. The man complains that no one helps him into the water when it stirs, and others always get there first. Jesus commands him to stand, lift his mat and walk, and at once he does. Because it is the Sabbath, the authorities rebuke him for carrying the mat; he blames the man who healed him, whose name he does not know, as Jesus has disappeared in the crowd. Later Jesus meets him in the temple and warns him to leave his sin behind, lest something worse befall him. The man reports to the authorities that it was Jesus, and they start to harass Jesus for Sabbath work. Jesus replies that his Father is still at work and so is he. Now they are more intent on killing him, for he not only breaks the Sabbath but claims God as his own Father, making himself God’s equal.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sabbath healing reveals Jesus's divine authority by the very nature of the opposition it generates. When Jesus says 'My Father is working until now, and I am working,' the Jewish leaders understand immediately what he is claiming: equality with God, the same authority over the Sabbath that God the Father has. This is not a misunderstanding that Jesus corrects; it is a correct understanding that Jesus confirms. The discourse that follows is the most comprehensive statement of the Son's relationship to the Father in the Gospels: the Son does nothing on his own, only what he sees the Father doing; the Father has given all judgment to the Son; the Son gives life to whom he will.

The Sabbath argument lands inside a debate the rabbis were already having. They knew God does not stop working on the seventh day — children are born and people die on it, and the giving of life and the judging of the dead were the standard examples of divine work that never ceases. The accepted solution was that God is exempt, since the whole universe is his house and he carries nothing out of it. Jesus takes that exemption for himself (My Father is working until now, and I am working) and then, over the next few verses, claims precisely the two works it was famous for: giving life (v. 21) and executing judgment (v. 22).

Verse 18 must not be softened. John does not write that they thought he was making himself equal with God, or that they misunderstood; he reports it as what was happening. The narrator agrees with their reading of the words and disagrees only with what they did about it. This closes off the idea that Jesus was a teacher of ethics whom his followers later inflated: nobody organises an execution over the golden rule. The possessive is the point — his own Father, private and particular, in a way that made his working and God's working one working.

Neither charge is right as they put it. He was not breaking the Sabbath; he was breaking their reading of it, and never once broke the law of God. And he was not making himself equal with God either — for the opposite reason. He made himself nothing. He was stating what was already the case, which is a larger offence than the one they charged.
verseByVerse.examples:
The thirty-eight-year illness is not incidental but emblematic: the man has exhausted every human resource and lies waiting for something that never comes by human effort. Jesus's intervention is sovereign and uninvited — the man does not ask for healing, does not know who Jesus is, and does not believe in him before the miracle. The healing comes entirely from Christ's initiative, which is the pattern of all saving grace. 'Do you want to be healed?' is the most searching question Jesus could ask, because chronic suffering can become a settled identity that is comfortable in its own way.

Do you want to be healed? sounds close to an insult to a man who has lain by a healing pool for thirty-eight years, and Jesus does not ask it of everyone he heals, which means it is meant for this history. Something happens to a want that has been disappointed for that long: it goes quiet, gets managed, and turns into a routine, until a life is built around the waiting and the waiting is the life. That is not weakness of character; most people can manage it in months. The question is the most respectful thing in the passage — he does not heal the man over his head, but asks somebody who has not been asked anything in decades what he actually wants.

This is the verse for the reader who long ago stopped asking for something: the marriage that has been like this for years, the child who does not call, the prayer abandoned around its fifth anniversary. The test is whether one can still say plainly what would be different if God moved — or whether the answer comes out as an explanation of why it will not happen, which is exactly what the man says next.

Two further mercies are worth naming. The healing came unrequested to a man who had given up asking, without faith, without confession, without his even knowing the name of the one who did it — grace arriving on its own initiative. And the mat was not left at the pool: a healed man walking away is a private mercy nobody need ever know about, but a healed man carrying his bed through the city is a public claim, the evidence held up in both arms. It is possible to be genuinely healed and entirely discreet about it. He is told to pick it up.

verseByVerse.quote: After this there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. Now there is in Jerusalem by the Sheep Gate a pool, in Aramaic called Bethesda, which has five roofed colonnades.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. Now there is in Jerusalem by the Sheep Gate a pool, in Aramaic called Bethesda, which has five roofed colonnades.

Setting. Chapter 5 marks a turning point. The third sign, a healing on the Sabbath, leads to open hostility and the first plot to kill Jesus (v. 18), and to his great discourse on his relationship with the Father.

A feast of the Jews. Unnamed; perhaps Pentecost, Tabernacles or Purim.

By the Sheep Gate. The Sheep Gate was in the north wall, near the temple, where sheep for sacrifice were brought in (Nehemiah 3:1).

A pool, in Aramaic called Bethesda. The ESV notes other spellings in the manuscripts (Bethzatha, Bethsaida). “Bethesda” may mean “house of mercy”. Archaeologists have found the remains of a double pool north of the temple, with porticoes on all four sides and a fifth across the middle, exactly as John describes. A striking confirmation of John’s accuracy.

Which has five roofed colonnades. “Has”: present tense, which may suggest John wrote before the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, or simply describes it vividly.

In a sentence. At a Jewish feast Jesus went to Jerusalem, where there was a pool called Bethesda near the Sheep Gate, surrounded by five covered colonnades.

On a Tuesday. John’s details have been confirmed by archaeology. The Gospel is history you can trust.
verseByVerse.note: The Sheep Gate was in the north wall, near the temple. The ESV notes that some manuscripts read Bethsaida. Archaeologists have uncovered twin pools there with colonnades on four sides and one across the middle.

parallels.desc: the Sheep Gate

verseByVerse.quote: In these lay a multitude of invalids — blind, lame, and paralyzed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In these lay a multitude of invalids: blind, lame, and paralysed.

A multitude of invalids. The pool was a gathering place for the sick and disabled, hoping for healing. A picture of human misery and helplessness.

Blind, lame, and paralyzed. Literally “withered”.

Textual note. The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 4, about an angel who stirred the water, so that the first person to step in was healed. It is missing from the earliest and best manuscripts and was probably added to explain verse 7, reflecting popular belief. Some think the pool was fed by an intermittent spring that bubbled up, which people believed had healing power.

In a sentence. Under the colonnades lay crowds of blind, lame and paralysed people.

On a Tuesday. The world is full of people waiting for help that never comes. Jesus comes to them.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 4, about an angel stirring the water and the first one in being healed — a popular belief explaining why the sick waited there.

verseByVerse.quote: One man was there who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years. When Jesus saw him lying there and knew that he had already been there a long time, he said to him, "Do you want to be healed?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
One man was there who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years. When Jesus saw him lying there and knew that he had already been there a long time, he said to him: do you want to be healed?

An invalid for thirty-eight years. Longer than many people lived then. Thirty-eight years may echo Israel’s thirty-eight years of wandering in the wilderness after their unbelief at Kadesh (Deuteronomy 2:14).

When Jesus saw him. Out of the multitude, Jesus chose this one. He took the initiative; the man did not ask. Grace is sovereign.

And knew that he had already been there a long time. Supernatural knowledge (2:25; 4:18).

Do you want to be healed? A strange question to a sick man. But after thirty-eight years, he may have given up hope, or grown used to his condition and the life of a beggar. Healing would mean new responsibilities. Jesus wakes him to desire. Do you really want to be made whole?

In a sentence. Jesus saw a man who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years, knew how long he had been there, and asked if he wanted to be healed.

On a Tuesday. Do you really want Jesus to make you whole, with everything that would change?
verseByVerse.note: Thirty-eight years may echo Israel’s thirty-eight years of wandering before entering the land (Deut 2:14), though John does not draw the link.

parallels.desc: thirty-eight years until that generation perished

verseByVerse.quote: The sick man answered him, "Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up, and while I am going another steps down before me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sick man answered him: sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up, and while I am going another steps down before me.

Sir, I have no one. The loneliest words. No friend, no family to help him. The paralytic in Mark had four friends (Mark 2:3); this man had none.

To put me into the pool when the water is stirred up. He believed the superstition, and it had failed him for years.

While I am going another steps down before me. A cruel competition, in which the weakest always lost.

He does not answer the question. He does not say yes. He explains why he cannot be healed. He does not know who is speaking to him (v. 13), and has no faith in Jesus. His hope is in the water.

In a sentence. The man answered that he had no one to help him into the pool when the water stirred, and someone always got there first.

On a Tuesday. If you feel you have no one, Jesus has come to you.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to him, "Get up, take up your bed, and walk." And at once the man was healed, and he took up his bed and walked. Now that day was the Sabbath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said to him: get up, take up your bed, and walk. And at once the man was healed, and he took up his bed and walked. Now that day was the Sabbath.

Get up, take up your bed, and walk. Three commands, all impossible. His word gives the power to obey. No pool, no stirring, no help needed. Jesus is greater than every superstition and every human remedy.

And at once the man was healed. After thirty-eight years, instantly.

And he took up his bed and walked. The bed was a light mat. Obedience.

Now that day was the Sabbath. The sentence that starts the conflict. Carrying a load on the Sabbath was forbidden by the rabbis’ rules (Jeremiah 17:21–22; Nehemiah 13:15–19). Jesus knew it was the Sabbath. He chose this day.

No faith mentioned. Unlike most healings, nothing is said of the man’s faith. A picture of sovereign grace: Jesus heals one who did not even know who he was.

In a sentence. Jesus told him to get up, pick up his mat and walk, and the man was healed at once and walked, and it was the Sabbath.

For worship. Jesus’ word gives power to do what it commands. Obey his word today.
verseByVerse.note: The bed was a light mat. Carrying a load on the Sabbath was forbidden by tradition, drawing on the prophets.

parallels.desc: a similar command to a paralytic
bear no burden on the Sabbath

verseByVerse.quote: So the Jews said to the man who had been healed, "It is the Sabbath, and it is not lawful for you to take up your bed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the Jews said to the man who had been healed: it is the Sabbath, and it is not lawful for you to take up your bed.

So the Jews said. In John, “the Jews” often means the Jewish religious authorities in Jerusalem.

It is the Sabbath, and it is not lawful for you to take up your bed. No joy that a man paralysed for thirty-eight years can walk. Only concern that a rule has been broken. The Mishnah lists carrying an object from one domain to another among the 39 kinds of forbidden work. The rule mattered more than the man.

In a sentence. The Jewish leaders told the healed man that it was unlawful for him to carry his mat on the Sabbath.

On a Tuesday. Don’t let rules blind you to the grace of God at work.
verseByVerse.note: In John, “the Jews” often means the Jewish religious authorities.

verseByVerse.quote: But he answered them, "The man who healed me, that man said to me, 'Take up your bed, and walk.'" They asked him, "Who is the man who said to you, 'Take up your bed and walk'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he answered them: the man who healed me, that man said to me, take up your bed, and walk. They asked him: who is the man who said to you, take up your bed and walk?

The man who healed me, that man said to me. He shifts the blame. If the healer had authority to heal, surely he had authority to tell him to carry his mat.

Who is the man who said to you. Not “who healed you?”, but “who told you to break the rule?” They are not interested in the miracle, only the offence.

In a sentence. He answered that the man who healed him told him to carry his mat, and they asked who it was.

On a Tuesday. Notice what people focus on when they hear of God’s work: the grace, or the rule-breaking?

verseByVerse.quote: Now the man who had been healed did not know who it was, for Jesus had withdrawn, as there was a crowd in the place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the man who had been healed did not know who it was, for Jesus had withdrawn, as there was a crowd in the place.

Did not know who it was. Healed without knowing his healer. Grace came before knowledge.

For Jesus had withdrawn, as there was a crowd in the place. He slipped away to avoid publicity.

In a sentence. The man did not know who had healed him, because Jesus had slipped away into the crowd.

On a Tuesday. God often blesses us before we know him well. Seek to know the one who has blessed you.

verseByVerse.quote: "Afterward Jesus found him in the temple and said to him, 'See, you are well! Sin no more, that nothing worse may happen to you.' The man went away and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had healed him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Afterwards Jesus found him in the temple and said to him: see, you are well! Sin no more, that nothing worse may happen to you. The man went away and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had healed him.

Afterward Jesus found him in the temple. Jesus sought him again. Perhaps he had gone to give thanks, now able to enter the temple.

See, you are well! You have been made whole.

Sin no more, that nothing worse may happen to you. Jesus does not say all illness is punishment for sin (9:3), but warns this man that sin has worse consequences than paralysis: eternal judgement. Perhaps his illness was connected to some sin. Physical healing is not enough; he needs to turn from sin. A body healed but a soul unrepentant would face something worse.

The man went away and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had healed him. Why? Perhaps naively, perhaps to protect himself, perhaps as testimony. Compare the man born blind, who boldly defended Jesus (9:30–33). This man seems to have reported him.

In a sentence. Jesus found him later in the temple, told him that he had been made well and should stop sinning or something worse would happen, and the man went and told the leaders it was Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Physical blessing is not salvation. Turn from sin, and trust Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus does not say all illness is punishment for sin, but warns that sin leads to worse than illness.

parallels.desc: go, and from now on sin no more

verseByVerse.quote: And this was why the Jews were persecuting Jesus, because he was doing these things on the Sabbath. But Jesus answered them, "My Father is working until now, and I am working."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This was why the Jews were persecuting Jesus, because he was doing these things on the Sabbath. But Jesus answered them: my Father is working until now, and I am working.

The Jews were persecuting Jesus. The tense means they kept on persecuting.

Because he was doing these things on the Sabbath. Repeatedly.

My Father is working until now, and I am working. A staggering claim. God rested on the seventh day from creation (Genesis 2:2–3). But Jewish teachers recognised that God keeps working on the Sabbath: giving life, sending rain, sustaining the universe, and judging. Otherwise the world would collapse. Jesus says: as my Father works on the Sabbath, so do I. He claims the same right as God to work on the Sabbath, because he does God’s work. And “my Father”: not “our Father”. A unique relationship.

In a sentence. The leaders persecuted Jesus for doing these things on the Sabbath, and he answered that his Father was still working, and so was he.

For worship. God is always at work, even on the day of rest. And Jesus does what the Father does.
verseByVerse.note: Jewish teachers recognised that God keeps working on the Sabbath, sustaining the world; Jesus claims the same right.

parallels.desc: lord even of the Sabbath

verseByVerse.quote: This was why the Jews were seeking all the more to kill him, because not only was he breaking the Sabbath, but he was even calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This was why the Jews were seeking all the more to kill him, because not only was he breaking the Sabbath, but he was even calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God.

Seeking all the more to kill him. The first time John mentions the plot to kill Jesus (7:1, 19, 25; 8:37, 40; 11:53).

But he was even calling God his own Father. “His own” (idion): uniquely, personally, in a way no one else could.

Making himself equal with God. They understood him perfectly. Jesus was claiming equality with God. Either he was a blasphemer, or he is God. He does not deny it; the discourse that follows explains it. Those who say Jesus never claimed to be God have not read John 5.

In a sentence. The leaders were even more determined to kill him, because he was not only breaking the Sabbath but calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God.

For worship. Jesus claimed equality with God, and died for it. Worship him as God.

parallels.desc: you, being a man, make yourself God

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–47 — The Son's Authority: Witness and Judgment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus explains that the Son acts in perfect union with the Father, doing whatever he sees the Father do, because the Father loves him and shows him all things. Like the Father, the Son gives life to whom he wills, and the Father has entrusted all judgment to him, so that the Son may be honoured as the Father is. Whoever hears Jesus and trusts the Father has eternal life already and has passed beyond condemnation. Even now the spiritually dead hear his voice and live, and one day everyone in the tombs will hear it and rise, to life or to judgment. Jesus does not testify alone: John the Baptist bore witness, Jesus’ works bear witness, the Father bears witness, and so do the Scriptures, which his hearers study while refusing to come to him for life. They seek honour from each other rather than from God. Moses, their hope, will accuse them, for he wrote about Jesus; if they do not believe Moses, they will not believe Jesus.
verseByVerse.theology:
The discourse on the Son's authority establishes that Jesus is not merely a great teacher or prophet but the one to whom the Father has delegated the twin divine prerogatives of life-giving and judgment. These are not shared with any creature; they belong to God alone. Yet the Father has given them to the Son precisely so that all will honor the Son as they honor the Father. The four witnesses — John, works, Father, Scripture — are not offered as proofs that compel belief but as witnesses whose rejection reveals the condition of the rejecting heart: no love of God, no desire for the glory that comes from God.

Life in himself (v. 26) is the highest thing said about God in the chapter. Everything that lives has life on loan — a tree from soil and light, a man from food and breath — and every such supply can be cut, which is why everything that lives also dies. To have life in himself is to hold it as a property rather than a supply, with nothing behind it that could fail; theologians call it aseity, and it belongs to God alone. That the Father granted the Son to have it is not an event in time and does not make it derived in the ordinary sense: it states the eternal relation between Father and Son. What the Father is, the Son is.

Verse 23 fixes the measure of honour with two words — just as — and forecloses the most popular way of handling Jesus. There is no arrangement in which a person keeps God and declines Christ; it is not offered. And the direction is the reverse of what is usually assumed: the Father has given life and judgment to the Son precisely so that all may honour the Son. Withholding that honour is not modesty on God's behalf but a failure to give the Father what he has said he wants.

Verse 29 sounds like salvation by works and cannot be, since verse 24 gives life to whoever hears my word and believes. The good and the evil are evidence rather than currency — the visible form of a life that had already crossed from death to life, or had not. And the apparent contradiction between 5:31 (if I alone bear witness about myself, my testimony is not true) and 8:14 (even if I do bear witness about myself, my testimony is true) resolves by what each answers: the first concerns legal standing, the second factual accuracy. He does not need corroboration in order to be right; he offers it because they need it in order to be persuaded.
verseByVerse.examples:
Jesus's claim to give life to whom he will (v. 21) and to execute judgment (v. 22) is either the most arrogant statement in human history or the most important truth in human history — there is no middle ground. The discourse forces a decision: either this man is deluded and dangerous, or he is who he says he is. The sequence of judgments in the discourse — present hearing (v. 24), coming resurrection (vv. 28-29) — establishes that the final judgment is already operative in every person's response to Christ.

Verse 35 is the saddest in the chapter and the tense is what makes it unbearable. He was a burning and shining lamp — the ordinary household oil lamp, the thing carried into a room after dark, and this Gospel has been careful that the Baptist was not the light (1:8). And they were willing to rejoice in it for a while. The whole country went out to the Jordan; it was the religious event of the decade; and it lasted about as long as such things last. By the time Jesus speaks, John's ministry is over. The mechanism has not changed — there is a way of consuming preaching as an experience, genuinely moved and warmly discussing it afterwards, and ending the season exactly where one started. The enjoyment is not fraudulent, which is what makes it dangerous: it feels like a response and it is a reaction.

Verse 39's search was no casual reading — these men counted the letters and knew which word stood at the centre of the Torah. They got a preposition wrong: they thought the life was located in the text, obtainable by handling it. Jesus does not deny that Scripture gives life; he denies the address. The distance between the scroll and the person was about four feet, and they would not cross it. It is entirely possible to conduct a serious study of Scripture as a closed system — the tracing of themes, the resolving of difficulties, the satisfaction of a passage coming clear — and for the whole exercise to terminate in itself. The test takes ten seconds: after the last passage studied, did it end in knowing something, or in wanting him?

Verse 44 is the only place in the Gospels where Jesus calls believing impossible for a stated reason, and the reason is an economy. Doxa means both glory and reputation, and these men held a currency they issued to one another — standing, deference, the seat at the front — which can only be earned inside the system and therefore only kept by not leaving. The way out is in the same verse and is not an instruction to care less about honour: the glory that comes from the only God. He does not tell them to want no approval. He tells them they are seeking it from a bankrupt issuer.

And the chapter's arrangement is its own argument. It opens with a man who could not reach the water, had nobody, and did not know the name of the one who healed him — and he was made whole. It closes with the best-taught men in the nation, holding every witness heaven could produce, who would not come. He got up. The men with all the evidence stayed sitting down.

verseByVerse.quote: "So Jesus said to them, 'Truly, truly, I say to you, the Son can do nothing of his own accord, but only what he sees the Father doing. For whatever the Father does, that the Son does likewise. For the Father loves the Son and shows him all that he himself is doing. And greater works than these will he show him, so that you may marvel.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So Jesus said to them: truly, truly, I say to you, the Son can do nothing of his own accord, but only what he sees the Father doing. For whatever the Father does, that the Son does likewise. For the Father loves the Son and shows him all that he himself is doing. And greater works than these will he show him, so that you may marvel.

The discourse. Jesus answers the charge that he made himself equal with God (v. 18). Not by denying it, but by explaining the relationship of the Son to the Father: perfect unity, with distinct roles.
