The Son can do nothing of his own accord. Not weakness, but unity. The Son never acts independently of the Father. He is not a rival god setting up on his own. He does nothing apart from the Father, as the Father does nothing apart from him.

But only what he sees the Father doing. Perfect knowledge of and conformity to the Father’s will.

For whatever the Father does, that the Son does likewise. “Whatever”: everything. The Son does all the works of God. Only one who is God can do everything God does.

For the Father loves the Son and shows him all that he himself is doing. Eternal love and complete openness between Father and Son.

And greater works than these. Greater than healing a paralysed man: giving life and judging (vv. 21–22).

Where Christians differ: the Son and the Father. Arians (and today Jehovah’s Witnesses) read “the Son can do nothing of his own accord” as proof that the Son is inferior to the Father. Verdict: the passage teaches that the Son is equal with the Father in nature and power (he does whatever the Father does, gives life, judges, receives equal honour), while distinct in person and relationship (the Father sends; the Son is sent and obeys). This is the doctrine of the Trinity: one God, three persons, equal in power and glory, distinct in relations (Westminster Shorter Catechism 6).

In a sentence. Jesus said that the Son does nothing on his own but only what he sees the Father doing, doing everything the Father does, because the Father loves him and shows him all he does, and will show him greater works still.

For worship. Father and Son are perfectly one in love and work. Worship the triune God.

verseByVerse.quote: "For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he will. For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he will. For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgement to the Son.

For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life. In the Old Testament, only God gives life to the dead (Deuteronomy 32:39; 1 Samuel 2:6; 2 Kings 5:7).

So also the Son gives life to whom he will. The Son does what only God does. “To whom he will”: by his sovereign choice. Spiritual life now (v. 24), and resurrection life at the last day (v. 29). Salvation is the sovereign gift of the Son.

For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son. The final judgement, which belongs to God alone (Genesis 18:25), is given to the Son (Acts 17:31). Two divine works: giving life and judging. Both belong to Jesus.

In a sentence. As the Father raises the dead and gives life, so the Son gives life to whom he chooses, and the Father has given all judgement to the Son.

For worship. The Son who gives life is also the Judge. Receive life from him now.

parallels.desc: I kill and I make alive

verseByVerse.quote: "that all may honor the Son, just as they honor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
That all may honour the Son, just as they honour the Father. Whoever does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him.

That all may honor the Son, just as they honor the Father. The purpose: equal honour. The same honour given to God is to be given to Jesus. Worship belongs to God alone (Isaiah 42:8). If the Son is to be honoured just as the Father, the Son is God.

Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him. You cannot honour God while rejecting Jesus. Every religion that respects God but denies Christ’s deity fails to honour God (1 John 2:23).

In a sentence. So that everyone will honour the Son as they honour the Father, for whoever does not honour the Son does not honour the Father who sent him.

For worship. Give Jesus the same honour you give the Father. Worship him as God.

parallels.desc: no one who denies the Son has the Father

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. He does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life. Truly, truly, I say to you, an hour is coming, and is now here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. He does not come into judgement, but has passed from death to life. Truly, truly, I say to you, an hour is coming, and is now here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.

Whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me. Hearing and believing: the way to receive life.

Has eternal life. Present tense. Already.

He does not come into judgment. No condemnation (3:18; Romans 8:1). Believers will stand before Christ (2 Corinthians 5:10), but not to be condemned.

But has passed from death to life. Perfect tense: has crossed over, and remains on the other side. From spiritual death (Ephesians 2:1) to eternal life. A complete change of state.

An hour is coming, and is now here. Already happening.

When the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live. The spiritually dead, who hear his voice in the gospel and are made alive (Ephesians 2:4–5). As Lazarus would hear his voice and come out of the tomb (11:43), the spiritually dead hear and live. Not that they decide to live; his voice gives life. Regeneration.

In a sentence. Whoever hears Jesus’ word and believes the Father has eternal life and has passed from death to life, and the time has come when the spiritually dead hear the Son of God and live.

For worship. If you believe, you have passed from death to life. You will never be condemned. Rejoice.

parallels.desc: dead in trespasses, made alive

verseByVerse.quote: "For as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself. And he has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself. And he has given him authority to execute judgement, because he is the Son of Man.

As the Father has life in himself. God is self-existent. He depends on nothing. Life is his by nature.

So he has granted the Son also to have life in himself. The Son too has life in himself: not borrowed, but his own (1:4). “Granted” does not mean the Son once lacked it; the eternal Son receives life eternally from the Father, as the Son eternally comes from the Father (eternal generation). And as incarnate, he has it in his human nature too, to give to others.

And he has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man. Daniel 7:13–14: the Son of Man receives dominion. And as a man, he can judge humanity fairly, having lived as one of us (Hebrews 4:15; Acts 17:31).

In a sentence. As the Father has life in himself, so he has given the Son life in himself, and authority to judge, because he is the Son of Man.

For worship. The Son has life in himself, and gives it to you. Draw your life from him.

parallels.desc: one like a son of man given dominion

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not marvel at this, for an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not marvel at this, for an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgement.

Do not marvel at this. If you are astonished at spiritual resurrection now, there is more.

An hour is coming. Not “and is now here”: this is the future, the last day.

When all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out. The bodily resurrection of all the dead, righteous and wicked, at the end (Daniel 12:2; Acts 24:15). Jesus will call, and every grave will open.

Those who have done good to the resurrection of life. To eternal life in the body.

And those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment. To condemnation, in the body.

What it does not mean. Not salvation by good works. In John, the “good” is above all believing in Jesus (6:29: this is the work of God, that you believe in him). Good deeds are the fruit and evidence of saving faith, not its ground (Ephesians 2:8–10; James 2:17–18). Those who have truly believed will have lived differently.

In a sentence. The time is coming when all the dead will hear his voice and rise, those who did good to life and those who did evil to judgement.

On a Tuesday. One day you will hear his voice from the grave. Are you ready for the resurrection of life?

parallels.desc: some to everlasting life, some to shame

verseByVerse.quote: "I can do nothing on my own. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just, because I seek not my own will but the will of him who sent me. If I alone bear witness about myself, my testimony is not true."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I can do nothing on my own. As I hear, I judge, and my judgement is just, because I seek not my own will but the will of him who sent me. If I alone bear witness about myself, my testimony is not true.

I can do nothing on my own. As in v. 19.

As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just. His judgement is perfectly just, because it is the Father’s.

Because I seek not my own will but the will of him who sent me. Perfect submission (4:34; 6:38).

If I alone bear witness about myself, my testimony is not true. The law required two or three witnesses; a man’s testimony about himself alone was not accepted in court (Deuteronomy 19:15). Jesus accepts the rule, and now calls his witnesses.

In a sentence. Jesus said he does nothing on his own, judging justly as he hears from the Father, and if he testified about himself alone his testimony would not count.

On a Tuesday. Seek God’s will, not your own. That is the path of true judgement.
verseByVerse.note: The law required two or three witnesses; a man’s testimony about himself did not count as valid evidence.

verseByVerse.quote: "There is another who bears witness about me, and I know that the testimony that he bears about me is true."
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is another who bears witness about me, and I know that the testimony that he bears about me is true.

There is another who bears witness about me. The other witness is probably the Father (v. 37), though some take it of John the Baptist (v. 33). Most likely the Father, the supreme witness.

And I know that the testimony that he bears about me is true. The Father cannot lie.

The witnesses. Jesus now calls four witnesses, as in a trial: John the Baptist (vv. 33–35), his works (v. 36), the Father (vv. 37–38), and the Scriptures, including Moses (vv. 39–47).

In a sentence. Another testifies about Jesus, and his testimony is true.

For worship. The Father himself testifies about Jesus. Believe his testimony.
verseByVerse.note: The other witness is probably the Father (v. 37), though some take it as John the Baptist (v. 33).

verseByVerse.quote: "You sent to John, and he has borne witness to the truth. Not that the testimony that I receive is from man, but I say these things so that you may be saved."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You sent to John, and he has borne witness to the truth. Not that the testimony that I receive is from man, but I say these things so that you may be saved.

You sent to John. The delegation of 1:19.

And he has borne witness to the truth. He testified that Jesus is the Lamb of God and Son of God (1:29, 34).

Not that the testimony that I receive is from man. Jesus does not depend on human testimony.

But I say these things so that you may be saved. Even in conflict, Jesus seeks their salvation. He mentions John for their sake, because they respected him.

In a sentence. They had sent to John, who testified to the truth, and Jesus mentions it not because he needs human testimony, but so that they might be saved.

On a Tuesday. Even Jesus’ hard words are spoken so that people may be saved.

verseByVerse.quote: "He was a burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He was a burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light.

He was a burning and shining lamp. A lamp, not the light itself (1:8). Burning: with zeal; shining: giving light. Past tense: John was now in prison or dead.

And you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light. For a while they enjoyed John’s ministry, the excitement of a prophet (Matthew 3:5). But they did not take his message seriously, or follow where he pointed. Enthusiasm without repentance.

In a sentence. John was a burning and shining lamp, and they were happy to enjoy his light for a while.

On a Tuesday. Enjoying a good preacher is not the same as obeying the message. Follow where the light points.

parallels.desc: I have prepared a lamp for my anointed

verseByVerse.quote: "But the testimony that I have is greater than that of John. For the works that the Father has given me to accomplish, the very works that I am doing, bear witness about me that the Father has sent me. And the Father who sent me has himself borne witness about me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the testimony that I have is greater than that of John. For the works that the Father has given me to accomplish, the very works that I am doing, bear witness about me that the Father has sent me. And the Father who sent me has himself borne witness about me.

The testimony that I have is greater than that of John. Better witnesses.

For the works that the Father has given me to accomplish. His signs and his whole ministry, culminating in the cross (17:4; 19:30).

Bear witness about me that the Father has sent me. The works show who he is (10:25, 37–38; 14:11).

And the Father who sent me has himself borne witness about me. At the baptism (Mark 1:11), in the Scriptures, and through the works. Perfect tense: a lasting testimony.

In a sentence. Jesus has a greater testimony than John’s: the works the Father gave him, which show the Father sent him, and the Father’s own testimony.

On a Tuesday. Look at Jesus’ works. They testify that the Father sent him.

parallels.desc: the Father’s voice at the baptism

verseByVerse.quote: "His voice you have never heard, his form you have never seen, and you do not have his word abiding in you, for you do not believe the one whom he has sent."
verseByVerse.commentary:
His voice you have never heard, his form you have never seen, and you do not have his word abiding in you, for you do not believe the one whom he has sent.

His voice you have never heard, his form you have never seen. At Sinai, Israel heard God’s voice and saw no form (Deuteronomy 4:12). But these leaders, despite their claims, do not truly know God. They have not heard his voice in the Scriptures, or seen his likeness, which is now visible in Jesus (14:9).

And you do not have his word abiding in you. They study it, but it does not live in them.

For you do not believe the one whom he has sent. The proof. If they knew God’s word, they would recognise his Son.

In a sentence. They had never heard the Father’s voice or seen his form, and his word did not live in them, because they did not believe the one he sent.

On a Tuesday. Does God’s word abide in you? Then you will recognise and believe his Son.

parallels.desc: you heard the sound of words, but saw no form

verseByVerse.quote: "You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me, yet you refuse to come to me that you may have life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me, yet you refuse to come to me that you may have life.

You search the Scriptures. They studied the Old Testament with great diligence, memorising, debating, counting letters. Or a command: search the Scriptures. Either way, they were serious Bible students.

Because you think that in them you have eternal life. They thought that studying the law and keeping it would give them life. Rabbis said: the more study of the law, the more life.

And it is they that bear witness about me. Key words. The purpose of Scripture is to point to Christ (Luke 24:27, 44). The whole Old Testament testifies to him.

Yet you refuse to come to me that you may have life. The tragedy: Bible study without coming to Christ. Life is not in the Bible itself, but in the one to whom it points. They searched for life in the book, and missed the life standing in front of them. The problem was not their mind but their will: “you refuse”.

In a sentence. They studied the Scriptures thinking that in them they had eternal life, but the Scriptures testify about Jesus, and they refused to come to him for life.

On a Tuesday. Read your Bible to come to Christ. Bible study that does not lead you to him misses the point.

verseByVerse.quote: "I do not receive glory from people. But I know that you do not have the love of God within you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do not receive glory from people. But I know that you do not have the love of God within you.

I do not receive glory from people. Jesus does not seek human approval or praise. He seeks his Father’s glory (7:18; 8:50).

But I know that you do not have the love of God within you. Love for God, or God’s love. Despite their religiousness, they did not love God. If they did, they would love the one he sent (8:42).

In a sentence. Jesus did not seek human praise, and he knew they did not have the love of God in them.

On a Tuesday. Religious activity is not the same as love for God. Do you love him?

verseByVerse.quote: "I have come in my Father's name, and you do not receive me. If another comes in his own name, you will receive him. How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have come in my Father’s name, and you do not receive me. If another comes in his own name, you will receive him. How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?

I have come in my Father’s name. With his authority, representing him.

And you do not receive me. Rejection (1:11).

If another comes in his own name, you will receive him. False messiahs, who came on their own authority, were often welcomed. Josephus records many. In AD 132, Simon bar Kokhba was hailed as Messiah by Rabbi Akiba and led a disastrous revolt. People prefer leaders who flatter them.

How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another. The root of their unbelief: love of human praise. They cared more about what their peers thought than what God thought. To believe in Jesus would cost them their reputation (12:42–43).

And do not seek the glory that comes from the only God? God’s approval is the only honour that matters.

In a sentence. Jesus came in his Father’s name and they rejected him, though they would accept someone coming in his own name, for they could not believe while they sought praise from each other rather than from the only God.

On a Tuesday. Whose praise do you seek? Love of human approval can keep you from Christ.

parallels.desc: Theudas and Judas the Galilean

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not think that I will accuse you to the Father. There is one who accuses you: Moses, on whom you have set your hope. For if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote of me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not think that I will accuse you to the Father. There is one who accuses you: Moses, on whom you have set your hope. For if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote of me.

Do not think that I will accuse you to the Father. Jesus does not need to.

There is one who accuses you: Moses. Moses, their great hero, the giver of the law they trusted, will be their prosecutor. The law they thought would save them will condemn them (Romans 3:19–20).

On whom you have set your hope. They hoped in Moses and the law for salvation.

For if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote of me. Moses wrote of Christ: the seed of the woman (Genesis 3:15), the offspring of Abraham (Genesis 22:18), the Passover lamb (Exodus 12), the sacrifices (Leviticus), the bronze serpent (Numbers 21:9; John 3:14), the prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15–18). To reject Jesus is to reject Moses.

In a sentence. Jesus said he would not need to accuse them, for Moses, in whom they hoped, accuses them, since if they believed Moses they would believe Jesus, for Moses wrote about him.

On a Tuesday. Read the books of Moses looking for Christ. He is there.

parallels.desc: a witness against you

verseByVerse.quote: "But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?

If you do not believe his writings. They claimed to honour Moses, but did not truly believe what he wrote.

How will you believe my words? If they will not believe the written Scriptures they revere, they will not believe Jesus’ spoken words. Faith in Scripture and faith in Christ stand or fall together. Jesus places his own words alongside Scripture.

In a sentence. If they did not believe Moses’ writings, how would they believe Jesus’ words?

For worship. Believe the Scriptures, and you will believe Christ. They speak with one voice.

5.title: The Son Has Life in Himself
5.text: <sup>1</sup>After this there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.<sup>2</sup>Now there is in Jerusalem by the Sheep Gate a pool, in Aramaic called Bethesda, which has five roofed colonnades.<sup>3</sup>In these lay a multitude of invalids—blind, lame, and paralyzed.<sup>5</sup>One man was there who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years.<sup>6</sup>When Jesus saw him lying there and knew that he had already been there a long time, he said to him, “Do you want to be healed?”<sup>7</sup>The sick man answered him, “Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool when the water is stirred up, and while I am going another steps down before me.”<sup>8</sup>Jesus said to him, “Get up, take up your bed, and walk.”<sup>9</sup>And at once the man was healed, and he took up his bed and walked. Now that day was the Sabbath.<sup>10</sup>So the Jews said to the man who had been healed, “It is the Sabbath, and it is not lawful for you to take up your bed.”<sup>11</sup>But he answered them, “The man who healed me, that man said to me, ’Take up your bed, and walk.’”<sup>12</sup>They asked him, “Who is the man who said to you, ’Take up your bed and walk’?”<sup>13</sup>Now the man who had been healed did not know who it was, for Jesus had withdrawn, as there was a crowd in the place.<sup>14</sup>Afterward Jesus found him in the temple and said to him, “See, you are well! Sin no more, that nothing worse may happen to you.”<sup>15</sup>The man went away and told the Jews that it was Jesus who had healed him.<sup>16</sup>And this was why the Jews were persecuting Jesus, because he was doing these things on the Sabbath.<sup>17</sup>But Jesus answered them, “My Father is working until now, and I am working.”<sup>18</sup>This was why the Jews were seeking all the more to kill him, because not only was he breaking the Sabbath, but he was even calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God.<sup>19</sup>So Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, the Son can do nothing of his own accord, but only what he sees the Father doing. For whatever the Father does, that the Son does likewise.<sup>20</sup>For the Father loves the Son and shows him all that he himself is doing. And greater works than these will he show him, so that you may marvel.<sup>21</sup>For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he will.<sup>22</sup>For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son,<sup>23</sup>that all may honor the Son, just as they honor the Father. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him.<sup>24</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life. He does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life.<sup>25</sup>“Truly, truly, I say to you, an hour is coming, and is now here, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.<sup>26</sup>For as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself.<sup>27</sup>And he has given him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man.<sup>28</sup>Do not marvel at this, for an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice<sup>29</sup>and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment.<sup>30</sup>“I can do nothing on my own. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just, because I seek not my own will but the will of him who sent me.<sup>31</sup>If I alone bear witness about myself, my testimony is not true.<sup>32</sup>There is another who bears witness about me, and I know that the testimony that he bears about me is true.<sup>33</sup>You sent to John, and he has borne witness to the truth.<sup>34</sup>Not that the testimony that I receive is from man, but I say these things so that you may be saved.<sup>35</sup>He was a burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light.<sup>36</sup>But the testimony that I have is greater than that of John. For the works that the Father has given me to accomplish, the very works that I am doing, bear witness about me that the Father has sent me.<sup>37</sup>And the Father who sent me has himself borne witness about me. His voice you have never heard, his form you have never seen,<sup>38</sup>and you do not have his word abiding in you, for you do not believe the one whom he has sent.<sup>39</sup>You search the Scriptures because you think that in them you have eternal life; and it is they that bear witness about me,<sup>40</sup>yet you refuse to come to me that you may have life.<sup>41</sup>I do not receive glory from people.<sup>42</sup>But I know that you do not have the love of God within you.<sup>43</sup>I have come in my Father’s name, and you do not receive me. If another comes in his own name, you will receive him.<sup>44</sup>How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?<sup>45</sup>Do not think that I will accuse you to the Father. There is one who accuses you: Moses, on whom you have set your hope.<sup>46</sup>For if you believed Moses, you would believe me; for he wrote of me.<sup>47</sup>But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?”
5.overview:
The third sign takes place in Jerusalem at the pool of Bethesda, whose five colonnades archaeologists have uncovered near the Sheep Gate. Among the crowds of sick people waiting for the water to stir lies a man who has been an invalid for thirty-eight years. Jesus asks whether he wants to be well, then tells him to pick up his mat and walk, and he does. But it is the Sabbath, and the authorities challenge the man for carrying his mat. When they learn it was Jesus, they begin to persecute him, and Jesus answers, “My Father is working until now, and I am working.” They understand him exactly: he is calling God his own Father and making himself equal with God, and they now seek to kill him.

Jesus’ reply (vv. 19–47) is one of the richest statements of his identity in the Gospels. The Son does nothing on his own, but whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise. Like the Father he gives life to whom he will, and the Father has entrusted all judgment to him, so that all should honour the Son as they honour the Father. Whoever hears his word and believes has eternal life now and has passed from death to life; and an hour is coming when all the dead will hear his voice and rise, to life or to judgment. Then, as in a courtroom, Jesus calls his witnesses: John the Baptist, his own works, the Father, and the Scriptures. His hearers search the Scriptures for life but refuse to come to the one they speak of; they seek glory from one another, not from God. Moses himself, whom they trust, will accuse them, for he wrote about Jesus.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — Feeding the Five Thousand and Walking on Water
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Some time later Jesus crosses the Sea of Galilee, followed by a huge crowd drawn by his healings. He goes up a hillside with his disciples. Passover is near. Seeing the crowd approach, he asks Philip where they could buy bread for them all, to test him, since he already knows what he will do. Philip calculates that even two hundred days’ wages would not buy each a mouthful. Andrew mentions a boy with five small barley loaves and two fish, but what use are they? Jesus has the people sit on the grass, about five thousand men. He takes the loaves, gives thanks and distributes them, and the fish too, as much as anyone wants. When all are satisfied, he tells the disciples to collect the leftovers so that nothing is wasted, and they fill twelve baskets. Seeing the sign, the people declare him the Prophet who was to come, and Jesus, knowing they mean to seize him and make him king, withdraws alone to the hills. At evening the disciples set off by boat for Capernaum in the dark, without him. A strong wind whips up the lake. After rowing three or four miles they see Jesus walking on the water towards them and are terrified, but he tells them it is he and not to fear. They gladly take him aboard, and at once the boat reaches the shore.
verseByVerse.theology: The feeding miracle and the sea-walking are connected signs: together they reveal Jesus as the one who commands both provision and chaos, who is both the Lord of creation and the bread of life. 'It is I' on the water (v. 20) is followed at once by the great 'I am' discourses of John's Gospel, beginning with 'I am the bread of life' in the discourse that follows. The crowd that wants to make Jesus an earthly king misunderstands the sign: they want the bread without the Bread-giver, the miracle without the meaning, the provision without the person.
verseByVerse.examples: The disciples' plan to divide the available food among five thousand is not faithlessness but the appropriate response of stewards who account for what they have. Jesus's question to Philip — 'where are we to buy bread?' — is a test, not a request for information. The walking on water is the most theologically revealing of the nature miracles: Jesus walks on the sea, which in the Old Testament is the domain of chaos and the realm only God can command (Job 38:16; Ps. 77:19).

verseByVerse.quote: After this Jesus went away to the other side of the Sea of Galilee, which is the Sea of Tiberias. And a large crowd was following him, because they saw the signs that he was doing on the sick.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this Jesus went away to the other side of the Sea of Galilee, which is the Sea of Tiberias. And a large crowd was following him, because they saw the signs that he was doing on the sick.

Setting. Chapter 6 contains two signs (the feeding of the five thousand and the walking on the water) and the great discourse on the bread of life. It ends with many disciples leaving Jesus. A turning point in his Galilean ministry.

The Sea of Galilee, which is the Sea of Tiberias. The Sea of Tiberias is another name for the Sea of Galilee, after the city Herod Antipas built on its western shore around AD 20 and named after the emperor Tiberius. John explains for readers outside Palestine.

Because they saw the signs. They followed for the miracles, not for who he was (v. 26).

In a sentence. Jesus crossed the Sea of Galilee, followed by a large crowd who had seen his healing signs.

On a Tuesday. Why do you follow Jesus: for what he can do for you, or for who he is?
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Tiberias is another name for the Sea of Galilee, from the city Herod Antipas built on its western shore and named after the emperor Tiberius.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus went up on the mountain, and there he sat down with his disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus went up on the mountain, and there he sat down with his disciples.

Jesus went up on the mountain. The hills east of the lake. Like Moses going up the mountain (Exodus 19; 24). The whole chapter will echo the exodus: the Passover, the mountain, the bread in the wilderness, the crossing of the sea, the grumbling.

And there he sat down with his disciples. The posture of a teacher.

In a sentence. Jesus went up a mountain and sat down with his disciples.

On a Tuesday. Take time to sit with Jesus, away from the crowd.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was at hand. Lifting up his eyes, then, and seeing that a large crowd was coming toward him, Jesus said to Philip, "Where are we to buy bread, so that these people may eat?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was at hand. Lifting up his eyes, then, and seeing that a large crowd was coming toward him, Jesus said to Philip: where are we to buy bread, so that these people may eat?

Now the Passover … was at hand. This is the second Passover John mentions (2:13; 11:55); the Passover setting colours the whole chapter. Passover recalled the exodus, when God fed Israel with manna in the wilderness. And at Passover the next year, Jesus would give his body and blood (vv. 51–56).

Seeing that a large crowd was coming toward him. Jesus sees the need.

Jesus said to Philip. Philip was from Bethsaida, nearby (1:44); he would know where food could be bought.

Where are we to buy bread, so that these people may eat? An echo of Moses: Where am I to get meat to give to all this people? (Numbers 11:13).

In a sentence. With Passover near, Jesus saw a large crowd coming and asked Philip where they could buy bread for them.

On a Tuesday. Jesus sees the needs around you. He asks what you will do.
verseByVerse.note: This is the second Passover John mentions; the Passover setting prepares for Jesus’ words about bread and his flesh and blood.

verseByVerse.quote: He said this to test him, for he himself knew what he would do. Philip answered him, "Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for each of them to get a little."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He said this to test him, for he himself knew what he would do. Philip answered him: two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for each of them to get a little.

He said this to test him. To stretch Philip’s faith. Would he look to his own resources, or to Jesus?

For he himself knew what he would do. Jesus is never at a loss.

Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough. The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage; two hundred denarii was about eight months’ wages. Philip calculated, and despaired. He looked at the problem, not at Jesus.

In a sentence. Jesus asked to test Philip, already knowing what he would do, and Philip answered that eight months’ wages would not buy enough for each to have a bite.

On a Tuesday. When God tests you, look to him, not to your calculations.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage; two hundred denarii was most of a year’s wages.

parallels.desc: where am I to get meat?

verseByVerse.quote: One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter's brother, said to him, "There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are they for so many?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, said to him: there is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are they for so many?

Andrew. Again bringing someone to Jesus (1:41; 12:22).

A boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish. Only John mentions the boy and the barley. Barley loaves were the cheap bread of the poor. An echo of Elisha, who fed a hundred men with twenty barley loaves, with some left over (2 Kings 4:42–44). Jesus is greater than Elisha. The fish were probably small dried or pickled fish.

But what are they for so many? Andrew brought what there was, even though it seemed useless. That is all Jesus asks.

In a sentence. Andrew said there was a boy with five barley loaves and two fish, but asked what use they were for so many.

On a Tuesday. Bring what little you have to Jesus. He can multiply it.
verseByVerse.note: Barley loaves were the cheap bread of the poor.

parallels.desc: Elisha feeds a hundred men with twenty barley loaves

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said, "Have the people sit down." Now there was much grass in the place. So the men sat down, about five thousand in number. Jesus then took the loaves, and when he had given thanks, he distributed them to those who were seated. So also the fish, as much as they wanted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said: have the people sit down. Now there was much grass in the place. So the men sat down, about five thousand in number. Jesus then took the loaves, and when he had given thanks, he distributed them to those who were seated. So also the fish, as much as they wanted.

Have the people sit down. Recline, as at a banquet.

Now there was much grass in the place. Spring, at Passover. Green pastures (Psalm 23:2). The good shepherd feeds his flock.

About five thousand in number. Men; with women and children, many more (Matthew 14:21).

And when he had given thanks. Eucharistēsas. John mentions only thanksgiving, not breaking, perhaps pointing to the Lord’s Supper, which he does not otherwise describe.

He distributed them. Jesus himself gives. The other Gospels say the disciples distributed.

As much as they wanted. Abundance. Not a token.

In a sentence. Jesus had the people sit on the grass, about five thousand men, gave thanks for the loaves and fish, and distributed as much as they wanted.

For worship. Christ gives as much as you want of himself. Come and eat.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had eaten their fill, he told his disciples, "Gather up the leftover fragments, that nothing may be lost." So they gathered them up and filled twelve baskets with fragments from the five barley loaves left by those who had eaten.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had eaten their fill, he told his disciples: gather up the leftover fragments, that nothing may be lost. So they gathered them up and filled twelve baskets with fragments from the five barley loaves left by those who had eaten.

When they had eaten their fill. Satisfied, fully.

Gather up the leftover fragments, that nothing may be lost. Only John records this command. God’s abundance is not wasteful. And “that nothing may be lost” anticipates v. 39: I should lose nothing of all that he has given me. The fragments picture the people Christ will not lose.

Twelve baskets. More left over than at the start. One for each apostle, and perhaps for the twelve tribes of Israel.

In a sentence. When everyone had eaten enough, Jesus had the disciples gather the leftovers so nothing would be lost, and they filled twelve baskets.

On a Tuesday. God’s generosity overflows, but he wastes nothing. Use his gifts carefully.

verseByVerse.quote: When the people saw the sign that he had done, they said, "This is indeed the Prophet who is to come into the world!" Perceiving then that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, Jesus withdrew again to the mountain by himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the people saw the sign that he had done, they said: this is indeed the Prophet who is to come into the world! Perceiving then that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, Jesus withdrew again to the mountain by himself.

This is indeed the Prophet who is to come into the world! “The Prophet” is the prophet like Moses whom Moses promised (Deuteronomy 18:15). Moses gave manna; this prophet gives bread. They are right, but they misunderstand.

They were about to come and take him by force to make him king. A political Messiah, to lead a revolt against Rome. Passover, the feast of liberation, heightened nationalist fervour. They wanted a king who would feed them and free them, on their terms.

Jesus withdrew again to the mountain by himself. He refused. His kingdom is not of this world (18:36). The same temptation Satan offered (Matthew 4:8–10): a crown without a cross. Matthew and Mark say he went to pray (Mark 6:46).

In a sentence. Seeing the sign, the people declared him the Prophet, and Jesus, knowing they meant to force him to be king, withdrew alone to the mountain.

On a Tuesday. Don’t try to make Jesus the king of your agenda. Let him be king on his terms.
verseByVerse.note: “The Prophet” is the prophet like Moses whom Moses promised. Many hoped for a Messiah who would lead a revolt against Rome.

parallels.desc: my kingdom is not of this world

verseByVerse.quote: When evening came, his disciples went down to the sea, got into a boat, and started across the sea to Capernaum. It was now dark, and Jesus had not yet come to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When evening came, his disciples went down to the sea, got into a boat, and started across the sea to Capernaum. It was now dark, and Jesus had not yet come to them.

His disciples went down to the sea. Mark says Jesus made them go (Mark 6:45), perhaps to remove them from the crowd’s political excitement.

It was now dark. In John, darkness often has symbolic weight (1:5; 3:2; 13:30).

And Jesus had not yet come to them. Alone in the dark, without Jesus.

In a sentence. In the evening the disciples set out by boat across the lake for Capernaum, and it was dark, and Jesus had not yet come to them.

On a Tuesday. There are times when it is dark and Jesus seems absent. He has not forgotten you.

verseByVerse.quote: The sea became rough because a strong wind was blowing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sea became rough because a strong wind was blowing.

The sea became rough. The Sea of Galilee lies low and ringed by hills; sudden strong winds funnel down onto it.

In a sentence. A strong wind blew and the sea grew rough.

On a Tuesday. Obeying Jesus does not mean calm seas. The disciples were where he sent them, in a storm.
verseByVerse.note: The Sea of Galilee lies low and ringed by hills; sudden strong winds are common.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had rowed about three or four miles, they saw Jesus walking on the sea and coming near the boat, and they were frightened. But he said to them, "It is I; do not be afraid."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they had rowed about three or four miles, they saw Jesus walking on the sea and coming near the boat, and they were frightened. But he said to them: it is I; do not be afraid.

When they had rowed about three or four miles. The ESV notes that the distance is literally twenty-five or thirty stadia. Roughly halfway across.

They saw Jesus walking on the sea. In the Old Testament, God alone treads on the waves of the sea (Job 9:8; Psalm 77:19). The sea pictures chaos. Jesus walks on it as its master.

And they were frightened. Terror.

It is I. Literally “I am” (egō eimi), the divine name (Exodus 3:14; Isaiah 43:10–11; 51:12). The God who walks on the sea says “I am”.

Do not be afraid. God’s word to his people throughout Scripture (Isaiah 43:1–2: when you pass through the waters, I will be with you).

In a sentence. After rowing three or four miles, the disciples saw Jesus walking on the water toward them and were terrified, but he said: I am; do not be afraid.

For worship. In your storm, hear him say: I am; do not be afraid.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the distance is literally twenty-five or thirty stadia. “It is I” can also be heard as the divine name, “I am.”

verseByVerse.quote: Then they were glad to take him into the boat, and immediately the boat was at the land to which they were going.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they were glad to take him into the boat, and immediately the boat was at the land to which they were going.

They were glad to take him into the boat. Or “they wanted to take him”. Fear became gladness.

And immediately the boat was at the land to which they were going. Another miracle. Psalm 107:29–30: he made the storm be still … and he brought them to their desired haven. With Jesus, they arrive.

In a sentence. They gladly took him into the boat, and at once the boat reached the shore they were heading for.

For worship. Take Jesus into your boat. He will bring you to your desired haven.

parallels.desc: he brought them to their desired haven

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–71 — The Bread of Life Discourse
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The crowd follows Jesus to Capernaum, wanting more bread. He urges them to seek food that lasts, given by the Son of Man, and tells them the work God asks is faith in the one he sent. When they demand a sign like the manna, he declares that he is the true bread from heaven, the bread of life, who satisfies hunger and thirst for ever. All the Father gives him will come, none will be turned away or lost, and he will raise them on the last day. As they grumble at his claim, he teaches that no one comes unless the Father draws and teaches them. The bread he will give for the world is his own flesh; only those who eat his flesh and drink his blood have life and remain in him. Many disciples are offended and leave. Jesus says his words are Spirit and life, but some do not believe. When he asks the Twelve whether they will go, Peter replies that only Jesus has the words of eternal life; they know he is the Holy One of God. Jesus warns that one of the Twelve, Judas, will betray him.
verseByVerse.theology: The Bread of Life discourse is simultaneously eucharistic (the language of eating and drinking Jesus's flesh and blood points to the Lord's Supper) and spiritual (the key interpretive statement is 'it is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all'). The flesh and blood Jesus speaks of is not a literal cannibalism but the reception of his atoning death: to eat his flesh and drink his blood is to appropriate by faith the benefits of his sacrifice. No one can come to Jesus unless the Father draws them; all who are given to the Son by the Father will come; all who come will be raised up on the last day. The sovereignty of grace and the necessity of faith are held together throughout.
verseByVerse.examples: The Bread of Life discourse sheds light on the Lord's Supper without being confined to it: feeding on Christ is spiritual, received by faith, not a physical re-sacrifice. The mass defection at the end of the discourse — 'many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him' — is the most important event in John 6: it reveals that the crowd's 'belief' was not genuine, and that the true disciples are known not by enthusiasm but by perseverance. Peter's confession — 'you have the words of eternal life' — is the greatest response to a hard teaching in the Gospels: when you cannot understand what Jesus is saying, you remain because of who he is.

verseByVerse.quote: On the next day the crowd that remained on the other side of the sea saw that there had been only one boat there, and that Jesus had not entered the boat with his disciples, but that his disciples had gone away alone. Other boats from Tiberias came near the place where they had eaten the bread after the Lord had given thanks.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the next day the crowd that remained on the other side of the sea saw that there had been only one boat there, and that Jesus had not entered the boat with his disciples, but that his disciples had gone away alone. Other boats from Tiberias came near the place where they had eaten the bread after the Lord had given thanks.

The crowd … saw that there had been only one boat. They were puzzled: Jesus had not left in the disciples’ boat, yet he was gone.

Other boats from Tiberias. Perhaps blown across by the storm.

Where they had eaten the bread after the Lord had given thanks. John calls Jesus “the Lord”, and stresses the thanksgiving.

In a sentence. The next day the crowd realised Jesus had not left with his disciples in the only boat, and other boats arrived from Tiberias.

On a Tuesday. Jesus is not limited by circumstances. He goes where he will.

verseByVerse.quote: So when the crowd saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples, they themselves got into the boats and went to Capernaum, seeking Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So when the crowd saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples, they themselves got into the boats and went to Capernaum, seeking Jesus.

Seeking Jesus. Diligently. But for the wrong reason (v. 26).

In a sentence. Seeing that neither Jesus nor his disciples were there, the crowd took the boats to Capernaum looking for him.

On a Tuesday. Seeking Jesus is good; examine why you seek him.

verseByVerse.quote: When they found him on the other side of the sea, they said to him, "Rabbi, when did you come here?" Jesus answered them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, you are seeking me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate your fill of the loaves."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they found him on the other side of the sea, they said to him: Rabbi, when did you come here? Jesus answered them: truly, truly, I say to you, you are seeking me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate your fill of the loaves.

Rabbi, when did you come here? Curiosity.

You are seeking me, not because you saw signs. Not because they understood the meaning of the feeding, as a sign pointing to who he is.

But because you ate your fill of the loaves. They wanted more free food. They saw the bread, but not the sign. Jesus exposes their motive: they want what he gives, not who he is.

In a sentence. When they found him and asked when he came, Jesus told them they were looking for him not because they understood the signs but because they had eaten their fill.

On a Tuesday. Do you want Jesus, or just what he can give? Seek the Giver, not just the gifts.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you. For on him God the Father has set his seal."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you. For on him God the Father has set his seal.

Do not work for the food that perishes. Physical food is necessary, but temporary. Don’t make it the goal of your life (Isaiah 55:2).

But for the food that endures to eternal life. Spiritual nourishment that never runs out.

Which the Son of Man will give to you. “Work for” it, yet it is a gift. Not earned, but sought and received.

For on him God the Father has set his seal. A seal marked ownership and guaranteed authenticity. The Father has authenticated Jesus as his own, at the baptism and through the signs. He is God’s certified Son.

In a sentence. Jesus told them not to work for food that perishes, but for food that lasts to eternal life, which the Son of Man, sealed by the Father, will give them.

On a Tuesday. How much of your energy goes into food that perishes? Seek the food that lasts.
verseByVerse.note: A seal marked ownership and guaranteed authenticity.

parallels.desc: why do you labour for that which does not satisfy?

verseByVerse.quote: "Then they said to him, 'What must we do, to be doing the works of God?' Jesus answered them, 'This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they said to him: what must we do, to be doing the works of God? Jesus answered them: this is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.

What must we do, to be doing the works of God? They take “work” literally: tell us what to do, what deeds, what rules, to earn this food.

This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent. Key words. Not works (plural), but one work: believe. Faith is not a work that earns salvation; it is the receiving of a gift. And it is “the work of God” in a double sense: the work God requires, and the work God does in us (v. 44, 65; Philippians 1:29). Salvation is not by doing but by believing in Jesus.

In a sentence. When they asked what works God requires, Jesus answered that the work of God is to believe in the one he has sent.

For worship. The only “work” God requires for salvation is to believe in Jesus. Rest in him.

verseByVerse.quote: So they said to him, "Then what sign do you do, that we may see and believe you? What work do you perform? Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness; as it is written, 'He gave them bread from heaven to eat.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So they said to him: then what sign do you do, that we may see and believe you? What work do you perform? Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness; as it is written: he gave them bread from heaven to eat.

Then what sign do you do, that we may see and believe you? Astonishing: they had just seen the feeding of five thousand. They want more. Perhaps a sign as great as Moses’ manna, which lasted forty years. One meal was not enough.

Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness. Exodus 16. There was a Jewish expectation that the Messiah would bring back the manna.

He gave them bread from heaven to eat. Psalm 78:24; Exodus 16:4. They challenge Jesus to match Moses.

In a sentence. They demanded a sign to make them believe, pointing out that their ancestors ate manna in the wilderness, bread from heaven.

On a Tuesday. Unbelief always wants more signs. Believe what God has already shown you.

parallels.desc: he gave them the grain of heaven
bread from heaven

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus then said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven. For the bread of God is he who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus then said to them: truly, truly, I say to you, it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven. For the bread of God is he who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.

It was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven. God gave it, not Moses.

But my Father gives you the true bread from heaven. Present tense: is giving, now. “True” (alēthinon): the real thing, of which the manna was a shadow. The manna fed bodies for a day; the true bread gives eternal life.

For the bread of God is he who comes down from heaven. Or “that which comes down”. The bread is a person: Jesus, who came down from heaven (3:13).

And gives life to the world. Not only to Israel, but to the world.

In a sentence. Jesus said it was not Moses but his Father who gives the true bread from heaven, the one who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.

For worship. Jesus is the true bread from heaven. Feed on him.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "Sir, give us this bread always." Jesus said to them, "I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They said to him: sir, give us this bread always. Jesus said to them: I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst.

Sir, give us this bread always. Like the Samaritan woman (4:15), they still think of physical bread.

I am the bread of life. Key words. This is the first of Jesus’ seven “I am” sayings in John: the bread of life (6:35), the light of the world (8:12), the door (10:7), the good shepherd (10:11), the resurrection and the life (11:25), the way, the truth and the life (14:6), the true vine (15:1). “I am” (egō eimi) echoes the divine name. Jesus does not just give bread; he is the bread. Not something he offers, but himself. Bread was the staple of life; without it, people died. Jesus is the essential nourishment of the soul.

Whoever comes to me shall not hunger. Coming to Jesus is like eating.

And whoever believes in me shall never thirst. Believing in Jesus is like drinking (4:14). Coming and believing are the same thing. The deepest hunger and thirst of the soul satisfied for ever.

In a sentence. When they asked for this bread always, Jesus said he is the bread of life, and whoever comes to him will never hunger, and whoever believes in him will never thirst.

For worship. Jesus is the bread of life. Come to him and believe, and you will never hunger again.
verseByVerse.note: This is the first of Jesus’ seven “I am” sayings in John.

parallels.desc: come, buy and eat

verseByVerse.quote: "But I said to you that you have seen me and yet do not believe."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But I said to you that you have seen me and yet do not believe.

You have seen me and yet do not believe. Seeing is not believing. They had seen the sign and the person, and still did not believe. Unbelief is not a lack of evidence. Why do some believe and others not? Jesus explains in the next verses.

In a sentence. Jesus said that they had seen him and still did not believe.

On a Tuesday. Pray for those who have seen and heard and still don’t believe. Only God can open their eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: "All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out. For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out. For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me.

All that the Father gives me will come to me. Key words. The Father has given a people to the Son (17:2, 6, 9, 24). They are given before they come. “All” of them will come: not might, but will. None will be missing. This is unconditional election and effectual calling: the Father chooses a people, gives them to the Son, and draws them so that they certainly come (v. 44).

And whoever comes to me I will never cast out. And the other side: no one who comes will be rejected. “Never” (ou mē): the strongest negative in Greek. A wonderful assurance for anyone who comes to Christ, however unworthy. You do not need to wonder whether you are chosen before you come; if you come, he will receive you.

For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me. Jesus’ mission is to do the Father’s will, which is to save all the Father has given him.

Where Christians differ: election. Arminians teach that God chooses those he foresees will freely believe. Verdict: the text puts the Father’s giving first, and the coming second, as its result: all that the Father gives will come. God’s choice is the cause of faith, not its result (also 6:44, 65; 10:26; Ephesians 1:4–5; Acts 13:48). Yet human responsibility is real: everyone who comes is welcomed, and those who refuse are responsible (5:40). Both truths are taught together, and we hold them together.

In a sentence. Everyone the Father gives Jesus will come to him, and he will never turn away anyone who comes, for he came down from heaven to do the will of the one who sent him.

For worship. If you have come to Christ, he will never cast you out. And you came because the Father gave you to him. Rest in that.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day.

This is the will of him who sent me. Jesus now spells out what the Father’s will is. It is a saving will, and the Son has come to carry it out to the end.

That I should lose nothing of all that he has given me. Key words. “All that he has given me” is neuter in Greek (pan ho), the whole company of the given seen as one gift. “Lose” (apollymi) is the same word used of the fragments in v. 12: gather them up “that nothing may be lost.” The Shepherd who would not lose a crust of barley bread will not lose one of his people. This is the perseverance of the saints, grounded not in the strength of the believer but in the will of the Father and the faithfulness of the Son (10:28–29; 17:12; 18:9).

But raise it up on the last day. Salvation is not complete until the body is raised. Jesus’ keeping reaches all the way through death to the resurrection at his return. The phrase “raise up on the last day” comes four times in this chapter (vv. 39, 40, 44, 54): it is the goal of everything Jesus does for his people.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that someone who makes a profession and then abandons Christ for ever was one of the given (see 1 John 2:19). Nor does it mean believers can live carelessly: those whom Christ keeps, he keeps believing and following (10:27).

Where Christians differ: can a true believer be lost? Many Arminians teach that a genuine believer may finally fall away. Verdict: this verse rules it out. If one given to the Son were lost, the Father’s will would fail and the Son would have failed in his mission. The warnings of Scripture are real, and they are one of the means by which Christ keeps his own; but the outcome is certain.

In a sentence. The Father’s will is that Jesus should lose none of those the Father has given him, but raise them all up on the last day.

On a Tuesday. Your perseverance rests in Christ’s hands, not in your grip. When you feel weak, remember: he does not lose what the Father has given him.

verseByVerse.quote: "For this is the will of my Father, that everyone who looks on the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this is the will of my Father, that everyone who looks on the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day.

For this is the will of my Father. The same will, now seen from the human side. Verse 39 spoke of what the Father gives; v. 40 speaks of what people do.

That everyone who looks on the Son and believes in him. Key words. “Looks” (theōreō) means to gaze, to look with attention. The crowd had seen him without believing (v. 36); this is seeing that leads to faith. The verse echoes the bronze serpent (3:14–15; Numbers 21:8–9): whoever looked, lived. “Everyone” is wide open: there is no one who looks and believes who is shut out.

Should have eternal life. Present possession: has it now.

And I will raise him up on the last day. And future completion: resurrection at the end. Eternal life now, and resurrection then.

Election and the open invitation. Verses 39 and 40 stand side by side on purpose. One speaks of the Father giving, the other of everyone who believes. They describe the same people. God’s choosing never makes the invitation less sincere; it is what guarantees that the invitation will not be refused by all.

In a sentence. The Father’s will is that everyone who looks to the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and Jesus will raise him up on the last day.

For worship. Look to the Son and believe. That is all, and it is everything.

verseByVerse.quote: So the Jews grumbled about him, because he said, "I am the bread that came down from heaven." They said, "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How does he now say, 'I have come down from heaven'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the Jews grumbled about him, because he said, “I am the bread that came down from heaven.” They said, “Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How does he now say, ‘I have come down from heaven’?”

So the Jews grumbled about him. “Grumbled” (gongyzō) is a deliberate word. It is the word the Greek Old Testament uses for Israel grumbling in the wilderness, the very place where the manna was given (Exodus 16:2, 7–8). They are acting out their fathers’ story while they talk about their fathers’ bread. “The Jews” in John often means the religious authorities and those who followed them in opposing Jesus, here people in the Galilean synagogue.

Because he said, “I am the bread that came down from heaven.” The claim to heavenly origin is what offends them.

Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? They know where he comes from, they think. They know his family. Ironically, they know only half the truth. John’s readers know he came from the Father (1:14), and many would know he was born of a virgin. Familiarity breeds contempt (compare Mark 6:3).

How does he now say, “I have come down from heaven”? Their objection is the incarnation itself: how can an ordinary man claim to come from heaven? This is still the stumbling block.

In a sentence. The Jews grumbled because Jesus claimed to be bread from heaven, since they knew his father and mother and thought they knew where he came from.

On a Tuesday. Do not let familiarity with Jesus dull your wonder. The man of Nazareth came down from heaven.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "Do not grumble among yourselves. No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. And I will raise him up on the last day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answered them, “Do not grumble among yourselves. No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. And I will raise him up on the last day.”

Do not grumble among yourselves. Jesus doesn’t argue with their objection about his family. He goes to the root: why they cannot believe.

No one can come to me. Key words. “Can” (dynatai) is about ability, not permission. It is not that no one may come, but that no one is able to come. Fallen human beings, left to themselves, are unable to come to Christ (3:3; 8:43; Romans 8:7–8).

Unless the Father who sent me draws him. “Draws” (helkō) is a strong word. It is used of drawing a net full of fish to land (21:6, 11), of drawing a sword (18:10), of dragging Paul and Silas into the marketplace (Acts 16:19). It is not a gentle suggestion that might be resisted, but an effective pull. God’s drawing does not force anyone against their will; it changes the will, so that the sinner comes gladly. That is what v. 45 will explain: the Father teaches, and the taught come.

And I will raise him up on the last day. The one who is drawn is the one who is raised. The same person runs from the beginning to the end: drawn, comes, raised. None drop out on the way.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that people who want to come to Christ are turned away because they are not drawn. Anyone who wants to come has already been drawn. Nor does it excuse unbelief: people do not come because they will not (5:40), and they are responsible for it.

Where Christians differ: is the Father’s drawing resistible? Arminians teach that God draws everyone (citing 12:32) with a grace that can be resisted, so that some who are drawn do not come. Verdict: in this verse the one who is drawn is the one who is raised up on the last day. If drawing could be resisted, the verse would promise resurrection to people who never come. The drawing is effectual. In 12:32 Jesus says he will draw “all people,” meaning all kinds of people, Gentiles as well as Jews (the Greeks of 12:20 have just asked to see him), not every single person. This is effectual calling: the Spirit’s work by which God persuades and enables us to embrace Jesus Christ, freely offered in the gospel.

In a sentence. Jesus told them to stop grumbling, because no one can come to him unless the Father who sent him draws him, and he will raise that one up on the last day.

On a Tuesday. If you have come to Christ, the Father drew you. Thank him. And when you share the gospel, pray: only the Father can draw.

parallels.desc: I will draw all people to myself

verseByVerse.quote: "It is written in the Prophets, 'And they will all be taught by God.' Everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me — not that anyone has seen the Father except he who is from God; he has seen the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is written in the Prophets, ‘And they will all be taught by God.’ Everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me — not that anyone has seen the Father except he who is from God; he has seen the Father.

It is written in the Prophets. The quotation is from Isaiah 54:13, a promise about the restored people of God in the new covenant age (compare Jeremiah 31:33–34).

And they will all be taught by God. “All” here means all God’s people, all the children of the new Jerusalem: in the new age, God himself teaches every one of them, not just prophets and priests.

Everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me. This explains what drawing is. The Father draws by teaching: he opens the mind and heart to hear and learn. And everyone who learns comes. Not some; everyone. Drawing is not force but inward teaching, which always succeeds. It is the same as the new birth (3:3–8) and the opening of Lydia’s heart (Acts 16:14).

Not that anyone has seen the Father except he who is from God. Jesus guards against a misunderstanding. Being taught by the Father doesn’t mean having visions of God. Only the Son has seen the Father (1:18). The Father teaches by pointing to the Son.

He has seen the Father. This is the authority of Jesus’ teaching: he speaks what he has seen.

In a sentence. The prophets promised that all God’s people would be taught by God, and everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to Jesus, the only one who has seen the Father.

For worship. The Father has taught you to come to the Son. Every true believer is a pupil of God.

parallels.desc: all your children shall be taught by the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes has eternal life. I am the bread of life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes has eternal life. I am the bread of life.

Truly, truly, I say to you. The solemn formula marks a summary of everything so far.

Whoever believes has eternal life. Simple and clear. Not whoever believes and does, but whoever believes. And has, now. Eternal life is the gift of God received by faith alone.

I am the bread of life. The great “I am” saying is repeated (v. 35). Everything in the discourse turns on this.

In a sentence. Jesus solemnly declared that whoever believes has eternal life, for he is the bread of life.

On a Tuesday. If you believe, you have eternal life today. Live from that, not towards it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died. This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that one may eat of it and not die."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died. This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that one may eat of it and not die.

Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died. The crowd had held up the manna as the great sign (v. 31). Jesus now points out its limit. It kept people alive for a day. It did not save them from death. The whole generation that ate it died in the wilderness, many in unbelief (Numbers 14:29; 1 Corinthians 10:5).

This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that one may eat of it and not die. Jesus is greater than the manna. The one who feeds on him will not die: not that he will escape the death of the body, but that death will not be the end (11:25–26). Eternal death is what is overcome.

In a sentence. Their fathers ate the manna and still died, but Jesus is the bread from heaven, so that whoever eats it will not die.

For worship. Moses’ bread fed bodies that died; Christ feeds souls that live for ever.

parallels.desc: your dead bodies shall fall in this wilderness

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh."
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh.

I am the living bread that came down from heaven. Living bread: bread that is alive, and gives life. A new form of the claim.

If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. Eating is a picture of believing (compare v. 35 with v. 47). As food becomes part of you and keeps you alive, so receiving Christ by faith unites you to him and gives you life.

And the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh. Key words. Here the discourse turns. “I will give”: future, looking to the cross. “For” (hyper) means on behalf of, in place of, the word of sacrifice (10:11, 15; 11:51–52). “My flesh”: his real human body (1:14), given up in death. The bread is not just Jesus’ teaching or his life, but his death. To feed on Christ is to trust in his sacrifice.

For the life of the world. “The world” in John is humanity in its rebellion against God, Gentiles as well as Jews. Christ’s death is not for Israel alone but for people of every nation (11:51–52).

Where Christians differ: does this mean Christ died for everyone alike? Some take “for the life of the world” to mean that Christ died equally for every human being. Verdict: in John, Christ lays down his life “for the sheep” (10:11, 15), for those the Father has given him (17:9, 19). “The world” here stresses the extent of his people, from every nation, and the greatness of the gift, not that every individual is saved. His death actually gives life, and it gives it to everyone who feeds on him. This is definite atonement: the death that truly secures life for all who are his.

In a sentence. Jesus is the living bread from heaven, and whoever eats it will live for ever, and the bread he will give for the life of the world is his flesh, given in death.

On a Tuesday. The bread of life was broken on the cross. Every time you trust Christ’s death for you, you are feeding on him.

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews then disputed among themselves, saying, "How can this man give us his flesh to eat?" So Jesus said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jews then disputed among themselves, saying, “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” So Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you.”

The Jews then disputed among themselves. “Disputed” (machomai) means fought, quarrelled. The grumbling has become open argument.

How can this man give us his flesh to eat? They take him literally and crudely, as Nicodemus took the new birth (3:4) and the woman took living water (4:11). The misunderstanding is part of John’s method: it leads to deeper teaching.

Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood. Jesus doesn’t soften it. He sharpens it. Now he adds the blood. Setting and background: drinking blood was strictly forbidden in the law (Genesis 9:4; Leviticus 17:10–14), because the life is in the blood. To a Jewish ear these words were shocking. Flesh and blood separated speak of a violent death: the body broken and the blood poured out. Jesus is speaking of his death as a sacrifice. To eat his flesh and drink his blood is to receive his death as your life, to take it into yourself by faith, to depend on it entirely.

You have no life in you. There is no other way to life. Without union with Christ crucified, there is only death.

What it does not mean. It does not mean literal eating of Jesus’ physical body. The crowd thought that, and Jesus corrects it in v. 63: the flesh is no help at all; his words are spirit. Nor does it mean that everyone who takes the Lord’s Supper has eternal life, or that no one who has not taken it can be saved. The thief on the cross never took it, and was with Christ that day.

Where Christians differ: John 6 and the Lord’s Supper. Roman Catholics read these verses as teaching transubstantiation, the bread and wine becoming Christ’s actual body and blood; Lutherans see Christ’s body present in, with and under the elements; some see here only a symbol of faith. Verdict: the Supper had not yet been instituted, and Jesus speaks to the crowd of something they must do now, on pain of having no life. Feeding on Christ is believing in him (vv. 35, 40, 47). John 6 is about faith, not first about the sacrament. Yet the same feeding is what happens at the Supper: there, as Calvin taught, believers by the Spirit truly feed on Christ’s body and blood, not by a change in the bread, but by being lifted up in faith to the living Christ, who nourishes them with himself. The Supper is a visible, sealing form of what John 6 describes.

In a sentence. When the Jews argued about how he could give his flesh to eat, Jesus said that unless they eat the flesh and drink the blood of the Son of Man, they have no life in them.

For worship. There is no life in us apart from Christ crucified. Feed on him by faith, daily, and at his table.
verseByVerse.note: Drinking blood was forbidden by the law, which made these words shocking.

parallels.desc: the life is in the blood

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day.

Whoever feeds on my flesh. Key words. The verb changes here from the usual word for eat (esthiō, phagein) to trōgō, to chew or munch. Some take it as a deliberately vivid, even crude word, insisting on the reality of the feeding. Others note it simply serves as the present tense of eating in later Greek. Either way, the present tense matters: it is the ongoing feeding of a life of faith, not a single act.

And drinks my blood has eternal life. The positive promise of v. 53: has eternal life now.

And I will raise him up on the last day. And resurrection to come. Compare v. 40: whoever looks on the Son and believes has eternal life and will be raised. The parallel shows what feeding means: believing.

In a sentence. Whoever feeds on Jesus’ flesh and drinks his blood has eternal life, and he will raise him up on the last day.

On a Tuesday. Faith is not a one-time meal. Keep feeding on Christ in his word, in prayer, at his table.

parallels.desc: a participation in the blood of Christ

verseByVerse.quote: "For my flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink. Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For my flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink. Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him.

For my flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink. “True” (alēthēs): real, genuine. Ordinary food is a shadow; Christ is the reality. He satisfies what bread only points to.

Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him. Key words. “Abides” (menō), remains, dwells: one of John’s great words (15:4–10; 1 John 2:24, 27). Feeding leads to union.
