As food becomes part of the body, the believer is joined to Christ, and Christ lives in the believer. This mutual indwelling is the heart of salvation: union with Christ.

In a sentence. Jesus’ flesh is real food and his blood real drink, and whoever feeds on them lives in him, and he in them.

For worship. You are in Christ, and Christ is in you. This is your life.

parallels.desc: abide in me

verseByVerse.quote: "As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever feeds on me, he also will live because of me. This is the bread that came down from heaven, not like the bread the fathers ate, and died. Whoever feeds on this bread will live forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever feeds on me, he also will live because of me. This is the bread that came down from heaven, not like the bread the fathers ate, and died. Whoever feeds on this bread will live forever.

As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father. The Son’s life comes from the Father (5:26). The Father is the living God, the fountain of life.

So whoever feeds on me, he also will live because of me. And as the Son lives from the Father, so the believer lives from the Son. Life flows from the Father, through the Son, to the believer. “Feeds on me”: now not flesh and blood but simply “me.” The point is the person of Christ, received.

This is the bread that came down from heaven, not like the bread the fathers ate, and died. The discourse ends where it began, with the manna (vv. 31–32). The contrast is complete.

Whoever feeds on this bread will live forever. The final word of the sermon: life for ever.

In a sentence. As the Son lives because of the Father, so whoever feeds on the Son will live because of him; unlike the manna, which could not keep the fathers from death, this bread gives life for ever.

On a Tuesday. Your life depends on Christ as completely as his depends on the Father. Draw from him today.

parallels.desc: Christ who lives in me

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said these things in the synagogue, as he taught at Capernaum. When many of his disciples heard it, they said, "This is a hard saying; who can listen to it?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus said these things in the synagogue, as he taught at Capernaum. When many of his disciples heard it, they said, “This is a hard saying; who can listen to it?”

Jesus said these things in the synagogue, as he taught at Capernaum. Setting and background. The whole discourse was given in the synagogue at Capernaum, Jesus’ base in Galilee. The remains of a later white limestone synagogue stand there, built on the dark basalt foundations of an earlier one, probably the one Jesus taught in.

When many of his disciples heard it. Not the Twelve, but a wider circle of followers. Being called a disciple did not mean being a true believer (v. 64).

This is a hard saying. Key words. “Hard” (sklēros) means harsh, offensive, unacceptable. It was not hard to understand; it was hard to accept. A crucified Messiah, a salvation received by depending wholly on him, and a God who must draw: these were offensive.

Who can listen to it? “Listen” here means accept, obey. They will not take it.

In a sentence. Jesus taught this in the synagogue at Capernaum, and many of his disciples said it was a hard saying that no one could accept.

On a Tuesday. Some of what Jesus says will offend you. The question is not whether it is hard, but whether it is true.
verseByVerse.note: The remains of a later synagogue at Capernaum stand on the foundations of an earlier one, perhaps the one where Jesus taught.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus, knowing in himself that his disciples were grumbling about this, said to them, "Do you take offense at this? Then what if you were to see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Jesus, knowing in himself that his disciples were grumbling about this, said to them, “Do you take offense at this? Then what if you were to see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?”

Knowing in himself that his disciples were grumbling about this. Jesus knows what is in people (2:24–25). The disciples are now grumbling like the crowd (v. 41).

Do you take offense at this? “Offense” (skandalizō): to trip, to stumble. The cross is the great stumbling block (1 Corinthians 1:23).

Then what if you were to see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before? The sentence is left unfinished in Greek. Two readings are possible. It could mean: if this offends you, how much more will his ascent, the full revelation of his heavenly origin, overwhelm you? Or: when you see him ascend, you will understand that he truly came from heaven, and that his words about his flesh were not about literal eating. In John, his going up includes the cross, resurrection and ascension together (3:13–14; 12:32–34). Either way, the ascension proves his claim that he came down from heaven (vv. 38, 42), and it shows that his flesh would not stay on earth to be literally eaten.

In a sentence. Knowing that his disciples were grumbling, Jesus asked whether they were offended, and what they would say if they saw the Son of Man ascending to where he was before.

For worship. The one who came down has gone up. Our Saviour reigns in heaven, where he was before.

verseByVerse.quote: "It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life. But there are some of you who do not believe." (For Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was who would betray him.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life. But there are some of you who do not believe. (For Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was who would betray him.)

It is the Spirit who gives life. Key words. Life comes from the Holy Spirit, as in the new birth (3:5–8). The Spirit is the one who makes the words of Jesus effective.

The flesh is no help at all. “Flesh” here means human nature on its own, apart from the Spirit, not Jesus’ own flesh given for the world (v. 51), which is the source of life. Merely human understanding, human effort, or literal physical eating, accomplishes nothing for salvation. This shuts out a crudely physical reading of the discourse.

The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life. Jesus’ teaching carries the Spirit and gives life. We feed on Christ by receiving his words in faith.

But there are some of you who do not believe. Among his disciples are unbelievers.

For Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was who would betray him. John’s comment. Jesus was not taken by surprise, not even by Judas. “From the beginning” probably means from the start of his ministry, or of their following. He chose the Twelve knowing what Judas would do (v. 70; 13:18).

In a sentence. Jesus said it is the Spirit who gives life, not the flesh, and his words are spirit and life, but some of them did not believe, for he knew from the beginning who did not believe and who would betray him.

On a Tuesday. Read Christ’s words and ask the Spirit to make them life to you. Without the Spirit, even the Bible is only ink.
verseByVerse.note: “Flesh” here means human nature on its own, apart from the Spirit.

parallels.desc: the Spirit gives life

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "This is why I told you that no one can come to me unless it is granted him by the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said, “This is why I told you that no one can come to me unless it is granted him by the Father.”

This is why I told you. The unbelief of some disciples is the explanation of v. 44.

No one can come to me unless it is granted him by the Father. Key words. “Granted” (dedomenon), given as a gift. Coming to Christ, faith itself, is a gift of God (Ephesians 2:8; Philippians 1:29). Three times in this chapter Jesus says it: the Father gives (v. 37), the Father draws (v. 44), the Father grants (v. 65). Unbelief is not God’s failure but human refusal; faith is not human achievement but God’s gift.

In a sentence. Jesus said that this was why no one can come to him unless the Father grants it.

For worship. Your faith is the Father’s gift. Give him the glory for it.

verseByVerse.quote: After this many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him. So Jesus said to the twelve, "Do you want to go away as well?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him. So Jesus said to the twelve, “Do you want to go away as well?”

After this many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him. The turning point of Jesus’ Galilean ministry. The day began with five thousand fed and a crowd wanting to make him king (v. 15). It ends with many walking away. “Turned back” literally means went away to the things behind, back to their old life. They had followed Jesus for bread and a political Messiah, not for himself. This is not true believers falling away, but false disciples being revealed (v. 64; 1 John 2:19).

So Jesus said to the twelve. The first mention of “the twelve” in John.

Do you want to go away as well? The Greek form expects the answer no. Jesus doesn’t beg them to stay or soften his teaching. He tests them, and invites a confession.

In a sentence. Many of his disciples turned back and stopped following him, so Jesus asked the Twelve whether they wanted to go away too.

On a Tuesday. Popularity is no measure of truth. Jesus let the crowds go rather than change his message. Do not follow a Christ made smaller to keep the crowd.

verseByVerse.quote: Simon Peter answered him, "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon Peter answered him, “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life.”

Simon Peter answered him. Peter speaks for the Twelve, as he does in the other Gospels (Matthew 16:16).

Lord, to whom shall we go? One of the great confessions of faith. Peter doesn’t claim to understand everything Jesus has said. But he knows there is no alternative. There is no one else to go to.

You have the words of eternal life. Peter has heard v. 63: Jesus’ words are spirit and life. He has believed it. Only Jesus has words that give eternal life.

In a sentence. Peter answered that there was no one else to go to, because Jesus has the words of eternal life.

For worship. When you don’t understand, and when others walk away, say with Peter: Lord, to whom shall we go?

parallels.desc: all the words of this Life

verseByVerse.quote: "and we have believed, and have come to know, that you are the Holy One of God." Jesus answered them, "Did I not choose you, the twelve? And yet one of you is a devil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
and we have believed, and have come to know, that you are the Holy One of God.” Jesus answered them, “Did I not choose you, the twelve? And yet one of you is a devil.”

And we have believed, and have come to know. Both verbs are in the perfect tense: we have come to believe and still do; we have come to know and still know. Faith and knowledge go together. Peter speaks of a settled conviction.

That you are the Holy One of God. Key words. “The Holy One of God” is a title used by a demon in Mark 1:24. It marks Jesus as set apart, belonging to God in a unique way, the one consecrated and sent by the Father (10:36). Later manuscripts read “the Christ, the Son of the living God,” borrowed from Matthew 16:16. Textual note: the earliest and best manuscripts read “the Holy One of God,” and the ESV rightly follows them.

Did I not choose you, the twelve? Jesus’ reply both encourages and warns. He chose them, not they him (15:16).

And yet one of you is a devil. “Devil” (diabolos): one who acts for the devil, an adversary. Not that Judas was a demon, but that he was the devil’s tool (13:2, 27). The choice of Judas was a choice to be an apostle, not the electing love that saves (17:12). Even among the twelve there was a traitor. Peter’s confession is true, but it is not the whole story of the Twelve.

In a sentence. Peter confessed that they had believed and knew Jesus to be the Holy One of God, and Jesus answered that he had chosen the Twelve, yet one of them was a devil.

On a Tuesday. Hold your confession firmly, and examine yourself humbly. Judas walked beside Jesus for three years.

parallels.desc: Peter’s confession

verseByVerse.quote: He spoke of Judas the son of Simon Iscariot, for he, one of the twelve, was going to betray him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He spoke of Judas the son of Simon Iscariot, for he, one of the twelve, was going to betray him.

He spoke of Judas the son of Simon Iscariot. “Iscariot” is often taken to mean man of Kerioth, a town in Judea (Joshua 15:25). If so, Judas was the only Judean among the Twelve, the rest being Galileans.

For he, one of the twelve, was going to betray him. “One of the twelve”: the tragedy is in the words. The betrayer was an insider. Jesus knew, and kept him close, and washed his feet (13:5, 26). Judas’ betrayal fulfilled Scripture (13:18; Psalm 41:9), yet he was fully responsible for it (Mark 14:21). God’s sovereignty and human guilt stand together here too.

In a sentence. Jesus was speaking of Judas son of Simon Iscariot, who, though one of the Twelve, was going to betray him.

For worship. Jesus loved and kept close the very man who would betray him. Such patience should melt us.
verseByVerse.note: “Iscariot” is often taken to mean “man of Kerioth,” a town in Judea, but that is uncertain.

6.title: The Bread of Life
6.text: <sup>1</sup>After this Jesus went away to the other side of the Sea of Galilee, which is the Sea of Tiberias.<sup>2</sup>And a large crowd was following him, because they saw the signs that he was doing on the sick.<sup>3</sup>Jesus went up on the mountain, and there he sat down with his disciples.<sup>4</sup>Now the Passover, the feast of the Jews, was at hand.<sup>5</sup>Lifting up his eyes, then, and seeing that a large crowd was coming toward him, Jesus said to Philip, “Where are we to buy bread, so that these people may eat?”<sup>6</sup>He said this to test him, for he himself knew what he would do.<sup>7</sup>Philip answered him, “Two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough for each of them to get a little.”<sup>8</sup>One of his disciples, Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, said to him,<sup>9</sup>“There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are they for so many?”<sup>10</sup>Jesus said, “Have the people sit down.” Now there was much grass in the place. So the men sat down, about five thousand in number.<sup>11</sup>Jesus then took the loaves, and when he had given thanks, he distributed them to those who were seated. So also the fish, as much as they wanted.<sup>12</sup>And when they had eaten their fill, he told his disciples, “Gather up the leftover fragments, that nothing may be lost.”<sup>13</sup>So they gathered them up and filled twelve baskets with fragments from the five barley loaves left by those who had eaten.<sup>14</sup>When the people saw the sign that he had done, they said, “This is indeed the Prophet who is to come into the world!”<sup>15</sup>Perceiving then that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, Jesus withdrew again to the mountain by himself.<sup>16</sup>When evening came, his disciples went down to the sea,<sup>17</sup>got into a boat, and started across the sea to Capernaum. It was now dark, and Jesus had not yet come to them.<sup>18</sup>The sea became rough because a strong wind was blowing.<sup>19</sup>When they had rowed about three or four miles, they saw Jesus walking on the sea and coming near the boat, and they were frightened.<sup>20</sup>But he said to them, “It is I; do not be afraid.”<sup>21</sup>Then they were glad to take him into the boat, and immediately the boat was at the land to which they were going.<sup>22</sup>On the next day the crowd that remained on the other side of the sea saw that there had been only one boat there, and that Jesus had not entered the boat with his disciples, but that his disciples had gone away alone.<sup>23</sup>Other boats from Tiberias came near the place where they had eaten the bread after the Lord had given thanks.<sup>24</sup>So when the crowd saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples, they themselves got into the boats and went to Capernaum, seeking Jesus.<sup>25</sup>When they found him on the other side of the sea, they said to him, “Rabbi, when did you come here?”<sup>26</sup>Jesus answered them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, you are seeking me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate your fill of the loaves.<sup>27</sup>Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give to you. For on him God the Father has set his seal.”<sup>28</sup>Then they said to him, “What must we do, to be doing the works of God?”<sup>29</sup>Jesus answered them, “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he has sent.”<sup>30</sup>So they said to him, “Then what sign do you do, that we may see and believe you? What work do you perform?<sup>31</sup>Our fathers ate the manna in the wilderness; as it is written, ’He gave them bread from heaven to eat.’”<sup>32</sup>Jesus then said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven.<sup>33</sup>For the bread of God is he who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.”<sup>34</sup>They said to him, “Sir, give us this bread always.”<sup>35</sup>Jesus said to them, “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst.<sup>36</sup>But I said to you that you have seen me and yet do not believe.<sup>37</sup>All that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out.<sup>38</sup>For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me.<sup>39</sup>And this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day.<sup>40</sup>For this is the will of my Father, that everyone who looks on the Son and believes in him should have eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day.”<sup>41</sup>So the Jews grumbled about him, because he said, “I am the bread that came down from heaven.”<sup>42</sup>They said, “Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How does he now say, ’I have come down from heaven’?”<sup>43</sup>Jesus answered them, “Do not grumble among yourselves.<sup>44</sup>No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him. And I will raise him up on the last day.<sup>45</sup>It is written in the Prophets, ’And they will all be taught by God.’ Everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me—<sup>46</sup>not that anyone has seen the Father except he who is from God; he has seen the Father.<sup>47</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes has eternal life.<sup>48</sup>I am the bread of life.<sup>49</sup>Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died.<sup>50</sup>This is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that one may eat of it and not die.<sup>51</sup>I am the living bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever. And the bread that I will give for the life of the world is my flesh.”<sup>52</sup>The Jews then disputed among themselves, saying, “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?”<sup>53</sup>So Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you.<sup>54</sup>Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him up on the last day.<sup>55</sup>For my flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink.<sup>56</sup>Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him.<sup>57</sup>As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever feeds on me, he also will live because of me.<sup>58</sup>This is the bread that came down from heaven, not like the bread the fathers ate, and died. Whoever feeds on this bread will live forever.”<sup>59</sup>Jesus said these things in the synagogue, as he taught at Capernaum.<sup>60</sup>When many of his disciples heard it, they said, “This is a hard saying; who can listen to it?”<sup>61</sup>But Jesus, knowing in himself that his disciples were grumbling about this, said to them, “Do you take offense at this?<sup>62</sup>Then what if you were to see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?<sup>63</sup>It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is no help at all. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.<sup>64</sup>But there are some of you who do not believe.” (For Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who did not believe, and who it was who would betray him.)<sup>65</sup>And he said, “This is why I told you that no one can come to me unless it is granted him by the Father.”<sup>66</sup>After this many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him.<sup>67</sup>So Jesus said to the twelve, “Do you want to go away as well?”<sup>68</sup>Simon Peter answered him, “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life,<sup>69</sup>and we have believed, and have come to know, that you are the Holy One of God.”<sup>70</sup>Jesus answered them, “Did I not choose you, the twelve? And yet one of you is a devil.”<sup>71</sup>He spoke of Judas the son of Simon Iscariot, for he, one of the twelve, was going to betray him.
6.overview:
The feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle, apart from the resurrection, recorded in all four Gospels. John sets it near Passover and tells it so that it opens into one of Jesus’ longest discourses. On a hillside by the Sea of Galilee Jesus feeds a vast crowd from a boy’s five barley loaves and two fish, and twelve baskets of leftovers are gathered. The crowd hails him as the Prophet like Moses and tries to force him to be their king, so he withdraws. That night, as his disciples row against a storm, he comes to them walking on the water and says, “It is I; do not be afraid,” words that echo the divine name.

Next day, in the synagogue at Capernaum, the crowd that ate the bread wants more. Jesus tells them to work for food that lasts, and that the work God requires is to believe in the one he has sent. They ask for a sign like the manna; he replies, “I am the bread of life.” All the Father gives him will come to him, and he will lose none of them but raise them up on the last day; no one can come unless the Father draws him. Then he says that the bread he will give is his flesh for the life of the world, and that unless they eat his flesh and drink his blood they have no life. Many disciples find this too hard and leave. When Jesus asks the Twelve whether they will go too, Peter answers for them all: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life.” Yet even among the Twelve is one who will betray him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With his life in danger in Judea, Jesus stays in Galilee until the Feast of Booths. His unbelieving brothers press him to go and make himself known; he answers that his time is not yet, and goes up privately later. In Jerusalem the crowds argue about him in hushed tones. Midway through the feast he teaches in the temple, and the leaders marvel at his learning. He says his teaching is from God, recognisable to anyone who wants to do God’s will; their anger at his Sabbath healing is inconsistent, since they circumcise on the Sabbath. People debate whether he could be the Messiah, since they think they know his origins. Jesus declares that he comes from the true God, whom they do not know. Attempts to arrest him fail, for his hour has not come, though many believe. When officers are sent, he speaks of going where they cannot follow. On the great last day he invites the thirsty to come to him and drink, promising rivers of living water, meaning the Spirit, to be given after his glorification. The crowd divides over whether he is the Prophet or the Christ, or merely a Galilean. The officers return saying no one has ever spoken like him. The Pharisees scorn them and the crowd, and when Nicodemus pleads for a fair hearing, they mock him as a Galilean.
verseByVerse.theology: The controversy in John 7 turns on the question of Jesus's origins and authority. Where is he from? Did he come from God or from himself? The crowd is divided: some say he is a good man; others say he leads the people astray. Jesus's teaching in the temple provokes astonishment: 'How is it that this man has learning, when he has never studied?' His answer is theological: his teaching is not his own but the Father's, and the one who seeks to do God's will will recognize its divine origin. The authority question and the origin question are ultimately the same question: who sent him?
verseByVerse.examples: The Feast of Tabernacles is the most eschatological of the Jewish festivals — it looks forward to the final harvest, the ultimate ingathering. Jesus's claim at the climax of the feast ('out of his heart will flow rivers of living water') is the claim to be the fulfillment of Israel's end-times hope. The officers who were sent to arrest Jesus and returned saying 'no one ever spoke like this man' (v. 46) give one of the most powerful testimonies to the authority of Jesus's teaching in the entire Gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: After this Jesus went about in Galilee. He would not go about in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him. Now the Jews' Feast of Booths was at hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus avoids Judea, where his life is in danger, as the Feast of Booths approaches.

Six months. From Passover (6:4) to Booths, in September or October: a period John passes over in a sentence.

The Feast of Booths. Sukkot (Leviticus 23:33–43; Deuteronomy 16:13–15), the most joyful of the pilgrim feasts. For eight days people lived in shelters of branches, recalling the wilderness, and celebrated the harvest. Daily water was carried from the Pool of Siloam and poured at the altar with prayers for rain, and huge lamps lit the temple courts. Both rituals lie behind Jesus’ words in 7:37–39 and 8:12.

Not afraid but wise. Jesus avoids danger until his hour.
verseByVerse.note: The Feast of Booths (Tabernacles) was the joyful autumn harvest festival. For a week people lived in shelters made of branches, remembering Israel’s years in the wilderness.

parallels.desc: the Feast of Booths

verseByVerse.quote: So his brothers said to him, "Leave here and go to Judea, that your disciples also may see the works you are doing. For no one works in secret if he seeks to be known openly. If you do these things, show yourself to the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
His brothers urge him to seek publicity in Jerusalem.

His brothers. James, Joseph, Simon and Judas (Mark 6:3).

Show yourself. Their advice is worldly: maximise exposure, go to the capital at the busiest time. They want a celebrity, perhaps reflected glory for the family.

On a Tuesday. Not every good opportunity for publicity is God’s timing. Seek his will before others’ expectations.
verseByVerse.note: His brothers were James, Joses, Judas and Simon.

verseByVerse.quote: For not even his brothers believed in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even Jesus’ own brothers do not yet believe in him.

Family unbelief. Those who grew up with him did not believe (Mark 3:21). After the resurrection, they did: Jesus appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7), the brothers prayed with the disciples (Acts 1:14), and James led the Jerusalem church and wrote a letter, as perhaps did Jude.

On a Tuesday. Keep praying for unbelieving family. Jesus’ own brothers took years, and a resurrection, to believe.
verseByVerse.note: James later led the church in Jerusalem, and the brothers were among the believers after the resurrection.

parallels.desc: with Mary and his brothers
he appeared to James

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "My time has not yet come, but your time is always here. The world cannot hate you, but it hates me because I testify about it that its works are evil."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus moves on his Father’s timetable, and the world hates him for exposing its evil.

My time. Kairos, the right moment, close to “my hour” (2:4). His movements are governed by the Father.

Your time is always here. Living by the world’s rules, they can come and go as they please.

The world hates me. Because he exposes it (3:19–20). The world loves its own (15:18–19).

On a Tuesday. If no one is ever uncomfortable with your faith, ask whether you are testifying to anything.

parallels.desc: if the world hates you

verseByVerse.quote: "You go up to the feast. I am not going up to this feast, for my time has not yet fully come." After saying this, he remained in Galilee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus refuses to go up on his brothers’ terms.

Did Jesus deceive them? He later goes (v. 10). Some see a change of plan; others say he refused to go up as they suggested, publicly, as a pilgrim seeking acclaim, or that he meant he would not go up in the sense of his final “going up” to the Father (20:17, the same verb). Textual note. Many manuscripts read “not yet going up” (ESV margin), probably a scribal attempt to remove the difficulty. Verdict: “not” is original; Jesus refused their agenda, not the feast itself, and went later in a different way.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add “yet” — “I am not yet going up.”

verseByVerse.quote: But after his brothers had gone up to the feast, then he also went up, not publicly but in private. The Jews were looking for him at the feast, and saying, "Where is he?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He goes up privately, and everyone is looking for him.

In private. Not in a pilgrim caravan, and not as a celebrity.

Where is he? Everyone is talking about him: the authorities to arrest him, the crowds out of curiosity.

verseByVerse.quote: And there was much muttering about him among the people. While some said, "He is a good man," others said, "No, he is leading the people astray." Yet for fear of the Jews no one spoke openly of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowds argue quietly about whether he is good or a deceiver.

Good or a deceiver? The two poles of opinion. Leading the people astray was a capital charge (Deuteronomy 13:1–5), and later Jewish sources accused Jesus of it.

C. S. Lewis. “A good man” is the one option Jesus does not leave open: a man who claimed what he claimed is either a liar, a lunatic or Lord.

Fear. Fear of authority silences people (9:22; 12:42; 19:38).

parallels.desc: a prophet who leads you astray
that impostor

verseByVerse.quote: About the middle of the feast Jesus went up into the temple and began teaching. The Jews therefore marveled, saying, "How is it that this man has learning, when he has never studied?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Midway through the feast Jesus teaches in the temple with learning that amazes them.

Never studied. He had not trained under a recognised rabbi, as Paul did under Gamaliel. Yet his knowledge of Scripture astonished them (Acts 4:13).

On a Tuesday. Formal qualifications are good, but they are not the measure of truth. Listen to faithful teachers whatever their credentials; and if you have credentials, do not trust them.
verseByVerse.note: “Never studied” means he had not been trained under a recognised rabbi.

parallels.desc: uneducated, common men

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus answered them, "My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me. If anyone's will is to do God's will, he will know whether the teaching is from God or whether I am speaking on my own authority."
verseByVerse.commentary:
His teaching is from God, and anyone willing to do God’s will can recognise it.

Not mine. His authority is not a school but his Father.

Willing, then knowing. The obstacle to recognising truth is often moral, not intellectual. Those who sincerely want to do God’s will come to recognise Jesus’ voice (10:4, 27).

On a Tuesday. If you are unsure about Christ, ask yourself: am I willing to do God’s will if it is shown to me? Start there, and pray.

verseByVerse.quote: "The one who speaks on his own authority seeks his own glory; but the one who seeks the glory of him who sent him is true, and in him there is no falsehood. Has not Moses given you the law? Yet none of you keeps the law. Why do you seek to kill me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
True teachers seek God’s glory; his opponents break the law while plotting to kill him.

A test of teachers. Whose glory do they seek? (5:41–44.)

None of you keeps the law. Their plot to kill him breaks the sixth commandment while claiming to defend the fourth.

verseByVerse.quote: The crowd answered, "You have a demon! Who is seeking to kill you?" Jesus answered them, "I did one work, and you all marvel at it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd accuses him of paranoia, and he points to the healing that offended them.

You have a demon. Perhaps meaning “you’re mad” or “paranoid”. The crowd, mostly pilgrims, may not know the leaders’ plans.

One work. The healing at Bethesda on the Sabbath (5:1–9), eighteen months earlier, still the talk of Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.note: The “one work” is the healing at the pool on the Sabbath.

verseByVerse.quote: "Moses gave you circumcision (not that it is from Moses, but from the fathers), and you circumcise a man on the Sabbath."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the law of Moses allows circumcision on the Sabbath.

From the fathers. Circumcision began with Abraham (Genesis 17:10–14), before Moses (Leviticus 12:3).

On the Sabbath. If the eighth day after birth fell on a Sabbath, rabbis ruled that circumcision overrode the Sabbath rest.
verseByVerse.note: Circumcision on the eighth day went ahead even when that day was a Sabbath. It began with Abraham, before Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: "If on the Sabbath a man receives circumcision, so that the law of Moses may not be broken, are you angry with me because on the Sabbath I made a man's whole body well? Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If they circumcise on the Sabbath, they should not condemn him for healing a whole man; they must judge rightly.

From the lesser to the greater. A rabbinic style of argument. If one part of the body may be “perfected” on the Sabbath, how much more the whole man?

Judge rightly. Do not judge superficially (1 Samuel 16:7; Isaiah 11:3).

What it does not mean. “Judge not” (Matthew 7:1) does not forbid all moral judgment. Jesus commands right judgment here.

On a Tuesday. Before criticising, look beyond appearances to the heart of the matter.

parallels.desc: judge righteously

verseByVerse.quote: Some of the people of Jerusalem therefore said, "Is not this the man whom they seek to kill? And here he is, speaking openly, and they say nothing to him! Can it be that the authorities really know that this is the Christ?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem’s people wonder whether the authorities think he is the Messiah.

Jerusalem residents. Unlike pilgrims, they know of the plot.

Openly. The authorities’ silence puzzles them.

verseByVerse.quote: "But we know where this man comes from, and when the Christ appears, no one will know where he comes from."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They think they know where Jesus comes from.

A hidden Messiah. Some Jewish traditions expected the Messiah to be hidden until he suddenly appeared (compare Malachi 3:1). Others, by contrast, knew he would come from Bethlehem (v. 42).

Irony. They think they know where Jesus is from, Nazareth, but do not know his true origin, from the Father.
verseByVerse.note: Some expected the Messiah to appear suddenly from hiding.

verseByVerse.quote: "So Jesus proclaimed, as he taught in the temple, 'You know me, and you know where I come from. But I have not come of my own accord. He who sent me is true, and him you do not know. I know him, for I come from him, and he sent me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They know his earthly home, but not the Father who sent him.

Cried out. A loud, public proclamation.

You know … you do not know. Perhaps ironic: “So you know me, do you?” They know his earthly home but not his Father.

I know him. Jesus alone truly knows the Father (1:18; Matthew 11:27).

verseByVerse.quote: So they were seeking to arrest him, but no one laid a hand on him, because his hour had not yet come. Yet many of the people believed in him. They said, "When the Christ appears, will he do more signs than this man has done?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one can seize him before his hour, and many believe.

His hour. God’s timetable governs events (8:20). Jesus is not a victim of circumstances.

Many believed. Faith of a sort, based on signs (2:23). But it is a beginning.

For worship. No one could touch Jesus before the Father’s time, and no one can touch you outside it (Psalm 31:15).

parallels.desc: his hour had come

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees heard the crowd muttering these things about him, and the chief priests and Pharisees sent officers to arrest him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The authorities send officers to arrest him.

An alliance. Chief priests (Sadducees) and Pharisees, usually rivals, unite against Jesus.

Officers. The Levite temple guard.
verseByVerse.note: The officers were the temple police.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus then said, "I will be with you a little longer, and then I am going to him who sent me. You will seek me and you will not find me. Where I am you cannot come."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus will soon return to the Father, where they cannot come.

A little longer. About six months until the cross.

Going to him who sent me. His death, resurrection and ascension as a return to the Father (13:1; 16:28).

You cannot come. Not merely physically: unbelief cannot follow him to the Father (8:21). Contrast what he says to the disciples (13:36; 14:3).

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews said to one another, "Where does this man intend to go that we will not find him? Does he intend to go to the Dispersion among the Greeks and teach the Greeks? What does he mean by saying, 'You will seek me and you will not find me,' and, 'Where I am you cannot come'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They mock the idea that he might teach the Greeks, not knowing that he will.

The Dispersion. Jews living outside the land, across the Greek-speaking world.

Unconscious prophecy. They mock, but it came true: through his apostles, Jesus did teach the Greeks (12:20–24; Acts). Like Caiaphas (11:49–52), they spoke better than they knew.
verseByVerse.note: The Dispersion means the Jews living scattered outside the land among the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: On the last day of the feast, the great day, Jesus stood up and cried out, "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, 'Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the great day of the feast Jesus calls the thirsty to come to him and drink, promising rivers of living water.

The water ceremony. Each morning of the feast a priest drew water from the Pool of Siloam in a golden pitcher and poured it at the altar, while the choir sang Isaiah 12:3: with joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation. It recalled the water from the rock in the wilderness (Exodus 17:6) and prayed for rain and for the promised outpouring (Zechariah 14:8; Ezekiel 47:1–12).

Stood and cried out. Rabbis sat to teach; Jesus stands and shouts, at the climax of the festival.

Come to me. Not to the temple or the ritual, but to him (Isaiah 55:1).

Out of whose heart? The Greek can be punctuated two ways: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me, and let him who believes in me drink. As Scripture says, out of his heart…” (meaning Christ’s heart, the source of the water, as the rock was, 1 Corinthians 10:4; and from his pierced side, 19:34); or (ESV) “Whoever believes in me… out of his heart” (meaning the believer’s, who becomes a channel of the Spirit to others, 4:14). Verdict: both are ancient and true; the Christological reading fits the stress on Jesus as the source, and the Spirit flows from him through believers.

As the Scripture said. No single verse matches; probably a combination of Ezekiel 47, Zechariah 14:8 and the rock in the wilderness.

For worship. Are you thirsty, dry, empty? Come to Jesus and drink.
verseByVerse.note: Later Jewish writings describe water being carried from the pool of Siloam and poured out at the altar each day of the feast. No single verse says these exact words; Jesus draws on several prophecies. The ESV notes a different punctuation that makes Jesus himself the source of the water.

parallels.desc: come to the waters
water flowing from the temple
living waters from Jerusalem

verseByVerse.quote: Now this he said about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive, for as yet the Spirit had not been given, because Jesus was not yet glorified.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The living water is the Spirit, to be given when Jesus is glorified.

John explains. The living water is the Holy Spirit (compare 4:10, 14).

Not yet. Literally “the Spirit was not yet”. The Spirit existed and worked in the Old Testament (Psalm 51:11; Numbers 11:25), but his full outpouring on all God’s people awaited Jesus’ glorification through the cross and resurrection (20:22; Acts 2:33).

Textual note. Some manuscripts add “given” or “upon them” to clarify. Verdict: the shorter, harder reading is original; translations rightly add “given” for sense.

Where Christians differ: the Spirit in the Old Testament. Some hold that Old Testament believers were not indwelt by the Spirit; others that they were regenerated by the Spirit, but without the fullness of the new covenant. Verdict: the Spirit gave new life to believers in every age (3:5, which Nicodemus should have known), but the indwelling fullness and universal gift belong to the new covenant after Pentecost.

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard these words, some of the people said, "This really is the Prophet." Others said, "This is the Christ." But some said, "Is the Christ to come from Galilee?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd is divided over whether he is the Prophet or the Messiah.

The Prophet and the Christ. Some saw them as two figures (1:20–21). Jesus is both.

From Galilee? They know only his upbringing.
verseByVerse.note: “The Prophet” is the prophet like Moses whom Moses promised.

verseByVerse.quote: "Has not the Scripture said that the Christ comes from the offspring of David, and comes from Bethlehem, the village where David was?" So there was a division among the people over him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some object that the Messiah comes from Bethlehem, unaware that Jesus does.

Bethlehem. Micah 5:2; 2 Samuel 7:12–16. John’s readers know that Jesus was born in Bethlehem and was of David’s line (Matthew 2:1–6; Luke 2:4). John lets the irony stand: the objection is true, and Jesus fulfils it.

Division. Schisma. Jesus divides people (9:16; 10:19; Luke 12:51).

On a Tuesday. When people dismiss Jesus on a point of fact, check the facts. The answer is often already known.
verseByVerse.note: They did not know that Jesus had been born in Bethlehem.

parallels.desc: from Bethlehem shall come a ruler

verseByVerse.quote: Some of them wanted to arrest him, but no one laid hands on him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one is able to arrest him.

Restrained. Again his hour has not come (v. 30).

verseByVerse.quote: The officers then came to the chief priests and Pharisees, who said to them, "Why did you not bring him?" The officers answered, "No one ever spoke like this man!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The officers return empty-handed: no one ever spoke like this man.

Disarmed by words. Sent to arrest him, they were arrested by him (Matthew 7:28–29).

For worship. No one ever spoke like Jesus. Read his words today and let them seize you.

verseByVerse.quote: The Pharisees answered them, "Have you also been deceived? Have any of the authorities or the Pharisees believed in him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees dismiss Jesus because no leaders believe in him.

Argument from authority. No expert believes, so it cannot be true. Ironically, one is about to speak up (v. 50), and others secretly believed (12:42).

On a Tuesday. “No serious scholar believes that” is not an argument. Truth is not decided by the elite.

parallels.desc: many even of the authorities believed

verseByVerse.quote: "But this crowd that does not know the law is accursed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They despise the crowd as ignorant of the law.

Contempt. Rabbinic writings sometimes used am ha’aretz, “people of the land”, with scorn for those ignorant of the finer points of the law.

Who is accursed? Those who reject Christ, not the ordinary people who hear him gladly (Mark 12:37; 1 Corinthians 1:26–29).
verseByVerse.note: Religious leaders despised ordinary people who did not know the finer points of the law.

parallels.desc: cursed be anyone who does not confirm the words of this law

verseByVerse.quote: Nicodemus, who had gone to him before, and who was one of them, said to them, "Does our law judge a man without first giving him a hearing and learning what he does?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nicodemus, one of their own, asks for a fair hearing.

Nicodemus again. Cautiously, procedurally, he speaks up (Deuteronomy 1:16–17; 17:4). The leaders who boast of knowing the law are not keeping it.

Growing courage. At night in chapter 3, a procedural question here, openly at the burial in 19:39.

On a Tuesday. When colleagues gang up on someone, ask for fairness. A small act of courage may be the beginning of a bigger one.
verseByVerse.note: Nicodemus was a member of the council.

parallels.desc: inquire diligently

verseByVerse.quote: They replied, "Are you from Galilee too? Search and see that no prophet arises from Galilee." They went each to his own house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They answer him with mockery, and are wrong about Galilee too.

Mockery. No answer to his point, only a sneer.

Wrong on the facts. Jonah came from Gath-hepher in Galilee (2 Kings 14:25), and possibly others. Textual note. One early papyrus (P66) reads “the Prophet”, which would mean the prophet like Moses. Verdict: “a prophet” is better attested; their sweeping claim is simply false.

Each to his own house. The end of 7:52 runs into 7:53, which begins the passage about the woman caught in adultery (7:53–8:11). The earliest manuscripts do not contain it; see the notes on chapter 8.
verseByVerse.note: They were wrong: the prophet Jonah came from Gath-hepher in Galilee. The ESV notes that the earliest manuscripts do not include 7:53–8:11 and brackets the passage.

parallels.desc: Jonah son of Amittai, of Gath-hepher
Galilee of the nations

7.overview:
Six months after the feeding of the five thousand, the Feast of Booths (Tabernacles) arrives: the joyful autumn festival when Israel lived in shelters of branches to remember the wilderness, and prayed for rain. Jesus’ unbelieving brothers urge him to go to Jerusalem and show himself; he refuses to move on their timetable, then goes up privately. Halfway through the feast he teaches openly in the temple, and the chapter becomes a swirl of opinions: he is a good man; he deceives the people; he has a demon; he is the Prophet; he is the Christ; he cannot be, because the Christ comes from Bethlehem. Jesus answers that his teaching comes from God, that anyone willing to do God’s will can recognise it, and that their anger at his Sabbath healing is hypocrisy, since they circumcise on the Sabbath. The authorities send officers to arrest him.

On the last and greatest day of the feast, when water from the Pool of Siloam was poured out at the altar, Jesus stands and cries out: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink,” and promises rivers of living water flowing from within. John explains that he meant the Spirit, who would be given once Jesus was glorified. The officers return without him, saying, “No one ever spoke like this man!” The Pharisees scorn them and the ignorant crowd, until Nicodemus, one of their own, asks whether the law condemns a man without a hearing, and is mocked for it. The chapter shows a people divided by Jesus, as every generation has been.

8.title: The Light of the World

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–30 — Light in the Darkness: The Second I AM
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus spends the night on the Mount of Olives and returns to the temple at dawn, where crowds gather and he sits to teach. The scribes and Pharisees bring a woman caught in adultery, stand her before everyone, and ask him whether she should be stoned as Moses commanded, hoping to trap him. Jesus bends down and writes on the ground with his finger. When they keep pressing, he straightens up and tells whoever among them is without sin to throw the first stone, then stoops and writes again. One by one, the oldest first, they leave, until only Jesus and the woman remain. He asks where her accusers are: has no one condemned her? No one, she says. Neither does he; she may go, and must leave her sin behind. Then Jesus declares that he is the light of the world: his followers will not walk in darkness but have the light of life. The Pharisees object that his self-testimony is invalid. He replies that his testimony is true because he knows where he came from and where he is going, and the Father who sent him also testifies; they do not know the Father, because they do not know him. He says this in the treasury, and no one seizes him, for his hour has not come. He warns that he is going away, and they will die in their sin, unable to follow; unless they believe that he is who he claims, they will die in their sins. When they have lifted up the Son of Man, they will realise who he is and that he speaks as the Father taught him, the Father who is always with him because he always pleases him. Many believe.
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter is saturated with the language of witness and judgment (a courtroom), light and darkness (the ceremonial torch-lighting of Tabernacles still in view), and the 'I AM' sayings that claim identity with the God who spoke to Moses. Jesus simultaneously judges (he is the one who judges truly, v. 16) and refuses to judge (he did not come to condemn, v. 15). This paradox is resolved in the cross: all judgment was poured out on him so that those who come to him face no condemnation.
verseByVerse.examples: The woman caught in adultery: the accusers depart one by one, beginning with the oldest (the most self-aware of their own sin). Only two are left: the woman and the one who could have condemned her. She goes free not because the law is set aside but because Jesus will shortly bear its full penalty. Every Christian stands where she stood: condemned by the law, set free by the one who alone can say 'neither do I condemn you,' because he bore the condemnation himself.

verseByVerse.quote: but Jesus went to the Mount of Olives. Early in the morning he came again to the temple. All the people came to him, and he sat down and taught them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This passage is probably not part of John’s original Gospel, but it preserves a true story of Jesus teaching in the temple at dawn.

Textual note: the woman caught in adultery. The story (7:53–8:11) is absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts (P66, P75, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus), from early translations and from the commentaries of the early Greek fathers. It first appears in Codex Bezae (fifth century), and in other manuscripts it is placed after 7:36, 7:44, 21:25 or Luke 21:38. Its vocabulary is more like Luke’s than John’s. Yet it was known early (perhaps by Papias, about AD 125) and has every mark of a true story about Jesus.

Where Christians differ. Some (especially those who follow the Byzantine text) defend it as part of John. Most evangelical scholars hold that it was not in the original Gospel but is a reliable early tradition. Verdict: it is probably not part of inspired Scripture as John wrote it, so no doctrine should rest on it alone; but it agrees fully with Jesus’ character in the Gospels and may be read and taught with that caution.

The Mount of Olives. Jesus lodged at Bethany or camped on the hillside during festivals (Luke 21:37).
verseByVerse.note: Jesus spent nights on the Mount of Olives during his time in Jerusalem. Teachers sat to teach.

verseByVerse.quote: The scribes and the Pharisees brought a woman who had been caught in adultery, and placing her in the midst they said to him, "Teacher, this woman has been caught in the act of adultery."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The religious leaders use a woman’s sin as bait to trap Jesus.

Where is the man? Caught in the act means two were involved; the law required both to die (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22). His absence exposes the injustice.

In the midst. Publicly shamed, used as bait.

On a Tuesday. Beware of using someone’s sin as a weapon in an argument. People are not exhibits.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now in the Law, Moses commanded us to stone such women. So what do you say?" This they said to test him, that they might have some charge to bring against him. Jesus bent down and wrote with his finger on the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They demand that Jesus choose between Moses’ law and his own mercy, and he stoops and writes on the ground.

The trap. If Jesus says “stone her”, he defies Rome, which reserved capital punishment (18:31), and loses his reputation for mercy. If he says “let her go”, he defies Moses.

Writing on the ground. What he wrote is not recorded. Suggestions: their sins; Jeremiah 17:13 (those who turn away will be written in the earth); the law, as God wrote it with his finger (Exodus 31:18); or simply a refusal to be hurried. Verdict: unknown, and the silence is part of the point.
verseByVerse.note: The law required both the man and the woman caught in adultery to be put to death; the man is missing. Rome did not allow the Jewish authorities to carry out executions, so the question was a trap either way.

parallels.desc: both of them shall die

verseByVerse.quote: And as they continued to ask him, he stood up and said to them, "Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her." And once more he bent down and wrote on the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus turns the law on the accusers’ own consciences.

The first stone. The law required witnesses to throw first (Deuteronomy 17:7). Jesus upholds the law but applies it to the accusers’ consciences.

What it does not mean. Not that sin should never be named or justice never done, or that only the sinless may judge. Jesus exposes hypocrisy and misuse of the law, not the rightness of courts (Romans 13:4).

On a Tuesday. Before you condemn someone, look in the mirror (Matthew 7:3–5; Galatians 6:1).
verseByVerse.note: Under the law the witnesses were to throw the first stones.

parallels.desc: the hand of the witnesses first against him

verseByVerse.quote: But when they heard it, they went away one by one, beginning with the older ones, and Jesus was left alone with the woman standing before him. Jesus stood up and said to her, "Woman, where are they? Has no one condemned you?" She said, "No one, Lord." And Jesus said, "Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The accusers leave one by one, and Jesus, the only sinless one, does not condemn her, but tells her to sin no more.

The oldest first. Perhaps the most self-aware, or the ones with the longest record.

Alone. Augustine: “Two were left, misery and mercy.”

Neither do I condemn you. The only sinless one, who could have thrown the stone, does not. Not because sin does not matter, but because he will bear its condemnation himself (Romans 8:1–3).

Go and sin no more. Forgiveness and repentance go together. Grace does not excuse sin; it frees from it (Titus 2:11–12). The order matters: first no condemnation, then a new life.

For worship. Thank Jesus that when your accusers have their case, he says, “Neither do I condemn you.”

parallels.desc: no condemnation

verseByVerse.quote: Again Jesus spoke to them, saying, "I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life." So the Pharisees said to him, "You are bearing witness about yourself; your testimony is not true." Jesus answered, "Even if I do bear witness about myself, my testimony is true, for I know where I came from and where I am going, but you do not know where I come from or where I am going.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is the light of the world, and his testimony is true because he knows where he comes from.

The lamps of the feast. On the first night of Booths, four great golden lamps were lit in the Court of the Women, near the treasury (v. 20), so that it was said every courtyard in Jerusalem was lit. Against that background Jesus claims to be the true light, not for one city but for the world (1:4–9; Isaiah 49:6).

Follows. As Israel followed the pillar of fire in the wilderness (Exodus 13:21).

The light of life. Light that gives life, and life lived in the light.

Self-testimony. In 5:31 Jesus conceded the legal point. Here he adds that his testimony is in fact true, because he alone knows his origin and destiny.

For worship. Follow the light today, one step at a time (Psalm 119:105).
verseByVerse.note: At the Feast of Booths great lamps were lit in the temple courts. This is the second of Jesus’ “I am” sayings in John.

parallels.desc: a pillar of fire to give them light
a light for the nations

verseByVerse.quote: "You judge according to the flesh; I judge no one. Yet even if I do judge, my judgment is true, for it is not I alone who judge, but I and the Father who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus does not judge by appearances, and his judgment is one with the Father’s.

According to the flesh. By appearances (7:24).

I judge no one. His purpose in coming was to save, not condemn (3:17). Yet he will judge (5:22, 27), and his judgment is perfectly just.

verseByVerse.quote: "In your Law it is written that the testimony of two people is true. I am the one who bears witness about myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness about me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus and the Father are the two witnesses the law requires.

Your law. Not disowning the law, but pressing them on their own ground (Deuteronomy 17:6; 19:15).

Two witnesses. The Son and the Father: a claim that only God could make.

parallels.desc: two or three witnesses

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him therefore, "Where is your Father?" Jesus answered, "You know neither me nor my Father. If you knew me, you would know my Father also." These words he spoke in the treasury, as he taught in the temple; but no one arrested him, because his hour had not yet come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To know Jesus is to know the Father, and no one can seize him before his hour.

Where is your Father? Perhaps a sneer about his birth (v. 41).

Know me, know the Father. The Son is the only way to know God (14:7–9).

The treasury. Probably the area in the Court of the Women where thirteen trumpet-shaped offering chests stood (Mark 12:41), close to the great lamps, and next to the chamber where the Sanhedrin met. He speaks almost under their noses.
verseByVerse.note: The treasury was probably in the Court of the Women, where the offering chests stood.

verseByVerse.quote: So he said to them again, "I am going away, and you will seek me, and you will die in your sin. Where I am going, you cannot come." So the Jews said, "Will he kill himself, since he says, 'Where I am going, you cannot come'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who reject him will die in their sin, unable to follow him.

Die in your sin. The most solemn warning: to die unforgiven, with sin unremoved.

Kill himself? Mockery: suicide was thought to lead to the depths of Hades, where they would certainly not go. Irony again: he will lay down his life, though not by his own hand (10:17–18).

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "You are from below; I am from above. You are of this world; I am not of this world. I told you that you would die in your sins, for unless you believe that I am he you will die in your sins."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unless they believe that he is the I am, they will die in their sins.

From below, from above. Two origins, two kingdoms (3:31; 18:36).

I am he. Literally “I am”, with no predicate. In Isaiah 43:10–13 God says, “that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he.” Jesus claims the divine self-identification.

Where Christians differ: must people believe Jesus is God? Some say it is enough to follow Jesus’ teaching. Jesus says faith in who he is, is necessary for salvation. Verdict: saving faith trusts Jesus as the one he says he is: the I AM, God the Son, come in the flesh (1 John 4:2–3; 5:20).
verseByVerse.note: “That I am he” is literally “that I am” — the divine name.

parallels.desc: that you may know and believe me, that I am he

verseByVerse.quote: So they said to him, "Who are you?" Jesus said to them, "Just what I have been telling you from the beginning. I have much to say about you and much to judge, but he who sent me is true, and I declare to the world what I have heard from him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus has been consistent from the beginning.

A difficult phrase. The Greek of Jesus’ reply is notoriously obscure. It may mean “What I have told you from the beginning”, or “Why do I speak to you at all?” Verdict: the ESV’s reading fits the context: he has been consistent from the start.

verseByVerse.quote: They did not understand that he had been speaking to them about the Father. So Jesus said to them, "When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he, and that I do nothing on my own authority, but speak just as the Father taught me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When they lift up the Son of Man on the cross, they will know who he is.

When you have lifted up. They will crucify him (3:14; 12:32–33). The cross will reveal who he is (Mark 15:39).

Then you will know. Not that all will believe, but that the truth will become plain: some will know to their salvation (Acts 2:36–41), others to their judgment.

For worship. At the cross we see who Jesus is: the great I AM, lifted up for sinners.
verseByVerse.note: In John, “lifted up” means both the cross and his exaltation.

parallels.desc: he shall be high and lifted up

verseByVerse.quote: "And he who sent me is with me. He has not left me alone, for I always do the things that are pleasing to him." As he was saying these things, many believed in him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Father is always with Jesus, because he always pleases him.

Not alone. Even facing hostility, Jesus has the Father’s presence (16:32). On the cross he will cry, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34), bearing our forsakenness.

Always. A claim of sinlessness (v. 46; Hebrews 4:15).

Many believed. But their faith is about to be tested (vv. 31–59).

parallels.desc: I am not alone, for the Father is with me

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–59 — The Children of Abraham and the Great I AM
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus tells Jews who had believed him that if they hold to his teaching, they are truly his disciples; they will know the truth, and it will free them. They protest that as Abraham’s descendants they have never been anyone’s slaves. Jesus answers that whoever sins is a slave to sin; a slave has no permanent place in the household, but a son does, so if the Son frees them, they will be truly free. They are Abraham’s descendants, yet they want to kill him because his word finds no room in them. If they were Abraham’s children, they would act as Abraham did. They insist God is their only Father; Jesus says that if he were, they would love him, since he came from God. They cannot hear his word because they belong to their father the devil, a murderer from the start and the father of lies. They do not believe him precisely because he tells the truth; none of them can prove him guilty of sin. They accuse him of being a Samaritan with a demon. He denies it: he honours his Father, who will vindicate him. Whoever keeps his word will never see death. They scoff: Abraham and the prophets died; is he greater than they? Jesus answers that his Father glorifies him, and that Abraham rejoiced to see his day. They object that he is not yet fifty, and Jesus replies that before Abraham came into being, he is. They pick up stones, but he slips away from the temple.
verseByVerse.theology: The passage presents two competing genealogies: Abraham's children versus the devil's children. The distinguishing mark is not ethnic lineage but moral resemblance — you are of your father the devil if you do his works (lying and murder). This is not ethnic polemic but spiritual diagnosis: the unregenerate heart, whatever its ancestry, is in bondage to the father of lies. The truth that sets free (v. 32) is not philosophical insight but the person of Christ himself (v. 36). Freedom is not the absence of constraint but the liberation of the will from slavery to sin, accomplished by the Son who is himself free.
verseByVerse.examples: The stoning attempt at chapter's end is the authorities' answer to 'Before Abraham was, I am.' They understand perfectly: this is a claim to be the eternal God, the I AM of Exodus 3. They reach for stones because they reject the claim as blasphemy. For the Christian, reading this from the other side of the resurrection, this is the moment where the curtain is drawn back and the eternal Word stands visible in human flesh, claiming what was always true. The authorities stone the wrong person for the right reason — he is exactly who he says he is.

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus said to the Jews who had believed him, "If you abide in my word, you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free."
verseByVerse.commentary:
True disciples remain in Jesus’ word, and the truth he reveals sets them free.

Abide. Continuing in Jesus’ word is the mark of true discipleship (15:7). Initial belief must become settled faith.

The truth. Not truth in general, but the truth revealed in Jesus, who is the truth (14:6).

Free. From sin (v. 34), not merely from ignorance.

What it does not mean. Often quoted on university buildings to mean that education liberates. Jesus means that knowing him frees from slavery to sin.

For worship. Thank Christ for the freedom that only he can give.

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, "We are offspring of Abraham and have never been enslaved to anyone. How is it that you say, 'You will become free'?" Jesus answered them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who sins is a slave of sin, whatever their ancestry.

Never enslaved? A remarkable claim from a people who had been slaves in Egypt and Babylon and were under Roman rule. They mean they have never been inwardly enslaved, as children of Abraham.

A slave to sin. Sin is not just an act but a master (Romans 6:16–20).

Where Christians differ: free will. Pelagians and many moderns hold that humans have a natural freedom to choose good. Augustine, Luther (“The Bondage of the Will”), Calvin and the Reformed confessions teach that fallen people freely choose what they want, but cannot by nature want God; their will is enslaved to sin until Christ sets it free (Westminster Confession 9.3–4). Verdict: bondage of the will: we are free to do what we love, but by nature we do not love God; only the Son makes us free indeed.
verseByVerse.note: Israel had been in bondage to Egypt, Babylon and now Rome; they meant they had never inwardly accepted slavery.

parallels.desc: slaves of sin

verseByVerse.quote: "The slave does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever. So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only the Son can free slaves and give them a place in the house for ever.

Slave and son. Ishmael and Isaac (Genesis 21:10; Galatians 4:21–31). A slave could be sold; a son is heir.

The Son. Only the Son of the house can free slaves and adopt them as sons.

Free indeed. Real freedom: not doing whatever we want, but being made able to do what God made us for.

On a Tuesday. What habit still enslaves you? Bring it to the Son, who sets free.
verseByVerse.note: A slave had no permanent place in a household; a son did.

parallels.desc: cast out this slave woman and her son

verseByVerse.quote: "I know that you are offspring of Abraham; yet you seek to kill me because my word finds no place in you. I speak of what I have seen with my Father, and you do what you have heard from your father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Physical descent from Abraham does not make them his children in spirit.

Descendants, but not children. Physical descent is not spiritual kinship (Romans 9:6–8; Galatians 3:7).

No place. His word makes no headway in them.

Your father. Not yet named, but soon (v. 44).

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, "Abraham is our father." Jesus said to them, "If you were Abraham's children, you would be doing the works Abraham did, but now you seek to kill me, a man who has told you the truth that I heard from God. This is not what Abraham did."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham’s true children believe God as Abraham did.

The works of Abraham. Abraham believed God (Genesis 15:6) and welcomed God’s messengers (Genesis 18). Children resemble their father.

A man. Jesus speaks of himself as fully human.

On a Tuesday. Religious heritage is a gift, but not a substitute for personal faith. Being raised in a Christian home does not make you a Christian.

parallels.desc: Abraham welcomes the LORD’s messengers

verseByVerse.quote: "You are doing the works your father did." They said to him, "We were not born of sexual immorality. We have one Father — even God." Jesus said to them, "If God were your Father, you would love me, for I came from God and I am here. I came not of my own accord, but he sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If God were their Father, they would love his Son.

Not born of immorality. Perhaps a jibe at Jesus’ birth, rumoured to be illegitimate (compare later Jewish polemic). Or a claim that they are not idolaters, spiritual adulterers (Hosea 2:4).

If God were your Father. Love for God shows itself in love for his Son (1 John 5:1).
verseByVerse.note: Their retort may hint at rumours about Jesus’ own birth.

parallels.desc: have we not all one Father?

verseByVerse.quote: "Why do you not understand what I say? It is because you cannot bear to hear my word. You are of your father the devil, and your will is to do your father's desires. He was a murderer from the beginning, and does not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him. When he lies, he speaks out of his own character, for he is a liar and the father of lies."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their resistance to the truth reveals their likeness to the devil, the liar and murderer.

Cannot hear. Moral inability: they do not want to hear.

Your father the devil. The strongest words in the Gospels. Jesus addresses particular opponents who are seeking to kill him (v. 40), not the Jewish people as a whole; he himself was a Jew, as were all his first disciples. The same charge applies to anyone, Gentile or Jew, who resists the truth and seeks to destroy (1 John 3:8–10).

What it does not mean. This verse has been abused to justify centuries of Christian persecution of Jews, an evil the church must repent of. Jesus’ words diagnose the spiritual state of his enemies; they give no licence for hatred (Romans 9:1–5; 10:1).

A murderer from the beginning. Through the lie in Eden he brought death (Genesis 3:4; Romans 5:12); Cain followed his example (1 John 3:12).

The father of lies. All deception ultimately originates with him (2 Corinthians 11:3; Revelation 12:9).
verseByVerse.note: The devil’s lie led to death in Eden; the first murder followed.

parallels.desc: “You will not surely die”

verseByVerse.quote: "But because I tell the truth, you do not believe me. Which one of you convicts me of sin? If I tell the truth, why do you not believe me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They reject Jesus because he tells the truth, and no one can convict him of sin.

Because I tell the truth. Those committed to a lie are repelled by truth.

Which of you convicts me? No one could answer. Jesus’ challenge is a claim of sinlessness that no prophet or apostle ever made (2 Corinthians 5:21; 1 Peter 2:22).

For worship. Praise the sinless Son, whose perfect life is credited to all who believe.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever is of God hears the words of God. The reason why you do not hear them is that you are not of God." The Jews answered him, "Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever belongs to God hears his words, and they answer with insults.

Of God. Belonging precedes hearing (10:26–27). Those born of God hear his voice.

A Samaritan. The worst insult they can think of: a heretic and half-breed. Perhaps also because he criticises Jews as Samaritans did.

A demon. When argument fails, insult remains.
verseByVerse.note: Calling a Jew a Samaritan was an insult.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "I do not have a demon, but I honor my Father, and you dishonor me. Yet I do not seek my own glory; there is One who seeks it, and he is the judge."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus honours his Father and leaves his vindication to him.

Calm reply. He ignores the insult “Samaritan”.

Not my own glory. He leaves vindication to the Father (1 Peter 2:23).

On a Tuesday. When insulted, you need not defend your reputation. Entrust it to God, who judges justly.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, if anyone keeps my word, he will never see death.' The Jews said to him, 'Now we know that you have a demon! Abraham died, as did the prophets, yet you say, 'If anyone keeps my word, he will never taste death.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever keeps Jesus’ word will never see death.

Never see death. Not that believers will not die physically, but that death will not be death for them: it has lost its sting (11:25–26; 1 Corinthians 15:55).

Taste death. They misquote him slightly, but the meaning is the same.

verseByVerse.quote: "Are you greater than our father Abraham, who died? And the prophets died! Who do you make yourself out to be?" Jesus answered, "If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me, of whom you say, 'He is our God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They ask whether he is greater than Abraham; Jesus says his Father glorifies him.

Greater than Abraham? As with Jacob (4:12), the answer is yes.

Who do you make yourself? The question of the whole Gospel.

My Father glorifies me. In the resurrection and exaltation (17:1, 5).

verseByVerse.quote: "But you have not known him. I know him. If I were to say that I do not know him, I would be a liar like you. But I do know him and I keep his word. Your father Abraham rejoiced that he would see my day. He saw it and was glad."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Abraham rejoiced to see the day of Jesus.

A liar like you. False modesty would be a lie.

Abraham rejoiced. When? Perhaps at the promise of a seed in whom all nations would be blessed (Genesis 12:3; 22:18), or at Isaac’s birth (Genesis 21:6), or the ram provided on Moriah (Genesis 22:8, 13–14), or by faith looking forward (Hebrews 11:13). Jewish tradition held that God showed Abraham the future.

For worship. Abraham longed to see Christ’s day. We live in it. Rejoice.

parallels.desc: having seen them and greeted them from afar

verseByVerse.quote: So the Jews said to him, "You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?" Jesus said to them, "Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before Abraham came to be, Jesus is: the eternal I am.

Not yet fifty. A round number for the age when a man was past his prime (Numbers 4:3). Jesus was in his early thirties (Luke 3:23).

Textual note. Some early manuscripts read “has Abraham seen you?”. Verdict: “have you seen Abraham?” is better attested; the sense is the same.

Before Abraham was, I am. Not “I was”: Abraham “came into being” (genesthai), but Jesus simply “is” (egō eimi). He claims eternal existence and the very name of God from the burning bush (Exodus 3:14; Isaiah 43:13; 48:12).

Where Christians differ. Jehovah’s Witnesses translate “I have been”, as a statement of pre-existence only. The contrast of tenses and the hearers’ response (v. 59) show that Jesus claimed more. Verdict: the historic Christian reading: Jesus claims to be the eternal God.

For worship. Bow before the I AM, who was before Abraham and is now and ever shall be.
verseByVerse.note: “I am” without anything added echoes the name God gave himself at the burning bush.

parallels.desc: “I AM WHO I AM”
from everlasting to everlasting

verseByVerse.quote: So they picked up stones to throw at him, but Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They try to stone him for blasphemy, and he leaves the temple.

Stones. The penalty for blasphemy (Leviticus 24:16). They understood his claim exactly. Building work on the temple meant stones were close at hand.

Hid himself. Not yet his hour. Perhaps a miraculous escape, perhaps slipping away in the crowd.

Leaving the temple. Symbolic: the glory of God departs from the temple, as in Ezekiel 10.

On a Tuesday. Jesus is not a safe, tame teacher. Either he is the I AM, or he is a blasphemer. There is no middle ground.
verseByVerse.note: Stoning was the penalty for blasphemy.
