Without knowing it, Caiaphas prophesies that Jesus will die for the nation and gather God’s scattered children into one.

An unwitting prophet. God can speak through unworthy people (Balaam, Numbers 22–24). Caiaphas meant expediency; God meant substitution.

For the nation. Substitution: one dies instead of many (Isaiah 53:5–6; 2 Corinthians 5:21).

The children of God scattered. Gentiles who will believe, already called God’s children before they are gathered, as the “other sheep” (10:16). God’s people are known to him before they come. The Reformed doctrine of election finds support here (Acts 18:10).

Gather into one. The goal of the cross is a united people, Jews and Gentiles in one body (Ephesians 2:14–16).

For worship. Thank God that Christ died to gather you, perhaps scattered far away, into his family.

parallels.desc: I will gather yet others

verseByVerse.quote: So from that day on they made plans to put him to death. Jesus therefore no longer walked openly among the Jews, but went from there to the region near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim, and there he stayed with the disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From that day they plan his death, and Jesus withdraws to Ephraim.

The decision. The death sentence is passed, in effect, before any trial.

Irony. Jesus gives Lazarus life, and it costs him his own. The one who raises the dead must die.

Ephraim. Probably et-Taiyibeh, about twelve miles north-east of Jerusalem, on the edge of the wilderness. Textual note. Some manuscripts add “Sapphurim”. Verdict: “Ephraim” alone is better attested.
verseByVerse.note: The town of Ephraim was probably north-east of Jerusalem, on the edge of the wilderness.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the Passover of the Jews was at hand, and many went up from the country to Jerusalem before the Passover to purify themselves. They were looking for Jesus and saying to one another as they stood in the temple, "What do you think? That he will not come to the feast at all?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As Passover approaches, people wonder whether Jesus will come.

Purification. Pilgrims who had contracted ritual impurity had to purify themselves, sometimes for a week, before eating Passover (Numbers 9:6–12; 2 Chronicles 30:17–18).

The third Passover. The last of Jesus’ ministry (2:13; 6:4). He will become the Passover Lamb (1:29; 19:36).
verseByVerse.note: Pilgrims came early to undergo purification rites so they would be ritually clean for the feast.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the chief priests and the Pharisees had given orders that if anyone knew where he was, he should let them know, so that they might arrest him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The authorities order anyone who knows where he is to report it.

A wanted man. The scene is set for Judas (12:4; 18:2–3).

On a Tuesday. Jesus will go to Jerusalem anyway (12:12). He knew the cost, and came for us.

11.text: <sup>1</sup>Now a certain man was ill, Lazarus of Bethany, the village of Mary and her sister Martha.<sup>2</sup>It was Mary who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair, whose brother Lazarus was ill.<sup>3</sup>So the sisters sent to him, saying, “Lord, he whom you love is ill.”<sup>4</sup>But when Jesus heard it he said, “This illness does not lead to death. It is for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.”<sup>5</sup>Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus.<sup>6</sup>So, when he heard that Lazarus was ill, he stayed two days longer in the place where he was.<sup>7</sup>Then after this he said to the disciples, “Let us go to Judea again.”<sup>8</sup>The disciples said to him, “Rabbi, the Jews were just now seeking to stone you, and are you going there again?”<sup>9</sup>Jesus answered, “Are there not twelve hours in the day? If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world.<sup>10</sup>But if anyone walks in the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him.”<sup>11</sup>After saying these things, he said to them, “Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I go to awaken him.”<sup>12</sup>The disciples said to him, “Lord, if he has fallen asleep, he will recover.”<sup>13</sup>Now Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought that he meant taking rest in sleep.<sup>14</sup>Then Jesus told them plainly, “Lazarus has died,<sup>15</sup>and for your sake I am glad that I was not there, so that you may believe. But let us go to him.”<sup>16</sup>So Thomas, called the Twin, said to his fellow disciples, “Let us also go, that we may die with him.”<sup>17</sup>Now when Jesus came, he found that Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days.<sup>18</sup>Bethany was near Jerusalem, about two miles off,<sup>19</sup>and many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them concerning their brother.<sup>20</sup>So when Martha heard that Jesus was coming, she went and met him, but Mary remained seated in the house.<sup>21</sup>Martha said to Jesus, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.<sup>22</sup>But even now I know that whatever you ask from God, God will give you.”<sup>23</sup>Jesus said to her, “Your brother will rise again.”<sup>24</sup>Martha said to him, “I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day.”<sup>25</sup>Jesus said to her, “I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live,<sup>26</sup>and everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. Do you believe this?”<sup>27</sup>She said to him, “Yes, Lord; I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world.”<sup>28</sup>When she had said this, she went and called her sister Mary, saying in private, “The Teacher is here and is calling for you.”<sup>29</sup>And when she heard it, she rose quickly and went to him.<sup>30</sup>Now Jesus had not yet come into the village, but was still in the place where Martha had met him.<sup>31</sup>When the Jews who were with her in the house, consoling her, saw Mary rise quickly and go out, they followed her, supposing that she was going to the tomb to weep there.<sup>32</sup>Now when Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell at his feet, saying to him, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.”<sup>33</sup>When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping, he was deeply moved in his spirit and greatly troubled.<sup>34</sup>And he said, “Where have you laid him?” They said to him, “Lord, come and see.”<sup>35</sup>Jesus wept.<sup>36</sup>So the Jews said, “See how he loved him!”<sup>37</sup>But some of them said, “Could not he who opened the eyes of the blind man also have kept this man from dying?”<sup>38</sup>Then Jesus, deeply moved again, came to the tomb. It was a cave, and a stone lay against it.<sup>39</sup>Jesus said, “Take away the stone.” Martha, the sister of the dead man, said to him, “Lord, by this time there will be an odor, for he has been dead four days.”<sup>40</sup>Jesus said to her, “Did I not tell you that if you believed you would see the glory of God?”<sup>41</sup>So they took away the stone. And Jesus lifted up his eyes and said, “Father, I thank you that you have heard me.<sup>42</sup>I knew that you always hear me, but I said this on account of the people standing around, that they may believe that you sent me.”<sup>43</sup>When he had said these things, he cried out with a loud voice, “Lazarus, come out.”<sup>44</sup>The man who had died came out, his hands and feet bound with linen strips, and his face wrapped with a cloth. Jesus said to them, “Unbind him, and let him go.”<sup>45</sup>Many of the Jews therefore, who had come with Mary and had seen what he did, believed in him,<sup>46</sup>but some of them went to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done.<sup>47</sup>So the chief priests and the Pharisees gathered the council and said, “What are we to do? For this man performs many signs.<sup>48</sup>If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation.”<sup>49</sup>But one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said to them, “You know nothing at all.<sup>50</sup>Nor do you understand that it is better for you that one man should die for the people, not that the whole nation should perish.”<sup>51</sup>He did not say this of his own accord, but being high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation,<sup>52</sup>and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad.<sup>53</sup>So from that day on they made plans to put him to death.<sup>54</sup>Jesus therefore no longer walked openly among the Jews, but went from there to the region near the wilderness, to a town called Ephraim, and there he stayed with the disciples.<sup>55</sup>Now the Passover of the Jews was at hand, and many went up from the country to Jerusalem before the Passover to purify themselves.<sup>56</sup>They were looking for Jesus and saying to one another as they stood in the temple, “What do you think? That he will not come to the feast at all?”<sup>57</sup>Now the chief priests and the Pharisees had given orders that if anyone knew where he was, he should let them know, so that they might arrest him.
11.overview:
The raising of Lazarus is the seventh and greatest sign in John, and the event that leads directly to the cross. Lazarus of Bethany, brother of Martha and Mary, falls ill, and the sisters send word to Jesus: “Lord, he whom you love is ill.” Because he loves them, Jesus waits two more days, then returns to Judea despite the danger, telling the disciples that Lazarus has fallen asleep and he is going to wake him. Thomas gloomily urges the others to go and die with him. By the time they arrive, Lazarus has been in the tomb four days. Martha meets Jesus with grief and faith mixed; he tells her, “I am the resurrection and the life,” and she confesses him the Christ, the Son of God. Mary falls at his feet weeping, and Jesus, deeply moved and troubled, weeps too. At the tomb he orders the stone removed, prays aloud to his Father, and cries, “Lazarus, come out.” The dead man walks out still bound in grave-clothes.

Many believe, but some report to the Pharisees, and the Sanhedrin meets in alarm: if Jesus goes on like this, the Romans will destroy the temple and the nation. The high priest Caiaphas declares that it is better for one man to die for the people than for the whole nation to perish. John comments that, without knowing it, he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, and to gather into one the scattered children of God. From that day they plan to kill him. Jesus withdraws to Ephraim, and as Passover approaches the crowds wonder whether he will dare to come to the feast. The one who gives life will give his own life, so that the dead may live.

12.title: The Hour Has Come

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–19 — The Anointing and the Entry
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Six days before Passover, at a dinner in Jesus’ honour in Bethany, with Martha serving and Lazarus at table, Mary anoints Jesus’ feet with a pound of expensive nard and wipes them with her hair, filling the house with fragrance. Judas, the future betrayer and a thief who pilfers from the common purse, protests that it could have been sold for the poor. Jesus defends her: she has kept it for his burial, and they will always have the poor, but not always him. Crowds come to see Jesus and the risen Lazarus, and the chief priests resolve to kill Lazarus too. Next day festival crowds carry palm branches out to meet Jesus, hailing him as the blessed King of Israel, and he rides in on a young donkey as the prophet foretold, though the disciples grasp this only later. Witnesses of Lazarus’s raising spread the news, drawing more people, and the Pharisees despair that the whole world is following him.
verseByVerse.theology: Mary's extravagance is the gospel's aesthetic: 'she has done a beautiful thing' (Matt. 26:10). The ointment worth a year's wages poured out on Jesus is the only appropriate response to the one who will pour out his life for the world. Judas' objection — it should have been sold and given to the poor — sounds pious but is calculated. He uses the language of charity to mask the language of control. The contrast between Mary's love and Judas' calculation is the contrast between authentic discipleship and the discipleship that has never really left the world's economy.
verseByVerse.examples: The triumphal entry is at once a royal procession and a misunderstood one. The crowd hails Jesus as king; they are right about the title and wrong about what it means. They expect a Davidic warrior-king who will restore national sovereignty; Jesus enters on a donkey, fulfilling Zechariah 9:9, the prophecy of the humble king of peace. The disciples do not understand this until after the resurrection (v. 16) — another instance of John's pattern where events are incomprehensible until the Spirit illuminates them in the light of the cross and resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: Six days before the Passover, Jesus therefore came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, whom Jesus had raised from the dead. So they gave a dinner for him there. Martha served, and Lazarus was one of those reclining with him at table.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six days before Passover, Jesus dines at Bethany with Lazarus at the table.

Six days. Probably the Saturday before Passover week. John’s chronology moves day by day towards the cross.

A dinner in his honour. Mark 14:3 places it at the house of Simon the leper, perhaps a friend or relative of the family.

Lazarus at table. A living testimony, eating with the one who raised him.

verseByVerse.quote: Mary therefore took a pound of expensive ointment made from pure nard, and anointed the feet of Jesus and wiped his feet with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume. But Judas Iscariot, one of his disciples (he who was about to betray him), said,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mary pours out costly perfume on Jesus’ feet in extravagant love.

Nard. An aromatic oil from a plant of the Himalayas, imported at great cost. A Roman pound (about 11 ounces, 325 grams) was a huge quantity.

The feet. Mark and Matthew say the head (Mark 14:3); probably both. John stresses the feet: the most humble act, and a foreshadowing of Jesus washing his disciples’ feet (13:5).

Her hair. A respectable woman did not let her hair down in public. Mary disregards propriety in devotion.

Where Christians differ: one anointing or two? Luke 7:36–50 describes a “sinful woman” anointing Jesus in Galilee, and medieval tradition merged Mary of Bethany, the sinful woman and Mary Magdalene. Verdict: Luke’s is a different, earlier event; Mark, Matthew and John describe the same anointing at Bethany. Mary of Bethany is not Mary Magdalene.

The fragrance. Love for Christ fills a house (2 Corinthians 2:14–16). Mark 14:9 says it would be told wherever the gospel is preached.

For worship. What costly thing could you pour out for Jesus?
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the pound was a Roman pound, about 11½ ounces. Nard was a costly perfume imported from India. A respectable woman did not normally let down her hair in public.

parallels.desc: a different woman in Galilee

verseByVerse.quote: "Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?" He said this, not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief, and having charge of the moneybag he used to help himself to what was put into it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judas objects in the name of the poor, but he is a thief.

Three hundred denarii. About a year’s wages for a labourer.

A pious objection. Concern for the poor can be a mask for other motives. The other Gospels say several disciples complained (Matthew 26:8); Judas led them.

A thief. John alone tells us. Greed opened the door to betrayal (Matthew 26:14–15).

On a Tuesday. If you handle money for a church or charity, be scrupulously accountable (2 Corinthians 8:20–21). And beware of criticising others’ generosity.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage; three hundred denarii was about a year’s wages.

parallels.desc: Judas had the moneybag

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said, "Leave her alone, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial. For the poor you always have with you, but you do not always have me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus defends Mary: she has anointed him for burial.

Keep it for my burial. Perhaps she had kept it for this; perhaps she sensed his death was near. Jesus interprets her act as an anointing for burial in advance.

The poor always with you. Deuteronomy 15:11, which continues: therefore open your hand to your brother, the needy and the poor. Jesus is not dismissing the poor.

What it does not mean. Not a reason to ignore poverty. Jesus’ point is that this moment of devotion to him, before his death, is unique.

Where Christians differ: worship or social action? Some set costly worship (beautiful buildings, music) against care for the poor; others the reverse. Verdict: both flow from love for Christ, and each needs the other; Judas cared for neither.
verseByVerse.note: Bodies were anointed with spices for burial.

parallels.desc: there will never cease to be poor in the land

verseByVerse.quote: When the large crowd of the Jews learned that Jesus was there, they came, not only on account of him but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead. So the chief priests made plans to put Lazarus to death as well, because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Crowds come to see Lazarus, and the chief priests plan to kill him too.

Curiosity. A man raised from the dead was a sensation.

Kill Lazarus too. Evil compounds itself. If you cannot deny the evidence, destroy it.

Going away. Leaving the authorities’ side.

On a Tuesday. A changed life is powerful testimony, and may attract opposition.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day the large crowd that had come to the feast heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem. So they took branches of palm trees and went out to meet him, crying out, "Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, even the King of Israel!" And Jesus found a young donkey and sat on it, just as it is written,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Festival crowds welcome Jesus as King of Israel, and he rides in on a young donkey.

The triumphal entry. Recorded in all four Gospels (Mark 11:1–10).

Palm branches. A symbol of Jewish nationalism since the Maccabees, who entered Jerusalem with palms after freeing it (1 Maccabees 13:51). The crowd hails a liberator king.

Hosanna. Hebrew for “save us, we pray” (Psalm 118:25–26), a pilgrim psalm sung at feasts, by now a shout of praise.

The King of Israel. Nathanael’s confession (1:49).

A donkey. Jesus responds to their nationalist hopes by choosing a humble mount, not a war horse.
verseByVerse.note: Palm branches had become a symbol of national victory and celebration. “Hosanna” means “save, we pray.”

parallels.desc: blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD
branches of palm trees at the Feast of Booths

verseByVerse.quote: "Fear not, daughter of Zion; behold, your king is coming, sitting on a donkey's colt!" His disciples did not understand these things at first, but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things had been written about him and had been done to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The humble King comes as Zechariah foretold, though the disciples understood later.

Zechariah 9:9. The king who comes humble and riding on a donkey, bringing peace to the nations (Zechariah 9:10). “Fear not” may come from Isaiah 40:9 or Zephaniah 3:16.

Understood later. After the resurrection and the giving of the Spirit (2:22; 14:26).

For worship. Welcome your King, who comes not to conquer by force but to make peace by his blood.
verseByVerse.note: A king riding a donkey came in peace, not on a warhorse.

parallels.desc: your king, mounted on a donkey
fear not, O Zion

verseByVerse.quote: The crowd that had been with him when he called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead continued to bear witness. The reason why the crowd went to meet him was that they heard he had done this sign.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The raising of Lazarus draws the crowd to Jesus.

Two crowds. Those from Bethany and those from Jerusalem, meeting on the road.

The sign. The raising of Lazarus drives the triumphal entry, and therefore the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: So the Pharisees said to one another, "You see that you are gaining nothing. Look, the world has gone after him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees despair: the world has gone after him.

The world. An exaggeration of frustration, but prophetic: immediately the Greeks arrive (v. 20).

On a Tuesday. No scheme can stop the spread of Christ’s kingdom.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–50 — The Hour Has Come: Lifting Up the Son of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Some Greeks who have come to worship at the feast ask Philip to let them see Jesus. When Philip and Andrew tell him, Jesus declares that the hour for the Son of Man’s glory has come. A grain of wheat stays alone unless it falls into the ground and dies; then it yields a great harvest. Whoever clings to life loses it, and whoever lets go of it in this world keeps it for eternity. His servants must follow him, and the Father will honour them. His soul is troubled, yet he will not ask to be spared this hour, for it is why he came; he prays that the Father will glorify his name. A voice from heaven replies that it has and will again. Some hear thunder, others an angel. Jesus says the voice was for them: now this world is judged, its ruler is driven out, and when he is lifted up he will draw everyone to himself, meaning the death he would die. The crowd asks how the Messiah, who remains for ever, can be lifted up, and who this Son of Man is. Jesus urges them to walk in the light while they have it and become children of light, then hides from them. Despite all his signs they do not believe, fulfilling Isaiah’s words about unbelief and hardened hearts; Isaiah said this because he saw Jesus’ glory. Even many leaders believe but keep quiet for fear of expulsion, preferring human praise to God’s. Jesus cries out that to believe in him is to believe in the one who sent him; he came as light so that believers need not stay in darkness. He does not judge those who reject his words now, for he came to save; but his word will judge them on the last day, for he speaks what the Father commanded, and the Father’s command is eternal life.
verseByVerse.theology: The hour is the theological center of John's gospel — referenced as 'not yet come' repeatedly throughout the narrative (2:4; 7:30; 8:20), now announced as arrived (v. 23). The hour is the cross-resurrection-ascension event, the moment when the Son of Man is simultaneously lifted up in humiliation and glorified in triumph. The cross is not the Father's defeat but his decisive victory; it is not the Son's shame but his glory. This is the theology that has to be maintained against every attempt to split the crucifixion from the resurrection: both are the one event called 'the hour.'
verseByVerse.examples: Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. This is the law of the kingdom: life through death, fruitfulness through sacrifice. Jesus applies it first to himself and then to his disciples. The disciple who 'hates his life in this world' — who does not cling to temporal existence at the cost of eternal loyalty — will find life preserved in ways that the self-preserver never can. The call to follow him is a call to follow him even into death.

verseByVerse.quote: Now among those who went up to worship at the feast were some Greeks. So these came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida in Galilee, and asked him, "Sir, we wish to see Jesus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greeks ask to see Jesus, a sign that the hour has come.

Greeks. Gentiles, probably God-fearers who worshipped Israel’s God but were not full converts (Acts 10:2). They could enter only the outer court of the temple.

Philip. A Greek name, from a town in a partly Gentile area (1:44).

We wish to see Jesus. Words carved on many pulpits, to remind preachers what people come for.

The world. They arrive just after the Pharisees say “the world has gone after him” (v. 19). The “other sheep” are coming (10:16).
verseByVerse.note: These Greeks were probably Gentiles who worshipped the God of Israel, like the centurion Cornelius. Philip had a Greek name.

parallels.desc: other sheep

verseByVerse.quote: Philip went and told Andrew; Andrew and Philip went and told Jesus. And Jesus answered them, "The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.

Andrew again. Bringing people to Jesus (1:41; 6:8).

The hour has come. All through the Gospel his hour had “not yet come” (2:4; 7:30; 8:20). The arrival of Gentiles signals that it is time: the cross will open the way for the nations.

Glorified. Through death. In John the cross is not defeat followed by glory, but itself the glory.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus’ “hour” in John is the time of his death and glorification.

verseByVerse.quote: "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit. Whoever loves his life loses it, and whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like a grain of wheat, Jesus must die to bear much fruit, and his followers must lose their lives to keep them.

The grain of wheat. One seed must be buried to produce a harvest. Jesus’ death will bring life to many, including the Greeks.

Love and hate. A Hebrew way of expressing preference (Luke 14:26). Not self-loathing, but putting Christ before self-preservation (Mark 8:35).

The principle for disciples. What is true of Christ is true of those who follow him: fruitfulness through dying to self (2 Corinthians 4:10–12). Tertullian: the blood of martyrs is seed.

On a Tuesday. What would it mean to let a seed die in your life: an ambition, a comfort, a reputation, so that others may live?

verseByVerse.quote: "If anyone serves me, he must follow me; and where I am, there will my servant be also. If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him. Now is my soul troubled. And what shall I say? 'Father, save me from this hour'? But for this purpose I have come to this hour."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Troubled, Jesus will not ask to be saved from the hour he came for.

Follow me. To the cross, and through it to glory (14:3; 17:24).

The Father will honour. The reward of service is honour from God himself.

Troubled. John’s version of Gethsemane (Mark 14:34–36). Jesus is truly human and feels the horror of what lies ahead.

For this purpose. He will not ask to be spared. He came to die.

For worship. Thank Jesus that, troubled as he was, he did not turn back.

parallels.desc: Gethsemane

verseByVerse.quote: "Father, glorify your name." Then a voice came from heaven: "I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again." The crowd that stood there and heard it said that it had thundered. Others said, "An angel has spoken to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus prays that the Father will glorify his name, and a voice from heaven answers.

Glorify your name. The prayer of Jesus’ whole life (17:4). Compare “hallowed be your name” (Matthew 6:9).

A voice from heaven. As at his baptism and transfiguration (Mark 1:11; 9:7). The only time in John.

Glorified and will glorify. In his life and signs; and again in the cross and resurrection.

Thunder. Those who will not hear God’s word hear only noise (Acts 9:7; 22:9).

parallels.desc: the Father’s voice at the baptism and transfiguration

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "This voice has come for your sake, not mine. Now is the judgment of this world; now will the ruler of this world be cast out."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the cross this world is judged and its ruler cast out.

For your sake. To confirm the meaning of what will happen.

The judgment of this world. At the cross the world’s rebellion is exposed and judged (16:11).

The ruler of this world. Satan (14:30; 16:11; 2 Corinthians 4:4). At the cross he is defeated and dethroned (Colossians 2:15; Hebrews 2:14; Revelation 12:9–11). Where Christians differ. Some think Satan is not yet bound and rules freely until the end. The amillennial reading sees here the binding of Satan (Revelation 20:2–3; Matthew 12:29): his power to deceive the nations is broken, so the gospel goes to all peoples. Verdict: Satan is a defeated enemy, still dangerous (1 Peter 5:8), but cast out from his throne by the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself." He said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lifted up on the cross, Jesus will draw people of every nation to himself.

Lifted up. On the cross (3:14; 8:28), and in exaltation.

All people. Where Christians differ. Universalists read this as a promise that everyone will be saved; Arminians as a universal drawing that may be resisted. Reformed interpreters note the context: Greeks have just come (v. 20), and “all” means all kinds of people, Gentiles as well as Jews (11:52); the drawing in 6:44 is effectual, since those drawn are raised. Verdict: through the cross Christ will draw people from every nation, effectively; not every individual, since this very chapter speaks of unbelief (v. 37).

Textual note. Some early manuscripts read “all things” (Colossians 1:20). Verdict: “all people” is the better reading.

For worship. Thank the crucified Lord who drew you to himself.
verseByVerse.note: In John, “lifted up” means both the cross and his exaltation.

parallels.desc: he shall be high and lifted up

verseByVerse.quote: So the crowd answered him, "We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever. How can you say that the Son of Man must be lifted up? Who is this Son of Man?" So Jesus said to them, "The light is among you for a little while longer. Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you. The one who walks in the darkness does not know where he is going."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd cannot fit a crucified Messiah into their hope, and Jesus urges them to walk while they have the light.

The Christ remains for ever. Psalm 89:36–37; Isaiah 9:7; Daniel 7:14. They understand “lifted up” as death and cannot fit it with their hope.

Who is this Son of Man? A real question, but Jesus answers with an urgent appeal instead of a lecture.

A little while. Opportunity does not last for ever (Isaiah 55:6).

parallels.desc: his offspring shall endure forever

verseByVerse.quote: "While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may become sons of light." When Jesus had said these things, he departed and hid himself from them. Though he had done so many signs before them, they still did not believe in him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
They must believe in the light while it is with them; then Jesus hides himself.

Sons of light. People who belong to the light (Ephesians 5:8; 1 Thessalonians 5:5). A phrase also used in the Dead Sea Scrolls.

Hid himself. The end of his public ministry. The light withdraws.

So many signs. The tragedy of John’s first half. Signs do not by themselves produce faith.

parallels.desc: walk as children of light

verseByVerse.quote: so that the word spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: "Lord, who has believed what he heard from us, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?" Therefore they could not believe. For again Isaiah said,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their unbelief fulfils Isaiah’s words about the Servant.

Isaiah 53:1. The opening of the song of the suffering Servant. Israel’s unbelief at the Servant was foretold (Romans 10:16).

The arm of the Lord. God’s saving power, revealed in the Servant.

parallels.desc: who has believed what he has heard from us?

verseByVerse.quote: "He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they see with their eyes, and understand with their heart, and turn, and I would heal them." Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaiah foretold their hardening, and he saw Jesus’ glory.

Could not believe. Isaiah 6:10. Their unbelief was both their choice (v. 37) and God’s judicial hardening (Romans 9:18; 11:7–10).

Where Christians differ: divine hardening. Some find it incompatible with God’s love and human responsibility. Reformed theology holds that God hardens those who have already resisted him, giving them over to the unbelief they chose (Romans 1:24–28), and that human responsibility and divine sovereignty are both real. Verdict: both are taught side by side; God is never the author of sin, yet nothing escapes his rule.

He saw his glory. In Isaiah 6 the prophet saw the LORD on his throne. John says he saw Jesus’ glory: Jesus is the LORD of Isaiah 6 (1:14, 18). Textual note. Some manuscripts read “when he saw”. Verdict: “because” is original; the sense is unchanged.

For worship. “Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts” (Isaiah 6:3), sung of Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Isaiah saw the Lord’s glory in the temple; John says that glory was Christ’s.

parallels.desc: make the heart of this people dull
I saw the Lord, high and lifted up

verseByVerse.quote: Nevertheless, many even of the authorities believed in him, but for fear of the Pharisees they did not confess it, so that they would not be put out of the synagogue; for they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many leaders believe secretly but will not confess him, loving human praise more than God’s.

Secret believers. Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea are examples (19:38–39), who eventually come out into the open.

Where Christians differ: secret faith. In the Reformation era Calvin criticised “Nicodemites”, Protestants who hid their faith and attended Mass to avoid persecution. Others counselled discretion in danger. Verdict: faith may begin quietly and should be wise in danger (Matthew 10:16), but true faith will confess Christ (Romans 10:9–10; Matthew 10:32–33); fear of people must not win.

The glory of men. The reason for silence (5:44).

On a Tuesday. Is there a place where you hide your faith because you value people’s approval more than God’s?
verseByVerse.note: Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea were among these secret believers.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus cried out and said, "Whoever believes in me, believes not in me but in him who sent me. And whoever sees me sees him who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
To believe in Jesus is to believe in the one who sent him.

Cried out. A final public summary of his message.

Believe in me, believe in him. To trust Jesus is to trust God (14:1). The Son is the full revelation of the Father (14:9).

verseByVerse.quote: "I have come into the world as light, so that whoever believes in me may not remain in darkness. If anyone hears my words and does not keep them, I do not judge him; for I did not come to judge the world but to save the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus came as light, to save the world, not to judge it.

Not remain. All begin in darkness; faith brings out of it (Colossians 1:13).

Not to judge. His purpose (3:17).

verseByVerse.quote: "The one who rejects me and does not receive my words has a judge; the word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day. For I have not spoken on my own authority, but the Father who sent me has himself given me a commandment — what to say and what to speak."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who reject his words will be judged by them on the last day.

The word will judge. Rejected words become evidence for the prosecution (Deuteronomy 18:18–19).

On a Tuesday. Every sermon you hear and every page of Scripture you read will either lead you to Christ or stand as a witness. Hear it with care (Hebrews 2:1–3).

parallels.desc: I will put my words in his mouth

verseByVerse.quote: "And I know that his commandment is eternal life. What I say, therefore, I say as the Father has told me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Father’s command, spoken through Jesus, is eternal life.

The Father’s command is life. God’s word is not merely rules but life-giving (6:63, 68; Deuteronomy 32:47).

The end of the public ministry. From chapter 13 Jesus speaks only to his disciples.

For worship. Thank the Father that his command, spoken through his Son, is eternal life.

12.text: <sup>1</sup>Six days before the Passover, Jesus therefore came to Bethany, where Lazarus was, whom Jesus had raised from the dead.<sup>2</sup>So they gave a dinner for him there. Martha served, and Lazarus was one of those reclining with him at table.<sup>3</sup>Mary therefore took a pound of expensive ointment made from pure nard, and anointed the feet of Jesus and wiped his feet with her hair. The house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume.<sup>4</sup>But Judas Iscariot, one of his disciples (he who was about to betray him), said,<sup>5</sup>“Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?”<sup>6</sup>He said this, not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief, and having charge of the moneybag he used to help himself to what was put into it.<sup>7</sup>Jesus said, “Leave her alone, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial.<sup>8</sup>For the poor you always have with you, but you do not always have me.”<sup>9</sup>When the large crowd of the Jews learned that Jesus was there, they came, not only on account of him but also to see Lazarus, whom he had raised from the dead.<sup>10</sup>So the chief priests made plans to put Lazarus to death as well,<sup>11</sup>because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus.<sup>12</sup>The next day the large crowd that had come to the feast heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem.<sup>13</sup>So they took branches of palm trees and went out to meet him, crying out, “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, even the King of Israel!”<sup>14</sup>And Jesus found a young donkey and sat on it, just as it is written,<sup>15</sup>“Fear not, daughter of Zion; behold, your king is coming, sitting on a donkey’s colt!”<sup>16</sup>His disciples did not understand these things at first, but when Jesus was glorified, then they remembered that these things had been written about him and had been done to him.<sup>17</sup>The crowd that had been with him when he called Lazarus out of the tomb and raised him from the dead continued to bear witness.<sup>18</sup>The reason why the crowd went to meet him was that they heard he had done this sign.<sup>19</sup>So the Pharisees said to one another, “You see that you are gaining nothing. Look, the world has gone after him.”<sup>20</sup>Now among those who went up to worship at the feast were some Greeks.<sup>21</sup>So these came to Philip, who was from Bethsaida in Galilee, and asked him, “Sir, we wish to see Jesus.”<sup>22</sup>Philip went and told Andrew; Andrew and Philip went and told Jesus.<sup>23</sup>And Jesus answered them, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.<sup>24</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.<sup>25</sup>Whoever loves his life loses it, and whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life.<sup>26</sup>If anyone serves me, he must follow me; and where I am, there will my servant be also. If anyone serves me, the Father will honor him.<sup>27</sup>“Now is my soul troubled. And what shall I say? ’Father, save me from this hour’? But for this purpose I have come to this hour.<sup>28</sup>Father, glorify your name.“ Then a voice came from heaven: ”I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.”<sup>29</sup>The crowd that stood there and heard it said that it had thundered. Others said, “An angel has spoken to him.”<sup>30</sup>Jesus answered, “This voice has come for your sake, not mine.<sup>31</sup>Now is the judgment of this world; now will the ruler of this world be cast out.<sup>32</sup>And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.”<sup>33</sup>He said this to show by what kind of death he was going to die.<sup>34</sup>So the crowd answered him, “We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever. How can you say that the Son of Man must be lifted up? Who is this Son of Man?”<sup>35</sup>So Jesus said to them, “The light is among you for a little while longer. Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you. The one who walks in the darkness does not know where he is going.<sup>36</sup>While you have the light, believe in the light, that you may become sons of light.” When Jesus had said these things, he departed and hid himself from them.<sup>37</sup>Though he had done so many signs before them, they still did not believe in him,<sup>38</sup>so that the word spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: “Lord, who has believed what he heard from us, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?”<sup>39</sup>Therefore they could not believe. For again Isaiah said,<sup>40</sup>“He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, lest they see with their eyes, and understand with their heart, and turn, and I would heal them.”<sup>41</sup>Isaiah said these things because he saw his glory and spoke of him.<sup>42</sup>Nevertheless, many even of the authorities believed in him, but for fear of the Pharisees they did not confess it, so that they would not be put out of the synagogue;<sup>43</sup>for they loved the glory that comes from man more than the glory that comes from God.<sup>44</sup>And Jesus cried out and said, “Whoever believes in me, believes not in me but in him who sent me.<sup>45</sup>And whoever sees me sees him who sent me.<sup>46</sup>I have come into the world as light, so that whoever believes in me may not remain in darkness.<sup>47</sup>If anyone hears my words and does not keep them, I do not judge him; for I did not come to judge the world but to save the world.<sup>48</sup>The one who rejects me and does not receive my words has a judge; the word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day.<sup>49</sup>For I have not spoken on my own authority, but the Father who sent me has himself given me a commandment—what to say and what to speak.<sup>50</sup>And I know that his commandment is eternal life. What I say, therefore, I say as the Father has told me.”
12.overview:
Chapter 12 closes the first half of John’s Gospel, the “book of signs”, and opens the way to the cross. Six days before Passover, at a dinner in Bethany with Lazarus at the table, Mary pours a pound of costly nard on Jesus’ feet and wipes them with her hair. Judas, a thief, complains about the waste; Jesus defends her: she has kept it for the day of his burial. The next day crowds wave palm branches and hail Jesus as the King of Israel as he rides into Jerusalem on a young donkey, fulfilling Zechariah. The Pharisees despair: “the world has gone after him.”

Then some Greeks ask to see Jesus, and he announces that the hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified. Like a grain of wheat he must fall into the ground and die to bear much fruit; whoever loves his life will lose it. His soul is troubled, but he will not ask to be saved from this hour; instead he prays, “Father, glorify your name,” and a voice from heaven answers. Lifted up from the earth, he will draw all people to himself, and the ruler of this world will be cast out. John then sums up Jesus’ public ministry: despite all his signs, most did not believe, fulfilling Isaiah’s words about blinded eyes and hardened hearts; even among the leaders some believed secretly but would not confess him, loving human glory more than God’s. Jesus’ final public appeal follows: he has come as light into the world, and his word will judge those who reject it on the last day.

13.title: The Foot Washing and the New Commandment

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — The Foot Washing: Love to the End
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Just before Passover, knowing his hour has come to return to the Father, Jesus shows the full extent of his love for his own. At supper, with Judas already moved by the devil to betray him, Jesus, conscious of his authority and his origin and destiny in God, lays aside his outer clothes, ties a towel around himself and washes the disciples’ feet. Peter protests and is told he will understand later; when he refuses, Jesus warns that without this washing Peter has no share in him. Peter then asks for a complete wash, but Jesus says the one already bathed needs only his feet cleaned; they are clean, except one. Back at table, Jesus explains that as their Lord and Teacher he has given them an example: they must wash each other’s feet, for no servant outranks his master, and blessing lies in doing it. He knows whom he chose, yet Scripture foretold that a companion at his table would turn against him. He tells them in advance so that they will believe. To receive his messengers is to receive him and the Father who sent him.
verseByVerse.theology: The foot washing is simultaneously a moral example (do as I have done) and a picture of the cleansing only Christ gives (you need to have your feet washed to have a part in me). Peter's characteristic resistance — then misunderstanding, then over-correction — clarifies both aspects: the washing Jesus gives is not merely a lesson in humility but the cleansing that makes fellowship with him possible. The once-washed disciple needs only the cleaning of feet — the ongoing renewal of those already justified, not re-justification. This is the distinction between initial cleansing (bath) and ongoing renewal (feet-washing): the one already clean needs only this.
verseByVerse.examples: You call me Teacher and Lord, and you are right, for so I am (v. 13). The authority of the foot-washing is its own argument. Jesus does not wash feet because he has forgotten who he is; he washes feet because he knows exactly who he is (v. 3-4). The servant heart flows from the secure identity: those who are anxious about their position never serve freely; those who know their position in Christ serve without self-protection. Genuine servanthood is not self-abasement but the overflow of a heart that has been secured by the Father's love.

verseByVerse.quote: Now before the Feast of the Passover, when Jesus knew that his hour had come to depart out of this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end. During supper, when the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon's son, to betray him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing his hour has come, Jesus loves his own to the very end, even as the devil moves Judas to betray him.

His hour has come. Announced in 12:23. The whole second half of the Gospel is that hour.

To the end. Eis telos: to the uttermost, completely, and to the finish. Echoed in the cry from the cross, “It is finished” (tetelestai, 19:30).

His own. Contrast 1:11, where “his own” rejected him. Now a new “his own”, the disciples.

Before the Passover. Where Christians differ: the date of the Last Supper. Matthew, Mark and Luke present it as a Passover meal (Mark 14:12). John seems to place Jesus’ death on the day the Passover lambs were killed (18:28; 19:14, 31). Explanations: different calendars in use (some groups followed a solar calendar); “Passover” in John meaning the whole week-long festival; or the Synoptics’ meal being an early Passover. Verdict: no consensus, but several reasonable harmonisations exist; the theological point is the same: Jesus is the Passover Lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7).

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “supper being ended” (KJV). Verdict: “during supper” is better attested and fits verse 26.

The devil and Judas. Satan prompts, but Judas consents (v. 27).
verseByVerse.note: John’s account of the last evening fills five chapters (13–17). “Simon’s son” is a different Simon from Peter.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going back to God, rose from supper. He laid aside his outer garments, and taking a towel, tied it around his waist.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Conscious of his supreme authority, Jesus takes the place of a slave.

Knowing … rose. His awareness of supreme authority leads not to grasping but to serving (Philippians 2:5–8).

Laid aside. The same verb as “lay down my life” (10:11, 17–18). The foot-washing is a picture of the cross.

A towel. The dress of a slave.

For worship. The hands that held all things took a towel. Worship the humble King.
verseByVerse.note: Washing guests’ feet was the job of the lowest household slave; roads were dusty and people wore sandals.

parallels.desc: I am among you as the one who serves

verseByVerse.quote: Then he poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples' feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him. He came to Simon Peter, who said to him, "Lord, do you wash my feet?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus washes the disciples’ dirty feet, and Peter protests.

Dirty feet. In sandals on dusty roads, feet were filthy. Washing them was a job for the lowest slave; Jewish slaves were sometimes exempted from it as too degrading.

No one else did it. Luke 22:24 records that they were arguing about who was greatest that evening.

You wash my feet? The emphasis in Greek falls on “you” and “my”.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "What I am doing you do not understand now, but afterward you will understand." Peter said to him, "You shall never wash my feet." Jesus answered him, "If I do not wash you, you have no share with me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unless Jesus washes us, we have no share in him.

Afterward. After the cross and resurrection.

Never. Pride disguised as humility: Peter will not let Jesus serve him.

No share. The deeper meaning: unless Jesus cleanses us from sin through his death, we have no part in him. Salvation means receiving his service.

On a Tuesday. Is there pride in you that resists being helped by God or by others?

verseByVerse.quote: Simon Peter said to him, "Lord, not my feet only but also my hands and my head!" Jesus said to him, "The one who has bathed does not need to wash, except for his feet, but is completely clean. And you are clean, but not every one of you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those already cleansed need only daily washing, but not all of them are clean.

All or nothing. Peter swings to the other extreme.

Bathed and feet. A guest bathed at home, then needed only his feet washed on arrival. Theologically: the once-for-all cleansing of justification and regeneration (Titus 3:5; 1 Corinthians 6:11) and the ongoing cleansing from daily sins through confession (1 John 1:9). A Christian does not need to be saved again each time he sins, but does need daily forgiveness.

Textual note. Some manuscripts omit “except for his feet”. Verdict: the longer reading is better attested.

Not all. Judas.
verseByVerse.note: Guests bathed before a banquet and needed only their feet washed on arrival.

parallels.desc: you are already clean

verseByVerse.quote: For he knew who was to betray him; that was why he said, "Not all of you are clean." When he had washed their feet and put on his outer garments and resumed his place, he said to them, "Do you understand what I have done to you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus washes even his betrayer’s feet, then asks whether they understand.

He washed Judas’s feet. Knowing everything, Jesus served his betrayer.

Do you understand? A teaching moment.

On a Tuesday. Who is your Judas, someone who has hurt you? Could you serve them?

verseByVerse.quote: "You call me Teacher and Lord, and you are right, for so I am. If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another's feet."
verseByVerse.commentary:
If their Lord and Teacher has washed their feet, they must wash one another’s.

Lord and Teacher. Humility does not deny his authority; it expresses it.

One another. Mutual service, not a hierarchy of servers and served.

Where Christians differ: an ordinance? Some churches (some Baptists, Brethren, Mennonites, Adventists) practise foot-washing as an ordinance alongside baptism and the Lord’s Supper; Roman Catholics wash feet on Maundy Thursday. Most Protestants see it as an example of humble service rather than a ritual command. Verdict: the command is to do humble, practical service for one another; foot-washing may be practised as a sign, but the substance matters more than the ceremony.

verseByVerse.quote: "For I have given you an example, that you also should do just as I have done to you. Truly, truly, I say to you, a servant is not greater than his master, nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus has given them an example: no servant is above his master.

An example. Hypodeigma, a pattern to copy (1 Peter 2:21).

Not greater. If the Master stoops, no servant is too important to serve.

On a Tuesday. What is the most menial task in your home, office or church? Do it, without being asked, and without telling anyone.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them. I am not speaking of all of you; I know whom I have chosen. But the Scripture will be fulfilled, 'He who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Blessing lies in doing what they know, and Scripture foretold a friend’s betrayal.

Knowing and doing. Blessing lies in obedience, not mere understanding (James 1:22–25).

Whom I have chosen. He chose the Twelve, Judas included (6:70), knowing what Judas would do.

Psalm 41:9. David betrayed by a close friend, probably Ahithophel (2 Samuel 15–17), who later hanged himself, as Judas did. Eating bread together was a bond of trust; lifting the heel is a picture of a violent kick or treachery.

Where Christians differ: was Judas free? If Scripture foretold it, was Judas responsible? Verdict: both: God foretold and ordained it, and Judas freely and culpably did it (Acts 2:23; Luke 22:22). God’s sovereignty does not remove human guilt.
verseByVerse.note: Lifting the heel against someone is a picture of treachery.

parallels.desc: my close friend, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me

verseByVerse.quote: "I am telling you this now, before it takes place, that when it does take place you may believe that I am he. Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever receives the one I send receives me, and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus foretells the betrayal so that they will believe he is the I am, and sends them with his authority.

I am he. Again the divine name (8:24, 28, 58). Fulfilled prophecy confirms who he is (Isaiah 41:21–23; 46:9–10).

Receiving messengers. Despite the betrayal, the mission continues. The apostles will carry Christ’s authority (20:21; Matthew 10:40).

parallels.desc: that you may know and believe that I am he

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–38 — The Betrayer Exposed and the New Commandment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Troubled in spirit, Jesus announces that one of them will betray him, and the bewildered disciples look at one another. At Peter’s signal, the disciple Jesus loves, reclining beside him, asks who it is. Jesus answers that it is the one to whom he gives the dipped morsel, and he hands it to Judas. Satan enters Judas, and Jesus tells him to act quickly; the others assume he is being sent on an errand with the common purse. Judas goes out into the night. Then Jesus says that the Son of Man is now glorified, and God in him. He will soon leave them, and they cannot follow yet. He gives them a new command, to love one another as he has loved them, the mark by which all will recognise his disciples. When Peter insists he will follow even to death, Jesus predicts that before the rooster crows Peter will disown him three times.
verseByVerse.theology: Love one another as I have loved you is the social ethics of the atonement made into community commandment. The 'as I have loved you' is the measure and the model: not abstract love or sentiment, but the costly, self-giving, foot-washing, cross-bearing love that Jesus has just demonstrated and is about to complete. This is a new commandment not because love was absent from the Mosaic law (Lev. 19:18) but because the standard is new: as I have loved you is qualitatively greater than 'as yourself.' The measure of Christian community love is the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: The prediction of Peter's denial is embedded within Peter's most confident declaration. He will not only follow Jesus but lay down his life for him. Jesus accepts neither the protest nor the probability: Will you lay down your life for me? Truly, truly, I say to you — the triple denial will come before morning. Jesus does not shame Peter but tells the truth that Peter needs to hear: his fidelity rests on a foundation Peter has not yet tested. The testing will come, the failure will happen, and the restoration that follows (ch. 21) will be built on a more honest foundation than confidence ever was.

verseByVerse.quote: After saying these things, Jesus was troubled in his spirit, and testified, "Truly, truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me." The disciples looked at one another, uncertain of whom he spoke.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Troubled, Jesus announces that one of them will betray him.

Troubled. The third time (11:33; 12:27). Betrayal by a friend wounds deeply.

Uncertain. Judas had hidden it well. No one suspected him.

On a Tuesday. If a friend has betrayed you, know that Jesus understands.

verseByVerse.quote: One of his disciples, whom Jesus loved, was reclining at table at Jesus' side, so Simon Peter motioned to him to ask Jesus of whom he was speaking.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciple Jesus loved reclines beside him, and Peter prompts him to ask.

Reclining. Guests lay on couches round a low table, propped on the left elbow. The beloved disciple was on Jesus’ right, so his head was near Jesus’ chest.

The disciple whom Jesus loved. First mentioned here (also 19:26; 20:2; 21:7, 20). Never named. He is the author of this Gospel (21:24). Where Christians differ: who was he? Church tradition from the second century (Irenaeus) identifies him as John son of Zebedee. Some modern scholars suggest Lazarus (11:3, 5), John the Elder, or an ideal figure. Verdict: John the apostle remains the most likely; he is otherwise strangely absent from this Gospel, and is always with Peter (Acts 3–4).

Loved. Not that Jesus loved the others less, but that this disciple knew himself loved.
verseByVerse.note: Guests reclined on couches, leaning on the left elbow; the one on the host’s right lay with his head near the host’s chest. The disciple “whom Jesus loved” is traditionally identified as John, the Gospel’s author.

verseByVerse.quote: So that disciple, leaning back against Jesus, said to him, "Lord, who is it?" Jesus answered, "It is he to whom I will give this morsel of bread when I have dipped it." So when he had dipped the morsel, he gave it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus offers Judas the morsel of friendship.

The morsel. Giving a choice piece of bread dipped in the sauce was a mark of honour and friendship. Jesus offers love to the end.

A quiet answer. Apparently only the beloved disciple hears it (v. 28).
verseByVerse.note: Handing a guest a dipped morsel was a mark of honour.

verseByVerse.quote: Then after he had taken the morsel, Satan entered into him. Jesus said to him, "What you are going to do, do quickly." Now no one at the table knew why he said this to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rejecting love’s last appeal, Judas gives himself to Satan, and Jesus sends him out.

Satan entered. Having rejected Christ’s final appeal of love, Judas gives himself fully to the enemy (Luke 22:3).

Do it quickly. Jesus is in control of the timing (10:18).

Where Christians differ: possession of a disciple? Can Satan enter a believer? Verdict: Judas was never a true believer (6:64; 17:12). Christians may be tempted and harassed, but are indwelt by the Spirit and cannot be possessed (1 John 4:4; 5:18).

verseByVerse.quote: Some thought that, because Judas had the moneybag, Jesus was telling him, "Buy what we need for the feast," or that he should give something to the poor. So, after receiving the morsel of bread, he immediately went out. And it was night.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judas goes out into the night.

The poor. Giving to the poor was customary on Passover night. Jesus and the disciples did it, as Judas’s pretended concern implies (12:5–6).

And it was night. Four of the most chilling words in Scripture. Judas walks out from the light of the world into darkness (3:19; 11:10; 12:35).

For worship. Thank Jesus that, though Judas went out into the night, the light of the world went on to the cross for you.
verseByVerse.note: Giving to the poor at Passover was a custom.

parallels.desc: send portions to anyone who has nothing ready
the power of darkness

verseByVerse.quote: When he had gone out, Jesus said, "Now is the Son of Man glorified, and God is glorified in him. If God is glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and glorify him at once."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the betrayal the Son of Man is glorified, and God in him.

Now. The betrayal sets the cross in motion. The moment of deepest treachery is the moment of glory.

Glorified. Five times in two verses. The cross reveals the glory of God’s love, justice and wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:23–24). The resurrection and ascension follow at once.

Textual note. Some early manuscripts omit “If God is glorified in him”. Verdict: probably original, omitted by accident through repetition.

verseByVerse.quote: "Little children, yet a little while I am with you. You will seek me, and just as I said to the Jews, so now I also say to you, 'Where I am going you cannot come.' A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another: just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus gives a new commandment: love one another as he has loved them.

Little children. The only time in this Gospel; a tender word, used often in 1 John.

You cannot come. Not yet (v. 36; 14:3).

A new commandment. Love was commanded in the law (Leviticus 19:18). What is new is the standard, “as I have loved you”, and the community: a new people bound together by Christ’s love (1 John 2:7–8). From the Latin mandatum novum comes “Maundy” Thursday.

As I have loved you. Washing feet, giving life.
verseByVerse.note: Love of neighbour was old; the new standard is “as I have loved you.”

verseByVerse.quote: "By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another." Simon Peter said to him, "Lord, where are you going?" Jesus answered him, "Where I am going you cannot follow me now, but you will follow afterward."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love for one another is the mark by which the world will know his disciples.

The mark of a Christian. Not miracles, knowledge or even doctrine alone, but love for fellow believers. Francis Schaeffer called it “the mark of the Christian”. Tertullian reports pagans saying, “See how they love one another.”

Follow afterward. In his own death as a martyr (21:18–19), and to glory.

On a Tuesday. Would your neighbours know you are a Christian by the way your church members treat one another?

parallels.desc: the death by which Peter would glorify God

verseByVerse.quote: Peter said to him, "Lord, why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you." Jesus answered, "Will you lay down your life for me? Truly, truly, I say to you, the rooster will not crow till you have denied me three times."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter vows to die for Jesus, and Jesus foretells his threefold denial.

I will lay down my life. Peter offers to do for Jesus what Jesus is about to do for him (10:11). Sincere, but self-confident.

Will you? A gentle, sad question.

Three times. Fulfilled in 18:15–27; restored three times in 21:15–17.

The rooster. Crowing marked the third watch, around 3 a.m.

On a Tuesday. Do not trust your own strength. The boldest promise can fail; rely on Christ’s faithfulness (Luke 22:31–32).

For worship. Jesus knew Peter would fail, and loved him to the end. He knows you, and loves you just the same.

13.text: <sup>1</sup>Now before the Feast of the Passover, when Jesus knew that his hour had come to depart out of this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end.<sup>2</sup>During supper, when the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon’s son, to betray him,<sup>3</sup>Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going back to God,<sup>4</sup>rose from supper. He laid aside his outer garments, and taking a towel, tied it around his waist.<sup>5</sup>Then he poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel that was wrapped around him.<sup>6</sup>He came to Simon Peter, who said to him, “Lord, do you wash my feet?”<sup>7</sup>Jesus answered him, “What I am doing you do not understand now, but afterward you will understand.”<sup>8</sup>Peter said to him, “You shall never wash my feet.” Jesus answered him, “If I do not wash you, you have no share with me.”<sup>9</sup>Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, not my feet only but also my hands and my head!”<sup>10</sup>Jesus said to him, “The one who has bathed does not need to wash, except for his feet, but is completely clean. And you are clean, but not every one of you.”<sup>11</sup>For he knew who was to betray him; that was why he said, “Not all of you are clean.”<sup>12</sup>When he had washed their feet and put on his outer garments and resumed his place, he said to them, “Do you understand what I have done to you?<sup>13</sup>You call me Teacher and Lord, and you are right, for so I am.<sup>14</sup>If I then, your Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.<sup>15</sup>For I have given you an example, that you also should do just as I have done to you.<sup>16</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, a servant is not greater than his master, nor is a messenger greater than the one who sent him.<sup>17</sup>If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.<sup>18</sup>I am not speaking of all of you; I know whom I have chosen. But the Scripture will be fulfilled, ’He who ate my bread has lifted his heel against me.’<sup>19</sup>I am telling you this now, before it takes place, that when it does take place you may believe that I am he.<sup>20</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever receives the one I send receives me, and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me.”<sup>21</sup>After saying these things, Jesus was troubled in his spirit, and testified, “Truly, truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me.”<sup>22</sup>The disciples looked at one another, uncertain of whom he spoke.<sup>23</sup>One of his disciples, whom Jesus loved, was reclining at table at Jesus’ side,<sup>24</sup>so Simon Peter motioned to him to ask Jesus of whom he was speaking.<sup>25</sup>So that disciple, leaning back against Jesus, said to him, “Lord, who is it?”<sup>26</sup>Jesus answered, “It is he to whom I will give this morsel of bread when I have dipped it.” So when he had dipped the morsel, he gave it to Judas, the son of Simon Iscariot.<sup>27</sup>Then after he had taken the morsel, Satan entered into him. Jesus said to him, “What you are going to do, do quickly.”<sup>28</sup>Now no one at the table knew why he said this to him.<sup>29</sup>Some thought that, because Judas had the moneybag, Jesus was telling him, “Buy what we need for the feast,” or that he should give something to the poor.<sup>30</sup>So, after receiving the morsel of bread, he immediately went out. And it was night.<sup>31</sup>When he had gone out, Jesus said, “Now is the Son of Man glorified, and God is glorified in him.<sup>32</sup>If God is glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and glorify him at once.<sup>33</sup>Little children, yet a little while I am with you. You will seek me, and just as I said to the Jews, so now I also say to you, ’Where I am going you cannot come.’<sup>34</sup>A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another: just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another.<sup>35</sup>By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”<sup>36</sup>Simon Peter said to him, “Lord, where are you going?” Jesus answered him, “Where I am going you cannot follow me now, but you will follow afterward.”<sup>37</sup>Peter said to him, “Lord, why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.”<sup>38</sup>Jesus answered, “Will you lay down your life for me? Truly, truly, I say to you, the rooster will not crow till you have denied me three times.
13.overview:
With chapter 13 the “book of glory” begins. The public ministry is over; for five chapters Jesus is alone with his disciples on the night before he dies, in what is often called the Upper Room or Farewell Discourse (13–17). John opens it with a sentence that sums up the cross: having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end. Knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, Jesus rises from supper, ties a towel round his waist and washes his disciples’ feet, the task of a slave. Peter protests, then asks to be washed all over; Jesus explains that one who has bathed needs only his feet washed, and that unless he washes Peter, Peter has no share with him. He tells them he has given them an example: as their Lord and Teacher has served them, they must serve one another.

Then Jesus, troubled, announces that one of them will betray him. At Peter’s prompting the disciple whom Jesus loved asks who it is; Jesus gives a morsel of bread to Judas, Satan enters him, and Judas goes out: “and it was night.” With the betrayer gone, Jesus speaks of his glorification and gives his disciples a new commandment: to love one another as he has loved them, so that all people will know they are his disciples. When Peter vows to lay down his life for him, Jesus foretells that before the rooster crows Peter will deny him three times. The chapter holds together the humility of Christ, the treachery of a friend, the weakness of the boldest disciple, and a love that does not let go.

14.title: I Am the Way, the Truth, and the Life

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The Way to the Father
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus calms his troubled disciples: as they trust God, they should trust him. In his Father’s house there is ample room, and he goes to prepare a place and will return to take them to himself. Thomas protests that they do not know the way; Jesus replies that he is the way, the truth and the life, the only route to the Father. To know him is to know the Father. When Philip asks to see the Father, Jesus says that anyone who has seen him has seen the Father, for the Father lives in him and does his works through him. Believers will do the same works and greater, because he is going to the Father, and he will do whatever they ask in his name for the Father’s glory.
verseByVerse.theology: I am the way, the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me is both comfort and exclusivity. Comfort: there is a way to the Father, it is real, it is accessible, it is Jesus. Exclusivity: this is the only way, and all other paths are paths that do not lead to the Father. The exclusivity is not arrogance; it is the necessary consequence of the incarnation. If God has come in one place, in one person, for one purpose, then there is one way home. The scandal of particularity cannot be removed without removing the gospel itself.
verseByVerse.examples: Whatever you ask in my name, this I will do (v. 13). Prayer in Jesus' name is not a formula attached to the end of requests; it is prayer aligned with his character, his purposes, and his glory. To ask in Jesus' name is to ask as he would ask, for what he would ask for, in the way that honors the Father through the Son. This is why prayer in Jesus' name is effective: it brings human desire into alignment with divine will, and divine will always accomplishes its purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: "Let not your hearts be troubled. Believe in God; believe also in me. In my Father's house are many rooms. If it were not so, would I have told you that I go to prepare a place for you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus calms troubled hearts: trust him as you trust God, for there is room in his Father’s house.

Troubled. Jesus himself was troubled (12:27; 13:21). Now he comforts them. The cure for a troubled heart is faith.

Believe in God; believe in me. The Greek can be read as statements or commands. Either way, trust in Jesus is set alongside trust in God, a claim to deity.

My Father’s house. Earlier the temple (2:16); now heaven, the presence of God.

Many rooms. Monai, dwelling places (the KJV’s “mansions” meant lodgings in 1611). The same root as “abide” (v. 23). Room enough for all.

Textual note. The punctuation is uncertain: “If it were not so, I would have told you, for I go to prepare a place” (KJV) or as a question (ESV). Verdict: either way, Jesus assures them of their place.

For worship. Read this at the bedside of the dying, and in your own anxious nights.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes an alternative reading of verse 2: “if it were not so, I would have told you, for I go to prepare a place for you.” Family houses were often extended with rooms as the family grew.

parallels.desc: I shall dwell in the house of the LORD forever

verseByVerse.quote: "And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also. And you know the way to where I am going."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus goes to prepare a place and will come again to take his people to himself.

Prepare a place. By his death, resurrection and ascension he opens the way (Hebrews 6:19–20; 9:24).

I will come again. Where Christians differ. Some see Jesus’ return at the end of the age; others his coming at each believer’s death, or his coming by the Spirit (v. 18). Dispensationalists see a secret rapture before the tribulation. Verdict: primarily his visible second coming (Acts 1:11; 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17), with no secret rapture; and he also comes to his people by the Spirit now (vv. 18, 23) and receives them at death (Philippians 1:23).

To myself. The heart of heaven is not the place but the person: to be with Christ (17:24).

Textual note. Later manuscripts read “where I go you know, and the way you know” (KJV). Verdict: the shorter text is original.

verseByVerse.quote: Thomas said to him, "Lord, we do not know where you are going. How can we know the way?" Jesus said to him, "I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is the way, the truth and the life, the only way to the Father.

Thomas. Honest, literal, pessimistic (11:16; 20:25). His question draws out one of the greatest sayings.

The way. Not a teacher who shows a way, but the way himself. Christians were first called “the Way” (Acts 9:2).

The truth. The full revelation of God (1:14, 17).

The life. Eternal life itself (11:25).

No one except through me. Where Christians differ. Pluralists hold all religions lead to God; inclusivists that people may be saved through Christ without knowing him. Verdict: the app’s exclusivist view: salvation is only through Christ and through conscious faith in him (Acts 4:12; Romans 10:13–15). Held with humility and urgency, not arrogance: it is good news for everyone, because the way is open to all who come.

On a Tuesday. When friends say all roads lead to God, ask them gently what Jesus said, and why he would die if there were another way.
verseByVerse.note: This is the sixth of Jesus’ “I am” sayings in John.

parallels.desc: no other name
the Way

verseByVerse.quote: "If you had known me, you would have known my Father also. From now on you do know him and have seen him." Philip said to him, "Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
To know Jesus is to know the Father, and Philip asks to see the Father.

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “If you know me, you will know my Father” (a promise, not a rebuke). Verdict: uncertain; both are true.

Show us the Father. Like Moses (Exodus 33:18). Philip wants a vision.

parallels.desc: please show me your glory

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to him, "Have I been with you so long, and you still do not know me, Philip? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father. How can you say, 'Show us the Father'? Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? The words that I say to you I do not speak on my own authority, but the Father who dwells in me does his works."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whoever has seen Jesus has seen the Father, who lives and works in him.

So long. Three years.

Seen me, seen the Father. Not that Jesus is the Father (modalism), but that the Son perfectly reveals him (1:18; Colossians 1:15; Hebrews 1:3).

In each other. Mutual indwelling (10:38).

For worship. If you want to know what God is like, look at Jesus washing feet, weeping at a grave and dying on a cross.

verseByVerse.quote: "Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father is in me, or else believe on account of the works themselves. Truly, truly, I say to you, whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do; and greater works than these will he do, because I am going to the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers will do greater works because Jesus goes to the Father.

Believe the works. Evidence for those who struggle (10:38).

Greater works. Where Christians differ. Some read this as promising believers greater miracles than Jesus did. Most interpreters, Reformed and others, take it to mean greater in scope: after Pentecost, through the Spirit, the gospel spreads across the world and thousands are brought to life (Acts 2:41). Verdict: the greater works are the spiritual harvest of the new covenant, made possible because Jesus goes to the Father and sends the Spirit; not a promise that every believer will work greater wonders.

Because I go. The key: Christ’s ascension and the Spirit’s coming.
verseByVerse.note: “Greater works” refers to the worldwide spread of the gospel after the Spirit came.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whatever you ask in my name, this I will do, that the Father may be glorified in the Son. If you ask me anything in my name, I will do it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus will do whatever is asked in his name, for the Father’s glory.

In my name. Not a formula tagged on, but praying as his representatives, in line with his character and will (1 John 5:14), for his glory.
