What it does not mean. Not a blank cheque for anything we want (James 4:3), as some prosperity preachers teach. The purpose is the Father’s glory.

Ask me. Prayer to Jesus himself is appropriate (Acts 7:59; 2 Corinthians 12:8). Textual note. Some manuscripts omit verse 14 or “me”. Verdict: both are probably original.

On a Tuesday. Pray boldly about the work God has given you, asking that Christ will be glorified in it.
verseByVerse.note: Praying “in my name” means praying as his representatives, according to his will.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–31 — The Promise of the Spirit and the Peace of Christ
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Love for Jesus shows itself in obeying him. He will ask the Father to give them another Helper, the Spirit of truth, who will stay with them for ever. The world cannot receive him, but they know him, for he lives with them and will be in them. Jesus will not leave them orphaned; he will come to them. Soon the world will not see him, but they will, and because he lives, they will live. Then they will know that he is in the Father, they in him and he in them. Whoever keeps his commands loves him and will be loved by the Father, and Jesus will show himself to them. Judas (not Iscariot) asks why he will reveal himself to them and not the world. Jesus replies that he and the Father will come and make their home with anyone who loves him and keeps his word. The Spirit, sent in his name, will teach them everything and remind them of all he said. He leaves them his peace, unlike the world’s, so they need not be troubled or afraid. If they loved him, they would be glad he is going to the Father, who is greater than he. He tells them now so they will believe when it happens. The ruler of this world is coming, but has no hold on him; he goes to show the world that he loves the Father and does what he commands. Then he tells them to get up and leave.
verseByVerse.theology: The Helper (Parakletos — Advocate, Comforter, Counselor) is described with four characteristics in the farewell discourse: he is the Spirit of truth (14:17), the Holy Spirit who teaches and reminds (14:26), the Spirit who testifies about Jesus (15:26), and the one who convicts the world (16:8). Each characteristic is an aspect of the single mission: to continue and apply what Jesus accomplished. The Spirit does not bring new revelation beyond Jesus but illuminates everything Jesus said and did, making it present and personal to each generation of believers.
verseByVerse.examples: My peace I give to you: not as the world gives. The world's peace is the absence of conflict, the management of anxiety, the temporary resolution of problems. Jesus' peace is an interior stability that coexists with external trouble — the shalom of the covenant, the wholeness that comes from being right with God and secure in his love. Not as the world gives: the two kinds of peace are not on the same spectrum; one is the presence of order, the other is the presence of God. The disciples will need this peace before the night is over.

verseByVerse.quote: "If you love me, you will keep my commandments. And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love for Jesus shows itself in obedience, and the Father will give another Helper to be with them for ever.

Love and obedience. Not obedience to earn love, but love expressed in obedience (vv. 21, 23; 1 John 5:3).

Another Helper. Paraklētos: one called alongside, an advocate, counsellor, comforter, helper. Used of Jesus himself (1 John 2:1). “Another” of the same kind: the Spirit continues Jesus’ presence and ministry.

For ever. Not temporarily, as on Old Testament prophets, but permanently.

The Trinity at work. The Son asks, the Father gives, the Spirit comes.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Helper” can also be rendered “Advocate” or “Counselor.” “Another” implies one like Jesus himself.

parallels.desc: an advocate with the Father

verseByVerse.quote: "even the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. You know him, for he dwells with you and will be in you. I will not leave you as orphans; I will come to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit of truth, unknown to the world, will live in believers.

Spirit of truth. He reveals and applies the truth of Christ (16:13).

The world cannot. Spiritual blindness (1 Corinthians 2:14).

With you, in you. Present with them in Jesus, and soon within them (20:22; Romans 8:9). Textual note. Some manuscripts read “is in you”. Verdict: “will be” is better.

A person. Jesus speaks of the Spirit as “he”, not “it”, though the Greek word for spirit is neuter. The Spirit is a person, not a force.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read “and is in you.”

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet a little while and the world will see me no more, but you will see me. Because I live, you also will live. In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus will not leave them orphans: because he lives, they will live.

Orphans. Disciples without their teacher were called orphans. Jesus promises not to abandon them.

I will come. In the resurrection appearances, and in the Spirit.

Because I live. Our life depends on his (Colossians 3:3–4).

In that day. After Easter and Pentecost they will understand the union: Father in Son, Son in believers.

For worship. Thank Christ: because he lives, you will live.

verseByVerse.quote: "Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me. And he who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him." Judas (not Iscariot) said to him, "Lord, how is it that you will manifest yourself to us, and not to the world?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who love Jesus keep his commands, and he reveals himself to them.

Has and keeps. Knowing his commands and doing them.

Loved by my Father. Not that obedience earns love (God loved first, 1 John 4:19), but that obedient disciples enjoy his love more deeply.

Judas, not Iscariot. Probably Thaddaeus, Judas son of James (Luke 6:16).

Why not the world? He expected a public messianic display.
verseByVerse.note: This Judas is Judas the son of James, probably the Thaddaeus of Matthew and Mark.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him. Whoever does not love me does not keep my words. And the word that you hear is not mine but the Father's who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Father and the Son will come and make their home with those who love Jesus.

Our home. Monē, the word for “rooms” in verse 2. Before we go to the Father’s house, the Father and the Son come to live in ours.

We. The Father and the Son. With the Spirit, the whole Trinity dwells in believers.

On a Tuesday. Your body and home are where God lives. Live accordingly (1 Corinthians 6:19).

parallels.desc: my dwelling place shall be with them

verseByVerse.quote: "These things I have spoken to you while I am still with you. But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit will teach the apostles all things and remind them of all Jesus said.

Teach and remind. A promise first to the apostles, guaranteeing the reliability of their witness to Jesus’ words: the basis of the New Testament (2 Peter 1:21; 3:2).

What it does not mean. Not that every believer will receive new revelation beyond Scripture. The Spirit teaches us today by illuminating what he caused the apostles to remember and write (1 John 2:20, 27).

In my name. The Spirit comes as Christ’s representative.

verseByVerse.quote: "Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Not as the world gives do I give to you. Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid. You heard me say to you, 'I am going away, and I will come to you.' If you loved me, you would have rejoiced, because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus leaves them his peace, and rejoices to return to the Father.

Peace. Shalom, the usual farewell, filled with new meaning: wholeness and reconciliation with God (Romans 5:1; Philippians 4:7).

Not as the world gives. The world’s peace is absence of trouble; Christ’s is presence of God in trouble (16:33).

The Father is greater. Where Christians differ. Arians used this to argue the Son is a lesser being. The church fathers answered that the Father is greater in relation to the Son’s incarnate state, humbled and about to die (Philippians 2:6–8), or as the source within the Trinity, not in nature (10:30). Verdict: equal in being, the Son in his humiliation joyfully returns to the glory he shared with the Father (17:5).
verseByVerse.note: “Peace” (shalom) was the everyday greeting and farewell. “The Father is greater” speaks of the Son in his humble human state, not a lesser divine nature.

parallels.desc: the LORD give you peace

verseByVerse.quote: "And now I have told you before it takes place, so that when it does take place you may believe. I will no longer talk much with you, for the ruler of this world is coming. He has no claim on me,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ruler of this world is coming, but has no claim on Jesus.

The ruler of this world. Satan, working through Judas and the authorities (13:27).

No claim on me. Literally “in me he has nothing”: no sin to accuse, no hold, no right. Jesus goes to the cross not as Satan’s captive but freely (10:18).

For worship. Because the enemy had no claim on Jesus, he has none on those who are in Jesus (Romans 8:1, 33–34).

verseByVerse.quote: "but I do as the Father has commanded me, so that the world may know that I love the Father. Rise, let us go from here."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus goes to the cross to show the world his love for the Father.

That the world may know. The cross displays the Son’s love for the Father, as well as the Father’s love for the world (3:16).

Rise, let us go. Puzzling, since chapters 15–17 follow before they leave (18:1). Where Christians differ. Some scholars think the chapters were rearranged or added later. Others suggest they got up and Jesus kept teaching as they walked through the city, past vines (15:1), or stood to sing a hymn (Mark 14:26). Verdict: a natural reading: they rose and Jesus continued speaking before or on the way.

On a Tuesday. Jesus goes to face death with determination. Whatever hard thing you must face, get up and go with him.
verseByVerse.note: Some think they left the upper room here, with chapters 15–17 spoken on the way; others that they rose but stayed.

Because I live, you also will live.<sup>20</sup>In that day you will know that I am in my Father, and you in me, and I in you.<sup>21</sup>Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me. And he who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him.”<sup>22</sup>Judas (not Iscariot) said to him, “Lord, how is it that you will manifest yourself to us, and not to the world?”<sup>23</sup>Jesus answered him, “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him.<sup>24</sup>Whoever does not love me does not keep my words. And the word that you hear is not mine but the Father’s who sent me.<sup>25</sup>“These things I have spoken to you while I am still with you.<sup>26</sup>But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you.<sup>27</sup>Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Not as the world gives do I give to you. Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid.<sup>28</sup>You heard me say to you, ’I am going away, and I will come to you.’ If you loved me, you would have rejoiced, because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I.<sup>29</sup>And now I have told you before it takes place, so that when it does take place you may believe.<sup>30</sup>I will no longer talk much with you, for the ruler of this world is coming. He has no claim on me,<sup>31</sup>but I do as the Father has commanded me, so that the world may know that I love the Father. Rise, let us go from here.
14.overview:
Jesus has just told his friends that he is leaving, that one of them will betray him and that Peter will deny him. Into their fear he speaks some of the most comforting words in Scripture: “Let not your hearts be troubled.” He is going to prepare a place for them in his Father’s house and will come again to take them to himself. When Thomas asks the way, Jesus answers, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.” When Philip asks to see the Father, Jesus replies that whoever has seen him has seen the Father. Those who believe will do greater works, because he is going to the Father, and whatever they ask in his name he will do.

The second half of the chapter introduces the Holy Spirit as “another Helper”, the Spirit of truth, who will be with them for ever and in them. Jesus will not leave them as orphans; he will come to them, and he and the Father will make their home with those who love him and keep his word. The Spirit will teach them all things and remind them of everything Jesus said, the promise that underlies the writing of the New Testament. He leaves them his peace, not as the world gives. The ruler of this world is coming, but has no claim on him; Jesus goes to the cross so that the world may know that he loves the Father. Here the doctrine of the Trinity is not argued but lived: the Father sends, the Son goes and prays, the Spirit comes, and all three make their home with the believer.

15.title: The True Vine

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — Abide in Me: The Vine and the Branches
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus calls himself the true vine, with his Father as the gardener who removes fruitless branches and prunes fruitful ones to make them more productive. The disciples are already made clean by his word. They must stay joined to him, for no branch bears fruit cut off from the vine, and without him they can achieve nothing; branches that do not remain are thrown out to wither and burn. If his words remain in them, their prayers will be answered, and their abundant fruit will glorify the Father and prove them disciples. He has loved them as the Father loves him, and they remain in his love by obeying him, as he obeys the Father, so that his joy may fill them. His command is that they love one another as he has loved them; the highest love gives its life for friends. They are his friends, not mere servants, for he has shared with them all he heard from the Father. He chose them, not they him, and appointed them to bear fruit that lasts.
verseByVerse.theology: I am the true vine: Israel was the vine God planted (Ps. 80:8; Isa. 5:1-7; Jer. 2:21; Ezek. 15; Hos. 10:1). Israel repeatedly failed as the vine. Jesus is the vine Israel was always meant to be — the true Israel, the faithful son, the one who bears fruit that lasts. The disciples are branches in this vine: their fruitfulness is entirely dependent on their connection to Jesus. Apart from me you can do nothing is the Reformed doctrine of total human dependence stated for the community of disciples. The branch does not produce fruit; it bears fruit — the distinction between human effort and Spirit-mediated connection.
verseByVerse.examples: You did not choose me, but I chose you (v. 16): the elective basis of discipleship. The disciples' following of Jesus is traced back to his choosing, not their decision. This does not make the disciples passive; they are appointed to go and bear fruit. But the initiative, the foundation, and the guarantee of fruitfulness reside in the one who chose, not in those who were chosen. Whatever fruit the Christian life produces is the fruit of the Vine, borne through the branches who abide.

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away, and every branch that does bear fruit he prunes, that it may bear more fruit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is the true vine, and the Father removes fruitless branches and prunes fruitful ones.

The true vine. The last of the seven “I am” sayings. Israel was God’s vine but bore bad fruit (Isaiah 5:1–7; Psalm 80:8–16). Jesus is the true Israel, the vine that bears the fruit God looked for. A golden vine decorated the temple entrance.

The vinedresser. The Father tends the vine with care.

Takes away. Airei can mean “lifts up”, and some read this as the gardener lifting a trailing branch off the ground. Where Christians differ: can true branches be lost? Arminians read verses 2 and 6 as warnings that true believers may finally fall away. Reformed interpreters see branches that are attached outwardly but never truly united to Christ, like Judas, who has just left (13:30; 1 John 2:19). Verdict: the warning is real and must be heard; those who truly abide are kept (10:28–29), and fruitlessness is the evidence of a false connection.

Prunes. Kathairei, cleans, linked with “clean” in verse 3. God’s discipline cuts back to increase fruitfulness (Hebrews 12:5–11).

On a Tuesday. When God cuts away things you loved, a job, a plan, a comfort, ask what fruit he may be preparing.
verseByVerse.note: The vine was a familiar picture of Israel, planted by God but often fruitless; Jesus is the true vine. This is the seventh of his “I am” sayings in John. Vinedressers cut away dead wood and pruned living branches hard.

parallels.desc: a vine brought out of Egypt
the vineyard that yielded wild grapes
discipline yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness

verseByVerse.quote: "Already you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you. Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Disciples, cleansed by his word, must abide in him, for no branch bears fruit alone.

Already clean. Through his word received in faith (13:10; 17:17). Pruning works on those already cleansed.

Abide. Menō, remain, stay, live. Used ten times in verses 4–10. Abiding is not a higher experience for advanced Christians but the ordinary life of faith: continuing to trust, depend on and obey Christ.

And I in you. Mutual indwelling: union with Christ.

parallels.desc: the washing of water with the word

verseByVerse.quote: "I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing. If anyone does not abide in me he is thrown away like a branch and withers; and the branches are gathered, thrown into the fire, and burned."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Apart from Jesus we can do nothing; branches that do not abide are thrown away.

Much fruit. Christlike character (Galatians 5:22–23), good works (Colossians 1:10), and new disciples (4:36; Romans 1:13).

Apart from me, nothing. Not that we can do a little without him, but nothing of eternal worth. The death of self-reliance (2 Corinthians 3:5).

Thrown into the fire. Vine wood is useless for anything except fuel (Ezekiel 15:1–8). A solemn picture of judgment on those who are never truly joined to Christ.

On a Tuesday. Begin each day with a conscious act of dependence: “Lord, without you I can do nothing.”
verseByVerse.note: Vine wood is useless for building; pruned branches were burned.

parallels.desc: the wood of the vine

verseByVerse.quote: "If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you. By this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit and so prove to be my disciples."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When his words abide in us, our prayers are answered and our fruit glorifies the Father.

His words in you. Abiding in Christ is inseparable from his words dwelling in us (Colossians 3:16). Scripture shapes what we ask.

Whatever you wish. When our desires are shaped by his words, our prayers align with his will (1 John 5:14).

The Father glorified. The purpose of fruit is God’s glory, not our reputation (Matthew 5:16).

Prove to be. Fruit shows discipleship. Textual note. Manuscripts vary between “that you become” and “and you will become”. Verdict: the sense is the same.

verseByVerse.quote: "As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you. Abide in my love. If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love, just as I have kept my Father's commandments and abide in his love."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus loves his disciples as the Father loves him, and they remain in that love by obedience.

As the Father has loved me. The measure of Christ’s love for his people is the eternal love of the Father for the Son.

Abide in my love. Not earn it, but stay in it, by obedience.

The pattern. Jesus himself lived in his Father’s love through obedience.

For worship. You are loved as the Father loves his Son. Rest in that.

parallels.desc: keep yourselves in the love of God

verseByVerse.quote: "These things I have spoken to you, that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be full. This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ commands lead to full joy, and the chief of them is love.

My joy. The joy of the Son in the Father’s love and will. Obedience leads to joy, not drudgery (Psalm 19:8).

Full. Complete (16:24; 17:13; 1 John 1:4).

As I have loved you. The new commandment again (13:34).

verseByVerse.quote: "Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends. You are my friends if you do what I command you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The greatest love lays down its life for friends.

Greater love. Inscribed on many war memorials. True of soldiers who died for comrades; supremely true of Christ. Yet Paul goes further: Christ died for us while we were enemies (Romans 5:8–10).

For his friends. Hyper, on behalf of. Christ’s death is for his own (10:11, 15).

If you do what I command. Friendship is not earned by obedience, but shown by it.

On a Tuesday. Laying down your life may mean giving time, comfort or preference for a friend in need (1 John 3:16–18).

parallels.desc: he laid down his life for us

verseByVerse.quote: "No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you. You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit and that your fruit should abide, so that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give it to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus calls them friends, not servants, and he chose them to bear lasting fruit.

Friends. Abraham was called God’s friend (Isaiah 41:8; James 2:23); so was Moses, spoken to face to face (Exodus 33:11). Now all disciples are Christ’s friends, sharing his confidence. They remain servants too (v. 20; Romans 1:1), but servants who are trusted friends.

I chose you. In the ancient world, students chose their rabbi. Here the master chose. Where Christians differ. Some say this refers only to the Twelve’s apostleship. Others extend it to God’s gracious choice of all believers (Ephesians 1:4). Verdict: spoken to the apostles, but expressing the principle of all salvation: grace begins with God’s choice (1 John 4:19).

Go and bear fruit. Mission: disciples go out, and their fruit lasts.

For worship. Thank Jesus that you are his friend because he chose you.
verseByVerse.note: Abraham and Moses were each called the friend of God.

parallels.desc: Abraham, my friend
as a man speaks to his friend

verseByVerse.quote: "These things I command you, so that you will love one another."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All his commands aim at love for one another.

The purpose. All of Jesus’ teaching aims at love.

A transition. From love among disciples to the world’s hatred (v. 18).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–27 — The World's Hatred and the Spirit's Witness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If the world hates them, they should remember it hated Jesus first. If they belonged to the world, it would love them, but because he chose them out of it, it hates them. No servant is greater than his master: those who persecuted him will persecute them, and those who kept his word will keep theirs. All this will happen because of his name, for they do not know the one who sent him. Had he not come and spoken, they would not be guilty, but now they have no excuse; to hate him is to hate his Father. Had he not done works no one else did, they would not be guilty, but they have seen and hated both him and the Father, fulfilling the words of their law that they hated him without cause. But when the Helper comes, the Spirit of truth whom Jesus will send from the Father, he will testify about Jesus, and the disciples must testify too, for they have been with him from the start.
verseByVerse.theology: The world's hatred of the church is not an accident to be explained away but a structural feature of the relationship between the kingdom of God and the kingdom of this world. Jesus does not promise that clever strategy or cultural accommodation will eliminate the hatred; he promises that the Spirit will sustain the witnesses through it. The Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father (v. 26) — a phrase that has generated centuries of debate about the procession of the Spirit — testifies about Jesus, and the disciples testify because they have been with Jesus from the beginning.
verseByVerse.examples: If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you (v. 20). The disciple is not above the master. This is simultaneously warning and honor: to be persecuted for Christ is to share in Christ's experience, to enter the fellowship of his sufferings. The church that is never persecuted has either been culturally absorbed to the point of invisibility or is living in an extraordinarily tolerant society — possibly both. The cross-bearing disciple should expect the world's hostility as confirmation, not contradiction, of authentic discipleship.

verseByVerse.quote: "If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you. If you were of the world, the world would love you as its own; but because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The world hates Jesus’ disciples because he chose them out of it.

The world. Humanity organised in opposition to God (1 John 2:15–17).

Chosen out of. Election separates believers from the world’s values, not from the world’s people (17:15).

Hate. Not always violence; sometimes mockery, exclusion or contempt (1 Peter 4:4).

On a Tuesday. Do not be surprised by hostility to your faith. And do not deserve it for the wrong reasons (1 Peter 4:15–16).

verseByVerse.quote: "Remember the word that I said to you: 'A servant is not greater than his master.' If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you. If they kept my word, they will also keep yours. But all these things they will do to you on account of my name, because they do not know him who sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Servants share their master’s persecution, and his reception.

A servant is not greater. Repeated from 13:16, now in a different sense: servants share their master’s rejection.

Kept your word. Some will receive the apostles’ message, as some received Jesus.

On account of my name. Persecution is ultimately about Jesus (Acts 5:41; 9:4).

verseByVerse.quote: "If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have been guilty of sin, but now they have no excuse for their sin. Whoever hates me hates my Father also."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having heard Jesus, the world has no excuse, and to hate him is to hate the Father.

Not guilty. Not sinless, but not guilty of the sin of rejecting the full revelation of God in Christ (9:41). Greater light brings greater responsibility (Luke 12:47–48).

Hates my Father. To reject the Son is to reject God (5:23).

verseByVerse.quote: "If I had not done among them the works that no one else did, they would not be guilty of sin, but now they have seen and hated both me and my Father. But the word that is written in their Law must be fulfilled: 'They hated me without a cause.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They have seen his works and hated him without a cause.

Works no one else did. The signs (9:32).

Without a cause. Psalm 35:19; 69:4, psalms of the righteous sufferer. “Law” means the whole Old Testament (10:34).

For worship. Jesus was hated without cause, so that we, who gave him every cause, might be loved.
verseByVerse.note: “Their Law” here means the Scriptures as a whole, including the Psalms.

parallels.desc: those who hate me without cause

verseByVerse.quote: "But when the Helper comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me. And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit and the apostles will together bear witness to Jesus.

Sent from the Father, by the Son. Both Father and Son send the Spirit (14:26; 16:7).

Proceeds from the Father. Where Christians differ: the filioque. The Nicene Creed (381) says the Spirit “proceeds from the Father”. The Western church later added “and the Son” (filioque), which the Eastern Orthodox reject, holding that the Spirit proceeds eternally from the Father alone. Western theology argues from the Son’s sending of the Spirit and texts calling him the Spirit of Christ (Romans 8:9; Galatians 4:6). Verdict: the Western and Reformed position, held charitably: the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, as the Son’s sending in time reflects eternal relations; but the addition to the creed was made without an ecumenical council, and the Eastern objection deserves respect.

Two witnesses. The Spirit and the apostles together (Acts 5:32). The Spirit’s testimony comes to us through their writings.

From the beginning. Eyewitnesses (Luke 1:2; 1 John 1:1–3; Acts 1:21–22).

On a Tuesday. When you speak of Christ, you do not speak alone: the Spirit testifies with you.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “Helper” can also be rendered “Advocate” or “Counselor.”

parallels.desc: we are witnesses, and so is the Holy Spirit

15.text: <sup>1</sup>“I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser.<sup>2</sup>Every branch in me that does not bear fruit he takes away, and every branch that does bear fruit he prunes, that it may bear more fruit.<sup>3</sup>Already you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you.<sup>4</sup>Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me.<sup>5</sup>I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.<sup>6</sup>If anyone does not abide in me, he is thrown away like a branch and withers; and the branches are gathered, thrown into the fire, and burned.<sup>7</sup>If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you.<sup>8</sup>By this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit and so prove to be my disciples.<sup>9</sup>As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you. Abide in my love.<sup>10</sup>If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love, just as I have kept my Father’s commandments and abide in his love.<sup>11</sup>These things I have spoken to you, that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be full.<sup>12</sup>“This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.<sup>13</sup>Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.<sup>14</sup>You are my friends if you do what I command you.<sup>15</sup>No longer do I call you servants, for the servant does not know what his master is doing; but I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you.<sup>16</sup>You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you that you should go and bear fruit and that your fruit should abide, so that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give it to you.<sup>17</sup>These things I command you, so that you will love one another.<sup>18</sup>“If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you.<sup>19</sup>If you were of the world, the world would love you as its own; but because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you.<sup>20</sup>Remember the word that I said to you: ’A servant is not greater than his master.’ If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you. If they kept my word, they will also keep yours.<sup>21</sup>But all these things they will do to you on account of my name, because they do not know him who sent me.<sup>22</sup>If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have been guilty of sin, but now they have no excuse for their sin.<sup>23</sup>Whoever hates me hates my Father also.<sup>24</sup>If I had not done among them the works that no one else did, they would not be guilty of sin, but now they have seen and hated both me and my Father.<sup>25</sup>But the word that is written in their Law must be fulfilled: ’They hated me without a cause.’<sup>26</sup>“But when the Helper comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me.<sup>27</sup>And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning.
15.overview:
In the Old Testament Israel was God’s vine, planted and tended by him but so often fruitless (Psalm 80:8–16; Isaiah 5:1–7; Jeremiah 2:21). Jesus now says, “I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser.” His disciples are the branches. Fruitless branches are removed; fruitful ones are pruned to bear more. The secret of fruitfulness is to abide in him, to remain joined to him by faith, his words living in them, as he lives in them: apart from him they can do nothing. Abiding means remaining in his love by keeping his commandments, the chief of which is to love one another as he has loved them, with the greatest love of all, laying down one’s life for one’s friends. He calls them no longer servants but friends, because he has made known to them all he heard from the Father. They did not choose him; he chose them and appointed them to go and bear lasting fruit.

The second half turns from love within the church to hatred from the world. If the world hates them, it hated him first; a servant is not greater than his master. Their hatred is without excuse, since Jesus spoke and did works no one else did, and it fulfils the psalm, “They hated me without a cause.” Yet the disciples will not be alone: the Helper, the Spirit of truth who comes from the Father, will bear witness about Jesus, and they too will bear witness, because they have been with him from the beginning.

16.title: The Spirit and the Joy of the Disciples

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The Spirit Convicts the World
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus forewarns the disciples so that persecution will not make them fall: they will be thrown out of synagogues, and their killers will think it service to God, not knowing the Father or the Son. Grief has filled them at the news of his departure, but his going is for their good, since only then will he send the Helper. The Spirit will prove the world wrong about sin, shown in its unbelief; about righteousness, proved by Jesus’ return to the Father; and about judgment, for the world’s ruler is condemned. There is more Jesus could tell them, more than they can now bear, but the Spirit of truth will lead them into all truth, speaking what he hears, revealing what is to come, and glorifying Jesus by making known what belongs to him, which is all that the Father has. Soon they will not see him, and soon after they will see him again.
verseByVerse.theology: The conviction work of the Spirit operates on three fronts: sin (the world's refusal to believe in Jesus), righteousness (the vindication of Jesus in his ascension to the Father), and judgment (the condemnation of the ruler of this world at the cross). This Trinitarian work of conviction is not coercive but illuminating — the Spirit opens eyes to what is actually true about the world's condition, about Jesus' identity, and about the decisive verdict already rendered at Calvary. Evangelism that presents the gospel as optional enhancement rather than rescue from genuine condemnation has not yet let the Spirit do his convicting work.
verseByVerse.examples: He will guide you into all truth (v. 13): the Spirit's hermeneutical function is ongoing, not merely the initial inspiration of the apostolic witness. The community that has the Spirit has access to the interpretive presence of the one who knows the mind of God (1 Cor. 2:10-11). This does not mean every Christian's interpretation is equally valid; it means that the Spirit-guided community reading the Spirit-inspired text under the guidance of the Spirit through his word can arrive at the truth Jesus promised. The church's theology is a work of the Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have said all these things to you to keep you from falling away. They will put you out of the synagogues. Indeed, the hour is coming when whoever kills you will think he is offering service to God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus warns his disciples of persecution so that they will not fall away.

Falling away. Skandalizō, stumbling. Forewarned is forearmed.

Out of the synagogues. As happened to the blind man (9:22, 34).

Service to God. Religious persecution feels righteous to the persecutor. Saul of Tarsus thought so (Acts 26:9–11; Philippians 3:6).

On a Tuesday. Around the world, Christians are still killed by people who believe they are serving God. Pray for the persecuted church today (Hebrews 13:3).
verseByVerse.note: Paul had been such a man, persecuting believers as a service to God.

parallels.desc: Paul’s zeal as a persecutor

verseByVerse.quote: "And they will do these things because they have not known the Father, nor me. But I have said these things to you, that when their hour comes you may remember that I told them to you. I did not say these things to you from the beginning, because I was with you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Persecution springs from not knowing God, and the warning will help them remember.

Ignorance of God. The root of persecution is not knowing God (1 Corinthians 2:8).

Remember. Fulfilled warnings strengthen faith (13:19; 14:29).

From the beginning. While Jesus was with them, he drew the hostility; after he leaves, they will face it.

parallels.desc: I had acted ignorantly in unbelief

verseByVerse.quote: "But now I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, 'Where are you going?' But because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Grief at his going fills their hearts.

None of you asks. Peter and Thomas did ask (13:36; 14:5), but now they are absorbed in their own grief rather than his destination: glory with the Father.

On a Tuesday. Grief can turn our eyes inward. Ask where Jesus is: at the Father’s right hand, for you.

verseByVerse.quote: "Nevertheless, I tell you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you. But if I go, I will send him to you. And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is better for them that he goes, for then he will send the Spirit, who will convict the world.

To your advantage. Astonishing: better to have the Spirit within than Jesus beside them. The Spirit makes Christ present everywhere, to all believers, at once.

Convict. Elenchō: expose, prove guilty, bring to conviction. The Spirit acts like a prosecutor, through the preaching of the apostles (Acts 2:37).

parallels.desc: they were cut to the heart

verseByVerse.quote: "concerning sin, because they do not believe in me; concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father, and you will see me no longer;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit shows the world its sin of unbelief and Jesus’ righteousness, proved by his return to the Father.

Sin. The root sin is unbelief (3:18–19). The Spirit shows people that their deepest problem is their rejection of Christ.

Righteousness. The world condemned Jesus as a sinner; his return to the Father proves him righteous (1 Timothy 3:16; Acts 2:24, 36). The Spirit also convicts the world of its false self-righteousness and shows the true righteousness that is in Christ.

parallels.desc: raised for our justification

verseByVerse.quote: "concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world is judged. I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit shows that the ruler of this world is judged.

Judgment. The world judged Jesus, but at the cross its ruler was judged (12:31). The Spirit convinces people that judgment is real, and that Satan is defeated.

Cannot bear them now. Not until after the cross, resurrection and Spirit.

On a Tuesday. Pray that the Spirit will convict people you love. Evangelism is his work through our words.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth, for he will not speak on his own authority, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will declare to you the things that are to come. He will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit will guide the apostles into all the truth and glorify Jesus.

Guide into all the truth. A promise to the apostles (v. 12): the Spirit will lead them to understand and complete the revelation of Christ, which they recorded in the New Testament.

Where Christians differ: new revelation? Some charismatic and Roman Catholic teaching sees here ongoing revelation through prophecy or church tradition. Reformed theology holds that this promise was fulfilled in the apostolic witness, now complete in Scripture (Jude 3; Hebrews 1:1–2), and that the Spirit now illuminates Scripture rather than adding to it. Verdict: the canon is closed and sufficient (Westminster Confession 1.6); the Spirit guides believers today into the truth already given.

Things to come. Perhaps the events of the cross and resurrection, and the future revealed in Revelation.

He will glorify me. The Spirit’s ministry is Christ-centred. A test of any claimed spiritual movement: does it glorify Jesus? J. I. Packer called it the Spirit’s floodlight ministry.

verseByVerse.quote: "All that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will take what is mine and declare it to you. A little while, and you will see me no longer; and again a little while, and you will see me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All the Father has belongs to Jesus, and in a little while they will see him again.

All that the Father has. A staggering claim of equality (17:10).

A little while. Hours until his death; three days until his resurrection.

Textual note. Later manuscripts add “because I go to the Father” (KJV), from verse 17. Verdict: not original here.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–33 — Sorrow Turned to Joy: I Have Overcome the World
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Puzzled, the disciples ask one another what he means by “a little while” and “going to the Father”. Knowing their question, Jesus tells them they will weep and mourn while the world rejoices, but their grief will become joy, like a woman whose pain in labour is forgotten in the joy of a new child. They grieve now, but he will see them again, and their joy no one will take away. In that day they will not need to ask him; the Father will give them whatever they ask in his name. Until now they have asked nothing in his name; they should ask and receive, so that their joy may be complete. He has spoken in figures, but soon he will speak plainly about the Father. They will ask in his name, not because he must plead for them, but because the Father himself loves them for loving and trusting his Son. He came from the Father into the world and is now leaving it to return. The disciples say that now he speaks plainly, and they believe he came from God. Jesus asks whether they really believe now. The hour has come when they will scatter, each to his home, and leave him alone; yet he is not alone, for the Father is with him. He has told them this so that in him they may have peace. In the world they will face trouble, but they should take courage: he has conquered the world.
verseByVerse.theology:
The chapter's second half turns on a claim about time. Everything Jesus promises here is stated as though it has already happened: the sorrow will turn into joy, the ruler of this world is judged, and — in the last verse — I have overcome the world, in the perfect tense, before the arrest. The disciples are being taught to live inside an outcome that is settled but not yet visible, which is the permanent situation of the church.

This is why the childbirth image governs the section. It is not a picture of pain compensated afterwards by an unrelated good, which is how providence is usually consoled about. It is a picture of pain that turns out to have been productive — the same event, read from the far end, carrying a meaning it could not disclose at the time. Applied to the cross, this is the interpretive key to the whole Gospel: the worst thing that ever happened is the thing the church sings about, and nothing had to be deleted for that to be true.

And the prayer promise sits in the middle of it for a reason. Prayer in the name of Jesus is not a technique for extracting outcomes; it is the practice of people who believe the outcome is already secured and are asking to be brought into line with it. Its stated end in verse 24 is not acquisition but fullness of joy.
verseByVerse.examples:
In the world you will have tribulation (v. 33) is the sentence to set against every version of Christianity that promises exemption. Not may, not could — will, spoken by the one person entitled to say it, on the last free evening of his life. And it stands beside in me you may have peace without contradiction, because the two prepositions name two locations and a believer is in both at once. That is why a Christian life so often feels like two contradictory reports about the same afternoon.

The pastoral use of verse 22 is worth naming: no one will take your joy from you is not a promise of cheerfulness. The joy in this passage is grounded in his seeing them, not in their managing to feel anything, which is precisely why it cannot be confiscated — nobody can reach the thing it depends on.

And verse 12 — you cannot bear them now — is the answer to the reader who suspects God is asking more than can be carried. Here is the Son measuring what he says against what eleven exhausted men can hold, and stopping short, on the one night when he had most to say and least time to say it.

verseByVerse.quote: So some of his disciples said to one another, "What is this that he says to us, 'A little while, and you will not see me, and again a little while, and you will see me'; and, 'because I am going to the Father'?" So they were saying, "What does he mean by 'a little while'? We do not know what he is talking about."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples are bewildered by the little while.

Confusion. Honest bewilderment. Even after three years, they cannot grasp a dying and rising Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus knew that they wanted to ask him, so he said to them, "Is this what you are asking yourselves, what I meant by saying, 'A little while and you will not see me, and again a little while and you will see me'? Truly, truly, I say to you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice. You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their sorrow will be turned into joy.

Jesus knew. He knows our unspoken questions.

The world will rejoice. At the crucifixion.

Sorrow into joy. Not replaced by joy, but turned into it: the same cross that caused their grief becomes the source of their joy.

parallels.desc: weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning

verseByVerse.quote: "When a woman is giving birth, she has sorrow because her hour has come, but when she has delivered the baby, she no longer remembers the anguish, for joy that a human being has been born into the world. So also you have sorrow now, but I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like a mother after childbirth, their pain will give way to a joy no one can take.

Birth pains. A prophetic picture of the pains before the messianic age (Isaiah 26:17–19; 66:7–14). Suffering that produces new life.

I will see you. After the resurrection (20:20: the disciples were glad when they saw the Lord).

No one will take. Resurrection joy is permanent, because the risen Lord never dies again.

On a Tuesday. Present suffering is not the end of the story. Hold on through the labour (Romans 8:18–23).

verseByVerse.quote: "In that day you will ask nothing of me. Truly, truly, I say to you, whatever you ask of the Father in my name, he will give it to you. Until now you have asked nothing in my name. Ask, and you will receive, that your joy may be full."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In that day they will pray to the Father in Jesus’ name and receive, so that their joy is full.

Ask nothing of me. Either they will no longer need to ask him questions, or they will pray directly to the Father.

In my name. A new way of praying, on the basis of Christ’s finished work and present intercession (Hebrews 4:14–16).

Textual note. Manuscripts place “in my name” either with “ask” or with “give”. Verdict: the sense is the same: prayer through Christ.

For worship. Pray today to the Father, through Jesus, by the Spirit.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have said these things to you in figures of speech. The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures of speech but will tell you plainly about the Father. In that day you will ask in my name, and I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Soon Jesus will speak plainly about the Father.

Plainly. After the resurrection and through the Spirit.

Not that I will ask. Not denying his intercession (Romans 8:34; Hebrews 7:25), but stressing that the Father himself loves them and does not need persuading.

verseByVerse.quote: "for the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came from God. I came from the Father and have come into the world, and now I am leaving the world and going to the Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Father himself loves them, because they love and trust his Son.

The Father himself loves you. Many Christians imagine a stern Father appeased by a loving Son. Jesus corrects it: the Father himself loves us (3:16).

Because you have loved me. Not the cause of God’s love, which is eternal and free, but the sphere in which it is enjoyed (14:21). Where Christians differ. Some read this as conditional love. Verdict: God’s electing love comes first (1 John 4:10, 19); his fatherly delight rests on those who love his Son.

The summary of the Gospel. From the Father, into the world, out of the world, to the Father: incarnation, death, resurrection, ascension.

verseByVerse.quote: His disciples said, "Ah, now you are speaking plainly and not using figurative speech! Now we know that you know all things and do not need anyone to question you; this is why we believe that you came from God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples think they understand at last.

Now we know. A genuine step forward, but overconfident. Their understanding is still partial.

You know all things. Seen in his knowledge of their question (v. 19).

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered them, "Do you now believe? Behold, the hour is coming, indeed it has come, when you will be scattered, each to his own home, and will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone, for the Father is with me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They will soon scatter, but the Father will be with Jesus.

Do you now believe? A gentle question: their faith is about to be tested.

Scattered. Zechariah 13:7: strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered (Mark 14:27).

Not alone. Even when friends desert him, the Father is with him. The cry of forsakenness (Mark 15:34) shows how deep the cross went, bearing our sin; but the Father’s love for the Son never ceased.

On a Tuesday. When others fail you, you are not alone if you belong to Christ (Hebrews 13:5).

parallels.desc: strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered

verseByVerse.quote: "I have said these things to you, that in me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Jesus there is peace, and he has overcome the world.

In me, in the world. Two spheres. Christians live in both: trouble in the world, peace in Christ.

Tribulation. Pressure, distress, persecution. Not a possibility but a promise (Acts 14:22; 2 Timothy 3:12).

What it does not mean. The gospel does not promise a trouble-free life.

I have overcome. Perfect tense, spoken before the cross as already done: the victory is certain (1 John 5:4–5; Revelation 5:5).

For worship. Take heart today. The world has done its worst to Jesus, and he has overcome.

parallels.desc: the victory that has overcome the world
