Indeed, the hour is coming when whoever kills you will think he is offering service to God.<sup>3</sup>And they will do these things because they have not known the Father, nor me.<sup>4</sup>But I have said these things to you, that when their hour comes you may remember that I told them to you. “I did not say these things to you from the beginning, because I was with you.<sup>5</sup>But now I am going to him who sent me, and none of you asks me, ’Where are you going?’<sup>6</sup>But because I have said these things to you, sorrow has filled your heart.<sup>7</sup>Nevertheless, I tell you the truth: it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you. But if I go, I will send him to you.<sup>8</sup>And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin and righteousness and judgment:<sup>9</sup>concerning sin, because they do not believe in me;<sup>10</sup>concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father, and you will see me no longer;<sup>11</sup>concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world is judged.<sup>12</sup>“I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.<sup>13</sup>When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth, for he will not speak on his own authority, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will declare to you the things that are to come.<sup>14</sup>He will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you.<sup>15</sup>All that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will take what is mine and declare it to you.<sup>16</sup>“A little while, and you will see me no longer; and again a little while, and you will see me.”<sup>17</sup>So some of his disciples said to one another, “What is this that he says to us, ’A little while, and you will not see me, and again a little while, and you will see me’; and, ’because I am going to the Father’?”<sup>18</sup>So they were saying, “What does he mean by ’a little while’? We do not know what he is talking about.”<sup>19</sup>Jesus knew that they wanted to ask him, so he said to them, “Is this what you are asking yourselves, what I meant by saying, ’A little while and you will not see me, and again a little while and you will see me’?<sup>20</sup>Truly, truly, I say to you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice. You will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will turn into joy.<sup>21</sup>When a woman is giving birth, she has sorrow because her hour has come, but when she has delivered the baby, she no longer remembers the anguish, for joy that a human being has been born into the world.<sup>22</sup>So also you have sorrow now, but I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.<sup>23</sup>In that day you will ask nothing of me. Truly, truly, I say to you, whatever you ask of the Father in my name, he will give it to you.<sup>24</sup>Until now you have asked nothing in my name. Ask, and you will receive, that your joy may be full.<sup>25</sup>“I have said these things to you in figures of speech. The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures of speech but will tell you plainly about the Father.<sup>26</sup>In that day you will ask in my name, and I do not say to you that I will ask the Father on your behalf;<sup>27</sup>for the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came from God.<sup>28</sup>I came from the Father and have come into the world, and now I am leaving the world and going to the Father.”<sup>29</sup>His disciples said, “Ah, now you are speaking plainly and not using figurative speech!<sup>30</sup>Now we know that you know all things and do not need anyone to question you; this is why we believe that you came from God.”<sup>31</sup>Jesus answered them, “Do you now believe?<sup>32</sup>Behold, the hour is coming, indeed it has come, when you will be scattered, each to his own home, and will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone, for the Father is with me.<sup>33</sup>I have said these things to you, that in me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world.”
16.overview:
Jesus warns his disciples plainly so that they will not fall away when persecution comes: they will be expelled from synagogues, and some will kill them thinking they are serving God. Sorrow fills their hearts at his going, but he tells them it is for their good, for unless he goes the Helper will not come. When the Spirit comes he will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness and judgment: sin, because they do not believe in Jesus; righteousness, because Jesus goes to the Father and is vindicated; judgment, because the ruler of this world is condemned. The Spirit of truth will guide the apostles into all the truth, declaring what is to come and glorifying Christ by taking what is his and making it known.

Then Jesus speaks of “a little while”: a little while and they will not see him, and again a little while and they will see him. The disciples are puzzled. He explains with the picture of a woman in labour, whose anguish gives way to joy when the child is born: they will grieve while the world rejoices, but he will see them again, and no one will take their joy from them. In that day they will pray to the Father in his name and receive, so that their joy may be full, for the Father himself loves them. When the disciples declare that now they understand and believe, Jesus warns that they will soon be scattered and leave him alone, yet he is not alone, for the Father is with him. His last words before his prayer are a promise for every age: “In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world.”

17.title: The High-Priestly Prayer

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–26 — Jesus Prays for Himself, the Disciples, and All Believers
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Raising his eyes to heaven, Jesus asks the Father to glorify the Son now that the hour has come, so that the Son may glorify him by giving eternal life to all the Father has given him. That life is knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent. Having finished his work on earth, Jesus asks for the glory he shared with the Father before creation. He has revealed the Father to those given him out of the world, and they have received his words and believed. He prays for them, not for the world: that the holy Father would keep them in his name and make them one; he has kept them, and none is lost except the son of destruction. The world hates them, but he asks not that they be removed from it, but guarded from the evil one, set apart by the truth of God’s word, and sent as he was sent; for them he consecrates himself. He prays too for all who will believe through their message, that they may be one as he and the Father are one, so that the world may believe and know the Father’s love. He longs for them to be with him and see his glory, and promises to keep making the Father known, so that the Father’s love and the Son himself may be in them.
verseByVerse.theology: The prayer is called the High-Priestly Prayer because it parallels the High Priest's prayer on the Day of Atonement — the one moment in the year when the high priest entered the Most Holy Place to intercede for the people. Jesus is simultaneously the priest and the sacrifice; he intercedes for his people while preparing himself for the offering that will accomplish what he prays for. His prayer for their sanctification (v. 17), protection (v. 11), joy (v. 13), and unity (v. 21-23) is the charter of the church's life.
verseByVerse.examples: That they may be one, as we are one (v. 22): the unity Jesus prays for is patterned on and derived from the inner-Trinitarian unity of Father and Son. This is not organizational uniformity or ecclesiastical merger but the living unity of love, shared purpose, and mutual indwelling. The church's unity is the Father's means of witnessing to the world (v. 21, 23): the divided church contradicts its own evangelistic witness. The prayer for unity is also the prayer for effective mission — they are inseparable in Jesus' own intercession.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus had spoken these words, he lifted up his eyes to heaven, and said, "Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son that the Son may glorify you, since you have given him authority over all flesh, to give eternal life to all whom you have given him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus prays for the Father to glorify the Son, who gives eternal life to all the Father has given him.

Lifted up his eyes. The posture of prayer (11:41; Psalm 123:1).

Father. Six times in the prayer: the intimacy of the Son.

Glorify your Son. Through the cross, resurrection and ascension, so that the Father’s love and righteousness are displayed.

All flesh. Universal authority (Matthew 28:18).

All whom you have given him. Five times in the prayer (vv. 2, 6, 9, 24): the Father’s gift of a people to the Son. Where Christians differ. Reformed theology sees here the covenant of redemption, the Father’s eternal gift of the elect to the Son, who secures their salvation. Others see a description of believers without implying prior choice. Verdict: the Reformed reading fits the repeated stress: the Son’s authority over all is exercised to give life to those the Father gave him (6:37–39; 10:29).
verseByVerse.note: John 17 is often called Jesus’ high priestly prayer: he prays for himself, his disciples and all future believers.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent. I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eternal life is knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ, and Jesus has finished his work.

Eternal life defined. Not only living for ever, but knowing God: a personal relationship of love and trust (Jeremiah 9:23–24; 31:34; 1 John 5:20).

The only true God, and Jesus Christ. Not setting Jesus outside the true God, but naming the Father as the one true God and the Son as the one through whom he is known. Jesus is himself the “true God” in 1 John 5:20.

Accomplished. Spoken in anticipation; on the cross, “It is finished” (19:30).

On a Tuesday. Do you know about God, or know God? Spend time with him today.
verseByVerse.note: “Know” in the Bible means a personal relationship, not mere information.

parallels.desc: that he understands and knows me
“It is finished”

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, Father, glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed. I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world. Yours they were, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asks for the glory he shared with the Father before the world, and has revealed the Father to his disciples.

Before the world existed. Jesus remembers pre-existent glory shared with the Father (1:1–2). Not a creature exalted, but the Son returning.

Where Christians differ. Adoptionists and some modern theologians say Jesus became Son of God at his baptism or resurrection. This verse speaks of eternal shared glory. Verdict: the eternal Son, who shares the Father’s glory (Isaiah 42:8) and so is God.

Your name. God’s character and identity, revealed through the Son (Exodus 34:5–7).

Kept your word. Generous, considering their failures. Jesus sees them by grace.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now they know that everything that you have given me is from you. For I have given them the words that you gave me, and they have received them and have come to know in truth that I came from you; and they have believed that you sent me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples have received Jesus’ words and believe that the Father sent him.

Received, known, believed. Faith comes through receiving Christ’s words (Romans 10:17).

The words. Jesus passes on the Father’s words; the apostles will pass on his (v. 20).

verseByVerse.quote: "I am praying for them. I am not praying for the world but for those whom you have given me, for they are yours. All mine are yours, and yours are mine, and I am glorified in them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus prays specifically for those the Father has given him.

Not for the world. Here, Jesus’ priestly intercession is specifically for his own. He does pray for his enemies elsewhere (Luke 23:34) and wants the world to believe (v. 21). Where Christians differ. Reformed theology sees the particularity of Christ’s intercession as matching the particularity of his atonement: he dies and prays for those the Father gave him (Romans 8:33–34). Verdict: Christ’s high-priestly work is effective for his people; the gospel invitation remains open to the world.

All mine are yours. A creature might say “all mine are yours”; only the Son can say “all yours are mine.”

Glorified in them. Remarkable: frail disciples bring glory to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "And I am no longer in the world, but they are in the world, and I am coming to you. Holy Father, keep them in your name, which you have given me, that they may be one, even as we are one. While I was with them, I kept them in your name, which you have given me. I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost except the son of destruction, that the Scripture might be fulfilled."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asks the holy Father to keep them united, as he has kept them, losing none but the son of destruction.

Holy Father. Only here: holiness and fatherhood together.

Keep them. Preserve them in faith. The Father keeps those the Son has kept (10:28–29; 1 Peter 1:5).

Your name, which you have given me. The divine name shared with the Son (Philippians 2:9). Textual note. Some manuscripts read “keep them in your name those whom you have given me”. Verdict: the harder reading, “which you have given me”, is original.

The son of destruction. Judas, the one destined for destruction; Paul uses the same title, “the son of destruction” (2 Thessalonians 2:3), for the man of lawlessness. Not an exception to Christ’s keeping, since he was never truly one of Christ’s sheep (6:64, 70), and Scripture foretold his betrayal (Psalm 41:9).
verseByVerse.note: “Son of destruction” describes one destined for destruction — Judas.

verseByVerse.quote: "But now I am coming to you, and these things I speak in the world, that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves. I have given them your word, and the world has hated them because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus wants them to share his joy, though the world hates them.

My joy. Even facing the cross, Jesus speaks of joy (15:11; Hebrews 12:2).

Hated. Because they are like him (15:18–19).

verseByVerse.quote: "I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one. They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asks not that they be taken from the world but kept from the evil one.

Not out of the world. No withdrawal into monasteries or Christian ghettoes. Disciples are to stay in the world as witnesses.

From the evil one. The devil (1 John 5:18–19; Matthew 6:13).

Where Christians differ: separation. Some traditions stress separation from culture; others engagement with it. Verdict: in the world, not of it: neither withdrawal nor worldliness, but holy presence (Philippians 2:15).

parallels.desc: deliver us from evil

verseByVerse.quote: "Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth. As you sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asks the Father to make them holy by his word of truth, and sends them into the world.

Sanctify. Set apart for God and make holy. Sanctification happens through the truth of God’s word (Psalm 119:9, 11; Ephesians 5:26).

Your word is truth. Not merely contains truth: is truth. A foundation for the authority and trustworthiness of Scripture.

As you sent me. The mission of the church continues the mission of the Son (20:21).

On a Tuesday. If you want to grow in holiness, feed on God’s word. And see your workplace and neighbourhood as the place you have been sent.
verseByVerse.note: To sanctify is to set apart for God and make holy.

parallels.desc: your law is true

verseByVerse.quote: "And for their sake I consecrate myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth. I do not ask for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus consecrates himself for them, and prays for all who will believe through their word.

I consecrate myself. As a priest is consecrated, or a sacrifice set apart for God (Exodus 28:41; Deuteronomy 15:19). Jesus dedicates himself to death as priest and offering (Hebrews 10:10, 14).

Through their word. The apostolic message, now Scripture. Every believer since comes to faith through the apostles’ word.

For worship. Jesus prayed for you by name, that night. Thank him.

parallels.desc: sanctified through the offering of his body

verseByVerse.quote: "that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me. The glory that you have given me I have given to them, that they may be one even as we are one,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus prays that all believers may be one as the Father and Son are one, so that the world may believe.

One. Modelled on the unity of Father and Son: a unity of love, truth and life, not merely organisation.

Where Christians differ: what kind of unity? Some (in parts of the ecumenical movement) see a call to one visible institutional church. Others see a spiritual unity already given in Christ, to be expressed in love and shared truth. Verdict: unity is both given and commanded: a spiritual reality in Christ (Ephesians 4:3–6), which must be visibly expressed in love, cooperation and shared confession of the truth, without sacrificing the gospel (Galatians 1:8–9).

So that the world may believe. Christian disunity hinders evangelism.

The glory. The glory of being God’s children, sharing his life and love (2 Corinthians 3:18).

verseByVerse.quote: "I in them and you in me, that they may become perfectly one, so that the world may know that you sent me and loved them even as you loved me. Father, I desire that they also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am, to see my glory that you have given me because you loved me before the foundation of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus wants his people to be with him and see his glory.

Perfectly one. Brought to completion.

Loved them as you loved me. The Father loves believers with the same love he has for his Son.

I desire. Jesus states his will. Heaven is the answer to this prayer.

To see my glory. The joy of heaven is seeing Christ (1 John 3:2; Revelation 22:4).

Before the foundation of the world. Eternal love within the Trinity, and eternal choice (Ephesians 1:4).

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “that which you have given me” (neuter, the whole people). Verdict: the neuter is probably original; the meaning is the same.

verseByVerse.quote: "O righteous Father, even though the world does not know you, I know you, and these know that you have sent me. I made known to them your name, and I will continue to make it known, that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus will keep making the Father known, so that the Father’s love and Jesus himself may be in them.

Righteous Father. Just in all his ways, including the cross, where his righteousness and love meet (Romans 3:25–26).

I will make it known. Through the Spirit, after the resurrection, and still today.

I in them. The final words of the prayer: Christ dwelling in his people.

For worship. The love of the Father for the Son is in you. Let that love shape your day.

17.text: <sup>1</sup>When Jesus had spoken these words, he lifted up his eyes to heaven, and said, “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son that the Son may glorify you,<sup>2</sup>since you have given him authority over all flesh, to give eternal life to all whom you have given him.<sup>3</sup>And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.<sup>4</sup>I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do.<sup>5</sup>And now, Father, glorify me in your own presence with the glory that I had with you before the world existed.<sup>6</sup>“I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world. Yours they were, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word.<sup>7</sup>Now they know that everything that you have given me is from you.<sup>8</sup>For I have given them the words that you gave me, and they have received them and have come to know in truth that I came from you; and they have believed that you sent me.<sup>9</sup>I am praying for them. I am not praying for the world but for those whom you have given me, for they are yours.<sup>10</sup>All mine are yours, and yours are mine, and I am glorified in them.<sup>11</sup>And I am no longer in the world, but they are in the world, and I am coming to you. Holy Father, keep them in your name, which you have given me, that they may be one, even as we are one.<sup>12</sup>While I was with them, I kept them in your name, which you have given me. I have guarded them, and not one of them has been lost except the son of destruction, that the Scripture might be fulfilled.<sup>13</sup>But now I am coming to you, and these things I speak in the world, that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves.<sup>14</sup>I have given them your word, and the world has hated them because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.<sup>15</sup>I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one.<sup>16</sup>They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.<sup>17</sup>Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth.<sup>18</sup>As you sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world.<sup>19</sup>And for their sake I consecrate myself, that they also may be sanctified in truth.<sup>20</sup>“I do not ask for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word,<sup>21</sup>that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me.<sup>22</sup>The glory that you have given me I have given to them, that they may be one even as we are one,<sup>23</sup>I in them and you in me, that they may become perfectly one, so that the world may know that you sent me and loved them even as you loved me.<sup>24</sup>Father, I desire that they also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am, to see my glory that you have given me because you loved me before the foundation of the world.<sup>25</sup>O righteous Father, even though the world does not know you, I know you, and these know that you have sent me.<sup>26</sup>I made known to them your name, and I will continue to make it known, that the love with which you have loved me may be in them, and I in them.”
17.overview:
Before going out to Gethsemane, Jesus lifts his eyes to heaven and prays aloud. Since the sixteenth century this has been called his “high-priestly prayer”: like the high priest on the Day of Atonement, he prays for himself, for his priests (the apostles), and for the people. It is the longest prayer of Jesus recorded, and lets us hear the Son speaking to the Father on the night before the cross.

First he prays for himself: the hour has come; may the Father glorify the Son, so that the Son may glorify him by giving eternal life to all the Father has given him. Eternal life is to know the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent. He asks to be restored to the glory he had with the Father before the world existed. Then he prays for his disciples: he has made the Father’s name known to those given him out of the world, and kept them, losing none but the son of destruction. He does not ask that they be taken out of the world, but kept from the evil one, made holy by the truth of God’s word, and sent into the world as he was sent. Finally he prays for all who will believe through their word: that they may be one, as the Father and the Son are one, so that the world may believe; and that they may be with him where he is, to see his glory and share the Father’s love. Every Christian is named in this prayer, and Christ’s intercession continues for them in heaven (Hebrews 7:25).

18.title: The Arrest, the Denial, and the Trial Before Pilate

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–27 — Gethsemane, the Arrest, and Peter's Denial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In a garden across the Kidron, Judas arrives with soldiers and temple guards. Jesus, knowing what lies ahead, steps forward and identifies himself, and at his “I am he” they fall back to the ground. He secures his disciples’ release, so that none of those given him is lost. When Peter cuts off the ear of Malchus, the high priest’s servant, Jesus orders him to put up his sword: he will drink the Father’s cup. Bound, he is taken to Annas, father-in-law of the high priest Caiaphas. Another disciple, known to the high priest, gets Peter into the courtyard, where Peter denies to the doorkeeper that he is a disciple and warms himself by the fire. Questioned about his teaching, Jesus says he has taught openly and they should ask those who heard him. An officer strikes him, and Jesus asks for evidence of any wrong he has said. Annas sends him to Caiaphas. Asked twice more, Peter denies Jesus again, and the rooster crows.
verseByVerse.theology: I am he — ego eimi — spoken in the garden, is the same divine Name Jesus has been claiming throughout the gospel. When he says it, the soldiers fall to the ground: the mere self-identification of the Son of God is enough to flatten an armed cohort. Jesus surrenders not because he is overpowered but because he chooses to. This is the theology of the atonement in action: the Lamb who lays down his own life, the Shepherd who gives himself for the sheep. The arrest is simultaneously Jesus' most vulnerable moment and his most sovereign act.
verseByVerse.examples: Peter's denial happens at the same fire where the servants are warming themselves — the detail is vivid and specific. He denies knowing Jesus to a slave girl, to bystanders, to a relative of the man whose ear he cut off. Three denials as predicted, completed at the crowing of the rooster. Peter's failure is not moral weakness alone but the collapse of self-confident discipleship — the faith that depends on its own resources rather than on grace. His restoration (ch. 21) will be built on a different foundation.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus had spoken these words, he went out with his disciples across the brook Kidron, where there was a garden, which he and his disciples entered. Now Judas, who betrayed him, also knew the place, for Jesus often met there with his disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus walks deliberately to the place where he knows he will be found: no one traps him; he gives himself up.

The Kidron. The ravine east of the city, between the temple and the Mount of Olives. David crossed it weeping when betrayed by Ahithophel and fleeing Absalom (2 Samuel 15:23, 30). The Son of David now crosses it, betrayed by a friend.

A garden. Mark and Matthew name it Gethsemane, “oil press” (Mark 14:32). Only John calls it a garden. Life was lost in a garden (Genesis 3); Jesus is arrested in one and buried in one (19:41).

Judas knew the place. Jesus did not hide. He went where Judas would look.
verseByVerse.note: The Kidron Valley lies between Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives; it is usually dry except in the rainy season. Matthew and Mark name the garden Gethsemane.

parallels.desc: David, betrayed, crosses the Kidron weeping

verseByVerse.quote: So Judas, having procured a band of soldiers and some officers from the chief priests and the Pharisees, went there with lanterns and torches and weapons. Then Jesus, knowing all that would happen to him, came forward and said to them, "Whom do you seek?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The powers of earth come armed against the light of the world, and he goes out to meet them, knowing everything.

A band of soldiers. Speira, a Roman cohort (nominally 600, probably a detachment), with the temple police. Rome and Jerusalem act together against Jesus.

Lanterns and torches. At Passover the moon is full; they bring lamps to search for the light of the world.

Knowing all. Jesus is not surprised. He goes out to them.

Whom do you seek? The question he asked the first disciples (1:38) and will ask Mary at the tomb (20:15).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the “band of soldiers” was a cohort, a tenth of a Roman legion — Roman troops joined with the temple police.

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, "Jesus of Nazareth." Jesus said to them, "I am he." Judas, who betrayed him, was standing with them. When Jesus said to them, "I am he," they drew back and fell to the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus speaks the name of God, armed men fall to the ground: he is arrested only because he allows it.

I am he. Egō eimi. At one level, “I’m the one.” At another, the divine name (8:58).

They fell to the ground. A reaction to the presence of God (Ezekiel 1:28; Daniel 10:9; Revelation 1:17). A brief unveiling of his majesty, showing that his surrender is voluntary (10:18).

Judas standing with them. John notes where the traitor now belongs.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “I am he” is literally “I am” here and in verse 8 — the words of the divine name.

parallels.desc: my adversaries stumble and fall

verseByVerse.quote: So he asked them again, "Whom do you seek?" And they said, "Jesus of Nazareth." Jesus answered, "I told you that I am he. So, if you seek me, let these men go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Good Shepherd places himself between the wolves and the sheep.

Let these go. Jesus bargains for his disciples’ freedom with his own surrender. A picture of substitution: he is taken, they go free.

On a Tuesday. Christ stands between you and what you deserve. Live as someone set free.

verseByVerse.quote: This was to fulfill the word that he had spoken: "Of those whom you gave me I have lost not one." Then Simon Peter, having a sword, drew it and struck the high priest's servant and cut off his right ear. (The servant's name was Malchus.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus keeps every one of his own, and Peter’s sword cannot help the kingdom of God.

I have lost not one. 17:12; 6:39. John applies Jesus’ words about eternal keeping to physical rescue: the one guarantees the other’s pattern.

Malchus. Only John names him and Peter. Luke the physician alone records that Jesus healed the ear (Luke 22:51).

The right ear. A detail of an eyewitness. Perhaps Peter aimed at his head.

Where Christians differ: Christians and force. Pacifists see here a ban on all violence. Others note that Jesus rebuked force used to defend his mission, not the state’s lawful use of the sword (Romans 13:4). Verdict: the kingdom of Christ never advances by the sword (v. 36); Christians may serve in lawful defence and justice, but never fight for the gospel with weapons.
verseByVerse.note: Only John names Peter as the swordsman and Malchus as the servant.

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus said to Peter, "Put your sword into its sheath; shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me?" So the band of soldiers and their captain and the officers of the Jews arrested Jesus and bound him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus chooses the cup of God’s wrath from his Father’s hand rather than escape by force.

The cup. In the prophets, the cup of God’s wrath against sin (Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15). In Gethsemane Jesus prayed that it might pass (Mark 14:36); now he accepts it as from his Father.

Bound. The one who binds the strong man (Mark 3:27) allows himself to be bound. Isaac too was bound for sacrifice (Genesis 22:9).

For worship. He drank the cup so that we receive the cup of salvation (Psalm 116:13).
verseByVerse.note: The “cup” pictures the suffering and judgment the Father had given him to bear.

verseByVerse.quote: First they led him to Annas, for he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year. It was Caiaphas who had advised the Jews that it would be expedient that one man should die for the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is brought before the man who had held the real power in Jerusalem for twenty years, and the prophecy of Caiaphas is on its way to fulfilment.

Annas. High priest AD 6–15, deposed by Rome but still powerful; five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas became high priest. Jews still regarded him as the true high priest, since the office was for life.

Caiaphas’s advice. 11:49–52. John reminds us of the substitution: one man for the people.

Only John. The other Gospels record the hearing before Caiaphas and the Sanhedrin; John records this preliminary hearing.
verseByVerse.note: Annas had been high priest from AD 6 to 15; five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office after him, and he remained the power behind it. Only John records this first hearing.

parallels.desc: the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas

verseByVerse.quote: Simon Peter followed Jesus, and so did another disciple. Since that disciple was known to the high priest, he entered with Jesus into the courtyard of the high priest, but Peter stood outside at the door. So the other disciple, who was known to the high priest, went out and spoke to the servant girl who kept watch at the door, and brought Peter in.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter follows Jesus into danger out of love, but walks into a temptation he is not ready for.

Another disciple. Probably the beloved disciple, John himself; how he was known to the high priest is unknown (perhaps family business in fish, or priestly relatives).

The courtyard. The open court of the high priest’s house, with servants on duty through the night.

On a Tuesday. Courage and weakness can live in the same heart. Know where you are vulnerable, and pray (Mark 14:38).
verseByVerse.note: The “other disciple” is often thought to be the beloved disciple, John.

verseByVerse.quote: The servant girl at the door said to Peter, "You also are not one of this man's disciples, are you?" He said, "I am not." Now the servants and officers had made a charcoal fire, because it was cold, and they were standing and warming themselves. Peter also was with them, standing and warming himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The boldest disciple collapses before a servant girl’s question, while his Lord stands firm before the high priest.

“You are not … are you?” The question expects “no”, and makes denial easy.

I am not. Ouk eimi. Jesus has just said “I am”; Peter says “I am not.” John draws the contrast.

A charcoal fire. The word appears again only in 21:9, where the risen Jesus restores Peter beside another charcoal fire.

Warming himself. Standing with the servants and officers, among the opposition.
verseByVerse.note: Jerusalem, high in the hills, can be cold on spring nights. John mentions a charcoal fire again when Peter is restored.

verseByVerse.quote: The high priest then questioned Jesus about his disciples and his teaching. Jesus answered him, "I have spoken openly to the world. I have always taught in synagogues and in the temple, where all Jews come together. I have said nothing in secret."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus has nothing to hide: his teaching was always public, and justice requires witnesses, not a forced confession.

About his disciples and teaching. Looking for a charge of sedition or false prophecy.

Openly. Synagogue and temple (6:59; 7:14, 26). Christianity is not a secret society.

Nothing in secret. Not that he never taught privately (chapters 13–17), but that he had no hidden doctrine different from his public message.

parallels.desc: I did not speak in secret

verseByVerse.quote: "Why do you ask me? Ask those who have heard me what I said to them; they know what I said." When he had said these things, one of the officers standing by struck Jesus with his hand, saying, "Is that how you answer the high priest?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus insists on due process and receives a blow for it, the first of many.

Ask those who heard. Jewish law required testimony from witnesses; the accused was not obliged to incriminate himself.

Struck. A slap (rhapisma), an insult and a breach of law. Isaiah 50:6: I gave my back to those who strike.

parallels.desc: you shall not revile God, nor curse a ruler

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "If what I said is wrong, bear witness about the wrong; but if what I said is right, why do you strike me?" Annas then sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus does not retaliate, but neither does he accept injustice in silence; he calmly names the wrong.

Bear witness about the wrong. A dignified, reasonable answer. Compare Paul’s flash of temper in a similar situation (Acts 23:2–5).

Turning the other cheek. Jesus shows what it means (Matthew 5:39): not passivity, but refusing revenge while calling for justice.

Sent bound to Caiaphas. The formal hearing before the Sanhedrin follows (Mark 14:53–65), which John does not narrate.

On a Tuesday. When treated unfairly at work or in the family, answer calmly and truthfully, without striking back (1 Peter 2:23).

verseByVerse.quote: Now Simon Peter was standing and warming himself. So they said to him, "You also are not one of his disciples, are you?" He denied it and said, "I am not." One of the servants of the high priest, a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off, asked, "Did I not see you in the garden with him?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter’s fear grows as the questions get closer to the truth.

A relative of Malchus. Only John records this: someone who had seen him in the garden. Peter’s lie now risks exposure.

Didn’t I see you? The sword stroke was remembered.

verseByVerse.quote: Peter again denied it, and at once a rooster crowed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ prophecy is fulfilled to the letter, and Peter’s self-confidence is broken, so that grace can rebuild him.

At once a rooster crowed. As Jesus foretold (13:38). Luke adds that the Lord turned and looked at Peter, and Peter went out and wept bitterly (Luke 22:61–62).

Not the end. Judas despaired; Peter wept and was restored (21:15–19). The difference was not the size of the sin but the response to it.

For worship. Thank Christ that he restores those who deny him and come back weeping.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28–40 — The Trial Before Pilate: What Is Truth?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At daybreak Jesus is taken to the Roman governor’s headquarters. His accusers stay outside to avoid defilement before eating the Passover, so Pilate comes out to them. They give no charge but insist he is a criminal; told to judge him by their own law, they say they are not allowed to execute anyone, fulfilling Jesus’ word about the kind of death he would die. Inside, Pilate asks Jesus if he is the King of the Jews. Jesus asks whether that is Pilate’s own question. Pilate retorts that he is no Jew; Jesus’ own people handed him over. Jesus answers that his kingdom does not come from this world, or his followers would fight. Pilate presses: so he is a king? Jesus says he was born to testify to the truth, and those who belong to the truth listen to him. Pilate asks what truth is, then goes out and declares him not guilty, offering to release him by the Passover custom. The crowd shouts for Barabbas, a bandit, instead.
verseByVerse.theology: Are you the King of the Jews? is the question Pilate must answer, and his ironic placard — THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS — will become the most accurate theological statement of the passion narrative. Jesus' kingdom is not from this world: it does not advance by the sword (as Peter demonstrated), does not require political coercion, does not depend on earthly armies. It advances by truth — by the witness of the one who is the truth, received by those who are of the truth. Pilate's question — What is truth? — is asked by the man standing in front of the answer.
verseByVerse.examples: The Barabbas exchange is the gospel in miniature: the guilty goes free, the innocent is condemned. Barabbas is released while the Son of the Father is crucified. He is a robber and insurrectionist — exactly the kind of person Jesus' opponents had accused Jesus of being. The crowd chooses the wrong son. In choosing Barabbas, they choose the kind of liberation they wanted — political, violent — and reject the liberation they needed — spiritual, sacrificial.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they led Jesus from the house of Caiaphas to the governor's headquarters. It was early morning. They themselves did not enter the governor's headquarters, so that they would not be defiled, but could eat the Passover. So Pilate went outside to them and said, "What accusation do you bring against this man?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The religious leaders are careful about ceremonial defilement while handing over an innocent man to be killed, and the true Passover Lamb is led to slaughter as the lambs are prepared.

The praetorium. The governor’s headquarters, probably Herod’s palace on the western hill, or the Antonia fortress. Pilate normally lived at Caesarea but came to Jerusalem at festivals to keep order.

Early morning. Roman officials began work at dawn.

Not defiled. Entering a Gentile house was thought to make a Jew unclean (Acts 10:28), which would prevent eating the Passover. Straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel (Matthew 23:24).

Eat the Passover. In John, the Passover meal is still to come, so Jesus dies as the lambs are slaughtered (19:14). See the note on 13:1.

What accusation? Pilate insists on a formal charge, as Roman law required.
verseByVerse.note: The governor’s headquarters is the praetorium. Entering a Gentile’s house would make them ritually unclean for the festival.

verseByVerse.quote: They answered him, "If this man were not doing evil, we would not have delivered him over to you." Pilate said to them, "Take him yourselves and judge him by your own law." The Jews said to him, "It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The accusers have no charge that will stand, but they want an execution they cannot carry out themselves.

Evasive. “Trust us, he is a criminal.”

Not lawful. Rome reserved capital punishment for its governors. (The stoning of Stephen was mob violence, Acts 7.) Pilate’s reply may be sarcastic: “Judge him yourselves,” knowing they want death.
verseByVerse.note: Rome kept the power of capital punishment for itself in Judea.

parallels.desc: Stephen stoned by a mob

verseByVerse.quote: This was to fulfill the word that Jesus had spoken to show by what kind of death he was going to die. So Pilate entered his headquarters again and called Jesus and said to him, "Are you the King of the Jews?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
By handing Jesus to Rome, his enemies ensure the death he foretold, crucifixion, being “lifted up”, and Pilate turns to the real question: kingship.

What kind of death. Jewish execution was by stoning; Roman, for rebels and slaves, by crucifixion. Jesus said he would be “lifted up” (12:32–33), and a crucified man was under God’s curse (Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:13).

Are you the King of the Jews? In Greek the “you” is emphatic: “You? The King of the Jews?” This bound, beaten man hardly looks like a rebel king. The charge that matters to Rome: treason.
verseByVerse.note: Stoning was the Jewish penalty for blasphemy; being “lifted up” pointed to Roman crucifixion.

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "Do you say this of your own accord, or did others say it to you about me?" Pilate answered, "Am I a Jew? Your own nation and the chief priests have delivered you over to me. What have you done?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus asks Pilate whether the question is his own, inviting him to consider who Jesus really is.

Your own accord? Is Pilate asking as a Roman fearing revolt, or as a man seeking truth?

Am I a Jew? Contempt: “Do I look like a Jew? Why would I care?”

Your own nation. Pilate is puzzled: why would Jesus’ own people hand over a would-be king of the Jews?

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting, that I might not be delivered over to the Jews. But my kingdom is not from the world." Then Pilate said to him, "So you are a king?" Jesus answered, "You say that I am a king. For this purpose I was born and for this purpose I have come into the world — to bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is a King, but his kingdom does not come from this world, does not use its weapons, and exists to bear witness to the truth.

Not of this world. Not from it in origin or nature, not that it has nothing to do with this world. His kingdom is real, present and will fill the earth (Daniel 2:44), but it does not advance by force.

My servants would fight. They did not (v. 11). A revolutionary would have used them.

You say that I am a king. A guarded yes.

To bear witness to the truth. His mission: to reveal God as he really is (1:18; 14:6).

Of the truth. Those who belong to the truth listen (10:27).

Where Christians differ: church and state. Some have sought a Christian state enforcing the faith; others withdraw from public life. Verdict: Christ’s kingdom works by word and Spirit, not the sword; Christians serve the common good in public life, but the church may never use coercion to spread the faith.

On a Tuesday. Is your hope pinned on a political victory? Christ’s kingdom is bigger and more certain.

parallels.desc: the good confession before Pontius Pilate

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate said to him, "What is truth?" After he had said this, he went back outside to the Jews and told them, "I find no guilt in him. But you have a custom that I should release one man for you at the Passover. So do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate dismisses the question of truth with a shrug, and in the same breath admits that the man before him is innocent.

What is truth? Perhaps cynical, perhaps weary, perhaps genuinely sceptical. Francis Bacon: “‘What is truth?’ said jesting Pilate, and would not stay for an answer.” Truth stood in front of him (14:6).

No guilt. The first of three declarations of innocence (19:4, 6). Jesus dies as the innocent for the guilty (1 Peter 3:18).

The Passover custom. Releasing a prisoner at Passover is otherwise unattested outside the Gospels, but fits Roman practice of local amnesties.

The King of the Jews. Pilate taunts the crowd with the title.

On a Tuesday. Our culture often asks “What is truth?” and does not wait for the answer. Keep pointing people to Jesus, the truth in person.

verseByVerse.quote: They cried out again, "Not this man, but Barabbas!" Now Barabbas was a robber.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd chooses a violent rebel over the Prince of Peace, and in the exchange the guilty man goes free while the innocent one dies.

Barabbas. Aramaic for “son of the father”. Mark calls him a murderer in an insurrection (Mark 15:7). Some manuscripts of Matthew 27:16–17 give his name as Jesus Barabbas.

A robber. Lēstēs, often used of insurgents and bandits.

A picture of substitution. Barabbas walks free because Jesus takes his place. Every believer is Barabbas.

For worship. Thank Jesus that he took the cross that was yours.
verseByVerse.note: Mark says Barabbas had committed murder in an insurrection; “robber” was often used for violent rebels.

So, if you seek me, let these men go.”<sup>9</sup>This was to fulfill the word that he had spoken: “Of those whom you gave me I have lost not one.”<sup>10</sup>Then Simon Peter, having a sword, drew it and struck the high priest’s servant and cut off his right ear. (The servant’s name was Malchus.)<sup>11</sup>So Jesus said to Peter, “Put your sword into its sheath; shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me?”<sup>12</sup>So the band of soldiers and their captain and the officers of the Jews arrested Jesus and bound him.<sup>13</sup>First they led him to Annas, for he was the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year.<sup>14</sup>It was Caiaphas who had advised the Jews that it would be expedient that one man should die for the people.<sup>15</sup>Simon Peter followed Jesus, and so did another disciple. Since that disciple was known to the high priest, he entered with Jesus into the courtyard of the high priest,<sup>16</sup>but Peter stood outside at the door. So the other disciple, who was known to the high priest, went out and spoke to the servant girl who kept watch at the door, and brought Peter in.<sup>17</sup>The servant girl at the door said to Peter, “You also are not one of this man’s disciples, are you?” He said, “I am not.”<sup>18</sup>Now the servants and officers had made a charcoal fire, because it was cold, and they were standing and warming themselves. Peter also was with them, standing and warming himself.<sup>19</sup>The high priest then questioned Jesus about his disciples and his teaching.<sup>20</sup>Jesus answered him, “I have spoken openly to the world. I have always taught in synagogues and in the temple, where all Jews come together. I have said nothing in secret.<sup>21</sup>Why do you ask me? Ask those who have heard me what I said to them; they know what I said.”<sup>22</sup>When he had said these things, one of the officers standing by struck Jesus with his hand, saying, “Is that how you answer the high priest?”<sup>23</sup>Jesus answered him, “If what I said is wrong, bear witness about the wrong; but if what I said is right, why do you strike me?”<sup>24</sup>Annas then sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest.<sup>25</sup>Now Simon Peter was standing and warming himself. So they said to him, “You also are not one of his disciples, are you?” He denied it and said, “I am not.”<sup>26</sup>One of the servants of the high priest, a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off, asked, “Did I not see you in the garden with him?”<sup>27</sup>Peter again denied it, and at once a rooster crowed.<sup>28</sup>Then they led Jesus from the house of Caiaphas to the governor’s headquarters. It was early morning. They themselves did not enter the governor’s headquarters, so that they would not be defiled, but could eat the Passover.<sup>29</sup>So Pilate went outside to them and said, “What accusation do you bring against this man?”<sup>30</sup>They answered him, “If this man were not doing evil, we would not have delivered him over to you.”<sup>31</sup>Pilate said to them, “Take him yourselves and judge him by your own law.” The Jews said to him, “It is not lawful for us to put anyone to death.”<sup>32</sup>This was to fulfill the word that Jesus had spoken to show by what kind of death he was going to die.<sup>33</sup>So Pilate entered his headquarters again and called Jesus and said to him, “Are you the King of the Jews?”<sup>34</sup>Jesus answered, “Do you say this of your own accord, or did others say it to you about me?”<sup>35</sup>Pilate answered, “Am I a Jew? Your own nation and the chief priests have delivered you over to me. What have you done?”<sup>36</sup>Jesus answered, “My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting, that I might not be delivered over to the Jews. But my kingdom is not from the world.”<sup>37</sup>Then Pilate said to him, “So you are a king?” Jesus answered, “You say that I am a king. For this purpose I was born and for this purpose I have come into the world— to bear witness to the truth. Everyone who is of the truth listens to my voice.”<sup>38</sup>Pilate said to him, “What is truth?” After he had said this, he went back outside to the Jews and told them, “I find no guilt in him.<sup>39</sup>But you have a custom that I should release one man for you at the Passover. So do you want me to release to you the King of the Jews?”<sup>40</sup>They cried out again, “Not this man, but Barabbas!” Now Barabbas was a robber.
18.overview:
John’s account of the arrest and trials shows Jesus not as a victim but as the one in control. In the garden across the Kidron, when soldiers and temple police come with Judas, Jesus steps forward and asks whom they seek; at his “I am he” they fall to the ground. He protects his disciples, rebukes Peter’s sword, and goes willingly to drink the cup his Father has given him. Bound, he is taken first to Annas, the former high priest and power behind the office, and questioned about his teaching, while outside in the courtyard Peter, warming himself at a charcoal fire, denies three times that he is a disciple, and the rooster crows.

At dawn he is brought to Pilate, the Roman governor. The Jewish leaders will not enter the praetorium, lest they be defiled before Passover, while they hand over the true Passover Lamb to be killed. Pilate moves in and out between the accusers outside and the prisoner inside. To his question, “Are you the King of the Jews?”, Jesus answers that his kingdom is not of this world; he came to bear witness to the truth, and everyone who is of the truth listens to his voice. Pilate replies, “What is truth?”, declares Jesus innocent, and offers to release him for Passover; the crowd demands Barabbas instead. The judge is on trial before the truth, and fails.

19.title: The Crucifixion and Burial of Jesus

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Crown of Thorns and the Cross
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pilate has Jesus flogged, and the soldiers mock him as king with a crown of thorns and a purple cloak, striking him. Pilate brings him out to the crowd to show he finds no fault, and presents him: “Behold the man!” The chief priests demand crucifixion. When they add that he claimed to be God’s Son, Pilate becomes more afraid and questions Jesus, who first stays silent, then tells him that his authority comes from above, and the one who delivered Jesus bears greater guilt. Pilate seeks to free him, but the leaders threaten that this would make him no friend of Caesar. At noon on the day of Preparation, seated on the judgment seat at the Stone Pavement, Pilate offers them their king; they cry for his death and declare Caesar their only king, and Pilate gives him up. Jesus carries his cross to Golgotha and is crucified between two others, beneath Pilate’s trilingual notice, “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews”, which Pilate refuses to alter.
verseByVerse.theology: Behold the man (v. 5) and Behold your King (v. 14) are Pilate's two presentations of Jesus to the crowd — each one a deeper truth than Pilate knows. Ecce Homo is the great statement of the incarnation: here is humanity in its representative, here is the man who is also the king. Pilate intends mockery and irony; the Spirit intends revelation. The crown of thorns (the curse of Gen. 3:18 placed on the head of the one who came to bear the curse), the purple robe (borrowed royalty that will soon be stripped), and the reed scepter — all are parodies of kingship that are simultaneously truths about the king who reigns from the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: They crucified him, and with him two others — one on either side (v. 18): the king flanked by his 'court,' the condemned alongside the condemned, the innocent among the guilty. The inscription in Hebrew, Latin, and Greek — the languages of religion, law, and culture — makes the proclamation universal: in every language, beside a road just outside the city, in the full light of Passover day, the truth is declared. The chief priests want it changed to 'he said he was king'; Pilate refuses: What I have written, I have written.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pilate took Jesus and flogged him. And the soldiers twisted together a crown of thorns and put it on his head and arrayed him in a purple robe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The King is crowned with thorns: the curse of the ground (Genesis 3:18) pressed onto the head of the one who came to remove it.

Flogged. Roman scourging used whips with pieces of bone or metal, and could tear flesh to the bone; some victims died of it. Pilate perhaps hoped a severe flogging would satisfy the crowd (Luke 23:16, 22). Isaiah 53:5: with his wounds we are healed.

Crown of thorns. A mock crown, perhaps of acanthus or date-palm spines, imitating the radiate crowns on emperors’ coins.

Purple robe. Probably a faded soldier’s cloak, the colour of royalty.
verseByVerse.note: Roman flogging used a whip weighted with bone or metal. Purple was the colour of royalty.

verseByVerse.quote: They came up to him, saying, "Hail, King of the Jews!" and struck him with their hands. Pilate went out again and said to them, "See, I am bringing him out to you that you may know that I find no guilt in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The soldiers mock Jesus as king without knowing that he is the King, and Pilate brings him out to declare him innocent again.

Hail, King of the Jews. A parody of “Hail, Caesar!” Every insult is unknowingly true.

No guilt. The second declaration (18:38).

verseByVerse.quote: So Jesus came out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe. Pilate said to them, "Behold the man!" When the chief priests and the officers saw him, they cried out, "Crucify him, crucify him!" Pilate said to them, "Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no guilt in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate presents a beaten, mocked man, perhaps hoping for pity, and the leaders demand his death; John wants us to look and see true humanity, and true God, in that bleeding figure.

Behold the man! Ecce homo. Pilate means “Look at this pathetic figure: is he a threat?” John may hear more: here is the true Man, the Son of Man, the second Adam (Zechariah 6:12; 1 Corinthians 15:45).

Crucify! The first time the word is used in John.

Take him yourselves. Sarcastic; they cannot legally. The third declaration of innocence.

For worship. Behold the man who was wounded for our transgressions (Isaiah 53:5).

parallels.desc: no beauty that we should desire him

verseByVerse.quote: The Jews answered him, "We have a law, and according to that law he ought to die because he has made himself the Son of God." When Pilate heard this statement, he was even more afraid.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The real charge comes out at last: Jesus claimed to be the Son of God, and Pilate, superstitious and uneasy, becomes afraid.

We have a law. Leviticus 24:16: blasphemy deserves death. They do not see that his claim might be true.

Son of God. To a Roman, a “son of the gods” was a divine man, a frightening figure. Pilate’s wife had already warned him (Matthew 27:19).

parallels.desc: whoever blasphemes the name of the LORD shall surely be put to death

verseByVerse.quote: He entered his headquarters again and said to Jesus, "Where are you from?" But Jesus gave him no answer. So Pilate said to him, "You will not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to release you and authority to crucify you?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate asks the deepest question of John’s Gospel, “Where are you from?”, but asks too late and with the wrong motive, so Jesus is silent.

Where are you from? The question running through the Gospel (7:27–28; 8:14; 9:29–30). Jesus is from the Father above.

Silence. Like the lamb before its shearers (Isaiah 53:7).

I have authority. Pilate boasts of power he is about to show he does not really have: he cannot even do what he believes is right.

parallels.desc: he opened not his mouth

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered him, "You would have no authority over me at all unless it had been given you from above. Therefore he who delivered me over to you has the greater sin." From then on Pilate sought to release him, but the Jews cried out, "If you release this man, you are not Caesar's friend. Everyone who makes himself a king opposes Caesar."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the Roman governor acts only under authority granted by God, so that the cross is both a human crime and a divine plan.

From above. From God (Romans 13:1). Pilate is responsible, but not sovereign.

The greater sin. Caiaphas, or Judas, who handed him over with fuller knowledge. Sin has degrees (Luke 12:47–48).

Where Christians differ: who killed Jesus? For centuries some Christians blamed “the Jews” collectively, with terrible consequences. Scripture names Jewish leaders, Pilate, Herod, Gentiles and the people of Israel together (Acts 4:27–28), and above all says that Christ died for our sins: we all put him there, and the Father gave him up (Romans 8:32; Isaiah 53:10). Verdict: no people bears collective guilt; every sinner shares in it, and God ordained it for our salvation (Acts 2:23).

Friend of Caesar. An official title for trusted associates. Releasing a would-be king could be reported to the suspicious emperor Tiberius as treason. Pilate’s career was at stake.
verseByVerse.note: “Friend of Caesar” was an honorary title for loyal officials; the threat was that Pilate would be reported to the emperor.

parallels.desc: there is no authority except from God

verseByVerse.quote: So when Pilate heard these words, he brought Jesus out and sat down on the judgment seat at a place called The Stone Pavement, and in Aramaic Gabbatha. Now it was the day of Preparation of the Passover. It was about the sixth hour. He said to the Jews, "Behold your king!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate sits as judge, but John lets us see that the real Judge stands before him, and the hour is the hour of the Passover lambs.

The judgment seat. The bēma. The Greek could mean that Pilate sat Jesus on the judgment seat in mockery; some ancient writers took it so. Verdict: more likely Pilate sat; but John’s irony is clear either way.

The Stone Pavement, Gabbatha. A paved area outside the governor’s residence; its location is uncertain.

The day of Preparation of the Passover. The day the Passover lambs were slaughtered, from noon onward. Jesus dies as the true Lamb (1:29; 1 Corinthians 5:7).

The sixth hour. About noon. Mark says Jesus was crucified at the third hour, 9 a.m. (Mark 15:25). Where Christians differ. Explanations include different time reckonings, approximate times in an age without clocks (the “third” and “sixth” hours being blocks of the morning), and a copying error. Verdict: both writers give approximate times for a morning of events; there is no real contradiction.

Behold your King! Pilate mocks them; John proclaims it.
verseByVerse.note: The judgment seat was the raised platform from which a Roman official gave judgment. The ESV notes that the sixth hour was about noon; Mark gives the third hour for the crucifixion — times were approximate and may be reckoned differently.

verseByVerse.quote: They cried out, "Away with him, away with him, crucify him!" Pilate said to them, "Shall I crucify your King?" The chief priests answered, "We have no king but Caesar." So he delivered him over to them to be crucified. So they took Jesus,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The leaders of God’s people renounce their true King and declare loyalty to Caesar, the climax of rejection in John’s Gospel.

Away with him. As the crowd cried at Paul’s arrest (Acts 21:36).

We have no king but Caesar. An astonishing betrayal of Israel’s faith that God alone is king (Judges 8:23; 1 Samuel 8:7). Every Passover they sang of God as King.

Delivered him over. Pilate hands him to them, that is, to their wishes, though Roman soldiers carry out the crucifixion.

On a Tuesday. Ask what “Caesar” claims your loyalty instead of Christ: money, nation, career, approval.

parallels.desc: they have rejected me from being king over them

verseByVerse.quote: And he went out, bearing his own cross, to the place called The Place of a Skull, which in Aramaic is called Golgotha. There they crucified him, and with him two others, one on either side, and Jesus between them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus carries the instrument of his own death outside the city, as the sin offering was taken outside the camp (Hebrews 13:11–13), and is crucified between criminals.

Bearing his own cross. The crossbeam. The other Gospels record that Simon of Cyrene was forced to carry it, probably after Jesus collapsed (Mark 15:21). John stresses that Jesus carries it himself, as Isaac carried the wood (Genesis 22:6).

Golgotha. Aramaic for skull; Latin calvaria (Calvary). Probably a rocky outcrop outside the city walls near a road. The Church of the Holy Sepulchre marks the traditional site, which archaeology supports as outside the walls at the time; Gordon’s Calvary is a later suggestion.

Crucified. The most shameful and painful Roman execution, reserved for slaves and rebels. Death came slowly by exhaustion and asphyxiation. Isaiah 53:12: numbered with the transgressors.

For worship. “When I survey the wondrous cross on which the Prince of glory died” (Isaac Watts).
verseByVerse.note: Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution; Simon of Cyrene was later made to carry it. Golgotha is Aramaic for “skull.”

parallels.desc: Isaac carries the wood

verseByVerse.quote: Pilate also wrote an inscription and put it on the cross. It read, "Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews." Many of the Jews read this inscription, for the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city, and it was written in Aramaic, in Latin, and in Greek.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pilate’s notice, written to insult, proclaims the truth to the whole world in its three great languages.

The titulus. A placard naming the crime. Here, the crime is being king.

Aramaic, Latin, Greek. The languages of religion, government and culture. The King of the Jews is announced to the nations.

Near the city. Crucifixions were placed by busy roads as a warning.
verseByVerse.note: Aramaic was the local language, Latin the language of Roman government, Greek the common language of the eastern empire.

verseByVerse.quote: So the chief priests of the Jews said to Pilate, "Do not write, 'The King of the Jews,' but rather, 'This man said, I am King of the Jews.'" Pilate answered, "What I have written, I have written."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chief priests want the claim disowned, but Pilate refuses: what God intended to be written stays written.

What I have written. A final act of spite against the leaders, but also, without knowing it, the last word of a pagan governor on Jesus’ identity.

On a Tuesday. God can use even the stubbornness of unbelievers to proclaim his truth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–42 — The Death and Burial of Jesus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The soldiers divide Jesus’ clothes in four and cast lots for his seamless tunic, fulfilling the psalm. Near the cross stand his mother, her sister, Mary the wife of Clopas and Mary Magdalene; Jesus entrusts his mother to the beloved disciple, who takes her into his home. Knowing his work is complete, Jesus says he is thirsty, to fulfil Scripture, and is given sour wine on a hyssop branch. Then he says, “It is finished,” bows his head and gives up his spirit. Because the Sabbath of Passover week is near, the leaders ask Pilate to have the legs of the crucified broken and the bodies removed. The soldiers break the legs of the two others, but finding Jesus already dead, one pierces his side with a spear, and blood and water flow out. The eyewitness testifies truthfully so that readers may believe; these things fulfilled the Scriptures that none of his bones would be broken and that they would look on the one they pierced. Joseph of Arimathea, a secret disciple, gets Pilate’s permission to take the body, and Nicodemus brings about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes. They wrap the body with the spices in linen, as Jews bury, and, because it is the day of Preparation and the tomb is near, lay him in a new tomb in a garden by the place of crucifixion.
verseByVerse.theology: It is finished is the single most important word of the gospel. It announces a completed action whose effects are permanent: the work of redemption is done, accomplished, complete — it does not require addition, continuation, or supplement. Every subsequent act of piety, every religious effort, every moral striving — none adds to what is finished on the cross. Salvation is received, not achieved; accepted, not earned.
verseByVerse.examples: The beloved disciple who stood at the cross (with Mary, Mary Magdalene, and Mary the wife of Clopas) is the model of discipleship under pressure: present where the cost is highest, faithful where the others fled. He sees the blood and water from the soldier's spear — the sign that Jesus is truly dead, truly human, truly sacrificed — and testifies that what he saw is true. His testimony is the foundation of the gospel that will go to the world.

verseByVerse.quote: When the soldiers had crucified Jesus, they took his garments and divided them into four parts, one part for each soldier; also his tunic. But the tunic was seamless, woven in one piece from top to bottom, so they said to one another, "Let us not tear it, but cast lots for it to see whose it shall be." This was to fulfill the Scripture which says, "They divided my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots." So the soldiers did these things.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the soldiers’ gambling fulfils Scripture: Jesus is stripped of everything, as the righteous sufferer of Psalm 22 foretold.

Four parts. A squad of four soldiers (Acts 12:4) took the condemned man’s clothes as perquisites: probably sandals, belt, head covering and outer garment.

The seamless tunic. Woven in one piece, like the high priest’s robe (Exodus 28:31–32; Josephus). Some see a hint that Jesus dies as High Priest; others a symbol of the church’s unity. John does not explain.

Psalm 22:18. The psalm of the forsaken righteous one, whose opening words Jesus cries from the cross (Mark 15:34). Its details of mockery, thirst and pierced hands and feet fit the crucifixion strikingly.

For worship. He was stripped so that we might be clothed with his righteousness (Isaiah 61:10).
verseByVerse.note: The four shares suggest a squad of four soldiers; the clothes of the condemned went to them.

parallels.desc: they divide my garments among them

verseByVerse.quote: but standing by the cross of Jesus were his mother and his mother's sister, Mary the wife of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene. When Jesus saw his mother and the disciple whom he loved standing nearby, he said to his mother, "Woman, behold, your son!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
While soldiers gamble, the women who love Jesus stay near him, and in his agony he provides for his mother.

The women. Probably four: his mother; her sister (perhaps Salome, the mother of James and John, Mark 15:40; Matthew 27:56, which would make John Jesus’ cousin); Mary the wife of Clopas; and Mary Magdalene. The men, except John, have fled.

Woman. As at Cana (2:4), a respectful address. Now his hour has come.

Behold your son. Jesus’ brothers did not yet believe (7:5). He entrusts Mary to a believing disciple.

Where Christians differ: Mary, mother of the church? Roman Catholic teaching reads this as giving Mary to all believers as their spiritual mother. Protestants see a son’s care for his widowed mother, fulfilling the fifth commandment. Verdict: a tender act of filial duty, and a picture of the new family of faith (Mark 3:35); it gives no basis for devotion to Mary as mediator.

parallels.desc: a sword will pierce your own soul

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to the disciple, "Behold, your mother!" And from that hour the disciple took her to his own home. After this, Jesus, knowing that all was now finished, said (to fulfill the Scripture), "I thirst."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus completes his care for his mother, and then, knowing all is finished, fulfils the Scripture of his thirst.

To his own home. John cared for Mary. Tradition says later at Ephesus.

Knowing that all was finished. Even in death he is in full awareness and control.

I thirst. Psalm 69:21; 22:15. The one who offered living water (4:14; 7:37) thirsts. A sign of his real humanity and real suffering.

parallels.desc: my tongue sticks to my jaws

verseByVerse.quote: A jar full of sour wine stood there, so they put a sponge full of the sour wine on a hyssop branch and held it to his mouth. When Jesus had received the sour wine, he said, "It is finished," and he bowed his head and gave up his spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ last word in John is a cry of triumph: the work the Father gave him to do is fully accomplished.

Sour wine. Cheap vinegar wine, the drink of soldiers and labourers.

Hyssop. A small, bushy plant, too flimsy, some say, to lift a sponge; a stalk or bundle could. Hyssop was used to daub the Passover lamb’s blood on the doorposts (Exodus 12:22). Textual note. One late manuscript reads hyssō, javelin, and some scholars have adopted this conjecture. Verdict: “hyssop” is in virtually all manuscripts, and its Passover echo is surely deliberate.

It is finished. Tetelestai: completed, accomplished, paid in full. The word appeared on receipts in the papyri. The work of redemption is done (17:4; Hebrews 10:12–14).

Where Christians differ: a finished sacrifice? Roman Catholic teaching holds that the Mass re-presents Christ’s sacrifice, offered for the living and the dead. The Reformers insisted that Christ’s sacrifice was once for all, complete and unrepeatable (Hebrews 7:27; 9:25–28); the Supper remembers and receives its benefits (Westminster Confession 29.2). Verdict: “It is finished” means nothing remains to be added, by priest, Mass or merit.

Gave up his spirit. Literally “handed over”. He did not have his life taken; he gave it (10:18).

For worship. Rest your whole weight on his finished work.
verseByVerse.note: Hyssop was the plant used to sprinkle the blood of the Passover lamb. “It is finished” is a cry of completion, not defeat.

parallels.desc: a bunch of hyssop

verseByVerse.quote: Since it was the day of Preparation, and so that the bodies would not remain on the cross on the Sabbath (for that Sabbath was a high day), the Jews asked Pilate that their legs might be broken and that they might be taken away. So the soldiers came and broke the legs of the first, and of the other who had been crucified with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The leaders, careful about the holiness of the Sabbath, ask for death to be hastened, and God uses even this to fulfil his word.

The day of Preparation. Friday.

A high day. The Sabbath of Passover week was especially holy.

Not remain on the cross. Deuteronomy 21:22–23: a hanged body must be buried the same day.

Broken legs. Crurifragium: breaking the legs with a mallet so that the victim could not push himself up to breathe, and died quickly. The skeleton of a crucified man found at Giv’at ha-Mivtar in Jerusalem (1968), with a nail through the heel, confirms details of the practice.
verseByVerse.note: The law forbade leaving a hanged body overnight; the coming Sabbath made it more urgent. Breaking the legs stopped a crucified man pushing up to breathe and hastened death.

parallels.desc: his body shall not remain all night on the tree

verseByVerse.quote: But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs. But one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and at once there came out blood and water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is truly dead, and from his pierced side flow blood and water, signs of the cleansing and life his death brings.

Already dead. No need to break his legs. Against later theories that he only fainted on the cross (the “swoon theory”), the soldiers, experts in death, confirm it, and the spear makes certain.

Blood and water. Physicians have suggested fluid from around the heart or lungs after trauma. John sees more: the blood of atonement and the water of the Spirit and cleansing (7:38–39; 1 John 5:6–8; Zechariah 13:1). Where Christians differ. Many church fathers saw the two sacraments, baptism and the Supper, flowing from Christ’s side. Verdict: the primary point is the reality of his death and the life that flows from it; a sacramental application is possible but secondary.

For worship. “Rock of Ages, cleft for me, let me hide myself in thee; let the water and the blood, from thy riven side which flowed, be of sin the double cure” (Augustus Toplady).

parallels.desc: the water and the blood
a fountain opened for sin

verseByVerse.quote: He who saw it has borne witness — his testimony is true, and he knows that he is telling the truth — that you also may believe. For these things took place that the Scripture might be fulfilled: "Not one of his bones will be broken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The eyewitness solemnly testifies so that we may believe, and shows that Jesus died as the true Passover Lamb.

He who saw it. The beloved disciple, the author (21:24). Testimony from someone at the foot of the cross.

That you also may believe. The purpose of the Gospel (20:31).

Not a bone broken. Exodus 12:46 and Numbers 9:12, of the Passover lamb; Psalm 34:20, of the righteous man.
verseByVerse.note: The Passover lamb’s bones were not to be broken.

parallels.desc: he keeps all his bones

verseByVerse.quote: And again another Scripture says, "They will look on him whom they have pierced." After these things Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly for fear of the Jews, asked Pilate that he might take away the body of Jesus, and Pilate gave him permission. So he came and took away his body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The pierced one will be looked upon, in mourning and in faith, and two secret disciples come out into the open to bury him.

Zechariah 12:10. God says that his people will look on “me, on him whom they have pierced”, and mourn, and a fountain will be opened for cleansing (13:1). Revelation 1:7 applies it to Christ’s return.

Joseph of Arimathea. A rich member of the council who had not agreed to the verdict (Luke 23:50–51; Matthew 27:57). Fear had kept him secret (12:42); now, at the worst moment, he takes a public stand.

Asked Pilate. Bodies of crucified criminals were often left for scavengers or thrown into a common grave. Joseph’s request was risky.
verseByVerse.note: Arimathea was a town of Judea. Joseph was a member of the council.

parallels.desc: they look on me, on him whom they have pierced

verseByVerse.quote: Nicodemus also, who earlier had come to Jesus by night, came bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about seventy-five pounds in weight. So they took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with the spices, as is the burial custom of the Jews.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nicodemus, who first came by night, brings a royal quantity of spices: the King is buried like a king.

Nicodemus. His journey from darkness to light is complete (3:1–2; 7:50–51).

About seventy-five pounds. One hundred Roman pounds, about 33 kg: an enormous amount, fit for royalty (2 Chronicles 16:14).

Myrrh and aloes. Aromatic resin and powdered wood, sprinkled among the linen strips to counter decay; not embalming.

As is the burial custom. Jews did not embalm or cremate.
